citations.quote:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For an integer $n\ge1$, a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, and an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, put $\mathcal D_K=\{\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq K\}$, using [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]. For integers $m\ge0$ set

$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in K}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|,\qquad d(\varphi,\psi)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty2^{-m-1}\min(1,p_m(\varphi-\psi)).$$

The topology is generated by the seminorms $p_m$: neighborhoods at zero contain finite intersections of $p_m<\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon>0$. Derivatives are continuous on $K$, so these suprema are finite; for $K=\varnothing$ all suprema are defined as zero and $\mathcal D_K=\{0\}$. For nonempty $K$, $p_0$ separates functions because all functions vanish off $K$. These are increasing seminorms and the displayed series converges since its terms are at most $2^{-m-1}$.

The term **fixed-support Fréchet space** refers to this topology and metric. Their agreement and completeness are established by the registered justifier [[lem-fixed-support-test-function-spaces-are-complete]], rather than included as unproved consequences of the name. If $K$ has empty interior, every test supported in $K$ is zero: a nonzero continuous value would have a neighborhood of nonzero values inside $K$.

A complex-linear functional $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$ is a distribution if and only if, for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, there are an integer $m_K\ge0$ and a finite constant $C_K\ge0$ such that
$$|u(\varphi)|\le C_K p_{m_K}(\varphi)\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D_K).$$
The quantifiers are $\forall K\,\exists(m_K,C_K)$; no simultaneous selection of witnesses is asserted or needed. The equivalence holds in ZF.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $F \subseteq X$ be closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]). Then $F$ is a compact subset of $X$: the metric
subspace $(F, d_F)$ is a compact metric space
([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]).

No choice principle is used.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ and $(Y, \mathcal{T}_Y)$ be topological spaces
([[def-topological-space]]), and let $\mathbb{R}$ carry its usual topology, the
metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metric-topology]],
[[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. **Continuous images.** If $f : X \to Y$ is continuous
   ([[def-continuous-map-top]]) and $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact
   ([[def-compact-space]]), then $f[X]$ is a compact subset of $Y$. More
   generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$ then $f[K]$ is a
   compact subset of $Y$.
2. **Extreme values.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact and nonempty and
   $g : X \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $g[X]$ has a maximum and a minimum
   ([[def-max-min]]): there are $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with
   $$g(x_{\min}) \;\le\; g(x) \;\le\; g(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X .$$
3. **Compact to Hausdorff.** If $(X, \mathcal{T}_X)$ is compact, $(Y,
   \mathcal{T}_Y)$ is Hausdorff ([[def-hausdorff-space]]) and $f : X \to Y$ is a
   continuous bijection, then $f$ is a homeomorphism
   ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]).

Nonemptiness in claim 2 is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for
$X = \varnothing$ the image is empty and has neither a maximum nor a minimum. **No
choice principle is used**: the one selection made below is over a finite index
set, where [[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying
$$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$
For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$,
$$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$
$$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Suppose $f$ is Riemann integrable on every $[c,b]$ with $a<c<b$. Its improper integral at the left endpoint is
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{c\downarrow a}\int_c^b f(x)\,dx,$$
provided the one-sided limit is a finite real number.

If instead $f$ is integrable on every $[a,c]$ with $a<c<b$, define
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx:=\lim_{c\uparrow b}\int_a^c f(x)\,dx.$$
Convergence always means existence of the displayed finite limit. The value assigned to $f$ at the singular endpoint, if any, is irrelevant because changing one endpoint value does not change any proper truncation integral.

If $f$ has a possible singularity at $c\in(a,b)$, define
$$\int_a^b f:=\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$$
only when the two one-sided improper integrals converge separately. Cancellation between divergent sides is not allowed.

Likewise, for any finite split point $s$, define
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f:=\int_{-\infty}^{s}f+\int_s^\infty f$$
only when both tails converge. More generally, an interval with several singular ends is split into finitely many one-ended pieces, each of which must converge separately. Independence of the permitted split point is a theorem, not part of this definition.

Suppose $0\le f\le g$ eventually toward a singular end. If the improper integral of $g$ converges there, then the integral of $f$ converges. If instead $|f|\le g$ eventually and $\int g$ converges, then $\int f$ converges absolutely and hence converges.

The same assertions hold separately at $+\infty$, at $-\infty$, and at either finite singular endpoint.

Every absolutely convergent improper integral converges. Moreover, on a one-ended interval,
$$\left|\int f\right|\le\int|f|.$$
For a mixed interval the same conclusion applies separately to each singular-end piece.

derivations.claim: If $I=\varnothing$, the stated functionals and all their derivatives are zero, proving the proper branch. Otherwise assume $I$ nonempty. The graph map $\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is $C^1$ on $I$ and injective, with values in $\Omega$; for $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ the pullback $\varphi:=\psi\circ\gamma:I\to\mathbb C$ is $C^1$, and $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq\gamma^{-1}[\operatorname{supp}\psi]$: if $\varphi(t)\ne0$ then $\gamma(t)\in\operatorname{supp}\psi$. In the proper branch $\gamma^{-1}[\operatorname{supp}\psi]$ is compact, so $\operatorname{supp}\varphi$ is a closed subset of a compact set, hence compact in $I$; thus $\varphi\in C_c^1(I)$ and $\varphi'$ is continuous.

In the proper branch, $\rho$ is a distribution. Let $K\subseteq\Omega$ be compact and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K$, so that $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq C_K:=\gamma^{-1}[K]$, a compact subset of $I$; if $C_K=\varnothing$ then $\varphi=0$. Otherwise $u:=\min C_K$ and $v:=\max C_K$ lie in $I$ with $C_K\subseteq[u,v]\subseteq I$, and $\lvert\varphi\rvert\le p_0(\psi)$ on $[u,v]$ because $\psi$ vanishes off $K$ and $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K\lvert\psi\rvert$; hence $\lvert\langle\rho,\psi\rangle\rvert\le2\lvert q\rvert\int_u^v\lvert\varphi\rvert\,dt\le2\lvert q\rvert(v-u)p_0(\psi)$ by [F5], a finite-order estimate of order zero, so $\rho$ is a distribution by [F1].

The automatic properness claims hold. If $\Omega=\mathbb R^3\times I$ and $K\subseteq\Omega$ is compact, then the time projection $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$ is a compact subset of $I$ by [F3] and $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is closed in $I$ (preimage of the closed set $K$ under the continuous map $\gamma$) with $\gamma^{-1}[K]\subseteq\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$; being closed in $I$ and contained in $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, it is closed in the subspace $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, hence compact as a closed subset of a compact metric space by [F3]. If $I=\mathbb R$, then $\gamma^{-1}[K]$ is closed and contained in the bounded set $\mathrm{pr}_t[K]$, hence compact in $\mathbb R$ by [F3].

In the proper branch, $J$ is a distribution: with the notation of step 2.1, $\lvert z'\rvert$ is continuous on $[u,v]$, hence bounded there by $M_K<\infty$, and $|\langle J_i,\psi\rangle|\le2\lvert q\rvert\int_u^v\lVert z'(t)\rVert_2\lvert\varphi(t)\rvert\,dt\le2\lvert q\rvert M_K(v-u)p_0(\psi)$, again a finite-order estimate of order zero.

Endpoint branch, well-definedness: let $I=(a,b)$, with $z$ extending continuously to $[a,b]$, $\int_a^b\lVert z'\rVert_2<\infty$ and both endpoint events in $\Omega$. Then $\varphi=\psi\circ\gamma$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$ with $\lvert\varphi\rvert\le p_0(\psi)$ and $|z_i'\varphi|\le p_0(\psi)\lVert z'\rVert_2$ on $(a,b)$; by the comparison test [F6] the improper integrals $\int_a^b\varphi$ and $\int_a^b z'\varphi$ converge absolutely (the first against the constant $p_0(\psi)$, the second against $p_0(\psi)\lVert z'\rVert_2$), so $\langle\rho,\psi\rangle:=q\int_a^b\varphi$ and $\langle J,\psi\rangle:=q\int_a^bz'\varphi$ are well-defined finite values; they are linear in $\psi$ by linearity of the truncated integrals and passage to the limit [F5, F6], and for $\psi\in\mathcal D_K$ they obey $\lvert\langle\rho,\psi\rangle\rvert\le2\lvert q\rvert p_0(\psi)(b-a)$ and $|\langle J_i,\psi\rangle|\le2\lvert q\rvert p_0(\psi)\int_a^b\lVert z'\rVert_2$, so they are distributions by [F1].

For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ in the proper branch, the pairing of the divergence is $\langle\partial_tho+\operatorname{div}J,\psiangle=-\langleho,\partial_t\psiangle-\langle J,
abla\psiangle=-q\int_I igl(\partial_t\psi(\gamma(t))+\langle z'(t),
abla\psi(\gamma(t))angle igr)dt$, the components of $
abla\psi$ being the spatial partial derivatives and $\operatorname{div}J$ the sum of the coordinate distributional derivatives of the components of $J$ by [F2].

By the chain rule [F4], $\frac{d}{dt}\varphi(t)=D\psi(\gamma(t))\gamma'(t)=\partial_t\psi(\gamma(t))+\langle\nabla\psi(\gamma(t)),z'(t)\rangle$, since $\gamma'=(z',1)$; hence the integrand of step 4.1 is exactly $\varphi'$.

Since $\varphi\in C_c^1(I)$ by step 1.1, there are $u<v$ in $I$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq[u,v]$ and $\varphi(u)=\varphi(v)=0$; by [F5] applied to the subinterval and by additivity of the integral over subintervals, $\int_I\varphi'=\int_u^v\varphi'=\varphi(v)-\varphi(u)=0$. Therefore $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=0$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, which is the identity $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$ of distributions.

Endpoint branch, identity: applying [F2] and the chain rule as in steps 4.1 and 5.1 gives $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=-q\int_a^b\varphi'(t)\,dt$, where $\varphi'$ is continuous on $(a,b)$ and $\lvert\varphi'\rvert\le C(1+\lVert z'\rVert_2)$ for a constant $C$ depending on the fixed test, so the improper integral converges absolutely by the comparison test [F6]; for $0<\varepsilon<(b-a)/2$ the proper fundamental theorem [F5] gives $\int_{a+\varepsilon}^{b-\varepsilon}\varphi'=\varphi(b-\varepsilon)-\varphi(a+\varepsilon)$, and the mixed improper integral is the limit of these truncations as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ [F6]; continuity of $\varphi$ at the endpoints gives $\varphi(b-\varepsilon)-\varphi(a+\varepsilon)\to\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)=\psi(z(b),b)-\psi(z(a),a)$. Hence $\langle\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J,\psi\rangle=q\psi(z(a),a)-q\psi(z(b),b)=\langle q\delta_{(z(a),a)}-q\delta_{(z(b),b)},\psi\rangle$ for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ by [F2], which is the endpoint identity. If $q=0$, each endpoint contribution and their sum vanish for every test; if $q\ne0$, division by $q$ shows that an individual contribution vanishes exactly when its endpoint test value is zero, and the sum vanishes exactly when the two endpoint test values are equal.

boundaries.evidence: In the proper branch step 2.1 treats C_K empty by phi=0, so the estimate holds; the endpoint branch has I=(a,b) nonempty with both endpoint events in Omega.
For q=0 both source functionals and each endpoint contribution vanish for every test, even when endpoint test values are nonzero; step 7.1 proves this directly from the exact endpoint pairing.
There is a single trajectory and a single charge q throughout; because gamma(t)=(z(t),t) is injective, each time is one event, and step 2.1 estimates one pulled-back test at a time.

Degenerate cases are treated explicitly: q=0, z constant, a pulled-back test that vanishes (step 2.1), and the failure of properness at finite endpoints, which is exactly the endpoint branch of steps 3.2 and 7.1 with its displayed delta terms.

Step 7.1 gives q times the difference of endpoint test values. Each contribution vanishes iff q=0 or its test value is zero; their sum vanishes iff q=0 or the two test values agree. The finite-window non-source-free Remark explicitly assumes q nonzero.
No choice principle is used or declared anywhere in steps 2.1-7.1: the proof works with the given trajectory, the given test function and finitely many estimates.

In step 7.1, if an individual endpoint contribution is zero and q is nonzero, divide by q to obtain zero test value. If the total pairing is zero and q is nonzero, divide by q to obtain equal endpoint values; q=0 supplies the other alternative.

In step 7.1, q=0 annihilates all contributions; a zero endpoint value annihilates its individual contribution, and equal endpoint values annihilate their difference. These prove both reverse implications by scalar algebra.

risk_review.notes: Read the Statement, all nine steps and twenty-four direct suppliers. Properness is the explicit compact-preimage condition, not graph containment: it gives compact pulled-back supports, bounded zprime on a fixed compact subinterval and order-zero component estimates. Automatic properness follows from closed preimages inside the compact time projection when Omega=R3 x I, or closed bounded subsets of R when I=R. For empty I all functionals vanish; singleton compact preimages support only the zero continuous pullback, so the zero-length bound is harmless. The current complex pairing and componentwise integral conventions are explicit; a factor 2 follows from separate real/imaginary bounds without requiring a vector-complex norm. In the endpoint branch absolute integrability of zprime and continuous endpoint events give convergence of both mixed improper pieces. The chain rule and FTC produce q delta_start minus q delta_end; the constant finite-window trajectory checks the sign and shows why containment is insufficient. No self-force or Maxwell law is inferred. Reader repair of complex typing/estimates accepted; initial raw bytes match post-reader hash. No missing choice assumption was found.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: The entries $Q_{ij}=F_iF_j-\tfrac12\delta_{ij}\langle F,F\rangle$ are sums of products of $C^1$ functions, hence $C^1$ on $U$ by [F3] and [F4], so both sides of the first identity are defined; moreover $\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\partial_j\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_lF_l=2\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_l\,\partial_jF_l$ by the product rule [F4].

For fixed $i$, $\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_jQ_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j(F_iF_j)-\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{3}\delta_{ij}\partial_j\langle F,F\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i+F_i\partial_jF_j\bigr)-\sum_{l=1}^{3}F_l\partial_iF_l=F_i\operatorname{div}F+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ by step 1.1, the product rule [F4] and the divergence formula [F2].

For a symmetric tensor and fixed $i$, the nine-term sum $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}$ vanishes: terms with $j=k$ have $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$, and for $j\ne k$ the pair $(j,k)$ and the pair $(k,j)$ contribute $\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}+\epsilon_{ikj}Q_{jk}=\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}-\epsilon_{ijk}Q_{kj}=0$, because $\epsilon$ changes sign under exchange of its last two indices and $Q$ is symmetric. This is the second claim.

The first coordinate of $F\times\operatorname{curl}F$ is, by [F1] and [F2], $F_2(\partial_1F_2-\partial_2F_1)-F_3(\partial_3F_1-\partial_1F_3)=F_2\partial_1F_2+F_3\partial_1F_3-F_2\partial_2F_1-F_3\partial_3F_1$; adding and subtracting $F_1\partial_1F_1$ shows that $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_1=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_1-F_j\partial_1F_j\bigr)$, and the same expansion in the second and third coordinates gives $-\bigl(F\times\operatorname{curl}F\bigr)_i=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\bigl(F_j\partial_jF_i-F_j\partial_iF_j\bigr)$ for every $i$. Substituting this into step 2.1 gives $\operatorname{div}Q=F\operatorname{div}F-F\times\operatorname{curl}F$, which is the first identity.

At each time the field $(x\times\Pi)_{i\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell}$ is spatially $C^1$, and differentiating the product in $x_\ell$ and summing over $\ell$ gives $(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i=\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell(\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\Pi_{k\ell})=\epsilon_{ijk}\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\bigl(\delta_{j\ell}\Pi_{k\ell}+x_j\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}\bigr)=\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}+\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\sum_{\ell=1}^{3}\partial_\ell\Pi_{k\ell}=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k$, where the term $\epsilon_{ijk}\Pi_{kj}$ vanishes by step 2.2 applied to the symmetric field $\Pi$; here $\delta_{j\ell}$ is the Kronecker symbol and the product rule [F4] was used in each summand.

Substituting $\partial_tg_k=-f_k-(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k$ and differentiating the product with the time-independent factor $x_j$ gives $\partial_t(x\times g)_i=\epsilon_{ijk}x_j\partial_tg_k=-\epsilon_{ijk}x_jf_k-\epsilon_{ijk}x_j(\operatorname{div}\Pi)_k=-(x\times f)_i-(\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi))_i$ by step 3.2; hence $\partial_t(x\times g)+\operatorname{div}(x\times\Pi)=-x\times f$, which is the third claim.

citations.quote:
Throughout, assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]); the surface integral of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and the domains of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] are developed under that convention.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open. Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface ([[def-codimension-and-hypersurface]], [[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]): every $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$ with $\varphi(S\cap U)=\varphi(U)\cap(\mathbb R^2\times\{0\})$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Such an $S$ is a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface, so the surface integral and the surface measure $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf 1_A\,dS$ of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]] apply; that measure is finite. The slice-chart definition has no manifold boundary; $S$ has no edge. If $S$ is empty, all surface functionals below are zero and the estimates are read separately without taking a supremum over the empty set.

A **two-sided presentation** of $S$ consists of a continuous unit normal field $n:S\to\mathbb R^3$ together with sides: $n(x)$ is orthogonal to $S$ at $x$ in the sense that $\langle n(x),\gamma'(0)\rangle=0$ for every $C^1$ path $\gamma:(-1,1)\to S$ with $\gamma(0)=x$ and $\lVert n(x)\rVert_2=1$; and $\Omega_-,\Omega_+\subseteq\Omega$ are open sets with

$$\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+,\qquad \Omega_-\cap\Omega_+=\varnothing,$$

such that for every $x\in S$ there is $\varepsilon=\varepsilon(x)>0$ with $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_+$ for all $0<s<\varepsilon$ and $x+sn(x)\in\Omega_-$ for all $-\varepsilon<s<0$. The normal $n$ points from the side $\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$; the orientation convention for normals is that of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

**The surface distribution $\delta_S$.** For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S\psi\,dS,$$

where the right-hand side is the surface integral of the restriction of $\psi$ to $S$, taken in the sense of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; complex-valued $\psi$ are integrated componentwise in real and imaginary parts. For a continuous **density** $a:S\to\mathbb R$ define

$$a\delta_S(\psi):=\int_S a\,\psi\,dS .$$

Both are complex-linear functionals on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, and both are distributions: $\delta_S,a\delta_S\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[def-distribution]]).

**Jumps across $S$.** Let $F:\Omega\setminus S\to\mathbb R^3$ be a field that is of class $C^1$ on $\Omega_-$ and on $\Omega_+$ separately and has one-sided continuous traces: there are continuous maps $F_+,F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3$ with

$$F_+(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_+}}F(y),\qquad F_-(x)=\lim_{\substack{y\to x\\ y\in\Omega_-}}F(y)$$

for every $x\in S$, the limits taken in $\mathbb R^3$. The **jump of $F$ across $S$** is the continuous map

$$[F]:=F_+-F_-:S\to\mathbb R^3 .$$

No continuity of $F$ across $S$ is assumed or implied; $F$ need not even be defined on $S$, and the two traces may differ.

### Well-definedness and finite order

*The surface functionals are distributions.* Fix a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$ and $\psi\in\mathcal D_K=\{\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega):\operatorname{supp}\psi\subseteq K\}$ with the seminorm $p_0(\psi)=\sup_K|\psi|$ of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]]. Since $\psi$ vanishes outside $K$ and is continuous, $\sup_S|\psi|\le p_0(\psi)$; and $\int_S|a\psi|\,dS\le\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\sup_S|\psi|\,S(S)$ with $\lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}<\infty$ by compactness of $S$ and continuity of $a$. Hence

$$|\delta_S(\psi)|\le S(S)\,p_0(\psi),\qquad |a\delta_S(\psi)|\le \lVert a\rVert_{\infty,S}\,S(S)\,p_0(\psi),$$

a finite-order estimate of order $0$ with constants independent of $K$; by the local finite-order characterization ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]) both functionals are distributions. This is the sense in which boundedness on the compact interface and finiteness of the surface measure give continuity of finite order. Linearity is immediate from linearity of the integral; the pairing is complex bilinear with no conjugation, as in [[def-distribution]].

*The field has locally integrable components.* The hypersurface $S$ is a Lebesgue-null set of $\mathbb R^3$: by the slice-chart property it is covered by finitely many compact pieces each of which is, in suitable $C^2$ coordinates, a graph over a compact subset of a coordinate plane, hence has content zero ([[thm-graph-of-continuous-function-on-a-compact-set-has-content-zero]]), and each piece has content zero in the ambient coordinates because it is the image under the $C^1$ chart inverse of a compact content-zero set ([[lem-c-one-images-of-content-zero-compact-sets-have-content-zero]]); a finite union of compact content-zero sets is compact and null ([[lem-null-sets-in-rn-closed-under-subsets-and-countable-unions]]), hence has content zero ([[lem-compact-null-iff-content-zero-in-rn]]), so $S$ has content zero in the sense of [[def-null-and-content-zero-in-rn]]. Now $F$ is continuous on $\Omega\setminus S=\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$. For each $x\in S$, the two one-sided limits are finite; hence there is a neighbourhood $U_x$ of $x$ on which $|F|$ is bounded on each side (use the defining limit with tolerance $1$ for each of $F_+(x)$ and $F_-(x)$). Away from $S$, continuity also gives a neighbourhood with a finite bound at every point. For a compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, these neighbourhoods cover $K$; take a finite subcover and the maximum of its finitely many bounds. This gives a finite $M_K$ such that $|F|\le M_K$ on $K\setminus S$. Extend $F$ by zero on the null closed set $S$; the extension is measurable because the two side restrictions are continuous, and

$$\int_K\lVert F\rVert_2\le M_K\lambda_3(K)<\infty,$$

the contributions from $K\cap S$ being null. Thus the components of $F$ are locally integrable on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], and define a regular distribution; the trace condition is exactly what makes the boundary values $F_\pm$ well-defined continuous functions on $S$, so the jump $[F]$ is continuous and bounded on $S$.

### Conventions and exclusions

The sign convention is fixed by the normal: $n$ points from $\Omega_-$ to $\Omega_+$, so $[F]=F_+-F_-$ is measured in the direction of $n$. This convention is used by the interface-derivative lemma on this page, where $\operatorname{div}F$ and $\operatorname{curl}F$ acquire the surface terms $n\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $n\times[F]\,\delta_S$; reversing $n$ reverses the signs of both sides consistently. The definition assumes a fixed stationary interface $S$: no time dependence of $S$ is part of the data, and the stationary jump formulas are not asserted for moving interfaces. The density $a$ is continuous, so $a\delta_S$ is defined by the displayed integral; no product of two arbitrary distributions, and no product of $\delta_S$ with a merely locally integrable field, is defined here. The definition is stated under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ because the surface measure it invokes is; the positivity of the surface measure of nonempty open pieces of $S$, and the finite-order estimates above, are its only uses here.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: By [F1] the components of $F$ and of its one-sided first derivatives are locally integrable on $\Omega$, the piecewise fields $\{\partial_iF_j\}$ are locally integrable, and $[F_j]$ is continuous on $S$; hence all the distributions displayed in the Statement are defined, and $n_i[F_j]\delta_S$ is the surface distribution of the continuous density $n_i[F_j]$ of [F1].

Reduction to finite chart boxes. At a point of $S$ use the $C^2$ slice diffeomorphism $\phi$ from [F1], with $\phi(S)=\{s=0\}$ locally. Choose a closed rectangular product box inside its open image, centred at the image point, and write $B$ for its open inverse image. Shrink the box so its closure is compactly contained in the chart and in $\Omega$. The two sets $B_\pm=B\cap\Omega_\pm$ are inverse images of the two open half-boxes: the local side designation is determined by the normal convention and continuity, and the half-boxes are connected. Each has a specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation, with the interface rectangle at $s=0$ and the finitely many outer rectangular faces transported by the $C^2$ chart inverse. Faces are regular parametrized compact patches. Their seams are transported line segments and vertices, hence null in ambient volume: the chart inverse has bounded first derivatives on the compact box, so a subdivision of each segment into $O(\delta^{-1})$ pieces has images covered by balls of radius $C\delta$, whose total three-dimensional content is $O(\delta^2)\to0$. For the required surface-null condition, parametrize each face by its two free box coordinates. Its seam preimage is a finite union of line segments, covered by $O(\delta^{-1})$ parameter squares of area $O(\delta^2)$; thus it has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. The chart surface density is bounded on the compact face, so its surface integral on those seams is zero. This verifies the finite-face and seam obligations in [F3], without asserting any property of a spherical chart cut. Compactness of the test support and [F4] now give finitely many such $B_1,\dots,B_N$ covering $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap S$, with compactly supported smooth cutoffs $\chi_k$ inside $B_k$ summing to one near that intersection. Write $\psi=\sum_k\chi_k\psi+(1-\sum_k\chi_k)\psi$; the last test vanishes near $S$, where the identity is the ordinary classical integration-by-parts identity. Thus it suffices to prove the displayed component identity for a test supported in one $B_k$.

Local computation: let $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$ have support in a chart box $B=B_k$ as in step 1.2. By [F2], $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=-\int_{\Omega}F_j\partial_i\varphi=-\int_{\Omega_+}F_j\partial_i\varphi-\int_{\Omega_-}F_j\partial_i\varphi$. On each side apply the divergence theorem [F3] to $G^\pm:=F_j\varphi\,e_i$. Its values and first spatial derivatives extend continuously to the closed half-box by the one-sided trace hypothesis and the product rule, so it belongs to $C^1(\overline{B_\pm})$ in the stated up-to-boundary convention, which requires no ambient extension. It vanishes near every outer box face because $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subseteq B$. For complex $\varphi$, apply the real divergence theorem separately to its real and imaginary parts; the outward normal of $\Omega_+$ on the interface face is $-n$ and that of $\Omega_-$ is $+n$, so $\int_{\Omega_+}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=-\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_+\varphi\,n_i\,dS$ and $\int_{\Omega_-}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)=\int_{S\cap B}(F_j)_-\varphi\,n_i\,dS$. Substituting $\int_{\Omega_\pm}F_j\partial_i\varphi=\int_{\Omega_\pm}\partial_i(F_j\varphi)-\int_{\Omega_\pm}(\partial_iF_j)\varphi$ gives $\langle\partial_iF_j,\varphi\rangle=\int_{\Omega}\{\partial_iF_j\}\varphi+\int_{S}((F_j)_+-(F_j)_-)\varphi\,n_i\,dS=\int_{\Omega}\{\partial_iF_j\}\varphi+\langle n_i[F_j]\delta_S,\varphi\rangle$, which is the componentwise identity.

Summing step 2.1 over $i$ (and using the definitions of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and of the piecewise fields) gives $\langle\operatorname{div}F,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega\{\operatorname{div}F\}\varphi+\langle n\cdot[F]\delta_S,\varphi\rangle$ for every test supported in some $B_k$, hence, by the finite partition of step 1.2, for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$; this is the divergence identity on $\Omega$.

Antisymmetrizing step 2.1 gives the curl identity: by [F5], $(\operatorname{curl}F)_k=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iF_j=\epsilon_{kij}\{\partial_iF_j\}+\epsilon_{kij}n_i[F_j]\delta_S=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_k+(n\times[F])_k\delta_S$ for each $k$, since $\epsilon_{kij}\{\partial_iF_j\}$ is the classical $k$-th component of the piecewise curl and $\epsilon_{kij}n_i[F_j]=(n\times[F])_k$ in the stated convention; hence, for every $\psi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)$, $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}_{\mathrm{piecewise}}+n\times[F]\delta_S$.
