Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ be a nonempty finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], written as $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ with its supplied decomposition into elementary Green regions of pairwise disjoint interiors and with the shared-arc structure of that definition, and let $\partial D$ be its positive boundary chain ([[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]). We require in addition that $D$ be Jordan measurable; this is explained below and holds for every finite elementary Green region. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let

$$r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$$

be a map that extends to a $C^2$ map ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) on an open neighbourhood of $D\times I\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Write $p=(u,v)$ for the parameter point, write $r_u(p,t),r_v(p,t),r_t(p,t)\in\mathbb R^3$ for the partial derivatives of that $C^2$ extension at $(p,t)$, and require

$$r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D^\circ\times I^\circ,$$

the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. For every $t\in I^\circ$ this gives rank two on $D^\circ$. It does not imply the connectedness or interior injectivity required by [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]]; neither is a standing hypothesis here. At endpoint or singleton times the rank condition is not imposed.

The **swept set** of the family is

$$S:=\bigcup_{t\in I}r(D\times\{t\})\subseteq\mathbb R^3,\qquad \Sigma:=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,\ t\in I\}\subseteq\mathbb R^4 .$$

A **velocity field for $r$** is a pair $(W,v)$ consisting of an open set $W\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ with $\Sigma\subseteq W$ and a map $v:W\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$ such that

$$v\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr)=r_t(p,t)\qquad\text{for every }(p,t)\in D\times I .$$

Such a pair is required to exist: the standing hypothesis of this definition is that a velocity field for $r$ is given, and $v$ denotes it. The equality above is what single-valuedness means here: whenever two parameter points at the same time map to the same spatial point, their time derivatives agree. Values at different times may differ.

Finally let $B:V\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ field on an open set $V\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ containing $\Sigma$. The **flux of $B$ through the patch at time $t\in I$** is

$$\Phi(t):=\int_D\bigl\langle B\bigl(r(p,t),t\bigr),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,du\,dv,$$

the integral being the Riemann integral over the compact Jordan measurable set $D$ of the displayed continuous integrand, and the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. This is a parametrized flux, counted with the supplied parametrization. When $(D,r(\cdot,t))$ satisfies the regular-patch definition, it agrees with [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. In general different parameter points may represent the same spatial point with different normals. At a rank-two slice the unit normal means $N(p,t)=(r_u\times r_v)/\lVert r_u\times r_v\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$, not necessarily a function of the spatial image alone.

For an injectively parametrized material-sheet interpretation, require in addition that $r(\cdot,t):D\to\mathbb R^3$ be injective for every $t\in I$. Injectivity alone does not imply $r_u\times r_v\ne0$: a regular-slice interpretation also requires this condition on $D^\circ\times I$, including endpoint and singleton times. These additional requirements are not standing hypotheses and are not used by the flux formula above.

### Well-definedness and conventions

*Jordan measurability of $D$.* Each piece is compact and Jordan measurable by [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]]. The topological boundary of their finite union is contained in the finite union of their content-zero boundaries: a point outside all those boundaries is either interior to one piece or exterior to every piece. Combining finite cube covers proves content zero without Countable Choice. Thus $D$ is compact and Jordan measurable by [[thm-jordan-boundary-criterion]]; the positive boundary chain $\partial D$ is separate supplied orientation data.

*Extension independence.* Each elementary piece is the closure of its interior by its strict graph inequalities, so $D=\overline{D^\circ}$. Two $C^2$ extensions agree on $D\times I$, and their spatial difference quotients agree at interior parameter points. Their continuous spatial partials therefore agree on all of $D\times I$: a nonzero difference at a boundary point would remain nonzero nearby and contradict the dense-interior equality. For nondegenerate $I$, the same argument on the dense set $D^\circ\times I^\circ$ makes $r_t$ extension-independent. For singleton $I=\{t_0\}$ it does not: the same zero restriction admits extensions $0$ and $(t-t_0)\chi(p)$ with different time derivatives. In that case the chosen extension is part of the velocity data; the flux still depends only on the spatial partials.

*Integrability.* For fixed $t\in I$, the map $p\mapsto B(r(p,t),t)$ is continuous on $D$ as a composition of continuous maps, the maps $p\mapsto r_u(p,t)$ and $p\mapsto r_v(p,t)$ are continuous on $D$, and the cross product and inner product are continuous bilinear operations; hence the integrand is continuous on the compact set $D$. A continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set is Riemann integrable over it ([[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]), so $\Phi(t)$ is defined for every $t\in I$.

*Degenerate time domains.* If $I$ is empty then $D\times I$ is empty, the family is vacuous and no flux value is asserted. If $I=\{t_0\}$ is a singleton, the compatibility condition still reads $v(r(p,t_0),t_0)=r_t(p,t_0)$, but it can always be met: choosing the extension $\tilde r(p,t):=r(p,t_0)$, which is constant in the time variable, gives $r_t\equiv0$ and admits the compatible $C^1$ velocity field $v\equiv0$. A different extension may require a different velocity field or may fail compatibility; as explained above, $r_t(p,t_0)$ is not determined by $r$ alone in this case. The flux $\Phi(t_0)$ involves only $r_u\times r_v$, so it is the parametrized flux of the fixed map and does not depend on that choice. The condition $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ is imposed only on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, so rank failures on the boundary of the parameter region (seams) are permitted exactly as in [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]], and at an endpoint time of a nondegenerate $I$ the definition asserts no regularity of the slice.

*No physical assertion.* This is a definition of a mathematical object: a time-dependent parametrized family, a velocity field compatible with it, and the flux integral. It asserts nothing about electromagnetic fields, about which vector fields occur in nature, or about the derivative of $\Phi$; the transport identity for $\Phi'$ is proved separately.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]). In the setting of [[def-em-moving-patch]]: $D\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a finite elementary Green region with positive boundary chain $\partial D$, $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval, $r:D\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ extends to a $C^2$ map on a neighbourhood of $D\times I$ with $r_u\times r_v\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I^\circ$, $(W,v)$ is a $C^1$ velocity field with $v(r(p,t),t)=r_t(p,t)$, and $B$ is a $C^1$ field on an open set containing the swept graph $\Sigma=\{(r(p,t),t):p\in D,t\in I\}\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, with flux

$$\Phi(t)=\int_D\bigl\langle B(r(p,t),t),\,r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\bigr\rangle\,dp .$$

For nondegenerate $I$, $\Phi$ is differentiable at interior times and relatively differentiable at included endpoints. Empty $I$ gives no flux values, and singleton $I$ gives one flux value but no derivative determined by that value. If the spatial divergence $\operatorname{div}B=0$, then for every time of such a nondegenerate $I$ whose slice has rank two, that is $r_u(p,t)\times r_v(p,t)\ne0$ for all $p\in D^\circ$,

$$\Phi'(t)=\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS-\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r .$$

By the standing hypothesis the slice has rank two at every interior time. At an included endpoint the displayed normal notation is used only if its slice also has rank two. Here $S(t)$ means the parametrized family $(D,r(\cdot,t))$, and $n$ means the parameter normal $N(p,t)=(r_u\times r_v)/\lVert r_u\times r_v\rVert_2$ on $D^\circ$. Define $\int_{S(t)}H\cdot n\,dS:=\int_D\langle H(r(p,t),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle\,dp$, including multiplicity; similarly $\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\operatorname{div}B\,dS:=\int_D\langle v(r(p,t),t),r_u\times r_v\rangle\operatorname{div}B(r(p,t),t)\,dp$. These agree with the ordinary flux definitions when the slice meets [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]] (through [[def-em-moving-patch]]); no image-wide normal or injectivity is assumed. If $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$, define $\oint_{\partial S(t)}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{\ell=1}^m\int_{r(\sigma_\ell,t)}G(\cdot,t)\cdot d\mathbf r$ using [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]] and [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. Without the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}B=0$ the additional term

$$\int_{S(t)}(v\cdot n)\,\operatorname{div}B\,dS$$

appears on the right-hand side. The identity is local in $t$ and is a statement about the parametrized mathematical object; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted.

A compact **Type I region** is

$$D=\{(x,y):a\le x\le b,\ \alpha(x)\le y\le\beta(x)\},$$

where $a<b$, the continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\alpha,\beta$ satisfy $\alpha\le\beta$, and $\alpha<\beta$ on $(a,b)$. A compact **Type II region** is defined analogously by continuous piecewise-$C^1$ functions $\lambda\le\rho$ on $[c,d]$:

$$D=\{(x,y):c\le y\le d,\ \lambda(y)\le x\le\rho(y)\}.$$

An **elementary Green region** admits both descriptions. By [[thm-fubini-over-a-region-between-continuous-graphs]], each Type I description is compact and Jordan measurable.

A **finite elementary Green region** is a nonempty finite union $D=D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_N$ of elementary Green regions with pairwise disjoint interiors. Pairwise intersections must be finite unions of complete shared boundary arcs and endpoints, and every positive-length internal arc must belong to exactly two pieces with opposite induced orientations. This supplied decomposition is part of the data; it is not inferred from an arbitrary closed curve.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $(D,\varphi)$ be a $C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region ([[def-the-induced-boundary-chain-of-a-c2-surface-patch]]), with positive boundary chain $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ and induced boundary chain $\varphi(\partial D)$, and let $F$ be a $C^1$ vector field on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ containing $\varphi[D]$. Then the circulation around the induced boundary chain equals the flux of the curl in the induced orientation:

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\bigl\langle(\operatorname{curl}F)\circ\varphi,\ \varphi_u\times\varphi_v\bigr\rangle.$$

The right-hand side is the flux of $\operatorname{curl}F$ through the patch in the orientation induced by $\varphi$, in the sense of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].

A **$C^2$ patch over a finite elementary Green region** is a regular parametrized surface patch $(D,\varphi)$ in the sense of [[def-admissible-regular-parametrized-surface-patch]] whose parameter region $D$ is supplied, in addition, with a decomposition making it a finite elementary Green region in the sense of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], and whose parametrization $\varphi$ is of class $C^2$ on an open neighbourhood of $D$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Both requirements on $D$ are part of the data: it is a compact Jordan parameter region, so it is the closure of its nonempty connected interior, and it carries a supplied elementary decomposition.

Let $\partial D=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)$ be the positive boundary chain of that decomposition, the finite list of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs of [[def-positive-orientation-for-elementary-region-boundaries]]. Then the **induced boundary chain** is the list of arcs obtained by composing the positive boundary chain of the parameter region with the parametrization, namely

$$\varphi(\partial D):=(\varphi\circ\sigma_1,\ldots,\varphi\circ\sigma_m),$$

each entry a piecewise-$C^1$ path in $\mathbb R^3$ in the sense of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]]. For a continuous vector field $F$ on a set containing $\varphi[D]$, the **circulation of $F$ around the induced boundary chain** is the finite sum

$$\oint_{\varphi(\partial D)}F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{l=1}^m\int_{\varphi\circ\sigma_l}F\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

with the vector line integrals of [[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]. The value does not depend on the order of the list, a finite sum of reals being independent of its order.

If instead $F$ is defined on an open set $U$ containing $\varphi[D]$, continuity of $\varphi$ and compactness of $D$ give an open neighbourhood $V$ of $D$ in the domain of $\varphi$ with $\varphi[V]\subseteq U$. On $V$, the **pulled-back functions** are the inner products of the field along the parametrization with the two parameter derivatives:

$$P^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_u\rangle,\qquad Q^{*}:=\langle F\circ\varphi,\varphi_v\rangle,$$

with the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The oriented area vector $\varphi_u\times\varphi_v$ and the flux it computes are those of [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. A merely continuous field on an arbitrary set containing $\varphi[D]$ is enough for circulation, but not for these neighbourhood-defined pullbacks.

For a Type I region of [[def-type-i-type-ii-and-elementary-green-regions]], the **positive boundary** traverses the lower graph from left to right, the right endpoint arc upward, the upper graph from right to left, and the left endpoint arc downward, omitting zero-length arcs. For a Type II description it traverses the right graph upward, the top endpoint arc from right to left, the left graph downward, and the bottom endpoint arc from left to right. In both cases the region remains locally on the left.

For a finite elementary Green region, delete every shared internal arc together with its oppositely oriented copy and retain the orientations of all surviving arcs. Reversal and concatenation are those of [[def-piecewise-c1-path-operations-and-oriented-reparametrizations]].

The surviving arcs form a finite list $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m$ of oriented piecewise-$C^1$ arcs, called the **positive boundary chain** $\partial D$. A finite elementary Green region need not be connected and need not be simply connected, so this list need not assemble into a single closed path. Accordingly, for a continuous field $G$ on a neighbourhood of $D$ the boundary integral is defined as the finite sum

$$\int_{\partial D}G\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{k=1}^m\int_{\sigma_k}G\cdot d\mathbf r,$$

and likewise $\int_{\partial D}P\,dx+Q\,dy$ for the field $(P,Q)$. When the surviving arcs do assemble into one closed path — in particular for a single elementary region, whose positive boundary is the concatenation of its four arcs — this sum is that path's integral, because vector line integrals add under concatenation ([[thm-line-integrals-under-reversal-and-concatenation]]). The value is independent of the order of the list, since a finite sum of reals does not depend on its order.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

For a regular patch $(D,\varphi)$, the parametrization induces on its interior the unit normal
$$N_\varphi=\frac{\varphi_u\times\varphi_v}{\|\varphi_u\times\varphi_v\|_2}.$$
The denominator is positive there by regularity and [[thm-surface-area-density-is-cross-product-norm]], and the vector is orthogonal to the tangent plane ([[def-tangent-plane-of-a-regular-surface-patch]]). Choosing $N_\varphi$ rather than $-N_\varphi$ is an **orientation**.

For a continuous vector field $F$, the flux in the orientation induced by $\varphi$ is $\int_D(F\circ\varphi)\cdot(\varphi_u\times\varphi_v)$. This is the scalar Riemann integral of a continuous function on $D$ ([[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); replacing the orientation by its negative negates the integrand.

derivations.claim: Setting and regularity. The map $r(u,v,t)=(a(t)u,a(t)v,0)$ is of class $C^2$ on the open set $\mathbb R^2\times I$, since it is polynomial in $(u,v)$ with $C^2$ coefficients, with $r_u=(a,0,0)$, $r_v=(0,a,0)$ and $r_u\times r_v=(0,0,a^2)\ne0$ on $D^\circ\times I$ because $a>0$; further $v(x,t)=\frac{a'(t)}{a(t)}(x_1,x_2,0)$ is $C^1$ jointly, and $v(r(u,v,t),t)=\frac{a'}{a}(au,av,0)=(a'u,a'v,0)=r_t(u,v,t)$, while $\operatorname{div}B=0$ for the constant field $B=e_3$. Thus the geometric and analytic hypotheses of [L1] hold, and $D$ is the elementary Green region of [L2]. At each time $D$ has connected interior and $r(\cdot,t)$ is injective since $a(t)>0$, so it is a regular patch for the Stokes application [L5].

The flux and its derivative. At each $\tau$, $\langle B(r),\ r_u\times r_v\rangle=\langle e_3,(0,0,a(\tau)^2)\rangle=a(\tau)^2$, a constant in $(u,v)$; hence by [L3] $\Phi(\tau)=\int_Da(\tau)^2\,du\,dv=a(\tau)^2$. Therefore $\Phi'(t)=2a(t)a'(t)$ for every $t\in I$ by the product rule of [L4].

The two terms on the right-hand side. Since $B$ is constant, $\partial_tB\equiv0$ and the surface integral $\int_{S(t)}\partial_tB\cdot n\,dS$ vanishes. For the boundary term, [L4] gives $v\times B=\frac{a'}{a}(x_1,x_2,0)\times(0,0,1)=\frac{a'}{a}(x_2,-x_1,0)$ and then $\operatorname{curl}(v\times B)=\bigl(0,0,\partial_1(-\tfrac{a'}{a}x_1)-\partial_2(\tfrac{a'}{a}x_2)\bigr)=(0,0,-2\tfrac{a'}{a})=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3$ at time $t$; consequently $(\operatorname{curl}(v\times B))\circ r=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3$ is constant on $D$, and patch Stokes [L5] together with the constant-integral fact [L3] gives $\oint_{\partial S(t)}(v\times B)\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_D\langle-2\tfrac{a'}{a}e_3,(0,0,a^2)\rangle\,du\,dv=-2\tfrac{a'}{a}a^2\int_Ddu\,dv=-2a(t)a'(t)$.

Comparison. The direct computations of steps 2.1 and 2.2 give $2a(t)a'(t)=0-(-2a(t)a'(t))$, so the transport formula holds here by direct computation without Choice; under the declared $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ it also instantiates [[lem-em-moving-flux]], with the boundary term contributing $+2a(t)a'(t)$ to $\Phi'$; if that boundary term is dropped, the identity would read $\Phi'(t)=0$, contradicting step 2.1 whenever $a'(t)\ne0$. The example therefore checks the sign convention and the necessity of the motion term at the stated $C^2$/$C^1$ regularity without singular support, and it asserts no physical law.

Let $4:=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $V:=\mathbb R^4$ be the set of all functions
$4\to\mathbb R$, with the pointwise vector-space structure of
[[def-function-space]]; so $V$ is the function space $F^X$ of
[[def-function-space]] at $F=\mathbb R$ and $X=4$, and its elements are written
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v^a:=v(a)$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the components
being indexed from $0$ and written with an upper index; the index conventions
used throughout this item are fixed below. Let $A$ be the same set
$\mathbb R^4$, whose elements are
now called **points**, together with the map

$$V\times A\to A,\qquad (v,p)\mapsto v+p,$$

given by pointwise addition of functions. Then the following three conditions
hold.

1. $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$ for all $v,v'\in V$ and all $p\in A$.
2. $0+p=p$ for every $p\in A$.
3. For all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$, namely
$v=q-p$.

Conditions 1 and 2 are read at each of the four coordinates from the field
axioms of $\mathbb R$, and condition 3 holds because $q-p$ satisfies
$(q-p)+p=q$ coordinatewise while any $v$ with $v+p=q$ agrees with $q-p$ at every
coordinate ([[def-vector-space]]). A triple consisting of a set $A$, a vector
space $V$ and a map $V\times A\to A$ satisfying 1–3 is called an **affine
space** with **translation space** $V$; the three conditions are its definition,
so by 1–3 the set $A$ above is an affine space with translation space $V$.

For $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $e_a\in V$ be given by $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and
$e_a(b):=0$ for $b\ne a$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]): every $v\in V$ equals $v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$, because
the two sides have the same value at each $b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$; and if
$c^0e_0+\dots+c^3e_3=0_V$ then evaluating at $b$ gives $c^b=0$, so the list is
linearly independent. We write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ and use the coordinate
columns of [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]] with respect to
this ordered basis.

**The Minkowski form.** Define

$$\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3,\qquad v,w\in V .$$

This is the standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ of
[[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first
coordinate reversed, together with the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates; directly from the
formula, for fixed $w$ the assignment $v\mapsto\eta(v,w)$ is a linear combination
of the component functions $v\mapsto v^a$, hence linear, and similarly in $w$,
so $\eta$ is a bilinear form, and $\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$ for all $v,w$, so it is
symmetric ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Its matrix in
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all
$v,w\in V$.

**Causal classification.** Let $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$. Then $v$ is
**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

**Orientation.** The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of
$\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ because $\eta$ is nondegenerate; thus $L$ is injective,
and an injective linear endomorphism of the four-dimensional space $V$ is
surjective by [[thm-rank-nullity]] together with
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], so $L$ is a bijection, and its inverse
$S:=L^{-1}$ is linear: for all $x,y\in V$ and all reals $a,b$, linearity of $L$
gives $L(aS(x)+bS(y))=ax+by$, and applying $S$ gives
$S(ax+by)=aS(x)+bS(y)$; thus $L$ is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]). The map $L$ is
**proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$.

**Frames.** A **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ together with an ordered
basis $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ such that
$\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ and
$u_0\in C^+$. The **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^4$ with
$p=o+x^0u_0+x^1u_1+x^2u_2+x^3u_3$; uniqueness holds because
$(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is an ordered basis, and $p-o$ is the unique element of $V$
carrying $o$ to $p$.

**Tensors and components.** For nonnegative integers $p,q$, a **tensor of type
$(p,q)$** on $V$ is a map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$ that is linear in
each argument separately, where $V^*$ is the algebraic dual of
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. An empty product is a singleton,
so a $(0,0)$ tensor is a scalar. Covectors are the $(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$
defines the $(1,0)$ tensor $\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$, and a **two-form** is a
skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor. These objects are maps, with arrays recording
their components in a chosen basis.

Fix a frame $(o,(u_a))$ and define its linear coordinate map
$B:\mathbb R^4\to V$ by $B\xi:=\sum_a\xi^au_a$. It is invertible because
$(u_a)$ is a basis, and $\eta(B\xi,B\zeta)=\eta(\xi,\zeta)$ by its defining
pairings. For a Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, put $N:=[L]_{(u_a)}$, identifying
its matrix with the linear map $B^{-1}LB$ on $\mathbb R^4$. With origin fixed
and new basis $u'_a:=L^{-1}u_a$, the coordinates of the same point obey
$x'=Nx$: indeed $p-o=Bx=L^{-1}Bx'$ is equivalent to this identity.
The basis is orthonormal since $L^{-1}$ preserves $\eta$, and it is a frame
when $L$ is orthochronous, since then $L^{-1}u_0\in C^+$.

For a fixed vector $v$, covector $\theta$ and two-form $F$, let
$\widehat v:=B^{-1}v$, $\widehat\theta_a:=\theta(u_a)$ and
$\widehat F_{ab}:=F(u_a,u_b)$ be their old component columns and matrix;
primes denote the corresponding components in $(u'_a)$. Then

$$\widehat v'=N\widehat v,\qquad \widehat\theta'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat\theta,\qquad \widehat F'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat F N^{-1}.$$

The vector law follows from $B'=L^{-1}B=BN^{-1}$. Substituting
$u'_a=\sum_bu_b(N^{-1})^b{}_a$ into $\theta(u'_a)$ and $F(u'_a,u'_b)$ gives
the other two laws by linearity and bilinearity. Equivalently, the coordinate
functional $\theta\circ B'$ is $(\theta\circ B)\circ N^{-1}$, the transpose
operation of [[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]], and the coordinate bilinear
form obeys $F(B'\xi,B'\zeta)=F(BN^{-1}\xi,BN^{-1}\zeta)$. The geometric
objects themselves are unchanged. In the standard frame $B=\operatorname{id}$,
$N$ is the standard coordinate matrix of $L$; in a general frame it is
$B^{-1}LB$.

Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate
$x^0$ has the dimension of length, and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$. No
physical claim is made here; in particular the identification of $A$ with
physical spacetime, of $C^+$ with the future light cone, and of $c$ with the
speed of light in vacuum are later physical premises.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

A real $x$ is **positive** when it has a representative $(a_n)$ together
with a rational $\delta > 0$ and an index $N$ such that $a_n > \delta$
for all $n \ge N$. Define

$$x \le y \iff x = y \;\text{ or }\; y - x \text{ is positive},$$

and $|x| = x$ if $x \ge 0$, $|x| = -x$ otherwise.

Let $\mathcal B=(b_0,\ldots,b_{n-1})$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The unique
coordinates $v=\sum_{j<n}x_jb_j$ form the **coordinate column**
$[v]_{\mathcal B}\in M_{n\times1}(F)$, whose $j$-th entry is $x_j$.

Let $\mathcal C=(c_0,\ldots,c_{m-1})$ be an ordered basis of $W$ and let
$T:V\to W$ be linear. The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and
$\mathcal C$** is the matrix
$[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is
$[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$. Equivalently, if
$T(b_j)=\sum_{i<m}t_{ij}c_i$, then
$([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C})_{ij}=t_{ij}$.

For an empty ordered basis, these definitions give the unique coordinate column
or matrix of the corresponding zero-sized shape.

Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over
a field $F$ ([[def-dimension]]).

If $\dim V=n\geq 1$, choose an ordered basis $\mathcal B$ and define

$$\det(T):=\det([T]_{\mathcal B}),$$

where $[T]_{\mathcal B}$ is the coordinate matrix of $T$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]) and the determinant on
the right is the matrix determinant
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]). If $V=\{0\}$, define $\det(T):=1$.

The positive-dimensional definition is justified by
[[thm-operator-determinant-is-basis-independent]], which proves that the value
does not depend on the chosen ordered basis.

Let $T$ be an operator on a positive-dimensional finite-dimensional vector
space over a field, let $\mathcal B$ be an ordered basis, and row-reduce
$A=[T]_{\mathcal B}$ to an upper triangular matrix $U$. Each row addition
leaves the determinant of the current matrix unchanged, each row swap changes
its sign, each row scaling by $c\neq0$ multiplies it by $c$, and $\det(U)$ is
the product of the diagonal entries of $U$. Consequently, if the reduction uses
$s$ swaps and scalings $c_1,\ldots,c_m$, then

$$\det(T)=(-1)^{s}\Big(\prod_{j=1}^{m}c_j\Big)^{-1}\det(U).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

Let $V$ and $W$ be vector spaces over the same field $F$. A function
$T:V\to W$ is **linear** when

$$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$

for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or
**linear transformation**.

derivations.claim: $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear: in components $(\Lambda_\beta u)^0=\gamma u^0-\gamma\beta u^1$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^1=-\gamma\beta u^0+\gamma u^1$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^2=u^2$, $(\Lambda_\beta u)^3=u^3$, so each component of $\Lambda_\beta u$ is a real linear combination of the components of $u$, and since addition and scalar multiplication in $V$ are pointwise, $\Lambda_\beta(au+a'u')=a\Lambda_\beta u+a'\Lambda_\beta u'$ for all reals $a,a'$; this is linearity in the sense of [L8].

(a) For all $v,w\in V$ one has $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$, and the same computation holds with $-\beta$ in place of $\beta$: substituting the displayed components into the form of [L1] gives $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\gamma^2[-(v^0-\beta v^1)(w^0-\beta w^1)+(v^1-\beta v^0)(w^1-\beta w^0)]+v^2w^2+v^3w^3$, the bracket expands to $-(1-\beta^2)v^0w^0+(1-\beta^2)v^1w^1$, and $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ by [L2], so the whole expression equals $-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3=\eta(v,w)$; only $\beta^2$ occurs, so the computation with $-\beta$ is identical.

(d) $\Lambda_{-\beta}\circ\Lambda_\beta=\operatorname{id}_V=\Lambda_\beta\circ\Lambda_{-\beta}$: the map $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is given by the same formulas with $-\beta$ and is linear by the same component computation as the one displayed for $\Lambda_\beta$, and using $\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ one computes $(\Lambda_{-\beta}(\Lambda_\beta v))^0=\gamma((\Lambda_\beta v)^0+\beta(\Lambda_\beta v)^1)=\gamma(\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)+\beta\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0))=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)v^0=v^0$ and likewise $(\Lambda_{-\beta}(\Lambda_\beta v))^1=\gamma((\Lambda_\beta v)^1+\beta(\Lambda_\beta v)^0)=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)v^1=v^1$, while both maps fix the last two components; the composite $\Lambda_\beta\circ\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is the same computation with $\beta$ and $-\beta$ interchanged. Hence $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ is a two-sided inverse of $\Lambda_\beta$, and by the uniqueness of the inverse in [L7], $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$.

At $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ is undefined: there $1-\beta^2=0$, while $a^{-1/2}$ is defined for $a>0$ and $0^r$ only for rational $r>0$ [L2], so the hypothesis $0\le\beta<1$ cannot be dropped.

(b, matrix) The matrix $M$ of $\Lambda_\beta$ in the basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ has first column the coordinate column $(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$, second column $(-\gamma\beta,\gamma,0,0)$ and last two columns those of the identity matrix (the matrix is symmetric, so these are also its first two rows): by [L4] its columns are the coordinate columns of the images of the basis vectors, and the displayed component formulas give $\Lambda_\beta e_0=\gamma e_0-\gamma\beta e_1$, $\Lambda_\beta e_1=-\gamma\beta e_0+\gamma e_1$, $\Lambda_\beta e_2=e_2$, $\Lambda_\beta e_3=e_3$.

(b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$: replacing the second row of the matrix of step 1.5 by (second row) $+\beta$(first row) gives the row $(0,\gamma(1-\beta^2),0,0)$, since its first entry is $-\gamma\beta+\beta\gamma=0$ and its second entry is $\gamma-\beta^2\gamma$. The resulting matrix is upper triangular with diagonal entries $\gamma$, $\gamma(1-\beta^2)$, $1$, $1$. By [L5] and [L6], the row addition preserves the determinant and $\det\Lambda_\beta=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1$ by [L2].

(c, inclusion) Both $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$ and $\Lambda_{-\beta}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$: if $v\in C^+$ then $v^0>0$ and $(v^1)^2\le(v^0)^2$, so $|v^1|\le v^0$ by [L3], and since $0\le\beta<1$ one has $(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)\ge\gamma(v^0-\beta|v^1|)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v^0>0$ and $(\Lambda_{-\beta}v)^0=\gamma(v^0+\beta v^1)\ge\gamma(1-\beta)v^0>0$, while $\eta(\Lambda_{\pm\beta}v,\Lambda_{\pm\beta}v)=\eta(v,v)\le0$ by step 1.2; these are exactly the two defining conditions of $C^+$.

(c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$: step 2.2 gives the inclusion $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)\subseteq C^+$ and also $\Lambda_{-\beta}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$, which by $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$ from step 1.3 says $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}(C^+)\subseteq C^+$; for $u\in C^+$ the vector $v:=\Lambda_\beta^{-1}u$ then lies in $C^+$ and satisfies $u=\Lambda_\beta v$, so $C^+\subseteq\Lambda_\beta(C^+)$, and with the inclusion the two sets are equal.
In particular every future causal vector has future causal image, namely the inclusion from step 2.2, and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$ for every $v$ is step 1.2 with $w=v$.

$\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map: it is linear by step 1.1, it satisfies $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w$ by step 1.2, and it has the two-sided inverse $\Lambda_{-\beta}$ by step 1.3, so it is a Lorentz map in the sense of [L1]; $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$ by step 2.1 makes it proper and $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$ by step 3.1 makes it orthochronous.

All claims of the statement are established — linearity in step 1.1, (a) in step 1.2, (d) in step 1.3, the excluded endpoint in step 1.4, (b) in steps 1.5 and 2.1, (c) in steps 2.2 and 3.1, the proper orthochronous Lorentz property in step 4.1 and the consequence for future causal vectors in step 3.2 — so the hypothesis is exactly as stated.

boundaries.reason: No quantified set in the statement or the proof can be empty: beta ranges over the nonempty interval [0,1) and every matrix computation is indexed by {0,1,2,3}.

boundaries.evidence: The included boundary beta=0 is harmless and is witnessed through step 2.1: gamma=1, the displayed formulas make Lambda_0 the identity, and the reduced triangular matrix has diagonal (1,1,1,1) with determinant 1.
The excluded value beta=1 is disposed of in step 1.4, where 1-beta^2=0 makes gamma undefined; determinantal properness is instead verified at the included endpoint beta=0 in step 2.1.
The degenerate case 1-beta^2=0 is exactly the excluded endpoint; within the hypothesis, step 2.1 keeps the reduced diagonal entry gamma(1-beta^2) nonzero, so no vanishing pivot is used.
The admissible interval [0,1) is handled at both ends: beta=0 is verified in step 2.1 and beta=1 is excluded with an explicit witness in step 1.4.

boundaries.reason: No selection is made: the argument works with the fixed real beta, the fixed basis vectors e_a and the displayed matrix entries.
The statement is a conjunction of clauses (a)-(d) with no biconditional, so no forward direction of an equivalence has to be discharged.
No converse is asserted: (d) is an equality of two explicitly computed composites, not one direction of an equivalence.
