Let $4:=\{0,1,2,3\}$ and let $V:=\mathbb R^4$ be the set of all functions
$4\to\mathbb R$, with the pointwise vector-space structure of
[[def-function-space]]; so $V$ is the function space $F^X$ of
[[def-function-space]] at $F=\mathbb R$ and $X=4$, and its elements are written
$v=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$ with $v^a:=v(a)$ for $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, the components
being indexed from $0$ and written with an upper index; the index conventions
used throughout this item are fixed below. Let $A$ be the same set
$\mathbb R^4$, whose elements are
now called **points**, together with the map

$$V\times A\to A,\qquad (v,p)\mapsto v+p,$$

given by pointwise addition of functions. Then the following three conditions
hold.

1. $(v+v')+p=v+(v'+p)$ for all $v,v'\in V$ and all $p\in A$.
2. $0+p=p$ for every $p\in A$.
3. For all $p,q\in A$ there is exactly one $v\in V$ with $v+p=q$, namely
$v=q-p$.

Conditions 1 and 2 are read at each of the four coordinates from the field
axioms of $\mathbb R$, and condition 3 holds because $q-p$ satisfies
$(q-p)+p=q$ coordinatewise while any $v$ with $v+p=q$ agrees with $q-p$ at every
coordinate ([[def-vector-space]]). A triple consisting of a set $A$, a vector
space $V$ and a map $V\times A\to A$ satisfying 1–3 is called an **affine
space** with **translation space** $V$; the three conditions are its definition,
so by 1–3 the set $A$ above is an affine space with translation space $V$.

For $a\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ let $e_a\in V$ be given by $e_a(b):=1$ for $b=a$ and
$e_a(b):=0$ for $b\ne a$. Then $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis of $V$
([[def-linear-basis]]): every $v\in V$ equals $v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$, because
the two sides have the same value at each $b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$; and if
$c^0e_0+\dots+c^3e_3=0_V$ then evaluating at $b$ gives $c^b=0$, so the list is
linearly independent. We write $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ and use the coordinate
columns of [[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]] with respect to
this ordered basis.

**The Minkowski form.** Define

$$\eta(v,w):=-v^0w^0+v^1w^1+v^2w^2+v^3w^3,\qquad v,w\in V .$$

This is the standard bilinear form $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i<n}x_iy_i$ of
[[def-standard-bilinear-form-on-a-coordinate-space]] with the sign of the first
coordinate reversed, together with the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]] on the last three coordinates; directly from the
formula, for fixed $w$ the assignment $v\mapsto\eta(v,w)$ is a linear combination
of the component functions $v\mapsto v^a$, hence linear, and similarly in $w$,
so $\eta$ is a bilinear form, and $\eta(v,w)=\eta(w,v)$ for all $v,w$, so it is
symmetric ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Its matrix in
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is

$$(\eta(e_a,e_b))_{a,b}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1),$$

and this matrix is its own inverse, the product of
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ with itself being the identity matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]); in particular it is invertible, so
$\eta$ is nondegenerate
([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]).

**Index conventions.** The components $v^a$ of a vector are the numbers in its
expansion $v=v^0e_0+\dots+v^3e_3$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, and
for a linear map $T:V\to V$ one writes $(Tv)^a$ for the components of $Tv$ and
$T^a{}_b$ for the matrix entries, so that $(Tv)^a=\sum_bT^a{}_bv^b$. Write
$\eta_{ab}:=\eta(e_a,e_b)$, so that
$(\eta_{ab})=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and let $(\eta^{ab})$ denote the
inverse matrix of $(\eta_{ab})$, that is, $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=1$ when
$a=c$ and $\sum_b\eta^{ab}\eta_{bc}=0$ when $a\ne c$. The **lowered** components
of $v$ are $v_a:=\sum_b\eta_{ab}v^b$, and the operation is inverted by
$v^a=\sum_b\eta^{ab}v_b$, because $\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is its own
inverse; explicitly $v_0=-v^0$ and $v_i=v^i$ for $i=1,2,3$. In these
conventions $\eta(v,w)=\sum_{a,b}\eta_{ab}v^aw^b=\sum_av_aw^a$ for all
$v,w\in V$.

**Causal classification.** Let $v\in V$ with $v\ne0$. Then $v$ is
**timelike** when $\eta(v,v)<0$, **null** when $\eta(v,v)=0$, and
**spacelike** when $\eta(v,v)>0$; it is **causal** when $\eta(v,v)\le0$. If the
nonzero $v$ is causal, then $v^0\ne0$: the inequality
$-(v^0)^2+(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2\le0$ gives
$(v^0)^2\ge(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2$, and $v^0=0$ would force
$(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2=0$, hence $v^1=v^2=v^3=0$ and $v=0$, contrary to the
hypothesis. A nonzero causal $v$ is therefore **future-directed** when $v^0>0$
and **past-directed** when $v^0<0$, and exactly one of these two alternatives
holds for a nonzero real $v^0$ ([[def-real-order]]). The **future causal cone**
is

$$C^+:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)\le0,\ v^0>0\},$$

whose elements are exactly the future-directed causal vectors; the zero vector
is not in $C^+$, because it fails $v^0>0$.

**Orientation.** The **standard orientation** of $V$ is the orientation class of
the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]).

**Lorentz maps.** A **Lorentz map** is a linear map $L:V\to V$
([[def-linear-map]]) that is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]) and satisfies

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V .$$

Writing $M:=[L]_{(e_0,\dots,e_3)}\in M_4(\mathbb R)$ for the matrix of $L$ in the
ordered basis $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), $M^{\mathsf T}$ for its
transpose ([[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]), and $\eta$ also for the matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the condition is the matrix identity

$$M^{\mathsf T}\eta M=\eta .$$

Expanding $Lv$ and $Lw$ in the basis gives
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\sum_{c,d}(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}v^cw^d$, whereas
$\eta(v,w)=\sum_{c,d}\eta_{cd}v^cw^d$, and the two sides agree for all $v,w$
exactly when $(M^{\mathsf T}\eta M)_{cd}=\eta_{cd}$ for every $c,d$, since
inserting the basis vectors $v=e_c$, $w=e_d$ gives the converse
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Equivalently, the matrix of $\eta$
in the basis $(Le_0,\dots,Le_3)$ is again
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$; this is the change-of-basis congruence of
[[thm-change-of-basis-for-a-bilinear-form-is-congruence]] for the basis change
from $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$ to its image under the invertible map $L$. The
invertibility requirement in the definition of a Lorentz map is in fact
automatic: if $L$ satisfies the displayed identity and $Lv=0$, then
$\eta(v,w)=\eta(Lv,Lw)=0$ for every $w$, so $v$ lies in the left radical of
$\eta$, which is $\{0\}$ because $\eta$ is nondegenerate; thus $L$ is injective,
and an injective linear endomorphism of the four-dimensional space $V$ is
surjective by [[thm-rank-nullity]] together with
[[thm-dimension-of-a-linear-subspace]], so $L$ is a bijection, and its inverse
$S:=L^{-1}$ is linear: for all $x,y\in V$ and all reals $a,b$, linearity of $L$
gives $L(aS(x)+bS(y))=ax+by$, and applying $S$ gives
$S(ax+by)=aS(x)+bS(y)$; thus $L$ is invertible
([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]). The map $L$ is
**proper** when $\det L=1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** when $L(C^+)=C^+$.

**Frames.** A **frame** of $A$ is a point $o\in A$ together with an ordered
basis $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ such that
$\eta(u_a,u_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ and
$u_0\in C^+$. The **coordinates** of $p\in A$ in that frame are the unique
$(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)\in\mathbb R^4$ with
$p=o+x^0u_0+x^1u_1+x^2u_2+x^3u_3$; uniqueness holds because
$(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is an ordered basis, and $p-o$ is the unique element of $V$
carrying $o$ to $p$.

**Tensors and components.** For nonnegative integers $p,q$, a **tensor of type
$(p,q)$** on $V$ is a map $(V^*)^p\times V^q\to\mathbb R$ that is linear in
each argument separately, where $V^*$ is the algebraic dual of
[[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. An empty product is a singleton,
so a $(0,0)$ tensor is a scalar. Covectors are the $(0,1)$ case, a vector $v$
defines the $(1,0)$ tensor $\theta\mapsto\theta(v)$, and a **two-form** is a
skew-symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor. These objects are maps, with arrays recording
their components in a chosen basis.

Fix a frame $(o,(u_a))$ and define its linear coordinate map
$B:\mathbb R^4\to V$ by $B\xi:=\sum_a\xi^au_a$. It is invertible because
$(u_a)$ is a basis, and $\eta(B\xi,B\zeta)=\eta(\xi,\zeta)$ by its defining
pairings. For a Lorentz map $L:V\to V$, put $N:=[L]_{(u_a)}$, identifying
its matrix with the linear map $B^{-1}LB$ on $\mathbb R^4$. With origin fixed
and new basis $u'_a:=L^{-1}u_a$, the coordinates of the same point obey
$x'=Nx$: indeed $p-o=Bx=L^{-1}Bx'$ is equivalent to this identity.
The basis is orthonormal since $L^{-1}$ preserves $\eta$, and it is a frame
when $L$ is orthochronous, since then $L^{-1}u_0\in C^+$.

For a fixed vector $v$, covector $\theta$ and two-form $F$, let
$\widehat v:=B^{-1}v$, $\widehat\theta_a:=\theta(u_a)$ and
$\widehat F_{ab}:=F(u_a,u_b)$ be their old component columns and matrix;
primes denote the corresponding components in $(u'_a)$. Then

$$\widehat v'=N\widehat v,\qquad \widehat\theta'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat\theta,\qquad \widehat F'=(N^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat F N^{-1}.$$

The vector law follows from $B'=L^{-1}B=BN^{-1}$. Substituting
$u'_a=\sum_bu_b(N^{-1})^b{}_a$ into $\theta(u'_a)$ and $F(u'_a,u'_b)$ gives
the other two laws by linearity and bilinearity. Equivalently, the coordinate
functional $\theta\circ B'$ is $(\theta\circ B)\circ N^{-1}$, the transpose
operation of [[def-transpose-of-a-linear-map]], and the coordinate bilinear
form obeys $F(B'\xi,B'\zeta)=F(BN^{-1}\xi,BN^{-1}\zeta)$. The geometric
objects themselves are unchanged. In the standard frame $B=\operatorname{id}$,
$N$ is the standard coordinate matrix of $L$; in a general frame it is
$B^{-1}LB$.

Finally, a fixed positive real $c$ is separate extra structure: the coordinate
$x^0$ has the dimension of length, and the time coordinate is $t:=x^0/c$. No
physical claim is made here; in particular the identification of $A$ with
physical spacetime, of $C^+$ with the future light cone, and of $c$ with the
speed of light in vacuum are later physical premises.

Let $0\le\beta<1$ and put $\gamma:=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}>0$
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). Define
$\Lambda_\beta:V\to V$ by $(\Lambda_\beta v)^0=\gamma(v^0-\beta v^1)$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^1=\gamma(v^1-\beta v^0)$, $(\Lambda_\beta v)^2=v^2$,
$(\Lambda_\beta v)^3=v^3$. Then $\Lambda_\beta$ is linear
([[def-linear-map]]), $\Lambda_\beta$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map,
and more precisely: (a) $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta w)=\eta(v,w)$ for
all $v,w\in V$; (b) $\det\Lambda_\beta=1$; (c) $\Lambda_\beta(C^+)=C^+$;
(d) $\Lambda_\beta^{-1}=\Lambda_{-\beta}$. In particular a future causal vector
has future causal image and $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=\eta(v,v)$
for every $v$ ([[def-real-order]], [[lem-of-square-monotone]]). The hypothesis
$0\le\beta<1$ is not removable: at $\beta=1$ the factor $\gamma$ is undefined.

Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]) and let
$z:J\to\mathbb R^4$ be of class $C^1$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) with $\eta(z'(s),z'(s))<0$ and
$z^0{}'(s)>0$ for every $s\in J$; $z'$ is the derivative of the vector-valued
curve ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) and such a $z$ is called a
$C^1$ future timelike curve. Put $g(s):=-\eta(z'(s),z'(s))>0$, fix $s_0\in J$,
and define $\tau(s):=c^{-1}\int_{s_0}^{s}\sqrt{g(u)}\,du$ for $s\in J$. Then:
(1) $g$ is continuous on $J$ and so is $s\mapsto\sqrt{g(s)}$, where
$\sqrt{\cdot}$ is the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]],
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]],
[[thm-composition-of-continuous-functions]]); (2) $\tau$ is differentiable on
$J$ with $\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{g(s)}>0$, hence $\tau$ is strictly increasing on
$J$, injective, and continuous
([[cor-primitives-of-a-continuous-function]],
[[thm-monotonicity-from-the-derivative]]); (3) the inverse
$\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to J$ is differentiable at every point $\tau(s)$ of the
interval $\tau[J]$, with $(\tau^{-1})'(\tau(s))=c/\sqrt{g(s)}$
([[thm-continuous-inverse]], [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]]); (4) the
reparametrized curve $z\circ\tau^{-1}:\tau[J]\to\mathbb R^4$ is differentiable
at every $\tau(s)$, with tangent $U(\tau(s)):=c\,z'(s)/\sqrt{g(s)}$ satisfying
$\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ ([[thm-chain-rule]],
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]]); (5) if instead
$\eta(z'(s),z'(s))=0$ for all $s\in J$, then $g=0$, $\tau\equiv0$ on $J$ and
$\tau$ is not injective, so a null curve carries no proper-time parametrization
([[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]); (6) if $z(s)=p+sv$ with
$\eta(v,v)<0$ and $v^0>0$, then
$\tau(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}\,(s-s_0)$ and
$U=c\,v/\sqrt{-\eta(v,v)}$ is constant
([[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]], [[def-derivative]]). The
identification of such straight lines with inertial motion is a physical premise
and is not asserted here.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be the four-dimensional real Minkowski vector space of
[[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]], with the fixed form of signature
$(-1,1,1,1)$. Let $F:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be a skew-symmetric bilinear form,
$F(u,v)=-F(v,u)$ for all $u,v\in V$
([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]]). Since $\eta$ is
nondegenerate, for each $u\in V$ there is exactly one $\Phi(u)\in V$ with
$\eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u)$ for all $w\in V$
([[thm-bilinear-forms-correspond-to-linear-maps-into-the-dual]],
[[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]), and
$\Phi:V\to V$ is linear ([[def-linear-map]]); with
$F_{\alpha\beta}:=F(e_\alpha,e_\beta)$ in the fixed ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of [[def-em-minkowski-affine-space]] and $(\eta^{\mu\alpha})$
the inverse matrix of $(\eta_{\alpha\beta})$, one has
$\Phi(u)^\mu=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\beta}u^\beta$, the
index-raised form of $F$. Then $\eta(u,\Phi(u))=0$ for every $u\in V$; in
components $u_\mu F^\mu{}_\nu u^\nu=0$, where
$u_\mu:=\sum_\alpha\eta_{\mu\alpha}u^\alpha$ and
$F^\mu{}_\nu:=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha\nu}$. Consequently, if
$J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a
nonempty open interval ([[def-interval]]), $U:J\to V$ is differentiable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and $m\,U'(s)=q\,\Phi(U(s))$ on
$J$ for some real $m\ne0$ and $q$, then $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on
$J$ ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-differentiable-implies-continuous]],
[[cor-zero-derivative-implies-constant]]). The same norm-conservation conclusion
holds for a family of skew forms $F_s$ and their pointwise operators $\Phi_s$
defined by $\eta(\Phi_s(u),w)=F_s(w,u)$, when $mU'(s)=q\Phi_s(U(s))$: no
derivative of $F_s$ is required. In particular one may evaluate a varying field
$F_x$ along a differentiable trajectory $x(s)$. This is a conditional statement
about the given equation; it does not assert that this equation governs any
particle.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

derivations.claim: (i) $\eta(v,v)=\eta(e_0,e_0)=-1<0$ and $v^0=1>0$, so $v$ is future timelike and unit in the sense $\eta(v,v)=-1$.
(ii, coordinates) For $0<\beta<1$, [L1] gives $\Lambda_\beta e_0=(\gamma(1-\beta\cdot0),\gamma(0-\beta\cdot1),0,0)=(\gamma,-\gamma\beta,0,0)$.
(iii, null tangent) The line $z(s)=(s,s,0,0)$ has the constant derivative $z'=(1,1,0,0)$, so $\eta(z',z')=-1+1=0$; its positive time component also makes the tangent future causal.

(iv, symmetric form) For $F:=\eta$, symmetry gives $\eta(u,w)=F(w,u)$ for every $w$, so $\Phi(u):=u$ satisfies the defining pairing. If another vector $y$ does so, $\eta(y-u,w)=0$ for every $w$, hence $y=u$ by nondegeneracy [F1]. Thus $\Phi=\operatorname{id}$ without using the skew hypothesis of [L3], and $\eta(v,\Phi(v))=-1\ne0$.

(v, skew sign witness) For the skew form with $F_{01}=1$, $F_{10}=-1$ and other coefficients zero, $F(w,e_0)=-w^1=\eta(-e_1,w)$ for every $w$, so $\Phi(e_0)=-e_1$ by [L3]. The raised-index formula gives $\Phi(e_0)^\mu=\sum_\alpha\eta^{\mu\alpha}F_{\alpha0}=-\eta^{\mu1}$, again the components of $-e_1$. Thus both signs agree and $\eta(e_0,\Phi(e_0))=0$.
(ii, excluded endpoint) At $\beta=1$, $1-\beta^2=0$, so $\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}$ is undefined by [L1]; the endpoint cannot be included in this formula.

(ii, norm) By step 1.2, $\eta(\Lambda_\beta v,\Lambda_\beta v)=-\gamma^2+\gamma^2\beta^2=-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$. Indeed [L5] with $a:=1-\beta^2>0$ gives $\gamma^2a=a^{-1/2}a^{-1/2}a=a^{-1}a=1$, and $\gamma>0$ by [L1] and [L5].

(iii, conclusion) $J:=\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval by [L4]. The line of step 1.3 has constant, hence continuous, derivative, so is $C^1$. The null clause of [L2] gives $g=0$ and $\tau\equiv0$, which is not injective; its future causal tangent therefore does not suffice for proper-time reparametrization.

All five checks are established — (i) in step 1.1, (ii) in steps 1.2, 2.1 and 1.6, (iii) in steps 1.3 and 2.2, (iv) in step 1.4, and (v) in step 1.5 — with no physical clock premise and no experimental claim.

boundaries.reason: Every object in the example is explicit, namely e_0, the boost, the line (s,s,0,0) and the two forms, so no set that could be empty is quantified over.

boundaries.evidence: The null line has eta(z prime,z prime)=0 in step 1.3 and its proper-time construction degenerates in step 2.2; the excluded endpoint beta=1 arises from 1-beta^2=0 in step 1.6.
The unit vector v=e_0 with eta(v,v)=-1 is the first check in step 1.1, and the symmetric-form clause uses F=eta with Phi=id in step 1.4.
The metric remains nondegenerate. The null tangent in steps 1.3 and 2.2 makes the proper-time construction constant and noninvertible; the timelike quadratic value is computed in step 2.1.
The boost clause uses 0<beta<1 and step 1.6 records that beta=1 makes gamma undefined; the null line is parametrized by all of R, whose open-interval property is used in step 2.2.

boundaries.reason: Each check is a finite computation in the standard frame, so nothing is chosen from a family.
The example verifies listed hypotheses by explicit computations and asserts no biconditional.

([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Write $y=\hat y+(y-\hat y)$ and apply the triangle inequality of [L2] together with the two assumed bounds: $|y|\le|\hat y|+|y-\hat y|\le s+\delta$.
If $\theta=\theta_0$ then $|\theta-\theta_0|=0\le (s+\delta)/m$, because $s\ge0$, $\delta\ge0$ give $s+\delta\ge0$ and $m>0$ makes $(s+\delta)/m\ge0$.

Suppose $\theta\ne\theta_0$ and put $a=\min(\theta,\theta_0)$, $b=\max(\theta,\theta_0)$, so $a<b$ and $\{a,b\}=\{\theta,\theta_0\}$. By [L1] the closed interval $[a,b]$ is contained in $I$; by [L3] the function $f$ is continuous on $I$, and by the restriction clause of [L4] the restriction $g=f|_{[a,b]}$ is continuous on $[a,b]$; by the locality clause of [L4] $g$ is differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ with $g'=f'$ there. The mean value theorem [L5] therefore yields $\xi\in(a,b)$ with $g(b)-g(a)=g'(\xi)(b-a)$. Since $g(b)-g(a)$ equals $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)$ up to the sign that reverses $b-a$ as well, and $g'(\xi)=f'(\xi)$, this is exactly $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)=f'(\xi)(\theta-\theta_0)$.

At the intermediate point of step 1.3 one has $f'(\xi)\ge m>0$, so $f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)$ has the sign of $\theta-\theta_0$, and therefore $|f(\theta)-f(\theta_0)|=f'(\xi)\,|\theta-\theta_0|\ge m\,|\theta-\theta_0|$.

Since $y=f(\theta)$ and $f(\theta_0)=0$, step 2.1 gives $m|\theta-\theta_0|\le|y|$, and step 1.1 gives $|y|\le s+\delta$. Hence $m|\theta-\theta_0|\le s+\delta$, and dividing by $m>0$ yields $|\theta-\theta_0|\le(s+\delta)/m$.

Every $\theta\in I$ compatible with the model requirement and the two bounds falls under one of the two cases: $\theta=\theta_0$ satisfies the bound by step 1.2, and $\theta\ne\theta_0$ satisfies it by step 3.1. Equivalently, if a proposed $\theta$ has $|\theta-\theta_0|>(s+\delta)/m$, then no assignment satisfying both stated bounds can also satisfy $y=f(\theta)$, so the specified model-plus-error-bound pair is incompatible with the premises; no probability, sampling, or statistical inference has been used.

Everything is scalar: one recorded value y-hat, one parameter theta and one lower bound m; the displacements are one-dimensional in steps 1.3 and 2.1, and the interval case with just two elements is the minimal one allowed by the statement of step 1.3.

boundaries.evidence: I need not be open: steps 1.3 and 2.1 use only the order-convexity [L1] of I and the restriction g = f on [a,b], so interval endpoints are covered; step 1.2 also covers theta = theta0 when theta0 is an endpoint of I.
