citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The characters
$(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z}$ form an orthonormal basis of the complex Hilbert space
$L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]): they are
orthonormal and their closed linear span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For every
$f\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ and every real $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$N\in\mathbb N$ with

$$\Bigl\|f-\sum_{|k|\le N}\widehat f(k)e_k\Bigr\|_2<\varepsilon .$$

Thus the symmetric partial sums of the Fourier series converge to $f$ in the
$L^2$ norm, and the finite-subset net of Fourier partial sums converges to $f$
as well. This is norm convergence only: no pointwise or uniform assertion is
made, and no ordering of $\mathbb Z$ other than the symmetric one is required.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $F:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and suppose one $L\ge0$ satisfies $\|F(t,x)-F(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t,x,y$. Then every IVP for $x'=F(t,x)$ has a unique global solution.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.

Assume Countable Choice for the Lebesgue regular-distribution convention. If $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is nonempty, open and connected and $\partial_j u=0$ for every $1\le j\le n$, then there is a unique $c\in\mathbb C$ such that $u(\psi)=c\int\psi$ for every test. Conversely every constant regular distribution has zero first derivatives. On a disconnected open set constants may differ on different connected components.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

derivations.claim:
A smooth field on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the parity pattern of the statement restricts to $Q$ as a tangential-electric and normal-magnetic perfect-conductor field: at the wall $x_1=0$ (and $x_1=L_1$), $E_1$ is even in $x_1$ while $E_2,E_3$ are odd, so $E_2=E_3=0$ there, which is $n	imes E=0$; $B_1$ is odd and $B_2,B_3$ even, so $B_1=0$ there, which is $n\cdot B=0$; the cyclic coordinates are identical. The parity conditions are closed linear conditions in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)$ because a sign change of a torus coordinate preserves $L^2$ convergence and distributional derivatives, and $\operatorname{div}E=0$ is the closed condition $\int E\cdot
abla\varphi\,d
u=0$ for every smooth periodic scalar test $\varphi$, and likewise for $B$, so $\mathcal C$ is a closed real subspace of the Hilbert space $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)^2$. The weak formulation used below is: $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;\mathcal C)$ is a weak solution when for every pair of smooth periodic vector fields $\Psi,\Theta$ compactly supported in $t$, $\iint E\cdot\partial_t\Psi\,d
u\,dt+(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}\iint B\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Psi\,d
u\,dt=0$ and $\iint B\cdot\partial_t\Theta\,d
u\,dt-\iint E\cdot\operatorname{curl}\Theta\,d
u\,dt=0$, which is exactly the statement that the two equations hold for $\partial_t$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]] (the spatial sign convention in $\operatorname{curl}$ is the distributional one, and for smooth periodic fields the pairing identities of the definition reduce to the displayed ones).

The characters $\Phi_n$ of [L1] are orthonormal in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$: orthogonality factors as a product of one-dimensional character pairings, and the $j$th factor is $1$ for equal coordinate indices and $0$ otherwise by the one-dimensional orthonormality of [L1]. They are complete: if $f\in L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$ is orthogonal to every $\Phi_n$, fix $n_2,n_3\in\mathbb Z$ and set $g(x_1):=\int f(x_1,x_2,x_3)e^{-i\pi(n_2x_2/L_2+n_3x_3/L_3)}\,d\nu_2d\nu_3$, an $L^2$ function of $x_1$ by Cauchy-Schwarz; its one-dimensional character coefficients all vanish, since they are the $\Phi_n$ pairings of $f$ with $n_1$ varying, so $g=0$ a.e. by the one-dimensional completeness of [L1]; applying this for all $n_2,n_3$ and iterating in the other two coordinates, with a countable union of exceptional null sets, gives $f=0$ a.e., so the closed span is all of $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb C)$. Parseval and mean-square convergence of finite partial sums follow from [L1] applied componentwise to the six real components of a pair of fields.

Group the character indices into the disjoint reflection orbits $O_p=\{n\in\mathbb Z^3:|n_j|=p_j\ (j=1,2,3)\}$ indexed by $p\in\mathbb N_0^3$. Let $P_p$ be the finite-dimensional real space of Fourier coefficient arrays $(v_n,w_n)_{n\in O_p}$ satisfying reality, the stated parities, and $k_n\cdot v_n=k_n\cdot w_n=0$, where $k_n=(\pi n_1/L_1,\pi n_2/L_2,\pi n_3/L_3)$. The divergence constraints are equivalent to these equations: testing against each character gives necessity, and an orbit sum with these equations has zero divergence pointwise. Projection onto a whole orbit commutes with coordinate reflections and reality. Thus whole-orbit truncations lie in $\mathcal C$ and converge in $L^2$ by step 2.1, proving density. The corresponding real products are the stated even-coordinate cosines and odd-coordinate sines, with zero-index sine terms absent. Parseval gives $\varepsilon\|E\|_2^2+\|B\|_2^2/\mu=\sum_p Q_p$, where $Q_p=\sum_{n\in O_p}(\varepsilon|v_n|^2+|w_n|^2/\mu)$. The mode equations are $v_n'=i(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1}k_n\times w_n$, $w_n'=-ik_n\times v_n$. Curl sends the magnetic parity pattern to the electric pattern and conversely: differentiating changes the parity of exactly the differentiated coordinate; the two terms in each curl component have the required pattern. These equations preserve reality and divergence, so define a real linear map on $P_p$. For real $k_n$, put $C=\overline v_n\cdot(k_n\times w_n)$. The scalar triple product gives $\overline w_n\cdot(k_n\times v_n)=-\overline C$, hence the energy derivative is $(2/\mu)\operatorname{Re}(iC+i\overline C)=0$. Therefore each $Q_p$ is conserved.

Enumerate $p\in\mathbb N_0^3$ by increasing $p_1+p_2+p_3$, then lexicographically within each finite level, writing $p^{(1)},p^{(2)},\dots$. Every coefficient belongs to exactly one $P_{p^{(m)}}$; let $A_m$ be the real matrix of the orbit operator of step 3.1 in the real basis obtained by Gaussian elimination on its finite linear constraints, with the coordinates in lexicographic order and the first available pivot chosen each time. This defines all bases without a countable choice of bases. Each $A_m$ is bounded, so the finite-dimensional linear system $z_m'=A_mz_m$ has a unique global solution through every real initial vector $z_m(0)$, by the global Lipschitz corollary of [L3]; no choice is needed for one system. For $M\ge1$ let $(E_M,B_M)$ be the sum of the first $M$ modal solutions with the initial amplitudes inherited from the given initial datum $(E_0,B_0)\in\mathcal C$. Each $(E_M,B_M)$ is a finite sum of smooth modes, hence smooth and in $\mathcal C$, solves the two equations pointwise, and satisfies $\varepsilon\|E_M(t)\|^2+\|B_M(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_{m\le M}Q_{p^{(m)}}(0)$ for all $t$ by the modal invariance of step 3.1. The omitted modes carry the nonnegative initial partial energies $R_M:=\sum_{m>M}Q_{p^{(m)}}(0)$, which decrease to $0$ because the total initial energy $\sum_mQ_{p^{(m)}}(0)=\varepsilon\|E_0\|^2+\|B_0\|^2/\mu$ is finite. For $M<M'$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, $\varepsilon\|(E_{M'}-E_M)(t)\|^2+\|(B_{M'}-B_M)(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_{M<m\le M'}Q_{p^{(m)}}(t)\le R_M$, because each omitted modal energy is constant; hence $(E_M,B_M)$ is Cauchy uniformly in $t$ in $L^2(\mathbb T;\mathbb R^3)^2$, and its uniform limit $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ exists and takes values in the closed subspace $\mathcal C$ of step 1.1, with $\varepsilon\|E(t)\|^2+\|B(t)\|^2/\mu=\lim_M\bigl(\varepsilon\|E_M(t)\|^2+\|B_M(t)\|^2/\mu\bigr)=\sum_mQ_{p^{(m)}}(0)$ for every $t$.

Let $(E,B)\in C(\mathbb R;\mathcal C)$ be any weak solution in the sense of step 1.1, and fix a mode index $m$ together with a real mode function $\varphi$ in the finite-dimensional space of modes belonging to the orbit $O_{p^{(m)}}$ (a smooth periodic vector field). Testing the two weak equations with $\psi(t)\varphi(x)$, where $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ is arbitrary, gives, in the sense of distributions on $\mathbb R$, the scalar equations $c_\varphi'=(\text{the corresponding finite linear combination of the other modal coefficients})$, where $c_\varphi(t)=\langle\varphi,(E,B)(t)\rangle$ is the coefficient pairing; these are continuous functions of $t$ because $(E,B)$ is continuous into $L^2$ and the pairing is continuous. Assembling the finitely many coefficients belonging to $O_{p^{(m)}}$ into a real vector $Z_m(t)$ gives a finite linear system $\partial_tZ_m=A_mZ_m$ with continuous right-hand side; applying the primitive construction componentwise on a compact interval $[a,b]$, every component of $A_mZ_m$ is continuous, hence Riemann integrable [L4], its oriented primitive $G$ is $C^1$ with $G'=g$ [L4], and the regular-distribution compatibility clause of [L4] (whose use here is covered by the standing $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) transfers this to distributional derivatives; subtracting the primitive from $Z_m$ shows that the difference has zero distributional derivative, hence is constant on the connected set $\mathbb R$ [L4]; continuity makes the equality pointwise. Therefore every modal coefficient is a classical $C^1$ solution of its finite linear system. Since $Z_m$ solves a linear constant-coefficient ODE, its value at every time is determined by $Z_m(0)$ by the global uniqueness part of [L3]; hence the weak solution $(E,B)$ is uniquely determined by its initial datum $(E(0),B(0))$, because the modal coefficients determine the fields by the completeness in step 3.1.

The energy of the constructed solution is constant. By step 4.1, for every $t$ one has $\varepsilon\|E(t)\|^2+\|B(t)\|^2/\mu=\sum_mQ_{p^{(m)}}(0)$, the same value at every $t$; and $\sum_mQ_{p^{(m)}}(0)=\varepsilon\|E_0\|^2+\|B_0\|^2/\mu$ by the Parseval identity of step 3.1, while the normalized torus measure and Lebesgue measure on $Q$ have the norm conversion $\int_Q|E|^2=L_1L_2L_3\|E\|_{L^2(\nu)}^2$ and likewise for $B$. Hence the energy $\tfrac12\int_Q(\varepsilon|E|^2+|B|^2/\mu)\,dx$ of the constructed solution equals its initial value at every time. By the uniqueness of step 4.2, every $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution in the class with the same initial datum is this solution, so energy conservation holds for every weak solution.

The limit $(E,B)$ of step 4.1 is a weak solution in the sense of step 1.1. Indeed, each truncation $(E_M,B_M)$ solves the equations pointwise, hence also in the pairing formulation, because for smooth periodic fields the distributional pairings coincide with the integral pairings and the cur sign convention is the same. For a smooth periodic test pair $(\Psi,\Theta)$ compactly supported in $t$, the differences satisfy $|\iint(E_M-E)\cdot\partial_t\Psi\,d\nu\,dt|\le\sup_{t}\|(E_M-E)(t)\|_{L^2}\cdot\int\|\partial_t\Psi(t)\|_{L^2}\,dt$, and $\int\|\partial_t\Psi(t)\|\,dt<\infty$ because $\Psi$ is compactly supported in time and continuous, so the bound tends to $0$ by the uniform convergence of step 4.1; the pairings with $\operatorname{curl}\Psi$ and $\operatorname{curl}\Theta$, and the corresponding pairings of $B_M$, are handled identically. Passing to the limit in the two displayed identities therefore shows that $(E,B)$ is a weak solution. The divergence constraints hold in the limit because the class $\mathcal C$ is closed, as recorded in step 1.1.

Collecting the results: step 3.1 proves claim (i), namely that the finite separated Fourier modes are dense in the class and that the class is complete for the $L^2$ pairing; steps 4.1 and 5.2 construct, for every initial datum in the class, a $C(\mathbb R;L^2)$ weak solution in the class, and step 4.2 proves that it is the only one, which is claim (ii); step 5.1 proves the energy constancy of claim (iii) for every weak solution. This proves every assertion of the statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^n)$ be compactly
supported, meaning that it has a representative which vanishes outside a
compact set. Then $Nf$ is finite almost everywhere, belongs to
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, and depends only on the $L^1$ equivalence
class of $f$. Its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f\quad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n).$$
The result includes $C_c$ data and compactly supported $L^p$ data for every
$1\le p\le\infty$. If $f=0$ almost everywhere outside a closed compact set
$K$, then $Nf$ is smooth and harmonic on $\mathbb R^n\setminus K$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Distributional derivatives satisfy $\partial^\alpha\partial^\beta u=\partial^{\alpha+\beta}u$ and are continuous linear maps on $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ for both the weak and strong distribution topologies. These claims hold in ZF. Assuming Countable Choice for the cited Riemann-to-Lebesgue comparison, if $f\in C^k(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ and $|\alpha|\le k$, then $\partial^\alpha u_f=u_{\partial^\alpha f}$. In particular distributional differentiation extends classical smooth differentiation.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $r$ be positive smooth. Every nonempty open $O\subseteq M$ has $\mu_r(O)>0$. If $d$ induces the manifold topology, then for every $p\in M$ and $R>0$ the ball $B_d(p,R)$ is Borel and has positive measure. If its closure in $M$ is compact, it also has finite measure.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $g\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]]) satisfy
$$\int_\Omega g\,\varphi\,dx=0\qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$$
([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]). Then $g=0$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$. Moreover, if $g$ is real-valued and $\int_\Omega g\varphi\,dx\ge0$ for every nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$, then $g\ge0$ almost everywhere.

derivations.claim: Substituting $z=x-y$ gives $Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(z)f(x-z)\,dz$, an absolutely convergent integral for every $x$: $f$ is bounded with support in some closed ball $\overline B_R(0)$, so the integrand is supported in $x-\overline B_R(0)$ and bounded there by $\|f\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$ with $\Phi\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$. The same substitution exhibits $Nf$ as the Newtonian potential of [L1], so the distributional identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ of [L1] holds.

Fix a multi-index $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)$ and a point $x$, and let $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a compact set containing $x$ in its interior. For $z$ in the fixed compact set $K-\operatorname{supp}f$ and $x'\in K$, the function $z\mapsto\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x'-z)$ is bounded by $\|D^\alpha f\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$, integrable on that compact set, and $z\mapsto\Phi(z)D^{\alpha+e_j}f(x'-z)$ likewise; moreover $D^\alpha f$ is uniformly continuous on the compact set $K-\operatorname{supp}f$ shifted appropriately. Applying the differentiation-under-the-integral-sign theorem [L2] successively in the three coordinates (the parameter being one coordinate of $x$ and the measure space $\mathbb R^3$ with the dominated bounds above) gives $D^\alpha Nf(x)=\int\Phi(z)D^\alpha f(x-z)\,dz=N(D^\alpha f)(x)$ at every $x$, and the resulting function is continuous in $x$ because the bound $\|D^\alpha f(x-z)-D^\alpha f(x'-z)\|_\infty|\Phi(z)|$ on the compact $z$-set is uniform in $x,x'$ near $x$ and tends to $0$. Hence $Nf$ has continuous derivatives of every order, so $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, and the identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$ holds for every multi-index $\alpha$; in particular the classical Laplacian $\Delta Nf=\sum_{j=1}^3N(\partial_j^2f)$ is a continuous function, and it is the classical Laplacian of the smooth function $Nf$.

By [L3] the distributional Laplacian of the smooth function $Nf$ is the regular distribution of the classical Laplacian, so the identity $-\Delta T_{Nf}=T_f$ of step 1.1 says that $\int_{\mathbb R^3}(f(y)+\Delta Nf(y))\varphi(y)\,dy=0$ for every test function $\varphi$. The function $g:=f+\Delta Nf$ is continuous by step 2.1, so it is locally integrable and the fundamental lemma [L5] gives $g=0$ almost everywhere. A continuous function vanishing almost everywhere vanishes everywhere: if $g(x_0)\ne0$, continuity gives $r>0$ with $|g|>|g(x_0)|/2>0$ on the nonempty open ball $B_r(x_0)$, which has positive Lebesgue measure by [L4], contradicting $g=0$ a.e.; hence $g(x_0)=0$ for every $x_0$. Therefore $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$.

For smooth compactly supported $\rho$, the derivative identity of step 2.1 with $\alpha=e_j$ shows that $\nabla N\rho$ is a smooth field, and $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth because $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$ is a constant. Countable Choice is inherited from the exact statement of the Newtonian-potential theorem [L1] and from the positive-density-measure corollary [L4]; the differentiation and upgrade arguments use no further choice. This proves the smoothness of $Nf$, the pointwise Poisson identity and the derivative identity $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$, and hence the smoothness of $E$.

boundaries.reason: No family or indexed aggregate occurs: the statement concerns one datum f and one potential Nf, the integration domain R^3 is nonempty, and the bounds of step 1.1 do not require supp f to be nonempty.

boundaries.evidence: The zero datum f = 0 is admitted: Nf = 0, the identity -Delta Nf = f holds with both sides zero, and the derivative identity D^alpha Nf = N(D^alpha f) is trivial; steps 1.1 and 3.1 apply to the identically zero function.

The first-order instance |alpha| = 1 is the base case of the multi-index argument of step 2.1, and the single-fluid case of the field E = -epsilon_0^{-1} grad N rho is the scalar-parameter instance of step 4.1; dimension three is fixed by the statement.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate parameter regime occurs: epsilon_0 > 0 is a positive scalar parameter and the argument holds x fixed while z varies over the pole-carrying compact set K - supp f; the singular kernel is retained in the integration and controlled by local integrability in step 2.1 rather than differentiated at the pole.

The spatial domain is all of R^3, so there is no boundary or interval endpoint; the only singular point is the pole z = 0, which is not excluded but handled by the estimate of step 2.1 and the density argument of step 3.1.

boundaries.evidence: AC_omega is declared and inherited exactly from the Newtonian-potential theorem [L1] and from the differentiation-under-the-integral and L^1 interfaces [L2] and [L5] used in steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1; step 4.1 records that no further choice is made.

boundaries.reason: The statement is a conjunction of smoothness and two identities, not a biconditional; steps 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 prove the forward assertions in order.

No converse is claimed: the item does not assert that every smooth solution of -Delta u = f with compactly supported f is the Newtonian potential, only that this explicit transform has the listed properties.

Moving derivatives onto f uses one fixed compact z-set for nearby x, dominated by |Phi| times the bounded derivatives of f; no kernel differentiation at its pole occurs. Exact Countable-Choice Newtonian supplier gives the distributional Poisson identity. Classical/distributional derivative compatibility and the fundamental lemma make f+Delta Nf zero a.e.; continuity and positive measure of open balls upgrade this pointwise. A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

In every real or complex inner-product space, for all vectors $x,y$,

$$\|x+y\|^2+\|x-y\|^2=2\|x\|^2+2\|y\|^2 .$$

Let $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$.
A map $B:X\times Y\to Z$ is **bilinear** when $x \mapsto B(x,y)$ is linear for
each fixed $y \in Y$ and $y \mapsto B(x,y)$ is linear for each fixed
$x \in X$.

It is a **bounded bilinear map** when there is a real constant $C \ge 0$ such
that

$$\|B(x,y)\| \le C\|x\|\,\|y\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X,\ y \in Y.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $\ell \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\ell$ is a
**greatest lower bound**, or **infimum**, of $S$ if both of the following hold:

- $\ell$ is a lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]), that is, $\ell \le s$ for
  every $s \in S$;
- $\ell' \le \ell$ for every lower bound $\ell'$ of $S$.

Written out in one line:

$$\ell \text{ is an infimum of } S \iff \big[(\forall s \in S)\, \ell \le s\big] \text{ and } \big[(\forall \ell' \in \mathbb{R})\, \big((\forall s \in S)\, \ell' \le s\big) \Rightarrow \ell' \le \ell\big].$$

An infimum, when it exists, is unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]), so we may write
$\inf S$ for it.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then $S$ has a
greatest lower bound in $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-infimum]]), and it is given by

$$\inf S = -\sup(-S), \qquad \text{where } -S = \{-s : s \in S\}.$$

In particular the complete ordered field $\mathbb{R}$ has the
greatest-lower-bound property, which is therefore not an extra axiom: it is a
consequence of the least-upper-bound property.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let $\ell$ be a
lower bound of $S$ ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then

$$\ell = \inf S \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \text{for every } \varepsilon > 0 \text{ there exists } s \in S \text{ with } s < \ell + \varepsilon.$$

In words: among the lower bounds of $S$, the infimum is exactly the one that
cannot be raised by any positive amount and still bound $S$ from below.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For every $v\in H$ one has $\tfrac12a(v,v)\ge\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2$ by the coercivity hypothesis and $-\ell(v)\ge-|\ell(v)|\ge-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$ by [F4], hence $J(v)\ge\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|$.

Expanding with bilinearity and symmetry of $a$ (the same expansion as the parallelogram identity [F2], applied to the quadratic form $v\mapsto a(v,v)$) gives $a\bigl(\tfrac{v+w}2,\tfrac{v+w}2\bigr)=\tfrac12a(v,v)+\tfrac12a(w,w)-\tfrac14a(v-w,v-w)$, hence $J\bigl(\tfrac{v+w}2\bigr)=\tfrac{J(v)+J(w)}2-\tfrac18a(v-w,v-w)$ for all $v,w\in H$.

Completing the square gives $\tfrac\alpha2\|v\|^2-\|\ell\|\,\|v\|=\tfrac\alpha2\bigl(\|v\|-\tfrac{\|\ell\|}\alpha\bigr)^2-\tfrac{\|\ell\|^2}{2\alpha}\ge-\tfrac{\|\ell\|^2}{2\alpha}$, so the image $S=\{J(v):v\in H\}$ is nonempty and bounded below in $\mathbb R$, and its infimum $m=\inf S\in\mathbb R$ exists by [F5].

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ the set $X_n:=\{v\in H:J(v)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}\}$ is nonempty: otherwise $m+\tfrac1{n+1}$ would be a lower bound of $S$ larger than $m$, contradicting [F5] (equivalently, [F5] with $\varepsilon=\tfrac1{n+1}$ produces $v$ with $J(v)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}$). Applying $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [F6] to the family $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ gives a sequence $(v_n)$ in $H$ with $J(v_n)<m+\tfrac1{n+1}$ for all $n$; since $m$ is a lower bound of $S$, also $J(v_n)\ge m$, so $J(v_n)\to m$.

Since $m$ is a lower bound of $S$ one has $J\bigl(\tfrac{v_n+v_k}2\bigr)\ge m$, so step 1.2 and the coercivity bound $a(v_n-v_k,v_n-v_k)\ge\alpha\|v_n-v_k\|^2$ give $\tfrac\alpha8\|v_n-v_k\|^2\le\tfrac{J(v_n)+J(v_k)}2-m\le\tfrac12\bigl(\tfrac1{n+1}+\tfrac1{k+1}\bigr)$; the right-hand side tends to $0$ as $n,k\to\infty$, so $(v_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $H$.
By completeness [F1] there is $u\in H$ with $\|v_n-u\|\to0$.

The functional $J$ is continuous in the norm: for $v,w\in H$ one has $|J(v)-J(w)|\le\tfrac12|a(v,v)-a(w,w)|+|\ell(v-w)|=\tfrac12|a(v+w,v-w)|+|\ell(v-w)|\le\bigl(\tfrac C2\|v+w\|+\|\ell\|\bigr)\|v-w\|$ by [F3] and [F4], which tends to $0$ as $v\to w$; hence $J(u)=\lim_nJ(v_n)=m$.

Fix $v\in H$ and consider $g(s)=J(u+sv)$; expanding with bilinearity and symmetry gives $g(s)=J(u)+s\bigl(a(u,v)-\ell(v)\bigr)+\tfrac{s^2}2a(v,v)$ for all $s\in\mathbb R$. Since $J(u)=m$ is the minimum of $J$, $g(s)\ge g(0)$ for all $s$: for $s>0$ division by $s$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)+\tfrac s2a(v,v)\ge0$, and letting $s\to0^+$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)\ge0$, while for $s<0$ the same division gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)+\tfrac s2a(v,v)\le0$, and letting $s\to0^-$ gives $a(u,v)-\ell(v)\le0$. Therefore $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$, and since $v\in H$ was arbitrary, $u$ solves the variational equation.

Uniqueness: if $u_1,u_2\in H$ both satisfy the equation, then testing the difference at $v=u_1-u_2$ gives $a(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)=0$, and coercivity gives $\alpha\|u_1-u_2\|^2\le a(u_1-u_2,u_1-u_2)=0$, so $\|u_1-u_2\|=0$ and $u_1=u_2$ by [F1].

Estimate: testing the equation at $v=u$ gives $a(u,u)=\ell(u)$, and coercivity together with [F4] gives $\alpha\|u\|^2\le a(u,u)=\ell(u)\le\|\ell\|\,\|u\|$; if $\|u\|=0$ then $0\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$ holds, and otherwise division by $\alpha\|u\|>0$ gives $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$. This proves existence, uniqueness and the estimate, and identifies the sole use of $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as the selection in step 3.1.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
citations.use: **FTC and Lipschitz bounds.** If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^m$ is differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ with $f'$ integrable, then $\int_a^bf'=f(b)-f(a)$; if moreover $\|f'\|\le M$ on $(a,b)$, then $\|f(t)-f(s)\|\le M|t-s|$ for all $s,t\in[a,b]$ ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]]). A continuous real function on $[a,b]$ is Riemann integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]), so the derivatives of the $C^1$ composites below are integrable.

citations.quote:
Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.
citations.use: **Differentiation under the integral sign.** For an open interval $I$, a measure space $X$ and $h:X\times I\to\mathbb C$ with integrable sections, a.e.-differentiable parameter dependence and an integrable dominating function for $\partial_th$, the function $t\mapsto\int h(x,t)d\mu(x)$ is differentiable with the expected derivative ([[thm-differentiation-under-the-integral-sign]]). It is applied below with the measure space $X=[0,L]$ carrying Lebesgue measure and the parameter running in an open interval, coordinatewise in the parameter; the bounded derivatives of the smooth kernels on compact sets supply the dominating functions.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.
citations.use: **Distributions.** $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) and the distributional derivative is $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). A complex-linear functional $u$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is a distribution exactly when for every compact $K$ there are $m_K\ge0$, $C_K\ge0$ with $|u(\varphi)|\le C_Kp_{m_K}(\varphi)$ on $\mathcal D_K$ ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]). The regular-functional map embeds $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo a.e. equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Constant-coefficient distributional derivatives commute ([[thm-distributional-differentiation-is-continuous-and-commutes]]).

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.
citations.use: **Distributions.** $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) and the distributional derivative is $\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle$ ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). A complex-linear functional $u$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$ is a distribution exactly when for every compact $K$ there are $m_K\ge0$, $C_K\ge0$ with $|u(\varphi)|\le C_Kp_{m_K}(\varphi)$ on $\mathcal D_K$ ([[thm-local-finite-order-characterization-of-distributions]]). The regular-functional map embeds $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo a.e. equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ ([[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]], [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]]). Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$
citations.use: **Tonelli and Fubini.** Nonnegative measurable integrands may be integrated in either order, and absolutely integrable integrands satisfy the Fubini identity ([[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]], [[thm-fubini-theorem-for-l-one-on-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]); translation is measure preserving, so $\int g(x-c)dx=\int g$ ([[thm-integrals-are-invariant-under-measure-preserving-maps]]).

citations.quote:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $f$ is integrable real or complex valued, $f\circ T$ is integrable and the same equality holds. Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);

   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

citations.quote:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$. Then the closed bounded interval
$[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]]) is compact ([[def-open-cover-r]]): every family of
open subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ whose union contains $[a,b]$ has a finite subfamily
whose union already contains $[a,b]$.

The proof is by repeated bisection. Supposing some open cover admits no finite
subcover, one halves the interval, keeps a half that still admits none, and
iterates; the halves shrink to a point, which the cover does reach, and a single
member of the cover then swallows a whole late-stage half. **The halving rule is
canonical**, taking the left half whenever the left half works, so the recursion
uses [[thm-recursion]] and no choice principle.
citations.use: **Compactness and distance.** $[0,L]$ is compact ([[thm-heine-borel-r]]), continuous images of compact sets are compact ([[thm-continuous-image-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]), compact subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are closed and bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), closed bounded subsets of $\mathbb R^3$ are compact ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]), and disjoint nonempty compact and closed sets in a normed space have a positive distance gap ([[lem-relative-compact-closed-sets-have-a-positive-distance-gap]]).

$f : X \to Y$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then:

1. If $(X,d_X)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]), the image
   $f[X] \subseteq Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$.
2. More generally, if $K \subseteq X$ is a compact subset of $X$, then $f[K]$ is
   a compact subset of $Y$.

No choice principle is used.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

For real $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2\le\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2$ ([[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]]); the pointwise divergence and curl are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

citations.quote:
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.
citations.use: **Sine and cosine.** $(\sin)'=\cos$ and $(\cos)'=-\sin$, $\sin0=0$, and $\sin$ and $\cos$ have fundamental period $2\pi$ ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-derivatives]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]).

citations.quote:
For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

derivations.claim: For $\psi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ the bound $|j(\psi)|\le|I|\int_0^L|\psi(\gamma(s))|ds\le|I|L\,p_0(\psi)$ holds, with $p_0$ the supremum seminorm over any compact set containing the bounded set $\gamma([0,L])$; the constant does not depend on the compact set $K$ supporting $\psi$, so [F4] makes $j$ a vector distribution of order $\le0$, supported in $\gamma([0,L])$.

Put $A_k(x)=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\Phi(x-\gamma(s))ds$ for $x\notin\gamma$ and $A_k=0$ on $\gamma$. For a compact $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ choose $R$ with $Q-\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_R(0)$; Tonelli [F5] and [F6] give $\int_Q|A_k|\le\mu_0|I|\int_0^L\int_{B_R}|\Phi|=(\mu_0|I|L R^2)/2$ and $\int_Q|\partial_jA_k|\le\mu_0|I|\int_0^L\int_{B_R}|\nabla\Phi|=\mu_0|I|LR$, so $A_k$ and each first partial derivative $\partial_jA_k$ belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and define regular distributions by [F4].

For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ with support in $B_R(0)$ and $0<\delta<R$, the divergence theorem [F8] on the annulus $\{\delta<|z|<R\}$, presented by the six signed-maximal-coordinate regular graph faces of each boundary sphere whose seam arcs have zero surface measure, applied to the $C^1$ field $\Phi\varphi\,e_j$ gives $\int_{\delta<|z|<R}\partial_j(\Phi\varphi)=\int_{S_R}\Phi\varphi\frac{z_j}{R}dS-\int_{S_\delta}\Phi\varphi\frac{z_j}{\delta}dS$, where the outer term vanishes and the inner term is bounded by $\|\varphi\|_\infty\frac{4\pi\delta^2}{4\pi\delta}=\|\varphi\|_\infty\delta\to0$; expanding $\partial_j(\Phi\varphi)=\partial_j\Phi\,\varphi+\Phi\,\partial_j\varphi$ and letting $\delta\to0$ with the absolutely integrable limits of [F6] yields $\langle\partial_jT_\Phi,\varphi\rangle=-\int\Phi\partial_j\varphi=\int(\partial_j\Phi)\varphi$, that is $\partial_jT_\Phi=T_{\partial_j\Phi}$ with $\partial_j\Phi(z)=-z_j/(4\pi|z|^3)$.

For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ one has $\langle\operatorname{div}j,\varphi\rangle=-\sum_kj_k(\partial_k\varphi)=-I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$ by [F4]; the chain rule [F1] gives $\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\varphi(\gamma(s))=(d/ds)(\varphi\circ\gamma)(s)$, and $s\mapsto(\varphi\circ\gamma)(s)$ is $C^1$ with continuous derivative on $[0,L]$, hence integrable, so the second FTC [F2] and the periodicity $\varphi(\gamma(L))=\varphi(\gamma(0))$ give $\int_0^L(d/ds)(\varphi\circ\gamma)ds=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}j=0$.

The pairing $j_\varepsilon(x)=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))$ uses the test function $y\mapsto\eta_\varepsilon(x-y)\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$, and expanding the definition of $j$ gives $j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds$ for every $x$; this is the mollified field of the Statement.

The translated identity $\partial_jT_{\Phi(\cdot-y)}=T_{\partial_j\Phi(\cdot-y)}$ follows from step 1.3 because the pairing is translation invariant [F5]; applying it under the absolutely integrable $s$-integral of step 1.2 gives $\partial_jT_{A_k}=T_{\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\partial_j\Phi(x-\gamma(s))ds}$, and with the componentwise distributional curl $\operatorname{curl}_ku=\sum_{i,j}\varepsilon_{kij}\partial_iu_j$ of [F12] one obtains $\operatorname{curl}T_A=T_B$ for the stated $B$, since $\varepsilon_{kij}\gamma_j'(s)\partial_i\Phi(x-\gamma(s))=\varepsilon_{kij}\gamma_j'(s)\frac{-(x-\gamma(s))_i}{4\pi|x-\gamma(s)|^3}=\frac{(\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s)))_k}{4\pi|x-\gamma(s)|^3}$ by [F12].

For scalar $\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3)$ set $H(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\Phi(z)\varphi(z+y)dz$, which is smooth near the compact curve $\gamma([0,L])$ by differentiation under the integral sign [F3] against the locally integrable $\Phi$; then $\langle\operatorname{div}T_A,\varphiangle=-\langle T_A,
abla\varphiangle=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\Bigl(\int\Phi(z)
abla\varphi(z+\gamma(s))dz\Bigr)ds=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot
abla H(\gamma(s))ds$, the interchange being justified by the Tonelli bound of step 1.2, and the chain rule together with the FTC and periodicity of $s\mapsto H(\gamma(s))$ gives $\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot
abla H(\gamma(s))ds=0$; hence $\operatorname{div}T_A=0$.

Componentwise, [F7] gives $-\Delta T_{A_k}=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\delta_{\gamma(s)}ds$: for a scalar test $\varphi$, Fubini [F5] and the translated fundamental-solution identity of [F7] yield $\langle-\Delta T_{A_k},\varphi\rangle=-\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\int\Phi(x-\gamma(s))\Delta\varphi(x)dx\,ds=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$; applying this to the components of a vector test $\psi$ gives $\langle-\Delta T_A,\psi\rangle=\mu_0I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))ds=\mu_0j(\psi)$, that is $-\Delta T_A=\mu_0j$.

For every multi-index $\alpha$ the integrand $\gamma'(s)D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))$ is smooth in $x$ with $s$-independent bound $\sup|D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon|$ over the compact parameter interval $[0,L]$, so differentiation under the integral sign [F3] coordinatewise gives $D^\alpha j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)D^\alpha\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds$ and $j_\varepsilon\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$; the integrand vanishes unless $x\in\gamma([0,L])+\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\gamma([0,L])+\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$, a closed bounded and hence compact set by [F11], so $\operatorname{supp}j_\varepsilon$ is compact.

Since $T_B=\operatorname{curl}T_A$ by step 2.3 and constant-coefficient distributional derivatives commute [F4], the alternating-symbol cancellations give $\operatorname{div}T_B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}T_A=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}T_A=\nabla\operatorname{div}T_A-\Delta T_A=0+\mu_0j=\mu_0j$; this proves the global distributional identities for $T_B$ without any limit through the singular support.

On $\mathbb R^3\setminus\gamma$ the field $B$ is given by the absolutely convergent integral of the Statement, with $|B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|}{4\pi}\int_0^L|x-\gamma(s)|^{-2}ds$ because $|\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))|\le|x-\gamma(s)|$ by [F12]; the same Tonelli computation as step 1.2 gives $\int_Q|B|\le\mu_0|I|LR$ on every compact $Q$, so $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $T_B$ is its regular distribution by [F4]; the curve is Lebesgue-null because for every $h>0$ the Lipschitz bound [F2] with $|\gamma'|=1$ covers $\gamma([0,L])$ by the $\lceil L/h\rceil$ balls of radius $h$ about the equally spaced points $jL/\lceil L/h\rceil$, whose total volume $\lceil L/h\rceil\frac43\pi h^3$ tends to $0$ as $h\to0$ by [F10], and arbitrary finite values assigned on that null set therefore give the same locally integrable class and a measurable representative; on a compact subset of the complement the distance gap of [F11] bounds the kernel and all its $x$-derivatives uniformly, so differentiation under the integral sign [F3] makes $B$ smooth off $\gamma$.

For every fixed $x$ one has $\operatorname{div}j_\varepsilon(x)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))ds=-I\int_0^L(d/ds)\bigl[\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\bigr]ds=0$: the chain rule [F1] identifies the integrand with the negative $s$-derivative, the composite is $C^1$ on $[0,L]$ with integrable derivative [F2], and periodicity gives equal endpoint values.
If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ and $|x|>a$, then $|x-\gamma(s)|\ge|x|-a$ for every $s$, so step 3.3 gives $|B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|}{4\pi}\frac{L}{(|x|-a)^2}$, the stated decay at infinity.

Let $K$ be nonempty compact with $d=\operatorname{dist}(K,\gamma([0,L]))>0$ by [F11], let $0<\varepsilon<d/2$, and let $A_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{j_\varepsilon(y)}{|x-y|}dy$ be the Newtonian potential of the smooth compactly supported $j_\varepsilon$; differentiating under the integral sign [F3] on $K$, where $|x-y|\ge d/2$ for $y\in\operatorname{supp}j_\varepsilon$ by step 3.1, gives the Biot-Savart field $B_\varepsilon(x)=\operatorname{curl}A_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int\frac{j_\varepsilon(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}dy$; substituting the formula of step 2.2 for $j_\varepsilon$, applying Fubini [F5] and translating $y=\gamma(s)+u$ with the measure-preserving change of variables [F5] yields $B_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\int_{\overline B_\varepsilon(0)}\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s)-u)}{|x-\gamma(s)-u|^3}\eta_\varepsilon(u)\,du\,ds$, all integrals absolutely convergent because $|x-\gamma(s)-u|\ge d-\varepsilon>0$.

For every multi-index $\alpha$ and $x\in K$, differentiate the absolutely convergent formulas of steps 3.3 and 4.3 under the integral signs [F3] and write $F_s(w)=\gamma'(s)\times w/|w|^3$: $D^\alpha B_\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\int D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s)-u)\eta_\varepsilon(u)duds$ and $D^\alpha B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^LD^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s))ds$; on the annulus $|w|\ge d/2$ one has $|D_wD^\alpha F_s(w)|\le C_\alpha|w|^{-3-|\alpha|}$ uniformly in $s$ because $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ and the derivatives of $w/|w|^3$ are homogeneous of the corresponding degrees, so the Lipschitz bound [F2] applied along the segment from $x-\gamma(s)$ to $x-\gamma(s)-u$ gives $|D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s)-u)-D^\alpha F_s(x-\gamma(s))|\le C_\alpha(d/2)^{-3-|\alpha|}|u|$; integrating against the unit-mass kernel supported in $\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ gives $|D^\alpha B_\varepsilon(x)-D^\alpha B(x)|\le\frac{\mu_0|I|L}{4\pi}C_\alpha(d/2)^{-3-|\alpha|}\varepsilon$, which tends to $0$ uniformly over $x\in K$ as $\varepsilon\to0$: the Biot-Savart fields converge with every derivative uniformly on $K$.

For $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and $x=z e_3$, step 3.3's formula has numerator $\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))=(z\cos(s/a),z\sin(s/a),a)$ and denominator $(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}$, so $B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}}\int_0^{2\pi a}(z\cos(s/a),z\sin(s/a),a)\,ds$; with $ds=a\,d\theta$, the transverse entries integrate to $0$ and the third entry integrates to $2\pi a^2$, because $\int_0^{2\pi}\cos=\int_0^{2\pi}\sin=0$ by the FTC and the fundamental period of [F13]; hence $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$, while no value of the singular line integral on the curve and no self-energy is asserted.

boundaries.evidence: The parameter aggregates are nonempty: the s-integral runs over the nondegenerate interval [0,L] with L > 0 in steps 1.1 and 2.1, the mollifier family is applied one kernel at a time in step 2.2 rather than chosen from, and the compact K of the convergence claim is assumed nonempty, the empty-K case being vacuous under the uniform estimates of step 5.1.

The zero-current case I = 0 gives j = 0, j_epsilon = 0 and B = 0 by steps 1.1, 2.2 and 3.3, so divergence-freeness and derivative convergence hold trivially; the divisions by epsilon and by |x - gamma(s)| are legitimate because epsilon > 0 and x stays off the curve on K.

The single-loop and single-kernel cases are exactly the ones handled: one closed curve with one current I in steps 1.1 and 1.2, one chosen radial kernel and its rescalings in step 2.2, and the first-order derivative case is the base instance of the arbitrary multi-index statement of step 3.1.

boundaries.reason: No degenerate parameter regime occurs: L > 0 and mu_0 > 0, the closed embedded C^2 curve has injective parametrisation on R/LZ so it has no self-intersection, and K stays at positive distance d from the curve in step 4.3, so |x - gamma(s)| never vanishes in the differentiated formulas.

boundaries.evidence: The parameter endpoints are handled by periodicity: step 2.1 integrates the chain rule over [0,L] and uses gamma(L) = gamma(0) and the closed-curve property, and step 4.1 evaluates the closed s-integral to zero; the limits epsilon tending to 0 and R tending to infinity are taken through positive values in steps 4.3 to 5.1.

AC_omega is declared and enters through the cited Lebesgue and distributional suppliers [F3], [F5] and [F10] used from step 1.2 onward and through the fundamental solution identity of [F7] in steps 2.5 and 3.2; the kernel family is universally quantified rather than selected, and no further choice principle is introduced.

boundaries.reason: The claim is a conjunction of divergence-freeness, smoothness and uniform derivative convergence, not a biconditional; steps 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 and 5.1 prove the forward assertions.

No converse is claimed: the item does not characterize all distributions whose mollifications approximate the Biot-Savart field, and step 4.1 proves divergence-freeness only for the explicitly constructed j_epsilon.
