Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[rem-real-and-complex-normed-space-convention]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$.

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain in $\mathbb R^3$ in the graph sense of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]; connectedness is unnecessary. Write $H^m(\Omega)=W^{m,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with the multi-index integral norm ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) and $H_0^1(\Omega)$ for the $H^1$ closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]). For every real $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ there is a unique $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)\cap H^2(\Omega)$ satisfying

$$\int_\Omega(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+uv)=\int_\Omega fv\qquad(v\in H_0^1(\Omega)).$$

It satisfies $(1-\Delta)u=f$ distributionally and almost everywhere as an $L^2$ identity, and

$$\|u\|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad\|u\|_{H^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}.$$

Moreover $D=\{\varphi\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega):\varphi|_{\partial\Omega}=0\}$ is dense in $H^2(\Omega)\cap H_0^1(\Omega)$ in the $H^2$ norm: every such $w$ has $\varphi_j\in D$ with $\varphi_j\to w$ in $H^2$. Here smoothness on the closure means restriction of a smooth function on a neighbourhood of the closure, equivalently the smooth chart representatives used below. In particular $\nabla\varphi_j\to\nabla w$ in the graph norm of $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$, with zero curl and $\operatorname{div}\nabla w=\Delta w$; every $\nabla\varphi_j$ is smooth and PEC since its tangential derivatives vanish at the boundary. For precision, let $X_\Omega$ be the graph-norm closure of smooth vector fields on a neighbourhood of the closure with $\nu\times v=0$ on the boundary, where $\nu$ is the outward Euclidean unit normal. The ambient graph space consists of real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional $\operatorname{div}v=\sum_i\partial_iv_i$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=(\partial_2v_3-\partial_3v_2,\partial_3v_1-\partial_1v_3,\partial_1v_2-\partial_2v_1)$ lie in $L^2$; its norm squared is $\|v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}v\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2^2$. Thus $\nabla w$ belongs to this explicitly defined $X_\Omega$, the same completion used by the later cavity item. No equality with every maximal trace realisation is asserted.

No smoothness of $f$, no classical boundary value for general $u$, and no general nonsmooth-domain, Neumann, interface, or variable-coefficient claim is included. Zero boundary condition means membership in $H_0^1$; the published trace theorem identifies its trace as zero.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be a complete orthonormal family in a real or complex Hilbert
space $H$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]) and
let $x\in H$, with partial sums
$P_Fx=\sum_{i\in F}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$ over finite $F\subseteq I$. Then:

1. $x$ is the norm limit of the finite-subset net $(P_Fx)$, that is
   $$x=\sum_{i\in I}\langle x,e_i\rangle e_i$$
   in the sense of convergence of the net of finite subsums;
2. **the coefficients are unique**: if $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ is a family in
   $\mathbb F$ whose finite-subset net $\sum_{i\in F}a_ie_i$ converges to $x$,
   then $a_i=\langle x,e_i\rangle$ for every $i\in I$;
3. the support $\{i : \langle x,e_i\rangle\ne0\}$ is at most countable, and the
   expansion does not depend on an ordering: if $(i_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ is a
   sequence of pairwise distinct elements of $I$ whose image contains the
   support, then the sequence of partial sums
   $\sum_{k<n}\langle x,e_{i_k}\rangle e_{i_k}$ also converges to $x$.

Claim 3 is the sense in which the expansion is **unconditional**: the sum is
independent of any ordering, because the finite-subset net converges and any
enumeration of a set containing the support by pairwise distinct indices is
cofinal in the squared mass.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

citations.quote:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

   section-integral functions are integrable; and

$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a

published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2.    is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let
$A \subseteq X$ and let $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ be the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-compact-space]]), that is $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \varnothing$.
2. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \varnothing$.

Claim 2 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

**Uniform normal collar and Gaffney identity.** Put $S=\partial\Omega$. On the smaller closed strip $|t|\le\eta/2$, the smooth positive volume Jacobian relative to $dS\,dt$ has constants $0<c\le J(p,t)\le C$ by [F7]; in a surface chart it is the absolute volume determinant divided by the positive Gram surface density, and the finite chart formula and change of variables of [F7] give $dx=J\,dS\,dt$. abla)N=0$. Also $
abla t=N$: the derivative of $t$ is zero on the vectors $D\Phi(	au,0)=	au+tD_	au n$, which are orthogonal to $n$, and is one on $\partial_t\Phi=n$. This is the signed-distance coordinate: for $x=\Phi(p,t)$ a closest point $q\in S$ exists by compactness, and minimizing squared distance in surface charts makes $x-q$ normal to $S$ with $|x-q|\le|t|<\minho$; injectivity of normal addition forces $q=p$, so $\operatorname{dist}(x,S)=|t|$ with the above inside/outside sign. For smooth $u$ with $n	imes u=0$, expansion and coordinate integration by parts [F1] give $\int_\Omega(|\operatorname{curl}u|^2+|\operatorname{div}u|^2-|
abla u|^2)=\sum_{i,j}\int_S(n_ju_j\partial_i u_i-n_ju_i\partial_i u_j)\,dS$. On $S$, $u=(u\cdot n)n$ and $\operatorname{div}u=\partial_N(u\cdot N)+(\operatorname{div}N)(u\cdot n)$: tangential derivatives of the zero tangential trace vanish there and $\partial_NN=0$. Substitution reduces the boundary term to $\int_S(\operatorname{div}N)|u\cdot n|^2dS$, the claimed Gaffney identity; its curvature is bounded on compact $S$.

**Boundary trace bound.** Use the inward coordinate $s=-t$ from step 1.1 and fix $0<h<\eta/2$. For $w(p,s)=u(p-sn(p))$, the FTC [F6] gives $|w(p,0)|^2\le |w(p,t)|^2+2\int_0^t|w(p,s)|\,|
abla u(p-sn(p))|ds$ for $0<t<h$, since $|\partial_sw|\le|
abla u|$. Average over $t\in(0,h)$, bound the resulting factor $(h-s)/h$ by one, and integrate over $S$. The lower Jacobian bound $J\ge c$ and the chart change-of-variables formula of step 1.1 yield $\|u\|_{L^2(S)}^2\le A h^{-1}\|u\|_2^2+2A\|u\|_2\|
abla u\|_2$, with $A=c^{-1}$, where Cauchy-Schwarz [F5] bounds the product integral on the interior collar. For every $\delta>0$, the algebraic square inequality gives $2Aab\le\delta b^2+A^2\delta^{-1}a^2$, hence $\|u\|_{L^2(S)}^2\le\delta\|
abla u\|_2^2+(A/h+A^2/\delta)\|u\|_2^2$. This uses the same finite compact cover and remains valid for disconnected domains.

Combining steps 1.1 and 2.1 with the bounded curvature term and absorbing the gradient contribution for small $\delta$ gives $\|u\|_{H^1}\le C(\|u\|_2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2+\|\operatorname{div}u\|_2)$ for smooth PEC fields, while conversely the graph norm is bounded by $C\|u\|_{H^1}$; hence the graph completion $X$ is a closed $H^1$-subspace of $H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with zero tangential trace, since the trace is continuous on $H^1$ and vanishes on the dense smooth PEC fields. The arbitrary-small-gradient trace estimate of step 2.1 holds for every $H^1$ field by smooth density and trace continuity [F2]. Graph completeness follows by passing the curl and divergence distributional test pairings to the componentwise $L^2$ limits [F5]; the two norm inequalities then identify this graph completion with a closed $H^1$ subspace.

The inclusion $X\hookrightarrow L^2$ is compact: extend a bounded family in $X$ to a fixed larger box by [F2], replace each extension by its average $P_hu$ over cubes of side $h$, and obtain the cube estimate locally as follows. On a cube $Q$ of side $h$, telescope $u(x)-u(y)$ along the three coordinate segments; ACL and Cauchy-Schwarz [F8, F5] bound each squared segment difference by $h$ times the line integral of the squared corresponding derivative. Product integration gives $\int_Q\int_Q|u(x)-u(y)|^2dx\,dy\le3h^2|Q|\int_Q|
abla u|^2$. Averaged Cauchy-Schwarz then gives $\int_Q|u-u_Q|^2\le3h^2\int_Q|
abla u|^2$. Apply this componentwise and sum over the finite cube partition to get $\|u-P_hu\|_2\le\sqrt3h\|
abla u\|_2$ uniformly; $P_h$ has finite-dimensional range and bounded images, so choosing $h$ small and a finite $\varepsilon$-net in that finite-dimensional range gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net for the family; total boundedness in the complete space $L^2$ gives compact closure, so $X	o L^2$ and $V	o H$ are compact inclusions.

On $X$ with the graph norm the shifted form $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega[\operatorname{curl}u\cdot\operatorname{curl}v+\operatorname{div}u\operatorname{div}v+u\cdot v]$ is symmetric, bounded and coercive with $a(u,u)=\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})}^2$, so the variational solver [F2] gives for every $f\in H$ a unique $K_0f\in X$ with $a(K_0f,v)=\int f\cdot v$ for all $v\in X$; $K_0$ is bounded $H\to X$ and $H\to L^2$; its divergence-free range is proved below.

Divergence preservation: for $f\in H$ put $q=\operatorname{div}K_0f$; testing the defining identity with the admissible smooth PEC gradients $v=
abla\varphi$ of zero-trace smooth $\varphi$ (for which $\operatorname{curl}
abla\varphi=0$, $\operatorname{div}
abla\varphi=\Delta\varphi$ and $n	imes
abla\varphi=0$) gives $\int_\Omega q(\Delta\varphi-\varphi)=0$ for all such $\varphi$, using $\int f\cdot
abla\varphi=0$ (each $f\in V$ has zero distributional divergence and the pairing is continuous in $L^2$) and $\int K_0f\cdot
abla\varphi=-\int q\varphi$.

For the datum $q\in L^2$ the Dirichlet resolvent [F4] gives $\varphi\in H^2\cap H_0^1$ with $(1-\Delta)\varphi=q$ and smooth zero-boundary approximants $\varphi_j	o\varphi$ in $H^2$ whose gradients $
abla\varphi_j	o
abla\varphi$ converge in the graph norm, so $
abla\varphi\in X$; passing the identity of step 5.1 to the limit by $L^2$ continuity gives $\int q(\Delta\varphi-\varphi)=-\|q\|_2^2$, hence $\|q\|_2=0$ and $q=0$; therefore $K_0$ maps $H$ into $V$, and $K=K_0|_H$ is bounded $H	o V$ and compact $H	o H$ by step 4.1.

Self-adjointness and trivial kernel: testing the defining equations of $Kf$ and $Kg$ with $Kg$ and $Kf$ respectively and using symmetry gives $(f,Kg)=a(Kf,Kg)=(Kf,g)$, so $K$ is self-adjoint; $(f,Kf)=\|\operatorname{curl}Kf\|_2^2+\|Kf\|_2^2>0$ for $f\ne0$, because $Kf=0$ would make $f$ orthogonal to the dense subspace $V$ of $H$, so $\ker K=\{0\}$.

By the compact self-adjoint spectral theorem [F3] applied to $K$, $H$ has an orthonormal basis $\{u_j\}$ of eigenfields $Ku_j=\kappa_ju_j$ with positive eigenvalues $\kappa_j$, finite multiplicities and $\kappa_j\to0$ (infinitely many only if $H$ is infinite dimensional, and any zero eigenvalue would contradict the trivial kernel); substituting into the full identity $a(Ku_j,v)=\int u_j\cdot v$ with $v\in X$, and using $\operatorname{div}u_j=0$ since $u_j\in V$, gives $\int\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=(\kappa_j^{-1}-1)\int u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$, so with $\lambda_j=\kappa_j^{-1}-1\ge0$ the eigenfields satisfy the full graph-class variational identity; testing with compactly supported smooth $v$ gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ distributionally with the inherited PEC trace.

The space $V$ with $\|u\|_V^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ is complete, being a closed subspace of the graph completion; the eigenidentity gives $(u,u_j)_V=(1+\lambda_j)(u,u_j)_H$, so $\{u_j/\sqrt{1+\lambda_j}\}$ is orthonormal in $V$ and its orthogonal complement vanishes, because orthogonality in $V$ forces all $H$-coefficients of $u$ to vanish; hence [F5] gives completeness in $V$ and the expansion $\|u\|_V^2=\sum_j(1+\lambda_j)|(u,u_j)_H|^2$.

Wave branch: for $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and data $q_0\in V$, $q_1\in H$ put $\alpha_j=(q_0,u_j)_H$ and $\gamma_j=(q_1,u_j)_H$; for $\lambda_j>0$ set $a_j(t)=\alpha_j\cos(v_{\mathrm{wave}}\sqrt{\lambda_j}t)+\gamma_j\sin(v_{\mathrm{wave}}\sqrt{\lambda_j}t)/(v_{\mathrm{wave}}\sqrt{\lambda_j})$, and for $\lambda_j=0$ set $a_j(t)=\alpha_j+t\gamma_j$; [F6] verifies the ODE and the initial values, and the positive-mode energy $|a_j'|^2+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_j|a_j|^2=|\gamma_j|^2+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_j|\alpha_j|^2$ is constant by [F6].

Since only finitely many eigenvalues lie in any bounded set and the zero sector is finite dimensional, the positive eigenvalues are bounded away from zero; the constant-energy identity therefore controls the $V$-displacement tail and the $H$-velocity tail uniformly in time, and the initial $V\times H$ summability of steps 9.1 and 10.1 makes all tails tend to zero, so finite modal sums converge in $C(K;V)$ for displacement and in $C(K;H)$ for velocity on every compact time interval $K$ with the prescribed initial data; the derivative statement passes to the limit by [F6]'s FTC estimate, and the finite equations pass to the variational equation in the distribution-in-time sense by $\|u\|_V$-convergence and density, while uniqueness follows from uniqueness of each scalar ODE and the completeness of the eigenbasis.

boundaries.evidence: The eigenbasis of step 8.1 is the complete orthonormal basis of the separable Hilbert space H, and in the trivial case H = {0} the index set is empty and every displayed series vanishes, all assertions holding vacuously; steps 9.1 to 11.1 impose no nonemptiness on the basis.

The zero eigenvalue sector is retained, not discarded: steps 7.1 and 8.1 show the kernel of K is trivial and the zero eigenspace finite dimensional, and step 10.1 gives the zero-mode coefficients a_j(t) = alpha_j + t gamma_j so the zero modes propagate linearly in time.

The single-mode sector is the finite-dimensional core of step 10.1: one eigenvalue with a one-dimensional eigenspace gives the explicit cosine/sine solution, and the first-order coefficient is gamma_j; the case of multiplicity one is included in the finite multiplicities of step 8.1.

The degenerate sector is handled explicitly: repeated eigenvalues have finite multiplicity by step 8.1, the zero eigenspace is kept with its linear-in-time coefficients in step 10.1, and step 11.1 uses that only finitely many eigenvalues lie in any bounded set.

boundaries.reason: No interval endpoint or boundary value of the time variable occurs: the solution is global in time in steps 10.1 and 11.1 and the spectral sums are controlled uniformly in t; the PEC boundary condition is encoded by membership in the graph completion X, not by an endpoint value of a parameter.

boundaries.evidence: The full Axiom of Choice is declared and used by the completion, trace, extension, Hilbert and compact-spectral suppliers, entering through [F2]-[F6] in steps 3.1 to 11.1, in particular the compact embedding and Hilbert-basis steps 4.1, 8.1 and 9.1; the Statement records that no weaker principle is claimed.

boundaries.reason: The claim is a conjunction of spectral, variational, distributional and wave assertions, not a biconditional; steps 4.1 to 9.1 prove the spectral and variational parts and steps 10.1 and 11.1 the wave part.

No converse is claimed: the item does not assert that the curl eigenfields are the only fields supporting the retained zero-mode dynamics, and the finite-mode example of step 11.1 is a check rather than a characterization.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and $n\ge1$. In the proof write $e_n$
for the last canonical basis vector $e_{n-1}$. Let
$H=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the upper
half-space, written $x=(x',t)$ with $x'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $t>0$. For every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$, every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ there is a bounded linear extension
operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(H;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (E_{k,p}u)|_H=u\ \text{almost everywhere on }H .$$
For $k\ge1$ one may take, with the unique coefficients
$(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb R^k$ satisfying
$\sum_{j=1}^k a_j(-j)^m=1$ for $m=0,1,\dots,k-1$,
$$E_{k,p}u(x',t)=u(x',t)\ \ (t>0),\qquad E_{k,p}u(x',t)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_ju(x',-jt)\ \ (t<0),$$
and for $k=0$ one may take the even reflection
$E_{0,p}u(x',t)=u(x',|t|)$. In particular $H$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension
domain in the sense of [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]
for every $k$ and every $p$, and no density assertion is made or needed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ with
$M_\eta:=\|D\eta\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb R^n)}$ and compact support; the case
$\eta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ is read by extending $\eta$ by zero.
Then for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$ and every $h\ne0$, on the shrunken set
$\Omega_{i,h}=\{x\in\Omega:x+he_i\in\Omega\}$ of
[[def-first-difference-quotient]] one has the exact identity
$$\delta_h^i(\eta u)-\eta\,\delta_h^iu=(\delta_h^i\eta)\,(\tau_{-he_i}u)\qquad\text{a.e. on }\Omega_{i,h},$$
where $\tau$ is the published translation $\tau_hu(x)=u(x-h)$ of
[[def-translation-of-a-function-on-rn]], so that
$(\tau_{-he_i}u)(x)=u(x+he_i)$. Consequently
$$\|\delta_h^i(\eta u)-\eta\,\delta_h^iu\|_{L^p(\Omega_{i,h})}\le M_\eta\,\|\tau_{-he_i}u\|_{L^p(\Omega_{i,h})}\le M_\eta\,\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
and more generally, on the domain where both sides are defined,
$$\delta_h^i\big(\eta^2\delta_h^iu\big)=\eta^2\delta_h^i\delta_h^iu+(\delta_h^i\eta^2)\,(\tau_{-he_i}\delta_h^iu).$$
The statement is quantitative in $\|D\eta\|_{L^\infty}$ and does not assume
any regularity of $u$ beyond $W^{1,p}$.

**Sobolev multiplier and support facts used below.** For every integer
$m\ge0$, $q\in W^{m,\infty}(U)$ and $z\in H^m(U)$ on an open set $U$,
$qz\in H^m(U)$ and
$$D^\alpha(qz)=\sum_{\beta\le\alpha}{\alpha\choose\beta}(D^\beta q)D^{\alpha-\beta}z,\qquad |\alpha|\le m,$$
with $\|qz\|_{H^m(U)}\le C(n,m)\|q\|_{W^{m,\infty}(U)}\|z\|_{H^m(U)}$.
Also, every compactly supported $z\in H^m(U)$ lies in $H^m_0(U)$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ ([[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]]). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and $n\ge1$. In the proof write $e_n$
for the last canonical basis vector $e_{n-1}$. Let
$H=\mathbb R^{n-1}\times(0,\infty)\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be the upper
half-space, written $x=(x',t)$ with $x'\in\mathbb R^{n-1}$ and $t>0$. For every
$k\in\mathbb N_0$, every $1\le p\le\infty$ and every
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ there is a bounded linear extension
operator
$$E_{k,p}:W^{k,p}(H;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (E_{k,p}u)|_H=u\ \text{almost everywhere on }H .$$
For $k\ge1$ one may take, with the unique coefficients
$(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb R^k$ satisfying
$\sum_{j=1}^k a_j(-j)^m=1$ for $m=0,1,\dots,k-1$,
$$E_{k,p}u(x',t)=u(x',t)\ \ (t>0),\qquad E_{k,p}u(x',t)=\sum_{j=1}^k a_ju(x',-jt)\ \ (t<0),$$
and for $k=0$ one may take the even reflection
$E_{0,p}u(x',t)=u(x',|t|)$. In particular $H$ is a $W^{k,p}$-extension
domain in the sense of [[def-sobolev-extension-domain-and-extension-operator]]
for every $k$ and every $p$, and no density assertion is made or needed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a **bounded smooth graph domain**: a nonempty bounded open set such that for every $x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood $W\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and a function $h\in C^\infty(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that $R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,

$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\},$$

which is the $C^\infty$ case of the bounded $C^k$ graph domain of [[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be an open set with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$. Then there exists a real-linear operator $E_\Omega$, determined only by $\Omega$, a finite smooth atlas and fixed cutoffs, such that for every open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and every function $u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ that is of class $C^\infty$ on the open set $\Omega\times J$ and whose every mixed derivative $D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u:\Omega\times J\to\mathbb R$ has a continuous extension to $\overline\Omega\times J$ ([[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]), the function $E_\Omega u$ is of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times J$, satisfies $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=u(x,\tau)$ for all $(x,\tau)\in\overline\Omega\times J$ and

$$D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)\big|_{\overline\Omega\times J}=\text{the continuous extension of }D^\alpha\partial_\tau^j u$$

for all multi-indices $\alpha$ and all $j\ge0$, and is spatially supported in one fixed compact subset of $V$, in the sense that there is a compact $K_\Omega\subseteq V$ with $E_\Omega u(x,\tau)=0$ for all $x\notin K_\Omega$, $\tau\in J$. In every seminorm formula below, a supremum over an empty indexing set is defined to be $0$; for a nonempty bounded family of nonnegative reals it denotes the usual least real upper bound. This convention applies also to the local seminorm formulas in the proof. For every compact $K\subseteq J$, every integer $m\ge0$ and every $j\ge0$,

$$\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j E_\Omega u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}\le C_m\sup_{\tau\in K}\|\partial_\tau^j u(\cdot,\tau)\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)},$$

where $\|w\|_{C^m(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\overline\Omega}|D^\alpha w(x)|$ and $\|W\|_{C^m(\mathbb R^3)}:=\sum_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^3}|D^\alpha W(x)|$, and the constant $C_m$ depends only on $m$, $\Omega$, the atlas and cutoffs. The extension commutes with every time derivative: $\partial_\tau^j(E_\Omega u)=E_\Omega(\partial_\tau^j u)$ for all $j\ge0$. No bound uniform over an unbounded $J$ is asserted. Vector-valued inputs of finite dimension are extended componentwise. The construction adds no choice principle: the finite atlas is selected from the cover of all admissible smooth chart patches, finite cutoffs come from the published choice-free compact cutoff lemma, and the infinite coefficient sequence is defined by the explicit formula below. The consuming elliptic or Sobolev argument retains whatever choice principles its own suppliers declare.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Define $H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\}$ and $H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$ with their graph norms, and let $X$ be the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n	imes u=0$; this is an explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor boundary class. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies the full graph-class variational identity $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$. The eigen equation is $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ distributionally with the PEC trace, and for every explicitly chosen mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every initial displacement $q_0\in V$ and velocity $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with those initial coefficients. Its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$; finite modal sums converge respectively in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$. The finite-dimensional $\lambda=0$ sector is retained with $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. This speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter, not a physical constant or prerequisite. Let $N$ be the smooth unit normal extended constantly along the normal collar lines, and $\kappa=\operatorname{div}N$ on $\partial\Omega$. For every smooth PEC field $w$ the Gaffney identity is $\int_\Omega(|\operatorname{curl}w|^2+|\operatorname{div}w|^2-|
abla w|^2)=\int_{\partial\Omega}\kappa|w\cdot
u|^2dS$. For every $\delta>0$ there is $C_{\Omega,\delta}<\infty$ such that $\|Tw\|_{L^2(\partial\Omega)}^2\le\delta\|

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let
$A \subseteq X$ and let $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ be the subspace
([[def-subspace-topology-top]]). Then:

1. **Compactness read in the ambient space.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$
   ([[def-compact-space]]), that is $(A, \mathcal{T}_A)$ is a compact space, if
   and only if for every family $\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathcal{T}$ with
   $A \subseteq \bigcup \mathcal{U}$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   $U_0, \dots, U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ with $A \subseteq U_0 \cup \dots \cup U_n$,
   or else $A = \varnothing$.
2. **The same in indexed form.** $A$ is a compact subset of $X$ if and only if
   for every set $I$ and every family $(U_i)_{i \in I}$ of open subsets of $X$
   with $A \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in I} U_i$ there are $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and
   indices $i_0, \dots, i_n \in I$ with
   $A \subseteq U_{i_0} \cup \dots \cup U_{i_n}$, or else $A = \varnothing$.

Claim 2 is the form used by almost every later proof on this page, because a
cover is usually produced by a rule that attaches an open set to each point or to
each index, and a set of open sets forgets that rule. No choice principle is used
anywhere below; the one place a selection is made is over a finite index set, and
[[lem-finite-choice]] is a theorem of ZF.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, used through the cited Countable-Choice and
Dependent-Choice interfaces (completed-product Fubini, approximate identities,
the fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions), for
the countable selections of cutoffs and mollifier scales below, and through the
earlier ACL reconstruction lemma. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be
open, $n\ge1$, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
For an almost-everywhere class $u$ on $\Omega$ the following are equivalent:

1. $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$;
2. $u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and $u$ has one measurable ACL representative
   $u^*$ whose classical coordinate derivatives $\partial_i u^*$ exist almost
   everywhere, are measurable, and belong to $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

In that case $\partial_i u^*$ is a representative of $D_i u$ for every
$i$, that is, $D_i u=\partial_i u^*$ almost everywhere.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, there is only the zero class, its representative
$u^*=0$ is ACL, and every displayed assertion holds vacuously.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume countable choice, let $n\ge1$, and use Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^n$. Translation $\tau_hf(x)=f(x-h)$ is an isometry of complex $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$ and depends norm-continuously on $h$ for $p<\infty$.

For complex $K\in L^1$ and $f\in L^p$, the convolution
$$(K*f)(x)=\int K(y)f(x-y)\,dy$$
exists absolutely a.e., defines a measurable class independent of representatives, and satisfies $\|K*f\|_p\le\|K\|_1\|f\|_p$.

If $K_\varepsilon\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ satisfy
$$\int K_\varepsilon=1,\qquad M:=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\|K_\varepsilon\|_1<\infty,\qquad \int_{|y|\ge\delta}|K_\varepsilon(y)|\,dy\longrightarrow0\quad(\delta>0),$$
then $K_\varepsilon*f\to f$ in $L^p$ for $p<\infty$, and uniformly for $f\in C_0(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. For fixed $K\in L^1$, $K*f\in C_0$ when $f\in C_0$. These assertions allow complex and sign-changing kernels. In particular $K_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}K(x/\varepsilon)$ is such an approximate identity whenever $K\in L^1$ and $\int K=1$.

If $\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ has mass one, $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$, and $f$ is complex locally integrable, then $\rho_\varepsilon*f$ is smooth and
$$\partial^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*f)=(\partial^\alpha\rho_\varepsilon)*f.$$
A compactly supported input gives a compactly supported output. No general $L^\infty$ translation-continuity or approximate-identity convergence is asserted.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

The first-order case m = 1 is membership in X with the H^1 equivalence of [F1], and r = 1 is the base of the bootstrap in step 7.1; step 5.1 advances one tangential direction k at a time.

The boundary is exactly where the regularity is proved: step 3.1 flattens charts and separates the vanishing tangential traces from the free normal trace, step 6.1 recovers the missing normal derivatives, step 7.1 bootstraps at fixed total order, and step 8.1 yields the classical boundary identity partial_nu u_n + kappa u_n = 0.

For $l\in\mathbb N_0$ and $z>0$ set

$$h_l(z)=(-i)^{l+1}\frac{e^{iz}}{z}\sum_{j=0}^{l}\frac{i^j\,(l+j)!}{j!\,(l-j)!\,(2z)^j}.$$

Then $h_l$ is a complex-valued $C^2$ function of $z>0$ solving

$$h_l''(z)+\frac2z h_l'(z)+\Bigl[1-\frac{l(l+1)}{z^2}\Bigr]h_l(z)=0,$$

it never vanishes on $(0,\infty)$, and its Wronskian-type identity $\operatorname{Im}\bigl(\overline{h_l(z)}\,h_l'(z)\bigr)=z^{-2}$ holds. For $k>0$ and $R>0$ the spherical Dirichlet-to-Neumann coefficient

$$t_l=\frac{k\,h_l'(kR)}{h_l(kR)}$$

satisfies the exact bounds

$$\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-\frac1R,\qquad |\operatorname{Re}t_l|\le\frac{l+1}{R},\qquad 0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k .$$

These are exact identities and inequalities for the displayed explicit functions, not asymptotic formulas; the argument uses only elementary differentiation and a constant Wronskian, so no large-$l$ asymptotic input is required.
citations.use: The degree-zero outgoing radial function is $h_0(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$ and the DtN coefficients of the spherical Hankel lemma satisfy $-(l+1)/R\le\operatorname{Re}t_l\le-1/R$ and $0<\operatorname{Im}t_l\le k$, with $t_l=kh_l'(kR)/h_l(kR)$ ([[lem-em-outgoing-spherical-hankel-dtn-bounds]]).

citations.quote:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the complete variational, Sobolev-extension and compact-spectral suppliers. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded $C^\infty$ domain. Define $H(\operatorname{curl})=\{u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3):\operatorname{curl}u\in L^2\}$ and $H(\operatorname{div})=\{u\in L^2:\operatorname{div}u\in L^2\}$ with their graph norms, and let $X$ be the graph-norm closure in $H(\operatorname{curl})\cap H(\operatorname{div})$ of the smooth fields on the closure with $n\times u=0$; this is an explicit weak perfect-electric-conductor boundary class. Put $V=\{u\in X:\operatorname{div}u=0\}$ and $H=\overline{V}^{\,L^2}$. Then the curl form on $V$ has a complete orthonormal $L^2$ eigenbasis with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$ of finite multiplicity tending to infinity whenever $H$ is infinite dimensional, and the zero eigenspace is finite dimensional and must be retained when the topology allows it. Each eigenfield $u_j\in V$ satisfies the full graph-class variational identity $\int_\Omega\operatorname{curl}u_j\cdot\operatorname{curl}v=\lambda_j\int_\Omega u_j\cdot v$ for every $v\in X$. The eigen equation is $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}u_j=\lambda_ju_j$ distributionally with the PEC trace, and for every explicitly chosen mathematical speed $v_{\mathrm{wave}}>0$ and every initial displacement $q_0\in V$ and velocity $q_1\in H$, the associated second-order wave has coefficients $a_j''+v_{\mathrm{wave}}^2\lambda_ja_j=0$ with those initial coefficients. Its displacement lies in $C(\mathbb R;V)$ and its velocity in $C(\mathbb R;H)$; finite modal sums converge respectively in $C(K;V)$ and $C(K;H)$ on every compact time interval $K$. The finite-dimensional $\lambda=0$ sector is retained with $a_j(t)=a_j(0)+ta_j'(0)$. This speed is a positive abstract mathematical parameter, not a physical constant or prerequisite. No identification with every maximal tangential-trace realisation, and no lossy, open or non-smooth-domain spectral claim, is made.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.
