citations.quote:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The cylinder $S=\{x:x_1^2+x_2^2=a^2\}$ is closed, hence Borel. For each $(x_2,x_3)\in\mathbb R^2$, its section $S^{(x_2,x_3)}:=\{x_1\in\mathbb R:(x_1,x_2,x_3)\in S\}$ consists of at most the two values $\pm\sqrt{a^2-x_2^2}$ when $|x_2|\le a$, and is empty otherwise. Each section is $\lambda_1$-null by [F4]. Tonelli and product-measure agreement [F4] give $\lambda_3(S)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\lambda_1(S^{(x_2,x_3)})\,d\lambda_2=0$.

The bounded Borel function $g_0:=e_3\mathbf 1_{\{\rho<a\}}$ agrees with $g$ off the null set $S$ of step 1.1, so completeness [F5] makes $g$ Lebesgue measurable with the same almost-everywhere class as $g_0$; by [F5] this class is locally integrable. Hence $T_g:=T_{g_0}$ is a well-defined distribution by [F2], and for the tests of [F1] the componentwise pairings of [F3] read $\langle\operatorname{curl}T_g,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}g_0\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3$ and $\langle\operatorname{div}T_g,\varphi\rangle=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}g_0\cdot\nabla\varphi\,d\lambda_3$, where the componentwise sums against the vector tests are the ordinary finite sums of the stated integrals.

Choose $R>a$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cup\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset W:=\{ho<R,\ |x_3|<R\}$ and put $V:=\{ho<a,\ |x_3|<R\}$. Since $\operatorname{curl}\psi$ and $
abla\varphi$ are supported in $W$, and $g_0$ equals $e_3$ on $V$, equals $0$ on the open set $W\setminus\overline V$, and the remaining part $W\cap\partial V$ lies in the null set $S$ of step 1.1, the two integrals of step 2.1 reduce to integrals over $V$: $\int_{\mathbb R^3}g_0\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\int_V e_3\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^3}g_0\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\int_V e_3\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3$.

The field $F_0:=\varphi e_3$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$, hence on a neighborhood of $\overline V$, and by [F9] its divergence is $\operatorname{div}F_0=\partial_3\varphi=e_3\cdot
abla\varphi$. The divergence theorem [F7] on the presentation [F6] gives $\int_V e_3\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\partial V}\varphi\,e_3\cdot
u\,dS$. On the lateral face $
u=e_ho$ and $e_3\cdot e_ho=0$ by [F8]; on the two disc caps $x_3=\pm R$ the test $\varphi$ vanishes because $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset\{|x_3|<R\}$; hence $\int_V e_3\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=0$. With steps 2.1 and 3.1 this proves $\langle\operatorname{div}T_g,\varphiangle=0$ for every scalar test.

The field $G_0:=\psi\times e_3$ is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$, and by [F8] its coordinates are $G_0=(\psi_2,-\psi_1,0)$, so by [F9] $\operatorname{div}G_0=\partial_1\psi_2-\partial_2\psi_1=(\operatorname{curl}\psi)_3=e_3\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi$. The divergence theorem [F7] on the presentation [F6] gives $\int_V e_3\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\partial V}G_0\cdot\nu\,dS$. The disc caps carry $\psi=0$ by the support condition, while on the lateral face $\nu=e_\rho$ and $G_0\cdot e_\rho=(\psi\times e_3)\cdot e_\rho=\psi\cdot e_\varphi$ by [F8]; therefore $\int_V e_3\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\rho=a,\ |x_3|<R}e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$, and by [F10] the last integral equals $\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$ because $e_\varphi\cdot\psi$ is compactly supported and vanishes off the compact band $\{\rho=a,\ |x_3|\le R\}$. With steps 2.1 and 3.1 this is $\langle\operatorname{curl}T_g,\psi\rangle=\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$ for every vector test, which is the claimed identification $\operatorname{curl}T_g=e_\varphi\,\delta_S$.

The one-sided values of $g$ across $S$ are $g_+=0$ and $g_-=e_3$, so $g_+-g_-=-e_3$ and, by [F8], $e_\rho\times(g_+-g_-)=e_\rho\times(-e_3)=e_\varphi$ and $e_\rho\cdot(g_+-g_-)=e_\rho\cdot(-e_3)=0$, which is the stated equivalence. The two distributional identities of steps 4.1 and 4.2 involve only integrals of locally integrable functions against smooth tests, so no product of two distributions is formed anywhere; the only multiplication on $S$ is that of the compactly supported function $e_\varphi\cdot\psi$ with the surface measure of [F10]. Countable Choice is used in step 1.1 through the product-measure and finite-null-set suppliers [F4] and is inherited only through the cited measure, surface and distribution interfaces [F11]; no stronger choice principle occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes $a>0$ and the nonempty cylinder; no family or cover is required to be nonempty. A test of empty support has zero pairing by steps 2.1 and 4.2, and the definition makes no nonemptiness claim.

If the vector test or scalar test is zero, both sides of the two identities of step 4.2 and step 4.1 vanish; the regular distribution is linear in its integrand, and the pairings of step 2.1 vanish for the zero test.
There is no counting parameter: the construction uses the single radius $a>0$ and one pair of tests; the classification of faces in step 3.1 is finite and no index degenerates at one.

The Statement requires $a>0$; $a=0$ would make $S$ the axis and is excluded. The half cylinder $V$ of step 3.1 is nondegenerate for every $R>a$, and the arbitrary values of $g$ on the null set $S$ are immaterial by step 2.1.

Proof 3.1 chooses |x_3|<R containing the test supports. The caps at x_3=±R contribute zero; the lateral face rho=a supplies the curl source integral in 4.2. F6 explicitly splits lateral charts into four faces with surface-null seams and rims.

Countable Choice is assumed; Proof 1.1 uses Tonelli, Euclidean product-measure agreement and finite-null-set suppliers F4. Completeness F5 justifies arbitrary finite surface values in 2.1; the existing surface and distribution interfaces carry the same assumption. No stronger Choice is used.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is a conjunction of two distributional identities and an equivalence of one-sided values, not an if-and-only-if claim.
No converse direction is asserted: the lemma computes both pairings for every test and records the one-sided values, and it claims no characterization.

risk_review.notes: Independently read Statement, F1–F11 and all six proof steps. Tonelli applies to the Borel cylinder with finite x1 sections under AComega; completeness permits arbitrary finite surface values. Four injective quarter-cylinder charts, cap normals and surface-null seams meet the piecewise divergence theorem. Compact support removes caps, div(varphi e3)=partial3 varphi gives zero, and div(psi cross e3)=(curl psi)3 gives +e_phi surface measure. Checked a>0, zero/empty tests, null-set representatives and both jump components; no physics premise or distribution product. Reader corrections accepted; supplementary bibliographic locators have not yet been independently checked.

citations.quote:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with $n\ge1$. A complex-valued function is smooth if its real and imaginary parts are $C^k$ for every finite $k$, in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Coordinate derivatives act on these two parts separately. We write $\partial^\alpha$ for the multi-index convention there, and $\partial^0\varphi=\varphi$.

The **test-function space** is $\mathcal D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb C)$: its members are smooth functions whose support, the closure in $\Omega$ of their nonzero set, is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Equivalently, the zero extension to $\mathbb R^n$ is smooth with compact support contained in $\Omega$: compactness gives a neighborhood of every boundary point disjoint from the support, where that extension vanishes. Functions are actual functions, not equivalence classes.

Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make this a complex vector space; the support of a sum lies in the union of the two compact supports. The zero function has empty support. If $\Omega=\varnothing$ there is just the empty function, which is the zero vector. The topology is specified in subsequent definitions. Distribution pairings throughout this page are complex bilinear, with no conjugation on test functions. One may restrict all constructions to real scalars.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, write $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ when $f:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_K|f|<\infty$ for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. This extends [[def-locally-integrable-function-on-r-n]]: equivalently, require integrability on every ball whose closure is a compact subset of $\Omega$. Such balls finitely cover each compact $K$, and conversely their closures are compact; on all of $\mathbb R^n$, any ball lies in a larger compact closed ball.

For a test $\varphi$ as in [[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], define the **regular functional**

$$\langle u_f,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega f(x)\varphi(x)\,dx.$$

This is well-defined since $|\int f\varphi|\le\sup_K|\varphi|\int_K|f|$ for $K=\operatorname{supp}\varphi$. It is complex-linear in $f$ and in $\varphi$ and depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $f$. For an empty support the integral is zero. The subsequent embedding theorem establishes continuity, so that this is a distribution, and injectivity modulo almost-everywhere equality. That theorem states the Countable Choice cost of its injectivity proof; no choice is needed to define the displayed pairing.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Every at most countable subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-countable]]) is Lebesgue measurable with

$$\lambda_n(E) \;=\; 0,$$

so $E$ is a $\lambda_n$-null set ([[def-measure-null-set-and-almost-everywhere]]).
In particular every singleton is null, and on the real line the set
$\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ of rational reals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) satisfies
$\lambda_1(\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}) = 0$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]), so
[[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]] makes
$\mathcal L(\mathbb R^n)$ a sigma-algebra. Let $n,m\in\mathbb N$ with
$n,m \ge 1$.

- A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is **Borel measurable** when
  it is measurable as a map

  $$f : (\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n)) \to (\mathbb{R}^m,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m))$$

  in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

- A function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is **Lebesgue measurable** when
  it is measurable as a map

  $$f : (\mathbb{R}^n,\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)) \to (\mathbb{R}^m,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^m)),$$

  where $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is the Lebesgue sigma-algebra of
  [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]].

When $m=1$, these are the corresponding notions for real-valued functions.

derivations.claim: The axis $Z=\{(0,0,x_3):x_3\in\mathbb R\}$ is closed, hence Borel. By [F3] in the product $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R$, $\lambda_3(Z)=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda_2(\{(0,0)\})\,dx_3=0$, because the singleton in $\mathbb R^2$ is null by [F5].

On $\mathbb R^3\setminus Z$ the components of $f$ are quotients of polynomials with nonvanishing denominator $x_1^2+x_2^2$, so by [F6] the partial derivatives exist and satisfy $\partial_1f_1=\frac{2x_1x_2}{\rho^4}$, $\partial_2f_2=-\frac{2x_1x_2}{\rho^4}$, $\partial_1f_2=\frac{x_2^2-x_1^2}{\rho^4}$, $\partial_2f_1=\frac{x_2^2-x_1^2}{\rho^4}$ and $\partial_3f=0$. Summing by [F7] gives $\operatorname{div}f=\partial_1f_1+\partial_2f_2=0$, and the curl coordinates are $\partial_1f_2-\partial_2f_1=0$, $\partial_3f_1-\partial_1f_3=0$ and $\partial_2f_3-\partial_3f_2=0$; hence $\operatorname{div}f=\operatorname{curl}f=0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\setminus Z$.

Fix $r>0$ and a height $h\in\mathbb R$, and let $\gamma(t)=(r\cos t,r\sin t,h)$, $t\in[0,2\pi]$, a closed $C^1$ path whose velocity is $\gamma'(t)=r\,e_\varphi(\gamma(t))$ by [F8]. On the trace, $f(\gamma(t))=r^{-1}e_\varphi(\gamma(t))$, so the integrand of the vector line integral of [F12] is the constant $f(\gamma(t))\cdot\gamma'(t)=r^{-1}\cdot r=1$, and the circulation is $\int_0^{2\pi}1\,dt=2\pi$.

Let $U=\mathbb R^3\setminus Z$ and define $\widetilde f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $\widetilde f=f$ on $U$ and $\widetilde f=0$ on $Z$. For every open $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, continuity of $f$ on $U$ makes $f^{-1}(O)$ open in $U$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$ because $U$ is open. The inverse image $\widetilde f^{-1}(O)$ is $f^{-1}(O)$ if $0\notin O$, and $f^{-1}(O)\cup Z$ if $0\in O$; both are Borel, since $Z$ is closed. The class $\mathcal C=\{B\subseteq\mathbb R^3:\widetilde f^{-1}(B)\text{ is Borel}\}$ is a sigma-algebra: inverse images preserve complements and countable unions. It contains every open set, hence every Borel set by [F5]. Thus $\widetilde f$ is Borel measurable without applying the cited full-space continuity result to $f$. For its local integrability, let $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ be compact and choose $R>0$, $H>0$ with $K\subset\{|x_3|\le H,\ \rho\le R\}$. By Tonelli [F3] and the polar formula [F4] in dimension two, applied to the nonnegative Borel function $u(x)=\rho^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\{|x_3|\le H,\ \rho\le R\}}(x)$ off $Z$, with $u=0$ on $Z$ (the same open-inverse-image argument proves measurability of $\rho^{-1}$ extended by zero, and restriction to this closed cylinder preserves it), $\int_{\mathbb R^3}u\,d\lambda_3=\int_{-H}^{H}\left(\int_{\rho\le R}\rho^{-1}\,d\lambda_2\right)dx_3=\int_{-H}^{H}R\,\sigma(S^1)\,dx_3=2HR\,\sigma(S^1)$, and this is finite because $\sigma$ is a finite measure [F4]. Since $|\widetilde f|=\rho^{-1}$ off $Z$ and $Z$ is null by step 1.1, $\mathbf 1_K|\widetilde f|\le u$ off a null set, so $\int_K|\widetilde f|\,d\lambda_3<+\infty$. Hence $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$ and $T_f$ is a well-defined distribution by [F1], [F2].

The regular-distribution pairings of [F1] and [F2] give $\langle\operatorname{curl}T_f,\psiangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3$ and $\langle\operatorname{div}T_f,\varphiangle=-\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3$, the integrands being dominated by $\|\operatorname{curl}\psi\|_\inftyho^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\operatorname{supp}\psi}$ and $\|
abla\varphi\|_\inftyho^{-1}\mathbf 1_{\operatorname{supp}\varphi}$, which are integrable by step 2.1. Fix $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cup\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset\{ho<R,\ |x_3|<R\}$ and put $V_\varepsilon:=\{\varepsilon<ho<R,\ |x_3|<R\}$ for $0<\varepsilon<R$. The functions $\mathbf 1_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi$ are dominated by $|f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi|$ and converge pointwise off the null axis $Z$ of step 1.1 to $f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi$; by [F11], $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\lim_{\varepsilon	o0}\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3$, and the same argument gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\lim_{\varepsilon	o0}\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot

On the neighborhood $\{\rho>\varepsilon/2\}$ of the compact closure $\overline{V_\varepsilon}$ the field $\psi\times f$ is $C^1$, since $f$ is smooth there, and by [F7] its divergence is $\operatorname{div}(\psi\times f)=f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi-\psi\cdot\operatorname{curl}f$; here $\operatorname{curl}f=0$ on $V_\varepsilon$ by step 1.2. Applying the divergence theorem [F9] on $V_\varepsilon$ gives $\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\partial V_\varepsilon}(\psi\times f)\cdot\nu\,dS$. On the same neighborhood the field $\varphi f$ is $C^1$, and $\operatorname{div}(\varphi f)=f\cdot
abla\varphi+\varphi\operatorname{div}f$ by [F7]; here $\operatorname{div}f=0$ on $V_\varepsilon$ by step 1.2. The divergence theorem [F9] gives $\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\int_{\partial V_\varepsilon}\varphi\,f\cdot
u\,dS$. On both cylinder faces $f\cdot
u=0$ because $f\perp e_ho$, and on the two cap annuli $\varphi=0$ because $\operatorname{supp}\varphi\subset\{|x_3|<R\}$; hence $\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=0$ for every $\varepsilon$.

With step 4.2, the identity $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=\lim_{\varepsilon	o0}\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3$ of step 3.1 gives $\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot
abla\varphi\,d\lambda_3=0$, and therefore $\langle\operatorname{div}T_f,\varphiangle=0$ for every scalar test $\varphi$ by step 3.1.

The double integral of step 4.1 has the limit $\int_0^{2\pi}\int_{-R}^{R}\psi_3(0,0,z)\,dz\,d\theta=2\pi\,A(\psi)$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. Indeed, $\psi_3$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^3$, hence uniformly continuous on the compact set $\{x:\rho\le R,\ |x_3|\le R\}$ by [F11], so for $\eta>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with $|\psi_3(\varepsilon\cos\theta,\varepsilon\sin\theta,z)-\psi_3(0,0,z)|\le\eta$ whenever $0<\varepsilon<\delta$ and $(\theta,z)\in[0,2\pi]\times[-R,R]$; dominated convergence [F11] on the finite-measure rectangle, or equivalently the estimate with the constant majorant $\eta$, gives convergence of the double integrals; the limit integrand does not depend on $\theta$, and finite linearity [F11] gives the iterated integral $\left(\int_0^{2\pi}1\,d\theta\right)\left(\int_{-R}^{R}\psi_3(0,0,z)\,dz\right)=2\pi\,A(\psi)$.

Combining steps 3.1, 4.1 and 5.2, $\langle\operatorname{curl}T_f,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb R^3}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\int_{V_\varepsilon}f\cdot\operatorname{curl}\psi\,d\lambda_3=\lim_{\varepsilon\to0}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_{-R}^{R}\psi_3(\varepsilon\cos\theta,\varepsilon\sin\theta,z)\,dz\,d\theta=2\pi\,A(\psi)$ for every vector test $\psi$, which is the claimed identification $\operatorname{curl}T_f=2\pi\,e_3\,\delta_Z$.

Steps 5.1 and 6.1 prove the two distributional identities of (c), step 1.2 proves the pointwise vanishing (b), and step 1.3 proves the circulation (d); step 2.1 is (a). Every pairing above is an integral of a locally integrable function against a smooth test, so no product of two distributions is formed. Countable Choice is used only through the measure and distribution interfaces [F13], namely Tonelli, polar coordinates, the nullity of countable sets and the regular-distribution embedding; no stronger choice principle occurs.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement fixes the field on the punctured space and requires no nonempty family; a test of empty support has vanishing pairings by the conventions of step 3.1, and the local-integrability claim of step 2.1 holds vacuously on the empty compact set.

For the zero field ($I=0$ in the later use) all pairings vanish by steps 3.1, 5.1 and 6.1; the divergence pairing of step 5.1 is zero identically, and the circulation of step 1.3 becomes $0$ only if the integrand is changed, so the asserted value $2\pi$ is stated for the fixed field $f$.
There is no counting parameter: one axis, one field and one pair of tests are fixed; the circle averages of step 5.2 involve a single compact interval and no degenerate index.

The circles of step 1.3 require $r>0$; the origin of the $(x_1,x_2)$-plane and the axis are excluded from the field domain and are Lebesgue null by step 1.1. The excision radius $\varepsilon$ in step 3.1 is strictly positive, and the limit $\varepsilon\to0$ is an improper limit, not a value at the axis.

The integration intervals $[-R,R]$ of steps 3.1 and 5.2 have endpoints carrying finitely many points in the average, so their values do not affect the integrals; the support condition of step 3.1 makes the faces at $\rho=R$ and $|x_3|=R$ contribute zero.

Countable Choice is assumed and used only through Tonelli, the polar formula, the nullity of countable sets and the distribution embedding cited in steps 1.1, 1.2, 2.1 and 7.1; no further selection occurs.

boundaries.reason: The Statement is a conjunction of computations (a)-(d), not an equivalence with a forward implication.
No converse is claimed: the lemma does not assert that a distribution with curl $2\pi e_3\delta_Z$ and vanishing divergence must equal $T_f$.

Annular charts and outward inner normal -e_rho give +psi3/epsilon, hence curl=+2pi e3 delta_Z; divergence boundary terms vanish. Uniform continuity justifies the shrinking-cylinder limit; finite L1 linearity handles the signed factorization. Checked r>0, arbitrary height, zero tests and reversal. citations.quote: Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. With $\omega_{n-1}=|S^{n-1}|>0$ in the published chart/polar convention, set $\Phi(x)=|x|^{2-n}/((n-2)\omega_{n-1})$ for $n\ge3$ and $\Phi(x)=-(2\pi)^{-1}\log|x|$ for $n=2$, $x\ne0$. Extend it as a locally integrable function at the pole. The one-dimensional analogue is $-\tfrac12|x|$; the subsequent $n\ge2$ Green theory does not silently include it.

Assume Countable Choice and $n\ge2$. For a measurable compactly supported
$f$, define
$$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\Phi(x-y)f(y)\,dy$$
at each $x$ where the integral is absolutely finite. Whenever this integral
is finite almost everywhere, $Nf$ also denotes its almost-everywhere class.
The following items establish everywhere convergence for bounded compact data
and almost-everywhere convergence for compact $L^1$ data; the definition itself
makes no unconditional convergence claim.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]], a finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation of a nonempty bounded open $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, consists of compact faces $S_1,\ldots,S_q$ covering its boundary, each a compact Borel subset of a regular $C^1$ hypersurface patch, and a compact edge set $E\subset\partial\Omega$. Require $S_j\cap E$ to have surface measure zero in each face, using [[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]]. E contains the boundaries of the faces relative to their patches and every overlap $S_i\cap S_j$, i different from j. At every point outside E the domain boundary is locally a single $C^1$ graph with Omega on one side. Each face carries this actual outward unit normal off E. Values assigned to the normal on E do not affect its integral.

For a specified finite gluing also list the open pieces with disjoint interiors, the shared faces, and their opposite outward normals. Require the pieces to cover the final domain up to their boundary faces, and the exposed faces to give its specified presentation. Internal faces are counted twice before cancellation, once from each side. The phrase piecewise smooth by itself supplies none of this data.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. If Omega has the specified finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, then $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F=\sum_j\int_{S_j}F\cdot\nu_j\,dS$, with faces counted once off E. All integrals are finite. In a specified finite gluing, the two fluxes on every shared face cancel.

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and $n\ge2$. The chart surface measure on $S^{n-1}$ equals the polar measure $\sigma$. Orthogonal transformations preserve it. The map $\omega\mapsto a+R\omega$, $R>0$, multiplies surface measure by $R^{n-1}$, and $|S^{n-1}|=n|B_1|$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.

derivations.claim: Since each $f_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, [F2] gives $A_i=N(f_i)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $D^\alpha A_i=N(D^\alpha f_i)$ for every multi-index $\alpha$; in particular $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ by [F3], and $\partial_iA_i=N(\partial_if_i)$ for each $i$. Summing over $i$ and using finite additivity of the integral [F8], $\operatorname{div}A=\sum_i\partial_iA_i=N(\sum_i\partial_if_i)=N(\operatorname{div}f)$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$, which is the first displayed identity; its integral is absolutely convergent because $|\operatorname{div}f|\le\|\operatorname{div}f\|_\infty$ is bounded and compactly supported and $\int_{B_R(x)}|x-y|^{-1}d\lambda_3<+\infty$ by [F7].

Fix $x\in\mathbb R^3$ and $j,k\in\{1,2,3\}$, let $\Phi(z)=1/(4\pi|z|)$, and choose $R>0$ with $\operatorname{supp}f\subset B_R(x)$. For $0<\varepsilon<R$ let $\Omega_\varepsilon:=B_R(x)\setminus\overline{B_\varepsilon(x)}$, presented as in [F5]. On a neighborhood of the compact closure the scalar product $y\mapsto f_k(y)\Phi(x-y)$ is $C^1$, and by [F4] its partial derivative is $\partial_{y_j}(f_k\Phi(x-y))=(\partial_jf_k)(y)\Phi(x-y)+f_k(y)\partial_{y_j}\Phi(x-y)$. Applying the divergence theorem [F5] to the field $f_k\Phi(x-\cdot)e_j$ on $\Omega_\varepsilon$ gives $\int_{\Omega_\varepsilon}(\partial_jf_k)\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\partial B_R(x)}f_k\Phi(x-y)(\nu_R)_j\,dS+\int_{\partial B_\varepsilon(x)}f_k\Phi(x-y)(\nu_\varepsilon)_j\,dS-\int_{\Omega_\varepsilon}f_k(y)\partial_{y_j}\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$. The outer sphere contributes $0$ because $f=0$ there; the inner sphere term is bounded in absolute value, by [F8] and the bound $|\Phi|=1/(4\pi|y-x|)=1/(4\pi\varepsilon)$ there, by $\|f_k\|_\infty\frac1{4\pi\varepsilon}\,|\partial B_\varepsilon(x)|=\|f_k\|_\infty\frac{|S^2|}{4\pi}\varepsilon\to0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ by [F6].

Let $\varepsilon\to0$ in the identity of step 1.2. The shell integrands $(\partial_jf_k)\Phi(x-y)\mathbf 1_{\Omega_\varepsilon}$ are dominated on $B_R(x)$ by $\|\partial_jf_k\|_\infty|\Phi|$, and the shell integrands $f_k\partial_{y_j}\Phi(x-y)\mathbf 1_{\Omega_\varepsilon}$ by $\|f_k\|_\infty|\partial_{y_j}\Phi|\le\|f_k\|_\infty\frac{1}{4\pi}|x-y|^{-2}$; both majorants are integrable on $B_R(x)$ by [F7], and both families converge pointwise off the null singleton $\{x\}$ to the corresponding unrestricted integrands. Dominated convergence [F9] therefore gives $\int_{B_R(x)}(\partial_jf_k)\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)=-\int_{B_R(x)}f_k(y)\partial_{y_j}\Phi(x-y)\,d\lambda_3(y)$; the left side is $N(\partial_jf_k)(x)=\partial_jA_k(x)$ by step 1.1, and since $\partial_{y_j}\Phi(x-y)=\frac{x_j-y_j}{4\pi|x-y|^3}$ for $y\ne x$, this reads $\partial_jA_k(x)=-\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f_k(y)(x_j-y_j)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy$, the integral being absolutely convergent because $|f_k(y)(x_j-y_j)|\le\|f_k\|_\infty|x-y|$ on $B_R(x)$ and $\int_{B_R(x)}|x-y|^{-2}d\lambda_3<+\infty$ by [F7].

Summing the identity of step 2.1 with the alternating symbol, $(\operatorname{curl}A)_i=\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_jA_k=-\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\varepsilon_{ijk}f_k(y)(x_j-y_j)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{(f(y)\times(x-y))_i}{|x-y|^3}\,dy$ by the component identity of [F10] and finite linearity of the integral [F8]; as this holds for each $i$, $\operatorname{curl}A(x)=\frac1{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy$, and the integral is absolutely convergent because $|f(y)\times(x-y)|\le\|f\|_\infty|x-y|$ and $\int_{B_R(x)}|x-y|^{-2}<+\infty$ by [F7]. With step 1.1 this proves both displayed identities at the arbitrary point $x$; the point was allowed to lie in $\operatorname{supp}f$, since the excision argument only removed a ball around it and used the bound on the differentiated kernel, so no smoothness of the kernel at the pole is assumed. Countable Choice is used only through the polar and surface-measure interfaces [F11] and the stated choice assumption of the smooth-newtonian supplier, and no stronger principle occurs.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$

Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.
