The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\varepsilon_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ and let $$Nf(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{f(y)}{4\pi|x-y|}\,dy .$$ Then $Nf\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, $-\Delta Nf=f$ pointwise, and for every multi-index $\alpha$ the spatial derivative satisfies $D^\alpha Nf=N(D^\alpha f)$. In particular, for smooth compactly supported $\rho$ the field $E=-\varepsilon_0^{-1}\nabla N\rho$ is smooth. The statement is about the explicit integral transform of compactly supported smooth data and does not assume smoothness of the kernel at the pole; the distributional identity $-\Delta Nf=f$ is the one supplied by the Newtonian-potential theorem ([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]]), upgraded here from a distributional to a pointwise identity for smooth data.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

derivations.claim: For each $i$ the datum $J_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, so [F1] gives $A_i=\mu_0N(J_i)\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$, the derivative identity $D^\alpha A_i=\mu_0N(D^\alpha J_i)$ for every multi-index $\alpha$, and $-\Delta A_i=\mu_0J_i$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$; since all components are smooth, $A\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ by [F2], and $-\Delta A=\mu_0J$ holds pointwise componentwise. This is (a).

Taking $\alpha=e_i$ in the derivative identity of step 1.1 and summing, $\operatorname{div}A=\sum_i\partial_iA_i=\mu_0\sum_iN(\partial_iJ_i)$; $N$ is componentwise linear by finite additivity of the integral over the compactly supported data, so this equals $\mu_0N(\sum_i\partial_iJ_i)=\mu_0N(\operatorname{div}J)$ pointwise, and $\operatorname{div}J=0$ gives $\operatorname{div}A=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. This is (b), and the hypothesis $\operatorname{div}J=0$ is used in no other step.

Since $A$ is $C^\infty$, the field $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$ is $C^\infty$ by [F2]. Then $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$ by [F3], and $\operatorname{curl}B=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}A=\nabla(\operatorname{div}A)-\Delta A$ by [F4]; substituting step 2.1 and step 1.1 gives $\operatorname{curl}B=0-(-\mu_0J)=\mu_0J$. Hence the magnetostatic pair of [F5] holds pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$.

Read step 3.1 inside the framework: [F5] identifies the pair $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ with the time-independent reduction of the adopted equations, and the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]](a) then holds for the fields $E:=0$, $\rho:=0$ on $\Omega\times I$ and the time-independent $B,J$ restricted to $\Omega\times I$: indeed $\operatorname{div}E=0=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ and $\partial_tB=0$ give $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and $\partial_tE=0$ with $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ gives $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$. Clauses (a)-(d) are steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1 together with the scope statement: $A$ is a vector potential for $B$ in the Coulomb gauge, the gauge condition $\operatorname{div}A=0$ is a construction choice, and no uniqueness of $A$, no uniqueness of $B$ and no statement for the ideal noncompact models of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c) is claimed. Countable Choice is used only through the Newtonian-potential supplier [F1] and the measure interfaces it inherits [F6]; no stronger choice principle occurs, and the vector identities of [F3], [F4] are choice-free.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length with period $L>0$: $\gamma(s+L)=\gamma(s)$ and $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ for every $s$, and the induced map $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is injective. Let $I\in\mathbb R$ and $\mu_0>0$, and for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)=:\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,$$

Here its scalar component distributions are $j_k(\varphi):=I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$ for scalar tests $\varphi$, $k=1,2,3$; for a scalar test the notation $j(\varphi)$ below denotes the vector $(j_1(\varphi),j_2(\varphi),j_3(\varphi))$. In the vector-test formula the pairing is the complex-bilinear Euclidean pairing (no conjugation) of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; restricted to real-valued $\psi$ this is the stated real functional. Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). For any family $(\eta_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of nonnegative smooth radial kernels with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta_\varepsilon=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ — including the rescalings $\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\varepsilon)$ of a chosen nonnegative unit-mass radial kernel supported in $\overline B_1(0)$ — the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon$ defined by the distribution pairing $j_\varepsilon(x):=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\,ds$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on every nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to

$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$$

([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). In addition, assigning arbitrary finite values on the curve gives a representative $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, smooth off $\gamma$, with $\operatorname{div}T_B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\mu_0j$ globally; the first identity is tested on scalar $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and the second on vector $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ for some $a>0$, then $|B(x)|\le\mu_0|I|L/\bigl(4\pi(|x|-a)^2\bigr)$ for $|x|>a$, so $B$ decays at infinity. For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. In the named inertial laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following additional classical physical idealization: a loop, infinite straight line or infinite cylindrical sheet source defined by [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1)-(c3), with zero charge density, is modeled by a time-independent $B$ satisfying exactly the admissibility predicate (c4), together with $E=0$ and $\rho=0$. Thus $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold distributionally on $\mathbb R^3$, with the stated off-source regularity, symmetry and decay; the electrostatic and temporal Maxwell identities are zero. This physical adoption extends to these explicitly declared source types only. It is separate from the earlier $L^1$-source and point/compact-sheet postulates, which do not include these line and noncompact sheet sources. No existence, uniqueness, finite self-energy, force product, self-force, apparatus accuracy, matter dynamics or empirical certainty is asserted.

Let the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal models be those of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. Its value is independent of the chosen larger bounding rectangle by finite rectangular subdivision and vanishing of the integrand off its support; the support itself need not be Jordan measurable. Thus this is a Riemann integral of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is absolutely finite because $J$ is bounded with compact support.

**(b) [Declared ideal thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $I\in\mathbb R$, the **magnetic moment** of the ideal loop current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1) is
$$m:=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds,$$
again a componentwise Riemann integral over the compact interval $[0,L]$ of continuous functions; for the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ traversed in the positive orientation this is $m=I\pi a^2e_3$.

**(c) [Status and scope].** In both clauses $m$ is a source moment of the declared current model: it is not a rest mass, not an intrinsic spin and not an observed quantity. The definition asserts no far-field property of $m$ (that is the content of [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]] under its hypotheses), no agreement between the two clauses in a common limit, and no moment for currents outside the two classes; no higher multipole is defined here. The finite Riemann moment definitions and circular-loop evaluation themselves are choice-free; no distribution-embedding or surface-measure theorem is used to compute these moments.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$ be any scalar parameter and let $J\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ and $\operatorname{supp}J\subset B_a(0)$, $a>0$, and put $m=\tfrac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). Then for $r=|x|\ge2a$ the vector potential and magnetic field $$A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad B=\operatorname{curl}A,$$ satisfy, uniformly in $n=x/r$, $$A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^3}\Bigr),\qquad B=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O\!\Bigl(\frac{\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1}{r^4}\Bigr).$$ The constants in the $O$ terms are absolute (the second follows by differentiating the first, not by differentiating an unspecified remainder), and $\|J\|_1=\int|J|$.

derivations.claim: The hypotheses of [F3] are exactly the hypotheses stated here for $J$ (smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free, contained in $B_a(0)$), and the objects of [F3] are the objects of this theorem: $A=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int J(y)|x-y|^{-1}dy$ componentwise and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ by [F1]. The moment of [F2] agrees with the Lebesgue moment of [F3]: each component $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ is smooth and compactly supported, hence bounded Borel and Riemann integrable on any nondegenerate closed rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$; by [F4] its Riemann integral over $Q$ equals its Lebesgue integral over $Q$, and since the integrand vanishes off $\operatorname{supp}J\subset Q$ this equals the Lebesgue integral over $\mathbb R^3$. Hence $\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy$ is the same vector in both items.

Substituting the identifications of step 1.1 into the conclusion of [F3] gives, for $r=|x|\ge2a$ and uniformly in the unit vector $n=x/r$, the displayed estimates $A(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{m\times x}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1r^{-3})$ and $B(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{3n(m\cdot n)-m}{r^3}+O(\mu_0a^2\|J\|_1r^{-4})$ for the framework's $A$ and $B$, with the lemma's uniformity and absolute constants and with $\|J\|_1=\int_{\mathbb R^3}|J|\,d\lambda_3$ as in the Statement.

The estimates of step 2.1 are the content of the Statement; no assertion is made for $r<2a$ or at the support, no higher multipole is defined, and the leading dipole term is not claimed to be exact. Countable Choice is used only through the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison [F4] and the measure and Newtonian interfaces [F5] of the cited suppliers; no stronger choice principle occurs.

Countable Choice is assumed and used only through the Riemann-Lebesgue comparison of step 1.1 and the measure and Newtonian interfaces of the cited suppliers, as recorded in step 3.1.

citations.quote:
Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

Let the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal models be those of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. Its value is independent of the chosen larger bounding rectangle by finite rectangular subdivision and vanishing of the integrand off its support; the support itself need not be Jordan measurable. Thus this is a Riemann integral of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is absolutely finite because $J$ is bounded with compact support.

**(b) [Declared ideal thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $I\in\mathbb R$, the **magnetic moment** of the ideal loop current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1) is
$$m:=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds,$$
again a componentwise Riemann integral over the compact interval $[0,L]$ of continuous functions; for the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ traversed in the positive orientation this is $m=I\pi a^2e_3$.

**(c) [Status and scope].** In both clauses $m$ is a source moment of the declared current model: it is not a rest mass, not an intrinsic spin and not an observed quantity. The definition asserts no far-field property of $m$ (that is the content of [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]] under its hypotheses), no agreement between the two clauses in a common limit, and no moment for currents outside the two classes; no higher multipole is defined here. The finite Riemann moment definitions and circular-loop evaluation themselves are choice-free; no distribution-embedding or surface-measure theorem is used to compute these moments.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ be a compact smooth current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$, let $A$ be the vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ its magnetostatic field, with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Biot-Savart integral represents the field,
$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy .$$
Moreover the same formula holds in the declared thin-loop limit, constructed in the all-space laboratory $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$: if $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length ($|\gamma'|\equiv1$), $I\in\mathbb R$, and $j_\varepsilon=j*\eta_\varepsilon$ are the mollified divergence-free compact currents of [[lem-em-thin-current-limit]] associated with the tangent line current of $\gamma$, then their fields (given by the displayed formula with $J:=j_\varepsilon$) converge, with every derivative uniformly on every compact $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to
$$B_\gamma(x)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds,$$
a locally integrable global distributional field with $\operatorname{div}B_\gamma=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B_\gamma=\mu_0J_\gamma$, smoothness off the curve and decay at spatial infinity, hence the admitted field of the declared ideal thin loop under [[post-em-ideal-magnetostatic-models]]. Its almost-everywhere representative on $\mathbb R^3$ is supplied by [[lem-em-thin-current-limit]], independently of the away-from-curve convergence. Nothing is asserted on the wire, about line self-energy, about the infinite-wire or sheet models, or for currents outside the compact smooth class and its declared thin-loop limit.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

For $a\in\Omega$, the **Dirac distribution at $a$** is the complex-linear functional $\delta_a(\varphi)=\varphi(a)$ on $\mathcal D(\Omega)$, with the bilinear convention of [[def-distribution]]. It is continuous: the seminorm $q(\varphi)=|\varphi(a)|$ restricts on each $\mathcal D_K$ to a seminorm bounded by $p_0$ (and is zero if $a\notin K$), so it is one of the admissible seminorms defining the test topology.

Its derivatives are those of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\partial^\alpha\delta_a,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha\varphi(a).$$
They are distributions by that definition; on each fixed-support stage the absolute value is at most $p_{|\alpha|}(\varphi)$. If $a\notin K$ all derivatives of the test vanish at $a$, so the bound has zero left side. For $\alpha=0$ this is $\delta_a$; a first derivative evaluates the negative first derivative of the test. No conjugation and no choice are involved. On the empty open set there is no permitted point $a$, rather than a new Dirac distribution. The sharp order of these distributions requires a test witness and is proved in the assigned example later.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt as physical postulates of this framework, on the spacetime and particle
model of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]] and
[[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] and on the special-relativity particle
model [[post-sr-massive-particle-dynamics]]:

(i) [Test charge in a prescribed external field] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ be a
constant charge parameter ([[def-em-sources]]), $m>0$ an externally supplied
rest mass, $x:J\to A$ a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline with
four-velocity $U$, and let $F$ be a prescribed field of
[[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph
of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle. Adopt the equation of
motion

$$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),$$

where, at each original parameter $s\in J$, $\Phi=\Phi_{x(s)}$ is the
raised-index operator of the field at $x(s)$, defined by
$\eta(\Phi_{x(s)}(u),w)=F(x(s))(w,u)$
([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]); equivalently
$m\,dU^\mu/d\tau=q\,F^{\mu\nu}U_\nu$. Here $dU/d\tau$ is the derivative of $U$
with respect to its proper-time function $\tau(s)$: explicitly
$dU/d\tau=U'(s)/\tau'(s)$, with
$\tau'(s)=c^{-1}\sqrt{-\eta(x'(s),x'(s))}>0$. It is the four-acceleration of the worldline
([[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]). The particle's own field
is excluded from $F$: this is the external-field coupling, and it defines no
self-force.

(ii) [Continuum matter coupling] For a smooth source $(\rho,J)$ of
[[def-em-sources]] interacting with the field through an explicitly stated
matter model to which this coupling applies, adopt the force density
$\rho E+J\times B$ (unit N m$^{-3}$) and the power density $J\cdot E$ (unit
W m$^{-3}$) as the electromagnetic source terms of that matter model, with the
spatial cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; they describe the local
interaction of the field with matter and are not a property of a prescribed
current alone.

(iii) [Scope] The rest mass and the charge are inputs; $m$ is not derived within
electromagnetism. The coupling is adopted for constant $q$ and $m>0$; no
magnetic-monopole coupling, no radiation reaction and no self-force are
included. In particular the nonrelativistic coordinate statement
$mr''=q(E+r'\times B)$ is not adopted as exact: the adopted statement is the
covariant one of clause (i), and any low-speed statement requires its own
approximation hypotheses and error bounds.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be

(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: Under the adopted coupling (W) the total force and torque of the parametrized wire are the integrals of the Statement: at arc-length parameter $s$ the element $d\gamma=\gamma'(s)ds$ carries current $I$, so $dF=I\gamma'(s)\times B(\gamma(s))ds$ and $dN=\gamma(s)\times dF$. The integrands are compositions and products of continuous maps on the compact interval $[0,L]$, hence continuous and Riemann integrable, so the componentwise integrals of [F1] are finite. This is (a).

Let $B$ be constant on a neighbourhood of the closed curve. Then $F=I\left(\int_0^L\gamma'(s)ds\right)\times B=I(\gamma(L)-\gamma(0))\times B=0$. For the torque, $F$'s definition and [F2] give $\gamma\times(\gamma'\times B)=(\gamma\cdot B)\gamma'-(\gamma\cdot\gamma')B$, so with the matrix $M_{jl}:=\int_0^L\gamma_j\gamma'_l\,ds$ one has $N=I\int_0^L(\gamma\cdot B)\gamma'\,ds-I\left(\int_0^L\gamma\cdot\gamma'\,ds\right)B=I\,B_jM_{jl}e_l$. The scalar $\gamma\cdot\gamma'=\frac12\frac{d}{ds}|\gamma|^2$ integrates to $0$ over the closed curve, and integrating $\frac{d}{ds}(\gamma_j\gamma_l)$ over the closed curve gives $M_{jl}+M_{lj}=0$, so $M$ is antisymmetric. For antisymmetric $M$, the moment $m_p=\frac I2\varepsilon_{pab}M_{ab}$ satisfies $I M_{jl}=\varepsilon_{jlp}m_p$ because $\varepsilon_{abp}\varepsilon_{pcd}=\delta_{ac}\delta_{bd}-\delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}$ gives $\varepsilon_{abp}m_p=\frac I2(M_{ab}-M_{ba})=IM_{ab}$. Substituting, $N=\varepsilon_{jlp}m_pB_j e_l=m\times B$ by the cyclic identity of the alternating symbol, and this is (b).

Let $J_{\rm seg}$ be the standalone open-segment current defined by $\langle J_{\rm seg},\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds$ for vector tests $\psi$. With the componentwise distributional divergence pairing of [F7], $\langle\operatorname{div}J_{\rm seg},\varphi\rangle=-I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\nabla\varphi(\gamma(s))\,ds=-I\int_0^L(\varphi\circ\gamma)'(s)\,ds=I(\varphi(\gamma(0))-\varphi(\gamma(L)))=I(\delta_{\gamma(0)}-\delta_{\gamma(L)})(\varphi)$ for every scalar test $\varphi$, the chain rule and the fundamental theorem of [F7] giving the middle equality. This is the endpoint identity asserted in the Statement, and it shows why the segment is treated as a local part of a fed or closed circuit.

Under the hypotheses of (c), step 1.1's formulas apply, and [F4] gives the decomposition $B(x)=B(0)+DB(0)x+R(x)$ with $|R(x)|\le\frac12M_2|x|^2$ for $|x|\le a$, together with the Lipschitz bound $|B(x)-B(y)|\le M_1|x-y|$ on the ball.

For the force in (c), the constant term vanishes as in step 1.2, and the linear term is $I\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_lB_k(0)M_{lj}e_i$ with the matrix $M$ of step 1.2. Substituting $IM_{lj}=\varepsilon_{ljp}m_p$ from step 1.2 and contracting by [F2], $I\varepsilon_{ijk}\partial_lB_k(0)M_{lj}e_i=(\delta_{il}\delta_{kp}-\delta_{ip}\delta_{kl})\partial_lB_k(0)m_pe_i=\bigl(\partial_i(m\cdot B)(0)-m_i\operatorname{div}B(0)\bigr)e_i=\nabla(m\cdot B)(0)$, since $m$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}B(0)=0$. By [F3] and step 2.1 the remainder obeys $|I\int_0^L\gamma'\times R(\gamma)\,ds|\le|I|\int_0^L|\gamma'|\,|R(\gamma)|\,ds\le\frac12|I|La^2M_2$, because $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $|\gamma(s)|\le a$. This proves the force assertion of (c) with $|R_F|\le\frac12|I|La^2M_2$.

For the torque in (c), split $B(\gamma(s))=B(0)+(B(\gamma(s))-B(0))$. The first part is the constant-field torque of step 1.2 with the constant field $B(0)$, that is $m\times B(0)$. For the remainder, [F2] gives $\gamma\times(\gamma'\times(B(\gamma)-B(0)))=\gamma'(\gamma\cdot(B(\gamma)-B(0)))-(B(\gamma)-B(0))(\gamma\cdot\gamma')$ and hence, by [F3] and step 2.1, $\left|I\int_0^L\gamma\times(\gamma'\times(B(\gamma)-B(0)))\,ds\right|\le|I|\int_0^L|\gamma|\,|\gamma'|\,|B(\gamma)-B(0)|\,ds\le|I|\,a\cdot1\cdot M_1a\cdot L$. This proves the torque assertion of (c) with $|R_N|\le|I|La^2M_1$.

For (d): by [F6] the external field of a compact smooth conserved current satisfies $B=\operatorname{curl}A$, hence is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with $\operatorname{div}B=0$; on the compact ball $\overline{B_a(0)}$ let $C_1,C_2$ be the maxima of the absolute coordinate first and second partial derivatives, finite by [F9], and put $M_1:=9C_1$, $M_2:=27C_2$. The coordinate sum bounds give $|DB(x)v|\le M_1|v|$ and $|D^2B(x)[v,w]|\le M_2|v||w|$. Integrating the first derivative along the segment from $x$ to $y$ gives $|B(x)-B(y)|\le M_1|x-y|$; integrating the identity of [F4] gives $|B(x)-B(0)-DB(0)x|\le\frac12M_2|x|^2$. All segments lie in the convex closed ball Hence the hypotheses of (c) are met on every such ball with finite constants.

Parts (a), (b), (c), (d) are steps 1.1, 1.2, 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3; the endpoint identity quoted in the Statement is step 1.3. The scope clause (e) records that only the external field acts, that the coupling (W) is an adopted idealisation motivated by the smooth continuum law [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) rather than derived from it, and that no self-field, self-force, radiation reaction, mechanical support, deformation or dynamical claim is made. Parts (a)-(c) are finite Riemann-integral calculations and use no Choice axiom; part (d) inherits Countable Choice only through the Newtonian-potential suppliers [F8]. The moment identity is contracted without dividing by $I$; for $I=0$ the moment, force, torque and both remainders vanish, and the algebra applies to every stated closed parametrized $C^2$ curve, including multiply traversed and self-intersecting ones, since only closure, unit speed and the finite moment integral are used.

boundaries.evidence: The curve is an arc-length parametrized $C^2$ map of the compact interval $[0,L]$, so its trace and the moment integral are nonempty for $L>0$; the zero values arise only from $I=0$ or a vanishing moment, both permitted by step 4.1.

For $I=0$ the moment, force, torque and both remainders of steps 3.1 and 3.2 vanish identically, and the identities $F=\nabla(m\cdot B)(0)+R_F$, $N=m\times B(0)+R_N$ reduce to $0=0$; the moment identity is contracted without dividing by $I$.

One curve and one external field are fixed; the matrix $M$, the moment $m$ and the two remainders involve no counting family, and no index degenerates at one; the case is read off the Statement and step 1.1 of the item.

Self-intersecting and multiply traversed closed curves are explicitly retained by step 4.1, and a vanishing moment $m=0$ is allowed; the constant-field case of step 1.2 is the degenerate case of a field with no variation and is handled exactly.

For an open curve the endpoint identity $\operatorname{div}J_{\rm seg}=I(\delta_{\gamma(0)}-\delta_{\gamma(L)})$ is proved in step 1.3; for a closed curve the endpoint values agree by hypothesis, and the segment of step 1.3 is a local part of a fed or closed circuit.
Parts (a)-(c) are finite Riemann-integral calculations and use no Choice axiom; part (d) inherits Countable Choice only through the Newtonian-potential suppliers, as recorded in step 4.1.

No converse is claimed: the theorem does not assert that an observed force determines the moment or the field.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $Z:=\{(0,0,x_3):x_3\in\mathbb R\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ be the third coordinate axis and let
$$f:\mathbb R^3\setminus Z\to\mathbb R^3,\qquad f(x)=\frac{(-x_2,\ x_1,\ 0)}{x_1^2+x_2^2},\qquad x=(x_1,x_2,x_3),$$
so that, in cylindrical notation $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$ and $e_\varphi=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$, one has $f=e_\varphi/\rho$ on the punctured space. Let $T_f$ be the regular distribution of $f$ on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and let $A$ be the $\mathbb R^3$-valued distribution
$$A(\psi):=\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,x_3)\,dx_3,\qquad\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
the third-direction line measure on $Z$. For an $\mathbb R^3$-valued distribution $T=(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ whose components are scalar distributions of [[def-distribution]], the pairings used below are the componentwise readings of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\operatorname{div}T,\varphi\rangle:=-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\langle T_i,\partial_i\varphi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}T,\psi\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\langle T_i,(\operatorname{curl}\psi)_i\rangle .$$
Then: (a) $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$; (b) $\operatorname{div}f=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}f=0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3\setminus Z$; (c) for every vector test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and every scalar test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$,
$$\langle\operatorname{curl}T_f,\psi\rangle=2\pi\,A(\psi),\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}T_f,\varphi\rangle=0,$$
that is, $\operatorname{curl}T_f=2\pi\,e_3\,\delta_Z$ and $\operatorname{div}T_f=0$ in the distributional sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; and (d) for every $r>0$ and $h\in\mathbb R$, the circulation of $f$ along the positively oriented circle $\gamma_{r,h}:[0,2\pi]\to\mathbb R^3\setminus Z$, $\gamma_{r,h}(t)=(r\cos t,r\sin t,h)$, traversed once with increasing $t$, is $2\pi$ ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]], read componentwise). No product of distributions is formed.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $a>0$, write $x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ and $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, let
$$S:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\rho=a\}$$
be the circular cylinder of radius $a$ about the third coordinate axis, with unit normal $e_\rho=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ pointing from the interior region $\{\rho<a\}$ to the exterior region $\{\rho>a\}$, and let $e_\varphi=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ and $e_3=(0,0,1)$. Let $g:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be the piecewise constant field
$$g(x):=\begin{cases}e_3,&\rho<a,\\ 0,&\rho>a,\end{cases}$$
extended arbitrarily on the three-dimensional Lebesgue-null set $S$, and let $T_g$ be its regular distribution ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). For an $\mathbb R^3$-valued distribution $T=(T_1,T_2,T_3)$ whose components are scalar distributions of [[def-distribution]], a scalar test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and a vector test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, the pairings used below are the componentwise readings of [[def-distributional-derivative]]:
$$\langle\operatorname{div}T,\varphi\rangle:=-\sum_{i=1}^{3}\langle T_i,\partial_i\varphi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}T,\psi\rangle:=\sum_{i=1}^{3}\langle T_i,(\operatorname{curl}\psi)_i\rangle .$$
Then for every vector test $\psi$ and every scalar test $\varphi$,
$$\langle\operatorname{curl}T_g,\psi\rangle=\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}T_g,\varphi\rangle=0,$$
that is, $\operatorname{curl}T_g=e_\varphi\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{div}T_g=0$ in the distributional sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]. The surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; since $\psi$ has compact support it equals the integral over any compact cylinder segment containing $\operatorname{supp}\psi\cap S$. Equivalently, with $g_\pm$ the one-sided values and the normal $e_\rho$ from the minus to the plus side, $g_+-g_-=-e_3$, $e_\rho\times(g_+-g_-)=e_\varphi$ and $e_\rho\cdot(g_+-g_-)=0$. No product of distributions is formed.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry: in (c2) and (c3), $B(x+he_3)=B(x)$ for every $h\in\mathbb R$, and $B(R_\theta x)=R_\theta B(x)$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, at off-source points, where $R_\theta(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,x_3)$; no symmetry is required in (c1); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3), $\sup_{(\theta,z)\in C}|B(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)|\to0$ as $r\to\infty$ for every nonempty compact $C\subset\mathbb R^2$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $\gamma:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ be piecewise-$C^1$. If $a=b$, define both line integrals below to be $0$. If $a<b$, choose an admissible partition $a=t_0<\cdots<t_m=b$ and a continuous derivative extension $v_i$ on each piece. Let $f$ be a continuous scalar field and $F$ a continuous vector field on a set containing the trace of $\gamma$. The **scalar line integral with respect to arc length** and the **vector-field line integral** are

$$\int_\gamma f\,ds:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}f(\gamma(t))\lVert v_i(t)\rVert_2\,dt,$$

$$\int_\gamma F\cdot d\mathbf r:=\sum_{i<m}\int_{t_i}^{t_{i+1}}\langle F(\gamma(t)),v_i(t)\rangle\,dt,$$

where the inner product is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. The summands exist by [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. Independence of the admissible partition is proved in [[lem-line-integrals-are-independent-of-the-piecewise-c1-partition]].

Assume the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]. Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]].

For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral. Independence and finiteness are established by the following chart-independence lemma.

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following

derivations.claim: The field of (a) is $B=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi}f$ with $f=\rho^{-1}e_\varphi$; by [F1] it is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ and $C^\infty$ off $\gamma$, with $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{curl}B=0$ pointwise off $\gamma$, and all these properties are stable under multiplication by the constant $\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi}$.

The field of (b) is $B=\mu_0Kg$ with $g$ the piecewise constant cylinder field: it is bounded, hence locally integrable, constantly $\mu_0Ke_3$ for $\rho<a$ and $0$ for $\rho>a$, so it is $C^\infty$ off $S$ with $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{curl}B=0$ there; it is invariant under translations along and rotations about the third axis, and its supremum on any compact set of cross-sectional parameters is $0$ for every $\rho>a$, hence its transverse far-zone supremum is $0$.

For the wire, $\langle\operatorname{curl}T_B,\psi\rangle=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi}\langle\operatorname{curl}T_f,\psi\rangle=\mu_0I\,A(\psi)=\mu_0\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle$ and $\langle\operatorname{div}T_B,\varphi\rangle=0$ for all tests by [F1] and [F3]; moreover $B$ depends only on $\rho$ through the scalar factor $\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}$ multiplying $e_\varphi$, so it is invariant under translations along $\gamma$ and rotations about it, and its transverse far-zone supremum is $\frac{\mu_0|I|}{2\pi\rho}\to0$.
