Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$ be a compact smooth current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$, let $A$ be the vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ its magnetostatic field, with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Biot-Savart integral represents the field,
$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y)\times(x-y)}{|x-y|^3}\,dy .$$
Moreover the same formula holds in the declared thin-loop limit, constructed in the all-space laboratory $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$: if $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length ($|\gamma'|\equiv1$), $I\in\mathbb R$, and $j_\varepsilon=j*\eta_\varepsilon$ are the mollified divergence-free compact currents of [[lem-em-thin-current-limit]] associated with the tangent line current of $\gamma$, then their fields (given by the displayed formula with $J:=j_\varepsilon$) converge, with every derivative uniformly on every compact $K$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to
$$B_\gamma(x)=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds,$$
a locally integrable global distributional field with $\operatorname{div}B_\gamma=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B_\gamma=\mu_0J_\gamma$, smoothness off the curve and decay at spatial infinity, hence the admitted field of the declared ideal thin loop under [[post-em-ideal-magnetostatic-models]]. Its almost-everywhere representative on $\mathbb R^3$ is supplied by [[lem-em-thin-current-limit]], independently of the away-from-curve convergence. Nothing is asserted on the wire, about line self-energy, about the infinite-wire or sheet models, or for currents outside the compact smooth class and its declared thin-loop limit.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry: in (c2) and (c3), $B(x+he_3)=B(x)$ for every $h\in\mathbb R$, and $B(R_\theta x)=R_\theta B(x)$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, at off-source points, where $R_\theta(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,x_3)$; no symmetry is required in (c1); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3), $\sup_{(\theta,z)\in C}|B(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)|\to0$ as $r\to\infty$ for every nonempty compact $C\subset\mathbb R^2$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Let the compact smooth current class and the declared ideal models be those of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(a) [Compact smooth currents].** Let $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. The **magnetic dipole moment** of $J$ is the vector
$$m:=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}y\times J(y)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3,$$
of unit A m$^2$. The integral is computed componentwise over any nondegenerate closed bounding rectangle $Q$ containing $\operatorname{supp}J$, using the continuous functions $y\mapsto(y\times J(y))_i$ on $Q$ and their zero extension outside $Q$. Its value is independent of the chosen larger bounding rectangle by finite rectangular subdivision and vanishing of the integrand off its support; the support itself need not be Jordan measurable. Thus this is a Riemann integral of continuous compactly supported functions ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); it is absolutely finite because $J$ is bounded with compact support.

**(b) [Declared ideal thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ and $I\in\mathbb R$, the **magnetic moment** of the ideal loop current of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1) is
$$m:=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds,$$
again a componentwise Riemann integral over the compact interval $[0,L]$ of continuous functions; for the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ traversed in the positive orientation this is $m=I\pi a^2e_3$.

**(c) [Status and scope].** In both clauses $m$ is a source moment of the declared current model: it is not a rest mass, not an intrinsic spin and not an observed quantity. The definition asserts no far-field property of $m$ (that is the content of [[pthm-em-magnetic-dipole-field]] under its hypotheses), no agreement between the two clauses in a common limit, and no moment for currents outside the two classes; no higher multipole is defined here. The finite Riemann moment definitions and circular-loop evaluation themselves are choice-free; no distribution-embedding or surface-measure theorem is used to compute these moments.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a closed embedded $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length with period $L>0$: $\gamma(s+L)=\gamma(s)$ and $|\gamma'(s)|=1$ for every $s$, and the induced map $\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ is injective. Let $I\in\mathbb R$ and $\mu_0>0$, and for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)=:\mathcal D(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]) define

$$j(\psi)=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,$$

Here its scalar component distributions are $j_k(\varphi):=I\int_0^L\gamma_k'(s)\varphi(\gamma(s))ds$ for scalar tests $\varphi$, $k=1,2,3$; for a scalar test the notation $j(\varphi)$ below denotes the vector $(j_1(\varphi),j_2(\varphi),j_3(\varphi))$. In the vector-test formula the pairing is the complex-bilinear Euclidean pairing (no conjugation) of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; restricted to real-valued $\psi$ this is the stated real functional. Then $\operatorname{div}j=0$ in the distributional sense ([[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-distribution]]). For any family $(\eta_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of nonnegative smooth radial kernels with $\int_{\mathbb R^3}\eta_\varepsilon=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\eta_\varepsilon\subseteq\overline B_\varepsilon(0)$ — including the rescalings $\eta_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-3}\eta(x/\varepsilon)$ of a chosen nonnegative unit-mass radial kernel supported in $\overline B_1(0)$ — the mollified fields $j_\varepsilon$ defined by the distribution pairing $j_\varepsilon(x):=j(\eta_\varepsilon(x-\cdot))=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\eta_\varepsilon(x-\gamma(s))\,ds$ are smooth, compactly supported and divergence-free, and their Biot-Savart fields converge, with every derivative uniformly on every nonempty compact $K\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ disjoint from $\gamma$, to

$$B(x)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^L\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(x-\gamma(s))}{|x-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$$

([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]). In addition, assigning arbitrary finite values on the curve gives a representative $B\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, smooth off $\gamma$, with $\operatorname{div}T_B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}T_B=\mu_0j$ globally; the first identity is tested on scalar $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and the second on vector $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^3)$. If $\gamma([0,L])\subseteq B_a(0)$ for some $a>0$, then $|B(x)|\le\mu_0|I|L/\bigl(4\pi(|x|-a)^2\bigr)$ for $|x|>a$, so $B$ decays at infinity. For the circle $\gamma(s)=a(\cos(s/a),\sin(s/a),0)$ and a point $z e_3$ on its axis the value is $B_z=\mu_0Ia^2/\bigl(2(a^2+z^2)^{3/2}\bigr)$. Nothing is asserted about the divergent line self-energy or about fields on the curve itself.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. In the named inertial laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following additional classical physical idealization: a loop, infinite straight line or infinite cylindrical sheet source defined by [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1)-(c3), with zero charge density, is modeled by a time-independent $B$ satisfying exactly the admissibility predicate (c4), together with $E=0$ and $\rho=0$. Thus $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold distributionally on $\mathbb R^3$, with the stated off-source regularity, symmetry and decay; the electrostatic and temporal Maxwell identities are zero. This physical adoption extends to these explicitly declared source types only. It is separate from the earlier $L^1$-source and point/compact-sheet postulates, which do not include these line and noncompact sheet sources. No existence, uniqueness, finite self-energy, force product, self-force, apparatus accuracy, matter dynamics or empirical certainty is asserted.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $c < d$ be reals and let $\varphi : [c,d] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable
at every point of $[c,d]$ as a function on $[c,d]$ ([[def-derivative]]), with
$\varphi'$ integrable on $[c,d]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex with at least two elements
([[def-interval]]) with $\varphi[\,[c,d]\,] \subseteq J$, and let $f : J \to
\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $J$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Then $(f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi'$ is integrable on $[c,d]$ and

$$\int_{\varphi(c)}^{\varphi(d)} f \;=\; \int_c^d (f\circ\varphi)\,\varphi' ,$$

the left-hand integral being the oriented one of [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Neither injectivity nor monotonicity of $\varphi$ is assumed**, and that is
exactly why the left-hand side is written with oriented limits: $\varphi(d)$ may
lie below $\varphi(c)$, and $\varphi$ may return to the same value many times.
The proof runs through a primitive of $f$ and the chain rule, and no inverse
function is ever formed.

**Continuity of $f$ is a hypothesis and cannot be weakened to integrability.**
With $f$ merely integrable the composite $f \circ \varphi$ need not be
integrable at all, so the right-hand side need not exist; that is
the false statement that weakens it on the companion page.

derivations.claim: Every axis point $ze_3$ lies at distance $\sqrt{a^2+z^2}\ge a>0$ from the circle, so it is off the curve; by [F1] the field of the declared ideal loop there is the absolutely convergent line integral $B(ze_3)=\frac{\mu_0I}{4\pi}\int_0^{2\pi a}\frac{\gamma'(s)\times(ze_3-\gamma(s))}{|ze_3-\gamma(s)|^3}\,ds$, the same integral being the Biot-Savart field of the compact smooth currents in the declared thin-current limit.

Substituting $t=s/a$, so that $ds=a\,dt$ and $\gamma'(s)=(-\sin t,\cos t,0)$ while $ze_3-\gamma(s)=(-a\cos t,-a\sin t,z)$, one has $\gamma'(s)\times(ze_3-\gamma(s))=(z\cos t,\ z\sin t,\ a)$ by [F3] (the first two components are $z\cos t$ and $z\sin t$ respectively, and the third is $a\cos^2t+a\sin^2t=a$), and $|ze_3-\gamma(s)|=(a^2+z^2)^{1/2}$ is constant. Hence the component integrals are continuous functions of $t$ on the compact interval $[0,2\pi]$.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]].

**(a) [Ideal infinite straight wire].** Let $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, let $J_{\rm w}$ be the declared ideal line current of amplitude $I$ along $\gamma$ ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c2)), and define, on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\gamma$,
$$B(x):=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi\rho}\,e_\varphi,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2},\qquad e_\varphi=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0).$$
Then $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ and of class $C^\infty$ off $\gamma$; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ pointwise off $\gamma$; $B$ is invariant under translations along $\gamma$ and rotations about it, and its transverse far-zone supremum tends to $0$ as $\rho\to\infty$; for every $r>0$ and $h\in\mathbb R$, the circulation of $B$ along $\gamma_{r,h}(t)=(r\cos t,r\sin t,h)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$, traversed once with increasing $t$, is $\mu_0I$ ([[def-scalar-and-vector-line-integrals-along-piecewise-c1-paths]]); and $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J_{\rm w}$ hold in the distributional sense of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c4). Hence $B$ is an admitted field of the declared wire model; the transverse decay excludes an added homogeneous longitudinal field, and no further selection, uniqueness or energy claim is made.

**(b) [Ideal infinite cylindrical sheet].** Let $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $K\in\mathbb R$, let $J_S$ be the declared ideal sheet current of amplitude $K$ along $S$ ([[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c3)), and define $B:=\mu_0Ke_3$ for $\rho<a$ and $B:=0$ for $\rho>a$. Then $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ and of class $C^\infty$ off $S$; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ pointwise off $S$; $B$ has the declared symmetry (translations along and rotations about the axis) and its transverse far-zone supremum is $0$; the one-sided jump across $S$, with $n=e_\rho$ from the interior to the exterior and $[B]=B_+-B_-$, is $n\times[B]=\mu_0Ke_\varphi$ and $n\cdot[B]=0$, the stationary tangential-sheet jump for this noncompact cylinder, established by the test-localized [[lem-em-ideal-cylindrical-sheet-field]] for the current density $Ke_\varphi$ (computed directly as $e_\rho\times(0-\mu_0Ke_3)=\mu_0Ke_\varphi$); and $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J_S$ hold in the distributional sense of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c4). Hence $B$ is an admitted field of the declared solenoid model.

**(c) [Scope].** Both models are declared noncompact idealisations: they are not finite-energy localized-current theorems; nothing is asserted about self-energy, inductance, self-force, the fields on the sources, or the approximation of any physical apparatus; and the fields are selected within the declared symmetry and decay class, not shown to be the only solutions of the magnetostatic equations off the sources without that class. The external force between two such wires is treated in [[ex-em-wire-force-coupling]] under the adopted thin-wire coupling.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry: in (c2) and (c3), $B(x+he_3)=B(x)$ for every $h\in\mathbb R$, and $B(R_\theta x)=R_\theta B(x)$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, at off-source points, where $R_\theta(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,x_3)$; no symmetry is required in (c1); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3), $\sup_{(\theta,z)\in C}|B(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)|\to0$ as $r\to\infty$ for every nonempty compact $C\subset\mathbb R^2$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Let $\gamma:[0,L]\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^2$ curve parametrized by arc length ($|\gamma'|\equiv1$) that is either closed ($\gamma(0)=\gamma(L)$ with matching one-sided derivatives) or a wire segment with free endpoints, let $I\in\mathbb R$, let $m=\frac I2\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\gamma'(s)\,ds$ be the finite Riemann source moment defined by this displayed integral in the closed case. For an embedded closed loop this agrees with [[def-em-magnetic-moment]](b); embeddedness is not required for the present parametrized-curve calculation. Let $B$ be a prescribed external magnetic field, of class $C^0$ on a neighbourhood of the trace of $\gamma$ in part (a) and of class $C^2$ on an open set containing the closed ball $\overline{B_a(0)}$ in parts (b)-(d). Adopt the thin-wire coupling hypothesis (W): for a general closed parametrized curve use the stated direct neutral-wire Riemann coupling (with multiplicity of traversal retained); in the embedded closed-loop specialization its source interpretation is exactly [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](c1); for an open curve use a compact segment of a fed or closed neutral circuit, including a segment of the declared infinite wire of (c2). Adopt separately for that parametrized wire or local segment the direct external magnetic coupling $dF=I\,d\gamma\times B$ and $dN=\gamma\times dF$, as an ideal extension motivated by the smooth continuum Lorentz law [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii); that smooth-source postulate does not itself include singular currents. An isolated static neutral open segment is not asserted: its standalone current satisfies $\operatorname{div}J_{\rm seg}=I(\delta_{\gamma(0)}-\delta_{\gamma(L)})$, so its endpoint feed/return cannot be suppressed in a global model. Force and torque here concern only the specified local segment under this adopted coupling. Then:

**(a) [Force and torque under (W)]**
$$F:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\times B(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad N:=I\int_0^L\gamma(s)\times\bigl(\gamma'(s)\times B(\gamma(s))\bigr)\,ds,$$
the componentwise Riemann integrals of continuous functions on the compact interval $[0,L]$ ([[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]).

**(b) [Constant field]** If $\gamma$ is closed and $B$ is constant on a neighbourhood of the loop, then $F=0$ and $N=m\times B$ exactly.

**(c) [Slowly varying field]** Let $\gamma$ be closed with $|\gamma(s)|\le a$ for all $s$, let $B$ be $C^2$ on an open set containing $\overline{B_a(0)}$ with constants $M_1,M_2$ such that $|B(x)-B(y)|\le M_1|x-y|$ and $|B(x)-B(0)-DB(0)x|\le\frac12M_2|x|^2$ for $|x|,|y|\le a$, and suppose $\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $B_a(0)$ (as holds for the external part of any smooth-branch vacuum field by [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]], [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then
$$F=\nabla(m\cdot B)(0)+R_F,\qquad N=m\times B(0)+R_N,$$
with $|R_F|\le\frac12|I|\,L\,a^2M_2$ and $|R_N|\le|I|\,L\,a^2M_1$, where $\nabla(m\cdot B)(0)$ is the gradient at $0$ of $x\mapsto m\cdot B(x)$ for the fixed vector $m$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(d) [Sufficient condition]** If the external field is the magnetostatic field of a compact smooth steady current $J_{\rm ext}\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J_{\rm ext}=0$ ([[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]], [[pthm-em-biot-savart]]), then it is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}B=0$, and meets the hypotheses of (c) on every ball $\overline{B_a(0)}$ with finite constants $M_1,M_2$.

**(e) [Scope]** Only the external field acts on the loop: the loop's own field, self-force, radiation reaction, mechanical support and material response are outside the statement, and no claim is made about the loop's dynamics, deformation or failure. The coupling (W) is an explicit idealisation of a neutral thin wire at rest in the laboratory frame; it is adopted, not derived, and the theorem is conditional on it. No measurement or uncertainty is involved. Parts (a)-(c), conditional on the explicit coupling (W) and the supplied curve and external field, are finite Riemann-integral calculations and use no Choice axiom. Part (d), transporting the Newtonian-potential construction, assumes Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Thus $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold distributionally on $\mathbb R^3$, with the stated off-source regularity, symmetry and decay; the electrostatic and temporal Maxwell identities are zero. derivations.claim: On the points $(d,0,x_3)$ of wire 2 one has $\rho=d$ and $(-x_2,x_1,0)=(0,d,0)$, so $e_\varphi=e_2$ and, by [F1], $B_1(d,0,x_3)=\frac{\mu_0I_1}{2\pi d}e_2$, constant along the whole line of wire 2.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The surface $S$ is Lebesgue-null in $\Omega$: by [L3] the finitely many regular charts $X_j:V_j\to S$ cover $S$, each image $X_j(V_j)$ is null in $\mathbb R^3$ by [L5] because $X_j$ is a $C^1$ map from the lower-dimensional open set $V_j\subseteq\mathbb R^2$, and a finite union of null sets is null by [L5]. Consequently, for $F\in\{B,D\}$ the distributional time derivative of the regular distribution of $F$ is the regular distribution of the piecewise classical time derivative: fix a test $\psi$ with support in a compact cylinder $\overline Q\times J\subseteq U$, so that $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=-\int_U F\partial_t\psi$; by [L8] applied after Fubini, this iterated integral equals $-\int_Q\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt\,dx$, and for every $x\in\Omega\setminus S$ the inner integrand is $C^1$ in $t$ with $\psi(x,\cdot)$ compactly supported in $J$, so [L8] gives $\int_JF(x,t)\partial_t\psi(x,t)\,dt=-\int_J\partial_tF(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dt$; since $S$ is null, replacing the outer integral over $\Omega\setminus S$ by one over $\Omega$ changes nothing, so $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$, where $\{\partial_tF\}$ is locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ extension hypothesis. In the weak-trace branch, the assumed $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ temporal derivatives instead make the same compact-test products integrable, so the identical Fubini and line-integration argument applies.

By [L1], applied to $D$, $B$, $E$, $H$ (each is $C^1$ on $\Omega_-\cup\Omega_+$ with one-sided $C^1$ traces under the joint extension hypothesis), the four spatial identities $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{div}B=\{\operatorname{div}B\}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S$, $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}H=\{\operatorname{curl}H\}+n\times[H]\delta_S$ hold as distributions on $U$ under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, with the piecewise fields locally bounded near $S$. More explicitly, apply [L1] at each fixed time to $\psi(\cdot,t)$ and integrate its identity in $t$. Fubini is justified by the compact-test integrability of the fields, their piecewise spatial derivatives and their surface-time traces; in the weak-trace branch these are exactly the additional stated $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ hypotheses, so the same transfer to spacetime distributions applies without a uniform bound.

Every smooth test supported away from $S\times I$ has zero sheet pairing; the fundamental lemma [L7] applied on that open complement therefore gives $g=0$ almost everywhere there. Since $S$ is null by step 1.1, Fubini [L8] makes $S\times I$ null locally in spacetime, so $g=0$ almost everywhere on $U$. Thus $\int_{S\times I}a\psi\,dS\,dt=0$ for every ambient smooth compact test $\psi$. In a sufficiently small rigid graph chart write $X(y)=(y,h(y))$, with a product box $V\times(z_-,z_+)\times J$ contained in the ambient chart/time domain. Then $t\mapsto\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in(a,b)$ with

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_Kf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x)=\int_K\partial_tf(x,t)\,d\lambda_n(x),$$

By [A2], $J_f\cdot E=E\cdot\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}\cdot E$, and $E\cdot\sigma E\ge0$ because $\sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite; the term is the Ohmic dissipation density of the model.

By [L1], $\operatorname{div}S=\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E-E\cdot\operatorname{curl}H$, so the two scalar identities of step 1.1 give $\operatorname{div}S=-(E\cdot J_f+E\cdot\partial_tD+H\cdot\partial_tB)$; differentiating $u$ in time and using the symmetry of $\varepsilon$ and $\mu$ with the product rule of [L2] gives $\partial_tu=\tfrac12\partial_t(E\cdot\varepsilon E)+\tfrac12\partial_t(H\cdot\mu H)=\partial_tE\cdot\varepsilon E+\partial_tH\cdot\mu H=E\cdot\partial_tD+H\cdot\partial_tB$ by [A2]; adding the two identities yields $\partial_tu+\operatorname{div}S=-J_f\cdot E$ on $\Omega\times I$, proving (a).

The finite union $\partial\Omega\prime$ is therefore volume-null. Hence the compact finite-measure set $K=\overline{\Omega\prime}$ and $\Omega\prime$ have the same integrals for the continuous functions used here. Apply [L3] to $K$ and $f=u$: $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u\,dx=\int_{\Omega'}\partial_tu\,dx$, where the regularity hypotheses on the fields supply the continuous $\partial_tu$ on a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Omega'}\times[a,b]$ for a compact interval $[a,b]\subset I$ containing $t$ in its interior; substituting the local balance of step 2.1 and applying the divergence theorem [L4] to $F=S$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega'}u=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E-\int_{\Omega'}\operatorname{div}S=-\int_{\Omega'}J_f\cdot E-\oint_{\partial\Omega'}S\cdot n\,dS$, under the $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis carried by [L4]. derivations.claim: Localize a test by a smooth partition of unity [L3] to finitely many rectangular boxes compactly contained in $U$; for boxes meeting the plane choose the height interval to straddle $z=0$. It suffices to prove the identity for each localized test and sum. Let $F\in\{E,B,D,H\}$ and let $\psi$ be supported in one such box. For fixed $(x,y,t)$ with $z\ne0$ the map $z\mapsto F(x,y,z,t)$ is $C^1$ on each part of that height interval and has the stated one-sided $C^1$ extensions at zero; applying [L1] on the two closed height subintervals and summing gives $\int_{\mathbb R}F\,\partial_z\psi\,dz=-[F](x,y,0,t)\,\psi(x,y,0,t)-\int_{\mathbb R}\{\partial_zF\}\psi\,dz$, because the outer boundary terms vanish by compact support; integrating over $x,y,t$ by [L2], with the plane $\{z=0\}$ null by [L4] so that the split into the two half-spaces is exact, gives $\langle\partial_zF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_zF\}\psi+\langle[F]\delta_S,\psi\rangle$ componentwise, i.e. $\operatorname{div}F=\{\operatorname{div}F\}+e_z\cdot[F]\,\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}F=\{\operatorname{curl}F\}+e_z\times[F]\,\delta_S$ by [L6], the tangential derivatives contributing no sheet term.

The same per-line integration by parts in $t$, with $\psi$ of compact $t$-support and the plane stationary and null by [L4], gives $\langle\partial_tF,\psi\rangle=\int_U\{\partial_tF\}\psi$ for every test $\psi$: time differentiation at the fixed plane contributes no sheet term, and the piecewise derivatives are locally bounded by the joint one-sided $C^1$ hypothesis.

Substituting the spatial identities of step 1.1 and the temporal identity of step 1.2 into the assumed equations [A2] gives four distributional identities of the form $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ on the local region, with locally integrable volume parts $g$: $u_{\{\operatorname{div}D\}-\rho_v}+(n\cdot[D]-\sigma_f)\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{div}B\}}+n\cdot[B]\delta_S=0$, $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+\{\partial_tB\}}+n\times[E]\delta_S=0$ and $u_{\{\operatorname{curl}H\}-J_v-\{\partial_tD\}}+n\times[H]\delta_S=0$, where the two half-space fields are $C^1$ with locally bounded derivatives and $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable.

[Coefficient extraction] Let $b\in C_c^\infty((-1,1))$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R$, with $b(0)=1$, $0\le b\le1$ [L3] and put $\psi_h:=\psi\,b(z/h)$ for a test $\psi$; testing an identity $u_g+a\delta_S=0$ of step 2.1 with $\psi_h$ gives $0=\int_Ug\psi_h+\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi_h$, whose second term tends to $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi$ because $b(z/h)\to b(0)=1$ everywhere on the plane and the integrands are dominated by $|a\psi|$ on the compactly supported part of the plane, while the first term tends to $0$ because $|\int_Ug\psi_h|\le\int_U|g\psi|\mathbf 1_{\{|z|\le h\}}$ with integrands converging to $0$ almost everywhere, dominated by the integrable $|g\psi|$, the exceptional set $\{z=0\}$ being null [L4]. Hence $\int_{\{z=0\}}a\psi=0$ for every test $\psi$; taking $\psi(x,y,z,t)=\eta(x,y,t)\beta(z)$ with $\eta$ supported in the tangential/time part of one of those local boxes and $\beta$ supported in its height interval with $\beta(0)=1$ reduces this to $\int a(x,y,0,t)\eta(x,y,t)\,dx\,dy\,dt=0$ for every $\eta$, so the continuous function $(x,y,t)\mapsto a(x,y,0,t)$ vanishes identically by [L5]. All four coefficients of step 2.1 therefore vanish pointwise on the plane.

Applying step 3.1 and the constitutive relations [A1]: (a) $n\times[E]=0$, so the tangential parts agree, $E_{2t}=E_{1t}$; (b) $n\cdot[D]=\sigma_f$ with $D_j=\varepsilon_jE_j$ on the two sides gives $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}-\varepsilon_1E_{1n}=\sigma_f$ and, since $\varepsilon_2>0$, $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}+\sigma_f/\varepsilon_2$; (c) if $\sigma_f=0$ the previous identity reads $\varepsilon_2E_{2n}=\varepsilon_1E_{1n}$, so $E_{2n}=(\varepsilon_1/\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}$ has the same sign as $E_{1n}$ and vanishes with it, and $E_{2n}=E_{1n}$ holds if and only if $(\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)E_{1n}=0$, i.e. when $E_{1n}=0$ or $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$; (d) $n\cdot[B]=0$ and $n\times[H]=0$, and in the nonmagnetic case $H=\mu_0^{-1}B$ on both sides the two identities give $[B_n]=0$ and $[B_t]=0$, hence $B_{2n}=B_{1n}$ and $B_{2t}=B_{1t}$ by the decomposition of [L6]. The scope (e) holds: the computation uses only the assumed local equations and the declared linear branch, asserts no global configuration, no existence, no further constitutive law and no empirical claim.

boundaries.evidence: Example and step 3.1: if a coefficient vanished identically the extraction still holds; the empty-support case of the test pairing is zero, and no nonemptiness of the plane's portion inside a compact cylinder or of the source support is assumed.

Steps 4.1: sigma_f=0 is treated explicitly in (c) (the normal relation becomes eps2 E_2n = eps1 E_1n, with common signs), the zero fields satisfy all four identities, and the zero free sheet current K_f=0 is the case used in (d).

Example and step 4.1: one planar interface, three spatial dimensions and the isotropic scalar permittivities eps1, eps2 are the case at hand; the normal/tangential decomposition against the single unit normal e_z gives one normal and two tangential components, and no anisotropic or multilayer case is claimed.

Step 4.1: the degenerate equal-permittivity case eps1=eps2 is retained (E_2n=E_1n for every E_1n) and distinguished from the generic case; the case E_1n=0 is retained as the other way the equality E_2n=E_1n can hold; no invertibility beyond eps2>0 is assumed.

Steps 1.1-3.1: all pairings are over compact test supports inside the local laboratory region, so no asymptotic or global endpoint of the noncompact plane arises; the fixed-volume/far-field endpoint case is not asserted, and the time derivative carries no sheet term because the interface is stationary.

Countable Choice is assumed for the distributional and surface-measure interfaces as in the Example; it is used in the sheet pairing and in the extraction through the measure-theoretic suppliers L2 and L4, while the per-line integration by parts and the final algebra of step 4.1 are choice-free.
Step 4.1(c): if E_2n=E_1n and sigma_f=0, then (eps1-eps2)E_1n=eps2E_2n-eps2E_1n=eps2(E_2n-E_1n)=0, so either E_1n=0 or eps1=eps2; the forward direction of the stated equivalence is this computation.

Step 4.1(c): conversely, if E_1n=0 then eps2E_2n=eps1E_1n=0 gives E_2n=0=E_1n, and if eps1=eps2 then eps2E_2n=eps1E_1n=eps2E_1n with eps2>0 gives E_2n=E_1n; the reverse direction is the other half of the same equivalence.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all five steps: the half-spaces are restricted to actual Omega, and compact tests localize to boxes inside the laboratory region. Height integration on the two C1 sides produces +jump delta; tangential and time derivatives have no sheet term. Fubini is justified by joint one-sided bounds. Thin cutoffs tend to zero off the null plane and remain one on it; dominated convergence removes the L1 volume part, and ambient product tests identify the continuous sheet coefficient. No global use of the compact-interface theorem is made on a noncompact plane. The normal formula divides only by epsilon2>0; both directions of equality include zero normal field and equal media, with either sign of sheet charge. Magnetic continuity additionally assumes the shared mu0 law. Reader domain/localization repairs accepted; the repaired transfer-only closure is irrelevant to this instantaneous branch. No existence or empirical claim.

On $r
e0$ the functions $z$ and $z\,r^{-3}$ are smooth and $r^{-3}$ is smooth away from the origin; the sum and scalar rules of [L1] give $\Delta z=0$ and $\Delta(z\,r^{-3})=z\,\Delta(r^{-3})+2\,
abla z\cdot
abla(r^{-3})$, with $\partial_ir^{-3}=-3x_ir^{-5}$ and $\Delta(r^{-3})=\sum_i\partial_i(-3x_ir^{-5})=-9r^{-5}+15r^{-5}=6r^{-5}$; hence $\Delta(zr^{-3})=6zr^{-5}+2\cdot(-3zr^{-5})=0$, so $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ on $r<a$ and $\Delta\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ on $r>a$; the interior potential is linear on the entire closed ball, including the origin, while the exterior expression and its gradient are smooth up to $S$ because $r\ge a>0$ on that closed exterior side.

Put $q:=z/r$ for the fixed directional factor along a radial line. At $r=a$: $\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}(a)=-CE_0aq$ and $\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}(a)=(-E_0a+d/a^2)q$, whose equality for every angle is the scalar equation $C=1-d/(E_0a^3)$; the radial derivatives are $\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=-CE_0q$ and $\partial_r\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}=(-E_0-2d/a^3)q$, whose equality after the weights $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}$ is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}C=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}(1+2d/(E_0a^3))$. Substituting the displayed $C$ and $d$ satisfies both equations (the determinant of the pair is $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}>0$), so the two matching identities hold. By the chain rule along any smooth surface chart, equal traces have equal tangential derivatives and hence equal tangential electric fields; conversely, equality of those derivatives makes the trace difference constant along every piecewise smooth path on the sphere, whose points are joined by great-circle arcs, without fixing its value. The displayed trace computation fixes it to zero. The weighted radial identity is exactly normal-$D$ continuity because $E=-\nabla\varphi$ and $D=\varepsilon E$. The asymptotics (c) follow from $|z|\le r$: $|\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}+E_0z|=|d||z|r^{-3}\le|d|r^{-2}$ and $\nabla(dzr^{-3})=d(r^{-3}e_3-3zr^{-5}x)$ has squared norm $d^2r^{-6}(1+3q^2)\le4d^2r^{-6}$ because $|q|\le1$, hence norm at most $2|d|r^{-3}$.

For the declared static completion, [L3] gives $\operatorname{div}D=\{\operatorname{div}D\}+n\cdot[D]\delta_S$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\{\operatorname{curl}E\}+n\times[E]\delta_S$, with analogous formulas for $B$ and $H$; by step 1.1 the piecewise classical divergences and curls of $D$ and $E$ vanish (each side is a constant multiple of the gradient of a harmonic function, so $\operatorname{div}E=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=0$ there, the latter by the mixed-partial commutation of [L1]), and by step 1.2 the normal jump $n\cdot[D]$ and tangential jump $n\times[E]$ vanish; since $B=H=0$ and $\rho_f=J_f=0$ with $\sigma_f=K_f=0$, all four distributional macroscopic equations hold on the local region and the hypotheses of [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]] ($S=\{r=a\}$ a compact embedded $C^2$ hypersurface in $\Omega$ because $\overline B_a\subseteq\Omega$, locally integrable fields, $C^1$ off $S$, joint one-sided $C^1$ extensions, stationary free sheet data) are verified.

For uniqueness, let $w_{\mathrm{in}}=\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}$ on $\overline{B_a}$ and $w_{\mathrm{out}}=\tilde\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}-\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ on $\{r\ge a\}$; both are harmonic with $C^2$ regularity on the closed regions, their traces and weighted radial derivatives agree on $S$ by the shared interface conditions, and $|w_{\mathrm{out}}|\le(M+|d|)r^{-1}$ for all sufficiently large $r\ge1$. Apply the first Green identity of [L2] with $u=v=w_{\mathrm{in}}$ on the ball $B_a$ and with $u=v=w_{\mathrm{out}}$ on the annulus $\{a<r<R\}$: since the Laplacians vanish, $\int_{B_a}|\nabla w_{\mathrm{in}}|^2=\oint_Sw_{\mathrm{in}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\int_{a<r<R}|\nabla w_{\mathrm{out}}|^2=\oint_{\{r=R\}}w_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}-\oint_Sw_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}$; multiplying by $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}$ and adding, the two surface terms on $S$ cancel by $w_{\mathrm{in}}=w_{\mathrm{out}}$ and $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{in}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}\partial_rw_{\mathrm{out}}$, while the term on $\{r=R\}$ is bounded by $(4\pi R^2)\cdot(M+|d|)R^{-1}\cdot C R^{-2}$ using [L2]'s Cauchy estimate on balls of radius $R/4$ centred at $|x|=R$, which lie in the exterior for large $R$ and carry the bound $|w_{\mathrm{out}}|\le C/R$, hence tends to $0$. For each fixed $L>a$, the nonnegative weighted energy on the ball and $a<r<L$ is at most that on the ball and $a<r<R$ for $R>L$, and the latter is bounded by the absolute outer boundary term, which tends to zero. Thus every fixed bounded-region energy is zero; continuity and the positive weights imply that both gradients vanish, so $w_{\mathrm{in}}$ is constant on the ball and $w_{\mathrm{out}}$ is constant on $r>a$; the decay forces that constant to be $0$, hence the common trace is $0$, and then $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ by the Dirichlet uniqueness of [L2] applied on the ball to $w_{\mathrm{in}}$ and the zero function.

The fields follow by differentiation: $E_{\mathrm{in}}=-\nabla\varphi_{\mathrm{in}}=CE_0e_3$ with $D_{\mathrm{in}}=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}CE_0e_3$ on $r<a$; outside, $\varphi_{\mathrm{out}}$ is the sum of the applied uniform potential and the potential $dzr^{-3}$ of a dipole at the origin with moment $p=4\pi\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}d\,e_3$, and direct differentiation of the defined dipole potential gives $E_p(x)=[3(p\cdot n)n-p]/(4\pi\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}r^3)$, so the exterior field has precisely that form; the interior polarisation is $P_{\mathrm{in}}=D_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_0E_{\mathrm{in}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}-\varepsilon_0)CE_0e_3$ and the exterior polarisation is $P_{\mathrm{out}}=(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}-\varepsilon_0)E_{\mathrm{out}}$, so the bound surface charge density is the singular coefficient of $\rho_b=-\operatorname{div}P$ at $S$, namely $\sigma_b=n\cdot(P_{\mathrm{in}}-P_{\mathrm{out}})$ in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, by applying [L3] to the piecewise smooth $P$ with jump $P_{\mathrm{out}}-P_{\mathrm{in}}$.

Steps 1.1-1.2 verify (a)-(c), step 2.1 verifies (b) and the distributional thin-interface reading, step 2.2 gives the uniqueness statement (d) with existence exhibited by the displayed pair, and step 2.3 gives the fields, polarisation, exterior dipole moment and bound surface charge of (e). citations.quote:
The curve is **$C^{1}$** when it is differentiable at every point of $I$ and
the derivative map $s \mapsto x'(s)$, $I \to V$, is continuous, meaning that
the $\mathbb{R}^{4}$-valued map $s \mapsto (x_A \circ x)'(s)$ is continuous
([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); by the equivalence of
transported norms this condition is independent of the inertial frame. It is
**$C^{k}$** for $k \ge 1$ when the derivative map is $C^{k-1}$, with the same
transported reading. A curve on a compact interval $[a,b]$ contained
in $I$ is **piecewise $C^{1}$** when there is a finite partition
$a = s_0 < s_1 < \cdots < s_m = b$ such that $x$ is $C^{1}$ on every open
subinterval $(s_{i-1},s_i)$ and the finite one-sided difference-quotient
derivatives at both ends of every piece exist in $V$. These are limits of
$\bigl(x(t+h)-x(t)\bigr)/h$ over the relevant side of the piece, not assertions
that $x'(s)$ has a limit as $s$ approaches a corner; their finiteness implies
continuity of $x$ at the corners (for a one-sided quotient derivative $v$ at $t$
one has $x(t+h)-x(t) = h\,(v+o(1))$ as $h \to 0$ on that side). No continuous
extension of the open-piece derivative is required. Derivatives at the endpoints
of $I$ are the one-sided difference-quotient limits over $I$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.
