citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Adopt the following reduced circuit model in the laboratory frame and SI units of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. The continuum material reference is [[post-em-material-closure]]; the terminal laws below are additional assumptions, rather than consequences of its pointwise constitutive relations or of Maxwell's equations.

(a) **Branch data.** Fix a nonempty interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$, a finite set of nodes $\mathcal N$, and a finite set of oriented branches $\mathcal E$, each with specified tail and head nodes. Designate $n$ inductive/resistive branches, $m$ capacitive branches and any source branches. On the first family specify currents $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ and separate voltage-drop vectors $V_L,V_R:J\to\mathbb R^n$; on the second specify charges $Q:J\to\mathbb R^m$, currents $I_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$ and voltage drops $V_C:J\to\mathbb R^m$. Currents $I$ and charges $Q$ admit $C^1$ extensions to an open interval containing $J$; included endpoint derivatives are their one-sided derivatives, and at a singleton the chosen extensions are part of the data supplying the jets. Voltages and source currents are continuous. The matrices $L,R\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ and $C\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ are constant, with $L^{\mathsf T}=L$, $C^{\mathsf T}=C$, $z^{\mathsf T}Cz>0$ for every $z\ne0$, $R^{\mathsf T}=R$, and $y^{\mathsf T}Ry\ge0$ for every $y$. These inequalities define positive definiteness and positive semidefiniteness here. Symmetry alone is imposed on a declared $L$; a smooth compact-current realization can supply its additional positivity. Geometry, orientations and source data are fixed.

(b) **Element and network relations.** Adopt
$$V_L=L\dot I,\qquad V_R=RI,\qquad I_C=\dot Q,\qquad V_C=C^{-1}Q.$$
Positive definiteness makes $C^{-1}$ well defined: $Cz=0$ implies $z^{\mathsf T}Cz=0$, hence $z=0$; an injective square finite matrix is invertible by [[thm-invertible-matrix-theorem]]. The voltage drop on an inductive/resistive branch is $(V_L+V_R)_\alpha$, with either element omitted by setting its corresponding matrix to zero; a capacitive branch has drop $(V_C)_\beta$. Thus the three voltage symbols refer to distinct element drops. In a purely inductive use, abbreviate $V_L$ by $V$. The linkage is $LI$ and the induced emf convention is $e_L:=-V_L$. The capacitor scalar law is $V_C=Q/C$ when $m=1$.

For a branch $b$ let $i_b$ be its oriented current and $v_b$ its voltage drop from tail to head (a source may have a negative drop). Define the incidence matrix by $A_{ab}:=\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{tail}(b)\}}-\mathbf1_{\{a=\operatorname{head}(b)\}}$. **Kirchhoff's current law** is $Ai(t)=0$, expressing no node-charge accumulation. A **closed walk** is a finite sequence of traversals of branches with matching successive nodes and final node equal to initial node. If its signed traversal count is $z_b$ (forward minus backward), **Kirchhoff's voltage law** is $\sum_bz_bv_b(t)=0$. Adopt it for every closed walk. Equivalently it suffices to impose it on a chosen linearly independent spanning set (basis) of the real span of their traversal-count vectors; this is the meaning of independent loops here. These are imposed ideal network constraints, not statements about arbitrary field circulations.

The bookkeeping energies are $\frac12I^{\mathsf T}LI$ and $\frac12Q^{\mathsf T}C^{-1}Q$. If a smooth compact conserved-profile realization of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b) is specified, identification of its linkage matrix with the declared $L$ is an additional model premise, not automatic.

(c) **Quasistatic regime.** Specify a geometric size $\ell>0$, a time scale $T>0$ and a chosen dimensionless tolerance $0<\epsilon_{\rm qs}<1$. The declaration $\ell/(cT)\ll1$ means $\ell/(cT)\le\epsilon_{\rm qs}$ with a tolerance regarded as small in the chosen application. Negligible radiation and leakage, ideal terminals and the fixed conductor geometry are separately adopted idealizations. Neither this inequality nor these idealizations give a quantitative error bound for an arbitrary full Maxwell solution; no universal accuracy is asserted.

(d) **Units and scope.** $V_L,V_R,V_C,v_b$ carry volts, $I,I_C,i_b$ amperes, $Q$ coulombs, $t$ seconds, $L$ henries ($\mathrm H=\mathrm V\,\mathrm s\,\mathrm A^{-1}$), $C$ farads ($\mathrm F=\mathrm C\,\mathrm V^{-1}$), and $R$ ohms ($\Omega=\mathrm V\,\mathrm A^{-1}$). The model excludes radiation, distributed-element, nonlinear, hysteretic, leakage and proximity effects; resistor loss is retained through $R$. Subluminal material speeds are required if a relativistic moving-matter interpretation is added. The model is adopted and contains no measurement or derivation from the vacuum Maxwell equations.

Assume the lumped circuit model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]) for clause (b), where it is inherited from the linkage suppliers.

For $y\in\mathbb R^n$ write $y_\alpha:=y(\alpha-1)$, and for $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ write $L_{\alpha\beta}:=L(\alpha-1,\beta-1)$, where $1\le\alpha,\beta\le n$, consistently with the zero-based coordinates of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the profile labels of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]. All sums over $\alpha,\beta$ below range from $1$ to $n$.

(a) [Terminal-energy bookkeeping] Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0,t_1\in J$, let $L\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be constant and symmetric, let $I:J\to\mathbb R^n$ be of class $C^1$ in the following sense: $I$ extends to a $C^1$ map on an open interval containing $J$, so that the derivatives used below are those of the extension (one-sided at included endpoints of $J$, and not intrinsic to a value restriction when $J$ is a singleton), and let $V(t):=L\dot I(t)$ be the terminal-voltage vector of the inductive branches as adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] (the Faraday branch: the terminal voltage of a branch is the rate of change of its flux linkage $\Phi=LI$). Then
$$\int_{t_0}^{t_1}\langle V(t),I(t)\rangle\,dt=\frac12\langle I(t_1),LI(t_1)\rangle-\frac12\langle I(t_0),LI(t_0)\rangle ,$$
and for $n=1$ with $L>0$ this reads $\int_{t_0}^{t_1}V I\,dt=\frac12L\bigl(I(t_1)^2-I(t_0)^2\bigr)$: the accumulated terminal energy equals the change of the inductor bookkeeping energy $\frac12LI^2$. The identity is exact for every such $C^1$ current and fixed geometry; it uses only symmetry of $L$, the product rule and the fundamental theorem of calculus. For a changing geometry the mechanical work done on the circuit is an additional term and is not covered here.

(b) [Identification with the frozen field energy] Suppose in addition that the currents are realized by fixed compact smooth conserved profiles $j_1,\dots,j_n$ of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), with instantaneous source $J_I(t):=\sum_\alpha I_\alpha(t)j_\alpha$, and that the inductance matrix is the linkage matrix of those profiles in the sense of [[pthm-em-inductance-reciprocity]]: $L_{\alpha\beta}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\iint\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x)$. Then for every $t\in J$
$$\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I(t),A_{J_I(t)}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I(t)}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
where $A_{J_I(t)}$ is the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential and $B_{J_I(t)}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I(t)}$ of that theorem: the right-hand side is the magnetic field energy of the frozen instantaneous configuration, and the accumulated terminal energy of (a) between $t_0$ and $t_1$ is the change of this field energy. The relation $V=L\dot I$ is the explicitly adopted terminal law of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the identification of the model's inductance matrix with the smooth-profile linkage matrix is part of the adopted model of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]].

(c) [Scope] no radiation, distributed-element, material-loss, moving-geometry or thin-wire self-inductance claim is made; the frozen-configuration energy is not asserted to be the energy of a time-dependent full Maxwell solution.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), with the exact meaning of [[def-countable-choice]]. Let $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $j_1,\dots,j_n\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}j_\alpha=0$ be fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles of the class of [[def-em-steady-current-regime]](b), extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. Fix amplitudes $I\in\mathbb R^n$, label them by $I_\alpha:=I(\alpha-1)$ for $1\le\alpha\le n$ in the zero-based convention of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and put $J_I:=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nI_\alpha j_\alpha$, let $A_{J_I}$ be the Coulomb-gauge Newtonian vector potential of [[pthm-em-magnetostatic-vector-potential]] applied to the conserved current $J_I$, and let $B_{J_I}=\operatorname{curl}A_{J_I}$. Define the linkage coefficients
$$L_{\alpha\beta}:=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\langle j_\alpha(x),j_\beta(y)\rangle}{|x-y|}\,d\lambda_3(y)\,d\lambda_3(x),\qquad\alpha,\beta=1,\dots,n .$$
The amplitudes $I_\alpha$ carry amperes and the profiles $j_\alpha$ are shapes per unit current, with units $\mathrm m^{-2}$; their numerical SI maps belong to the stated smooth class. Consequently $J_I$ has unit $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$, $A_{J_I}$ has $\mathrm T\,\mathrm m$, $L_{\alpha\beta}$ has H, the linkage has Wb and $U$ has joules. $A_{j_\alpha}$ denotes the linear potential response per ampere. Then:

(a) [Finiteness and self-energy] every $L_{\alpha\beta}$ is a finite real number: the defining double integral converges absolutely, and in particular every self-coefficient $L_{\alpha\alpha}$ is finite, so the compact smooth profiles carry a finite self-energy. This is a statement about the smooth profiles only; no finite value is assigned to a zero-radius thin-wire self-inductance.

(b) [Reciprocity and flux linkage] $L_{\alpha\beta}=L_{\beta\alpha}$ for all $\alpha,\beta$; $A_{J_I}=\sum_{\alpha}I_\alpha A_{j_\alpha}$ componentwise; and for every $\beta$ the linkage integral is
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle j_\beta,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3=\sum_{\alpha=1}^nL_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha .$$
Thus the numbers $L_{\alpha\beta}$ are the linkage coefficients of the profiles: the linkage of profile $\beta$ with the field of the superposition is the linear combination $\sum_\alpha L_{\beta\alpha}I_\alpha$.

(c) [Magnetic energy and positivity] with $U(I):=\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\langle J_I,A_{J_I}\rangle\,d\lambda_3$,
$$U(I)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^nL_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha I_\beta=\frac1{2\mu_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}|B_{J_I}|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge0,$$
all quantities finite; moreover $U(I)=0$ holds precisely when $J_I=0$ on $\mathbb R^3$. Identify these profile-labelled coefficients with the standard matrix by $L(i,j):=L_{i+1,j+1}$ for $0\le i,j<n$. Consequently the symmetric matrix $L$ is positive semidefinite, and it is positive definite exactly when the profiles are pointwise linearly independent, i.e. when $\sum_\alpha I_\alpha j_\alpha\equiv0$ forces $I=0$.

(d) [Scope] the theorem concerns fixed compact smooth conserved current profiles and their Coulomb-gauge fields. It asserts no thin-wire, sheet or singular self-inductance; no time-dependent, moving, radiating or material configuration; and no uniqueness of the vector potential. The identification of these coefficients with the inductance matrix of the adopted lumped circuit model, and of the linkage derivatives with terminal voltages, is adopted in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; the strict material-loop theorem applies separately only to an actual moving sheet and compatible smooth Maxwell fields satisfying its hypotheses. No terminal-voltage law for arbitrary varying frozen profiles is inferred from the present magnetostatic computation.

For the Lebesgue/surface/distributional source and admissibility branches (c)-(d), assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The smooth formulation in (a) and the smooth conserved-current predicate in (b) do not themselves use Choice. Let the laboratory region and its chart, the field and source objects and the units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]], [[def-em-sources]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and fix $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$.

**(a) [Steady-current regime].** A steady-current (magnetostatic) configuration on $\Omega\times I$ consists of a field pair $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ and source fields $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that are independent of $t$ and satisfy the smooth branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with the operators of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For such a configuration the formal distributional branch of [[pthm-em-charge-continuity]] gives $\operatorname{div}J=0$ distributionally; this is pointwise when $J$ is $C^1$. In the jointly $C^2$ field/$C^1$ source branch its classical proof applies directly. The locally integrable distributional reading here inherits Countable Choice, whereas the stated classical $C^2/C^1$ compatibility calculation is choice-free, and the four adopted equations are equivalent to the electrostatic pair and the magnetostatic pair
$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J .$$

**(b) [Compact smooth current class].** The compact smooth current class of this framework consists of the currents $J\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with $\operatorname{div}J=0$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^3$. A magnetostatic field of such a current is a field $B$ of class $C^1$ on $\mathbb R^3$ satisfying $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ on $\mathbb R^3$ with the extended $J$. This is the hypothesis class of the vector-potential, Biot-Savart and dipole theorems of this page; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of $B$ in the class.

**(c) [Ideal source objects].** Define three ideal current source objects outside the compact class, together with the data selecting their fields. Curve parameters $s$ and $L$ and the radius $a$ carry metres; the signed line-current amplitude $I$ carries amperes and the signed sheet-current amplitude $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$. The field $B$ carries tesla, as in [[def-em-si-conventions]].

**(c1) [Closed thin loop].** For a closed embedded $C^2$ curve $\gamma:\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R^3$ with $|\gamma'|\equiv1$ ($L>0$) and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal loop current is the distribution
$$\langle J_\gamma,\psi\rangle:=I\int_0^L\gamma'(s)\cdot\psi(\gamma(s))\,ds,\qquad \psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3),$$
with $\rho_\gamma:=0$.

**(c2) [Infinite straight wire].** For $\gamma(s)=(0,0,s)$, $s\in\mathbb R$, and $I\in\mathbb R$, the ideal wire current is
$$\langle J_{\rm w},\psi\rangle:=I\int_{\mathbb R}\psi_3(0,0,s)\,ds,$$
with $\rho_{\rm w}:=0$.

**(c3) [Infinite cylindrical sheet].** For $a>0$, $S=\{\rho=a\}$, $\rho=\sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2}$, $e_\rho:=\rho^{-1}(x_1,x_2,0)$ and $e_\varphi:=\rho^{-1}(-x_2,x_1,0)$ on $\{\rho>0\}$, and $K\in\mathbb R$, the ideal solenoid sheet current is
$$\langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=K\int_S e_\varphi\cdot\psi\,dS$$
([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]], read on compact cylinder segments), with $\rho_S:=0$. All three pairings are finite because $\psi$ has compact support.

**(c4) [Admissibility].** A field $B$ is admitted for one of these declared models when: $B$ is locally integrable on $\mathbb R^3$ (hence a distribution by [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]) and $C^1$ off the support of the current; $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=0$ hold pointwise off that support; the distributional identities $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J$ hold against every scalar divergence test $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and vector curl test $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ in the sense of [[def-distributional-derivative]]; $B$ has the model's declared symmetry: in (c2) and (c3), $B(x+he_3)=B(x)$ for every $h\in\mathbb R$, and $B(R_\theta x)=R_\theta B(x)$ for every $\theta\in\mathbb R$, at off-source points, where $R_\theta(x_1,x_2,x_3)=(x_1\cos\theta-x_2\sin\theta,x_1\sin\theta+x_2\cos\theta,x_3)$; no symmetry is required in (c1); and $B$ obeys the decay requirement: $|B(x)|\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$ in (c1), and in (c2), (c3), $\sup_{(\theta,z)\in C}|B(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)|\to0$ as $r\to\infty$ for every nonempty compact $C\subset\mathbb R^2$. The companion examples exhibit and verify the fields of the two axisymmetric models in this class; the definition itself asserts no existence, uniqueness, finite energy or limiting relation for the declared models, and no compact-class theorem of this page applies to them.

**(d) [Scope].** This is a model restriction: the steady-current regime for compact smooth currents, and three explicitly declared ideal noncompact or singular models. It excludes point charges, weaker-regularity volume sources, moving sheets, normal sheet currents and any claim of empirical exactness; the equations in (c4) define a mathematical admissibility predicate; its physical adoption for these source objects is a separate postulate, and no product of distributions is formed.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

derivations.claim: Clause (a): by [F5], $\frac12\langle I(t),LI(t)\rangle=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2$, which is the displayed $W(t)$. Differentiating termwise with the product and scalar rules of [F6] gives $\dot W=L_1I_1\dot I_1+M(\dot I_1I_2+I_1\dot I_2)+L_2I_2\dot I_2=(L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2)I_1+(M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2)I_2=V_1I_1+V_2I_2$, since $[L\dot I]_\alpha=V_\alpha$; the sign reading of the mutual term is immediate from $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+\frac12L_2I_2^2+MI_1I_2$ for $M>0$.

Clause (b): under the realization hypothesis, $W(t)=\frac12\sum_{\alpha,\beta}L_{\alpha\beta}I_\alpha(t)I_\beta(t)=U(I(t))\ge0$ at each $t$ by [F3], the block $L$ being by hypothesis the linkage matrix of the two profiles. Substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2-M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; substituting $I=(\sqrt{L_2},+\sqrt{L_1})$ gives $W=L_1L_2+M\sqrt{L_1L_2}\ge0$, that is $M\ge-\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; together, $|M|\le\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. If $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$, the same expansion gives $W=L_1L_2-sM\sqrt{L_1L_2}=L_1L_2-L_1L_2=0$, so by the vanishing clause of [F3] the associated current $J_I$ vanishes pointwise.

Clause (c): with $N_1=\sqrt{L_1/\Lambda}$ and $N_2=\sqrt{L_2/\Lambda}$ one has $L_1=\Lambda N_1^2$, $L_2=\Lambda N_2^2$ and $M=\sqrt{L_1L_2}=\Lambda N_1N_2$ because $N_1N_2=\sqrt{L_1L_2}/\Lambda$. Hence, using $V_\alpha=\sum_\beta L_{\alpha\beta}\dot I_\beta$, $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda N_2(N_1\dot I_1+N_2\dot I_2)=N_2\dot\Phi_c$ with $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)$; dividing by $N_1,N_2>0$ gives the common ratio, and $e_\alpha=-V_\alpha$ reverses the common sign. For the energy, $W=\frac12L_1I_1^2+MI_1I_2+\frac12L_2I_2^2=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+N_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$ by the displayed relations and the binomial expansion.

Clause (d), strict-linkage non-identity: suppose $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$ and $V_2=kV_1$ held for all $C^1$ currents on $J$; then $\sum_\beta L_{2\beta}\dot I_\beta=k\sum_\beta L_{1\beta}\dot I_\beta$ for every such current. Fix any point $t_0\in J$ (any point when $J$ is a singleton) and, for each vector $a=(a_1,a_2)\in\mathbb R^2$, take the affine history $I(t)=c+(t-t_0)a$ (any fixed $c\in\mathbb R^2$) on $J$, which is the restriction of the affine map of $t$ on $\mathbb R$ and hence carries the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension with $\dot I\equiv a$; substituting gives $(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2=0$ for all $a$, hence $L_{21}=kL_{11}$ and $L_{22}=kL_{12}$, i.e. $\operatorname{row}_2L=k\operatorname{row}_1L$. Then $L_1k=M$ and $L_2=kM=M^2/L_1$, so $L_1L_2-M^2=0$, contradicting $L_1L_2-M^2>0$ from $|M|<\sqrt{L_1L_2}$; hence no such $k$ makes the ratio a universal identity. Accidental satisfaction occurs: any history with $\dot I$ in the kernel of the nonzero functional $a\mapsto(L_{21}-kL_{11})a_1+(L_{22}-kL_{12})a_2$ satisfies $V_2=kV_1$ at every time, that kernel containing the nonzero vector $(L_{22}-kL_{12},-(L_{21}-kL_{11}))$ because the row difference is nonzero; in particular the constant currents give $V_1=V_2=0$. For the reversed winding with $M=s\sqrt{L_1L_2}$, put $\Phi_c=\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)$; then $V_1=L_1\dot I_1+M\dot I_2=\Lambda N_1(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=N_1\dot\Phi_c$ and $V_2=M\dot I_1+L_2\dot I_2=\Lambda sN_2(N_1\dot I_1+sN_2\dot I_2)=sN_2\dot\Phi_c$ because $s^2=1$, so $V_1/N_1=V_2/(sN_2)=\dot\Phi_c$, and $W=\frac12\Lambda(N_1I_1+sN_2I_2)^2=\Phi_c^2/(2\Lambda)$.

Steps 1.1-1.4 establish (a)-(d): steps 1.1-1.2 give (a) and the bound and null-direction clauses of (b), and steps 1.3-1.4 give the common-flux model (c) and the limitations (d). The computation is conditional on the adopted lumped model [F1], its units are [F7], and no leakage, loss, material or measurement claim is added; the terminal-voltage jets on a singleton interval are those of the specified extension. Countable Choice is used only through the realization clause (b), via [F3]; the algebraic clauses (a), (c) and (d) are choice-free.

boundaries.evidence: The block has the fixed size $2$ and $L_1,L_2>0$; the algebra of steps 1.1-1.4 needs no nonemptiness beyond these hypotheses, and the zero-current case is covered separately.

For $I_1=I_2=0$ step 1.1 gives $W=0$ and $V_1=V_2=0$; step 1.4's kernel description includes the constant (hence zero-derivative) histories, and the common-flux relations of step 1.3 degenerate to $\Phi_c=0$ with $W=0$.
The turns ratio is fixed by the model data: $N_1=N_2=1$ when $L_1=L_2=\Lambda$, as step 1.3 displays, and no other counting parameter occurs.

At perfect linkage the null direction $I=(\sqrt{L_2},-s\sqrt{L_1})$ is a genuinely nonzero current vector, so step 1.2 exhibits a nontrivial kernel of $L$; under strict linkage step 1.4 uses $L_1L_2-M^2>0$, i.e. positive definiteness, and the contradiction follows from the forced vanishing of that determinant.

The interval $J$ may be non-open; the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension of the currents supplies the derivatives used in steps 1.1-1.4, and no separate endpoint claim is made. J is nonempty, including singleton specified jets; the affine-history counterargument can select t0. Lambda has unit H and N1,N2 are positive real dimensionless effective winding factors, not promised integer counts.
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used only through the realization clause (b) via [F3] in step 1.2; the algebraic clauses (a), (c) and (d) of steps 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 are choice-free, as step 2.1 records.
No if-and-only-if claim is made; the vanishing clause used in step 1.2 is the quoted equivalence of [F3], and the item proves equalities (the bound, the ratio, the energy) rather than equivalences.

There is no converse direction; step 1.4 proves a negative statement (failure of a universal voltage ratio) by contradiction and exhibits accidental histories satisfying the ratio without claiming that they realise the ideal model.

Assume the lumped circuit model and its units as in [[post-em-circuit-approximation]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval ([[def-interval]]) and let $t_0\in J$. For a nondegenerate $J$, derivatives are domain-relative, with one-sided values at included endpoints, in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; the functions constructed below also admit the stated $C^k$ open-neighbourhood extensions. If $J=\{t_0\}$, the formulas specify the initial values and the jets of the explicitly constructed extensions below, rather than an intrinsic derivative of a singleton restriction. The RL solution, the LC candidate and the bookkeeping-energy algebra use no choice principle. Only the optional geometric capacitor identification in (b) assumes full Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ consequence ([[def-countable-choice]]), exactly as [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] requires. The inductive energy is that of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]].

(a) [RL circuit] Let $L>0$ and $R\ge0$ be constants and let $V:J\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then the initial value problem
$$L\dot I(t)+R\,I(t)=V(t),\qquad I(t_0)=I_0\in\mathbb R,$$
has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate $J$, namely
$$I(t)=\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)\Bigl[I_0+\frac1L\int_{t_0}^{t}\exp\!\Bigl(\frac{R(s-t_0)}{L}\Bigr)V(s)\,ds\Bigr],$$
and along it the inductive bookkeeping energy satisfies the power identity
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\Bigl(\frac12LI(t)^2\Bigr)=L\dot I(t)I(t)=V(t)I(t)-R\,I(t)^2 ,$$
i.e. the terminal power splits into the rate of change of the inductive energy and the Ohmic term $RI^2$. (For $R=0$ the same formula reduces to $I=I_0+L^{-1}\int_{t_0}^tV$.) For $J=\{t_0\}$ its unique restriction is $I(t_0)=I_0$; the canonical extension obtained using the constant source $V(t_0)$ has jet $\dot I(t_0)=(V(t_0)-RI_0)/L$ and satisfies the same power algebra. No uniqueness of arbitrary extension germs is asserted.

(b) [LC oscillation] Let $L>0$, $C>0$ and set $\Omega:=(LC)^{-1/2}>0$, $z_0:=Q_0-\mathrm i\,I_0/\Omega$, $w(t):=z_0\exp(\mathrm i\Omega(t-t_0))$ with the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]], and $Q(t):=\operatorname{Re}w(t)$. Then $Q$ is of class $C^2$ on $J$, $Q(t_0)=Q_0$, $Q'(t_0)=I_0$, and
$$L\,Q''(t)+\frac{Q(t)}{C}=0\qquad\text{on }J ;$$
equivalently, with the real trigonometric functions of [[thm-eulers-formula]],
$$Q(t)=Q_0\cos\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{I_0}{\Omega}\sin\bigl(\Omega(t-t_0)\bigr).$$
Moreover the total bookkeeping energy
$$E(t):=\frac12L\,Q'(t)^2+\frac{Q(t)^2}{2C}$$
satisfies $E'(t)=Q'(t)\bigl(LQ''(t)+Q(t)/C\bigr)=0$ on $J$, hence $E$ is constant with value $\frac12LI_0^2+\frac{Q_0^2}{2C}$: the two terms are the adopted capacitive and inductive bookkeeping energies, the latter as in [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](a), so in the lossless loop their sum is conserved. For the additional geometric identification, explicitly choose the fixed compact separated conductor arrangement of [[pthm-em-capacitance-energy]] with bounded smooth ambient domain, connected vacuum, grounded outer boundary, zero volume source and its unit-Dirichlet solutions; drive only conductor 1 and ground the others, set the circuit parameter $C$ equal to that arrangement's $C_{11}>0$, and at each time set $V_1=Q/C_{11}$. Under full AC that supplier gives the frozen electrostatic field energy $Q^2/(2C_{11})$. An arbitrary declared $C>0$ is model data and is not automatically the capacitance of a particular arrangement. Any magnetic field-energy identification likewise requires the extra smooth-profile linkage realization of [[pthm-em-inductor-energy]](b), under its $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ hypothesis. Neither frozen realization is an asserted time-dependent full Maxwell solution. At a singleton time the entire LC candidate supplies the jets $\dot Q=I_0$, $\ddot Q=-Q_0/(LC)$ and the same constant energy.

(c) [Scope] both statements are consequences of the expressly adopted circuit reduction, with the sign conventions and relations of [[post-em-circuit-approximation]]; they assert no general network completeness, no derivation from the full time-dependent Maxwell system, no radiation or distributed-element effect and no empirical claim.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

$$\exp(x)\to+\infty\quad(x\to+\infty),\qquad \exp(x)\to0\quad(x\to-\infty),$$
and the range of $\exp$ is contained in $(0,\infty)$ and is unbounded above with infimum $0$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

derivations.claim: Define the candidate $\varphi(t):=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ on $J$. The function $t\mapsto-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ is affine with derivative $-\frac RL$ by [F3], and $\exp'=\exp$ by [F2], so the chain rule [F4] gives $\varphi'(t)=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\left(-\frac RL\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)=-\frac RL\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)$. Therefore $L\varphi'(t)+R\varphi(t)=-R\left(\varphi(t)-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)+R\varphi(t)=V_0$ identically, and $\varphi(t_0)=\frac{V_0}{R}+\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)=I_0$.

Stationary solutions: if $I\equiv c$ is constant, then $L\dot I+RI=Rc$, so the equation $L\dot I+RI=V_0$ holds exactly when $c=V_0/R$; since $R>0$ there is exactly one such constant, namely $I\equiv V_0/R$.

Limit statement: if $J$ is unbounded above, then for $t\in J\cap[t_0,+\infty)$ the argument $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}$ satisfies $-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\to-\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$ because $R/L>0$, so [F5] gives $\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)\to0$ and hence $I(t)\to V_0/R$ along that ray; the time constant is $\tau:=L/R$, so the decay factor is $\exp(-(t-t_0)/\tau)$.

Deviation identity: subtracting $V_0/R$ from the displayed formula gives $I(t)-V_0/R=\left(I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right)\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$; since $\exp(x)>0$ for real $x$ by [F6], taking absolute values preserves the exponential factor, so $|I(t)-V_0/R|=\left|I_0-\frac{V_0}{R}\right|\exp\left(-\frac{R(t-t_0)}{L}\right)$ for every $t\in J$.

Identification of the solution: by step 1.1 the candidate $\varphi$ is a $C^1$ solution of the initial value problem (its derivative exists on all of $J$ through the stated extension convention) and by [F1] the initial value problem with the constant source $V\equiv V_0$ has exactly one $C^1$ solution on every nondegenerate $J$; hence the displayed $I$ equals $\varphi$ there and is the unique solution, and for $J=\{t_0\}$ the restriction and jets are those of [F1] with $V(t_0)=V_0$, namely $I(t_0)=I_0$ and $\dot I(t_0)=(V_0-RI_0)/L$.

Steps 1.1-1.4 and 2.1 establish the formula, its uniqueness, the deviation identity with time constant $\tau=L/R$, the unique stationary solution, the limit behaviour on intervals unbounded above, and the singleton reading. The computation uses only the adopted lumped model and its constant positive elements, with units [F7]; no radiation, distributed-element, material or measurement claim is added, and the RL existence and uniqueness supplier is the choice-free clause (a) of [F1].

boundaries.evidence: The hypothesis $t_0\in J$ excludes an empty interval; no family or indexed set is present, and step 2.1 disposes of the singleton case $J=\{t_0\}$.
For $V_0=0$ the formula gives $I(t)=I_0\exp(-R(t-t_0)/L)$ with $V_0/R=0$; for $I_0=0$ and $V_0=0$ it gives $I\equiv0$, and step 1.1 verifies the equation $0=0$ in that case.
The circuit is scalar (one branch); the single time constant is $\tau=L/R$ as recorded in step 1.3, and no counting parameter occurs.
For $J=\{t_0\}$ step 2.1 gives the restriction $I(t_0)=I_0$ and the jet $(V_0-RI_0)/L$ from [F1]'s canonical extension, and asserts no intrinsic derivative of the singleton restriction.

For non-open $J$ the derivative is read through the stated $C^1$ open-neighbourhood extension; step 1.1 differentiates on all of $J$ through that convention and step 2.1 invokes [F1]'s endpoint and singleton clauses.
The example uses no choice: [F1]'s RL clause is explicitly choice-free (step 2.1) and the calculus and exponential suppliers used in steps 1.1-1.4 are choice-free.
The only uniqueness statement is that $I\equiv V_0/R$ is the unique stationary solution, proved in step 1.2 by solving $Rc=V_0$; no if-and-only-if is asserted.
There is no converse direction; the limit of step 1.3 is one-directional ($t\to+\infty$ along a ray of $J$) and does not claim convergence in the reverse time direction.

citations.quote:
**Regularity convention for a possibly non-open parameter interval.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval and let $k\in\mathbb N$. A map on $U\times I$ is **jointly $C^k$** when it is the restriction of a $C^k$ map on some open neighbourhood $N\subseteq\mathbb R^4$ of $U\times I$, in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; it is **jointly $C^\infty$** when it is the restriction of one smooth map on such an open neighbourhood. For open $I$ these are exactly the usual open-domain classes; at included endpoints of a nondegenerate interval, time derivatives are the corresponding relative one-sided derivatives. For empty or singleton $I$ the convention still asserts extension existence and the spatial identities below, but it does not determine time jets uniquely from the restricted values alone. The convention does not require a fixed uniform enlargement of an unbounded $I$.

**Vector witness.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and star-shaped with centre $a\in U$ ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval, let $k\ge1$, and let $B:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$ ([[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]). Then

$$A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr)\times(x-a)\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the curl being taken in the spatial variables and the cross product being that of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

**Scalar witness.** If in addition $C:U\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $U$ for every $t\in I$, then

$$\phi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\bigl\langle C\bigl(a+s(x-a),t\bigr),\,x-a\bigr\rangle\,ds$$

is jointly $C^k$ on $U\times I$ and

$$\nabla\phi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)\qquad(t\in I),$$

the gradient and inner product being those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. For jointly $C^\infty$ data both potentials are jointly $C^\infty$. No global potential on a non-star-shaped open set is claimed, and the restrictions are continuous at included endpoints by joint regularity.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $c>0$ and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ be open. A **scalar-vector potential pair** of class $C^k$ on $\Omega$, for an integer $k\ge1$, is a pair $(\varphi,A)$ with $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ each of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], the components of $A$ being of class $C^k$ separately; the pair is **smooth** when both members are $C^\infty$, and **continuous**, or of class $C^0$, when both members are continuous. A pair defined on a set of the form $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ with $t_0<T$ is of class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, **in the extension sense** when there are an open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ and a potential pair of class $C^k$ on the open set $\mathbb R^3\times J$ whose restriction to $\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T]$ the given pair is; the same wording is used for $C^\infty$ and for the single functions $\varphi$ and $\chi$ below.

All operators $\nabla$, $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\Delta$ below act on the three spatial coordinates with $t$ fixed: for $\Omega_t:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:(x,t)\in\Omega\}$, apply the cited three-dimensional operators to the restrictions $x\mapsto\varphi(x,t)$, $x\mapsto A(x,t)$ or $x\mapsto u(x,t)$ on the open set $\Omega_t$. In particular $\nabla\varphi=(\partial_{x_1}\varphi,\partial_{x_2}\varphi,\partial_{x_3}\varphi)$ and $\Delta u=\sum_{i=1}^3\partial_{x_i}^2u$; $\partial_t$ differentiates only the time coordinate.

For a potential pair of class $C^k$ with $k\ge1$ its **electric field** and **magnetic field** are

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. Both $E(\varphi,A)$ and $B(\varphi,A)$ are maps $\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$.

For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is the function

$$G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi,$$

also of class $C^{k-1}$, and the pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega$ when $G(\varphi,A)=0$ throughout $\Omega$.

For $k\ge2$ and a function $\chi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^k$, a **gauge function**, the **gauge transform** of the pair is

$$T_{\chi}(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

again a potential pair, of class $C^{k-1}$.

Finally, for a function $u:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ put

$$Wu:=c^{-2}\partial_t^2u-\Delta u,$$

with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and $\partial_t^2$ the second partial derivative in $t$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]); this is the normalization $W=c^{-2}\Box_c$ of the wave operator $\Box_c=\partial_t^2-c^2\Delta$ of speed $c$ of [[def-wave-equation-cauchy-data-and-wave-speed]]. For a map $U:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ of class $C^2$ with components $U_1,\dots,U_m$, one writes $WU:=(WU_1,\dots,WU_m)$ componentwise.

Nothing in this definition asserts that a gauge function with prescribed auxiliary data exists, that every potential pair is gauge equivalent to a pair in Lorenz gauge, or that $Wu=g$ is solvable: those are conclusions with their own hypotheses. The signs $-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $A+\nabla\chi$, the factor $c^{-2}$ in $G$, and the spelling *Lorenz* are part of the convention.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$

$$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle\nabla f,F\rangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$

If moreover $n=3$, then

$$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=\nabla f\times F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$

Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $\nabla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $\phi:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$. Then $\nabla\phi$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\nabla\phi=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

derivations.claim: Hypothesis check and vector step. The set $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped with centre $a$ and $I$ is an interval, and by [F2] the field $B$ is jointly $C^k$ with $\operatorname{div}B(\cdot,t)=0$ on $\Omega$ for every $t\in I$, the divergence being that of [F9]. Since $k\ge2\ge1$, the vector witness of [F1] applies and produces the field $A(x,t):=\int_0^1s\,B(a+s(x-a),t)\times(x-a)\,ds$, which is jointly $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ and satisfies $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ for every $t\in I$.

Converse. Let $\varphi$ and $A$ be jointly $C^\infty$ on $\Omega\times I$ and put $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B:=\operatorname{curl}A$. All functions are restrictions of $C^\infty$ maps on an open neighbourhood of $\Omega\times I$, so the identities below may be checked there and restricted. The field $A$ is $C^\infty$, hence $C^2$, and [F7] gives $\operatorname{div}B=\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}A=0$. For the curl of $E$, the linearity of the curl [F5] gives $\operatorname{curl}E=-\operatorname{curl}\nabla\varphi-\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA$; the first term vanishes by [F8] applied to the $C^2$ function $\varphi$, and for the second, the component formula of [F9] turns each coordinate of $\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA$ into a difference of mixed derivatives $\partial_t\partial_x$ and $\partial_x\partial_t$ of the $C^2$ components of $A$, which [F6] identifies, so $\operatorname{curl}\partial_tA=\partial_t\operatorname{curl}A=\partial_tB$. Hence $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ on $\Omega\times I$.

The auxiliary field $C:=E+\partial_tA$. The fields $E$ and $A$ are restrictions to $\Omega\times I$ of $C^k$ maps on a common open neighbourhood; the time partial derivative of each component of the $C^k$ map extending $A$ exists and is $C^{k-1}$ there by [F4] and [F9], and the class is closed under sums by [F4], so $C$ is jointly $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$ in the restriction convention.

The auxiliary field is curl-free at every time. Fix $t\in I$. By linearity of the curl [F5] and the componentwise commutation of $\partial_t$ with the spatial partial derivatives of the jointly $C^2$ field $A$, which is [F6] applied to the component functions, $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)+\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}A)(\cdot,t)$, the operators and the derivative being those of [F9]. By step 1.1, $\operatorname{curl}A(\cdot,t)=B(\cdot,t)$ as functions of the position variable, so $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}A)(\cdot,t)=\partial_tB(\cdot,t)$; by [F2], $\operatorname{curl}E(\cdot,t)=-\partial_tB(\cdot,t)$. Substituting gives $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=-\partial_tB(\cdot,t)+\partial_tB(\cdot,t)=0$.

Scalar step and the pair identities. By step 2.1 the field $C$ is jointly $C^{k-1}$ with $k-1\ge1$, and by step 2.2 it satisfies $\operatorname{curl}C(\cdot,t)=0$ on $\Omega$ for every $t\in I$; the scalar witness of [F1] therefore gives the jointly $C^{k-1}$ function $\varphi(x,t):=-\int_0^1\langle C(a+s(x-a),t),x-aangle\,ds$ with $
abla\varphi(\cdot,t)=-C(\cdot,t)$ for every $t\in I$. Since $C=E+\partial_tA$ by step 2.1, this reads $
abla\varphi=-E-\partial_tA$, that is $E=-
abla\varphi-\partial_tA$ on $\Omega	imes I$; together with $\operatorname{curl}A=B$ from step 1.1 this exhibits $(\varphi,A)$ as a potential pair with field pair $(E,B)$ in the sense of [F3], with $\varphi$ jointly $C^{k-1}$ and $A$ jointly $C^k$.

If $E$ and $B$ are jointly $C^\infty$, the vector witness of [F1] applied to $B$ gives a jointly $C^\infty$ field $A$ with $\operatorname{curl}A=B$, the field $C=E+\partial_tA$ is jointly $C^\infty$ by the closure and differentiation rules of [F4], and the scalar witness of [F1] applied to $C$ gives a jointly $C^\infty$ scalar $\varphi$ with $\nabla\varphi=-C$; the identities of step 3.1 then hold with both potentials jointly $C^\infty$.

Conclusion and bookkeeping. Steps 1.1 through 3.1 produce, for every integer $k\ge2$, a jointly $C^{k-1}$ scalar $\varphi$ and a jointly $C^k$ vector $A$ with $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ and $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ on $\Omega\times I$; step 4.1 supplies the jointly $C^\infty$ choice when the data are jointly $C^\infty$; and step 1.2 proves the converse implication.
