citations.quote:
Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter**
$q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the
sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is
not asserted.

(b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on
$\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$,
$J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of
class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the
**frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density**
(A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if
$V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define

$$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$

by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by
[[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the
full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]),
as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded
Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$,
define

$$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$

where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is
defined through its positive and negative parts
([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]],
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The
function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open
$O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively
open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of
$\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$
([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely
finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by
[[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by
[[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the
monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound
$\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator
integral being its simple-function value
([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the
positive and negative parts are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On
the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption,
$Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]].
The
empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains
defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current
flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced
orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]].
Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are
different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them.

(c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and
$j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the
charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model,
and hence the component transformation law of
[[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts.
This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents.

(d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch]
Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a
$C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier
$\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so
$u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic
convention is $j^0=c\rho$,

$$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$

Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$,
including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent
to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike
$U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge
density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or
proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its
coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is
$v^i:=cu^i$.

For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the
material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model
condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch,
$U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and

$$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$

Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model:
in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The
equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$
(equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are
retained.

(e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and
their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved
for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and

$$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$

Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

derivations.claim: On $W$ the source terms vanish, so the Faraday and Ampère equations become $\partial_tB=-\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_tE=c^2\operatorname{curl}B$, the second obtained from $\operatorname{curl}B=c^{-2}\partial_tE$ by multiplying by $c^2$; both displays hold pointwise on $W$, and each side is a continuous combination of first partial derivatives of $E,B$, and is therefore $C^1$ because $E,B$ are jointly $C^2$ there.

The conclusion is local on the open set $W$ and uses only the smooth branch: no decay, boundedness, compact-support, finite-energy or boundary hypothesis was imposed or needed, the weak branch and singular source support are excluded, and no empirical or existence claim is made.

Differentiating the two displays of step 1.1 in time gives $\partial_t^2E=c^2\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}B)$ and $\partial_t^2B=-\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}E)$ on $W$; by step 1.1's differentiability and [F4] the time derivative commutes with every spatial partial derivative, so $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}B)=\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tB)$ and $\partial_t(\operatorname{curl}E)=\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tE)$; substituting the displays of step 1.1 yields $\partial_t^2E=c^2\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tB)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E$ and $\partial_t^2B=-\operatorname{curl}(\partial_tE)=-c^2\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B$ on $W$.

Fix $(x,t)\in W$; by [F1] the spatial field $E(\cdot,t)$ is $C^2$ on the open set $\Omega$, so [F3] gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E=\nabla\operatorname{div}E-\Delta E$ at $(x,t)$, and the Gauss equation $\operatorname{div}E=0$ of [F2] on $W$ turns this into $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E=-\Delta E$; the identical computation with $B$ gives $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}B=-\Delta B$. Substituting these into step 2.1 gives $\partial_t^2E=c^2\Delta E$ and $\partial_t^2B=c^2\Delta B$ on $W$, that is $\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E$ and $\Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B$ componentwise: each component $v$ of $E$ or of $B$ satisfies $c^{-2}\partial_t^2v=\Delta v$ on $W$.

The derivation used both Gauss constraints through step 3.1; without $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ one obtains only the curl-curl forms of step 2.1. No converse holds: on $W=\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the time-independent field $E(x)=(x_1,0,0)$, $B=0$ is $C^\infty$, is affine in $x_1$ so that $\Delta E=0$ and $\partial_t^2E=0$, and therefore satisfies both vector wave equations, while $\operatorname{div}E=1$ violates the constraint $\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ with $\rho=0$; hence it lies in no source-free smooth Maxwell branch and the wave equations do not imply the four Maxwell equations.

Steps 1.1, 2.1, 3.1 and 4.1 derive the two displayed vector wave equations on $W$ from the four smooth-branch equations with vanishing sources, record the hypotheses actually used (time differentiation, Clairaut commutation, the curl-curl identity and the two Gauss constraints), and exhibit a witness showing that the implication is one-directional; step 1.2 records the scope.

citations.quote:
Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for
the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the
laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with
$\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of
[[def-em-si-conventions]].

(a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional
derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let
$\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative
$\partial_t$ at fixed position of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$

(b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued
fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on
$I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). Let
$\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and $\partial_t$ act as
distributional derivatives, componentwise, and let $\psi$ range over
$C_c^\infty(I\times\Omega)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]).
Then the same four identities hold in the sense of [[def-distribution]]: the
pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\qquad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish for every such $\psi$, all derivatives being distributional
derivatives ([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(c) [Scope] The postulate contains no magnetic charge: $\operatorname{div}B=0$
and no magnetic-source term appears in $\operatorname{curl}E$. Sources that
are not locally integrable functions (point or sheet sources) are covered by
neither branch and require their own definition. The equations are adopted
classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from
charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity
postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of
inertial frame.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$, $\|u\times v\|_2^2=\det G(u,v)$, and this value is positive exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.

Equivalently,
$$\|u\times v\|_2^2=\|u\|_2^2\|v\|_2^2-\langle u,v\rangle^2.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Assume the smooth branch of the vacuum Maxwell postulate
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of
[[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, the divergence and curl of
[[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the Laplacian $\Delta$ of
[[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]. Let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be
jointly $C^2$ fields of [[def-em-fields]], let $(\rho,J)$ be the source fields
of [[def-em-sources]], and let $W\subseteq\Omega\times I$ be open with
$\rho=0$ and $J=0$ on $W$ (a source-free region). Then on $W$, componentwise,

$$\Delta E=c^{-2}\partial_t^2E,\qquad \Delta B=c^{-2}\partial_t^2B;$$

equivalently each of the six Cartesian components of $E$ and of $B$ satisfies
the scalar wave equation $c^{-2}\partial_t^2v=\Delta v$ of speed $c$ on $W$.

(a) [Hypotheses actually used] The derivation differentiates the Faraday and
Ampère equations in time, commutes the time derivative with
$\operatorname{curl}$ (Clairaut's theorem, available for jointly $C^2$ fields),
uses the curl-curl identity of [[cor-the-curl-of-a-curl-of-a-c2-field]], and
uses the two Gauss equations $\operatorname{div}E=0$,
$\operatorname{div}B=0$ on $W$. The two evolution equations alone are not
sufficient for the conclusion without the constraint equations.

(b) [One-directional] No converse is asserted. The two vector wave equations do
not imply the four source-free Maxwell equations: the constraints
$\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{div}B=0$ and the two curl relations are not
recovered, and solutions of the six uncoupled scalar wave equations need not
lie in a source-free smooth Maxwell branch. The correctly constrained
initial-value problem is a separate result on this page.

(c) [Scope] Only the smooth branch is covered. No decay, boundedness, compact
support, finite-energy or boundary hypothesis is imposed or needed; the
conclusion is local on $W$, asserts no value of any field or derivative at a
point of singular source support, and does not cover the weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. The result is conditional on the adopted postulates
and makes no empirical claim.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$
For every real $\theta$, $\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

derivations.claim: For the fields of [F1] with phase $\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$, differentiation through the real part gives componentwise $\partial_{x_j}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,k_je\,\exp(i\theta))$ and $\partial_tE=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\,e\,\exp(i\theta))$, hence $\operatorname{div}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,(k\cdot e)\exp(i\theta))$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=\operatorname{Re}(i\,(k\times e)\exp(i\theta))$; replacing $e$ by $b$ gives the same four displays with $B$ and $b$. Indeed each component of $(x,t)\mapsto e_j\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is a composition of the entire exponential with the real-linear maps $(x,t)\mapsto i\theta(x,t)$ and multiplication by the constant $e_j$, so the chain rule [F4] gives $\partial_{x_j}(e_j\exp(i\theta))=e_j\exp(i\theta)\,ik_j$ and $\partial_t(e_j\exp(i\theta))=e_j\exp(i\theta)(-i\omega)$; the derivative of the real part equals the real part of the derivative because $\operatorname{Re}$ is $\mathbb R$-linear [F4], and summing coordinates with the coordinate formulas for divergence and curl [F4] and the cross-product formula [F3] gives the displays.

citations.quote:
Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and $\omega>0$, let $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$,
and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave pair of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on
the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with phase
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$. Suppose the amplitude conditions of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] hold, so that $k\cdot e=0$ and
$b=k\times e/\omega$. By that theorem, if the pair is nonzero then it also
satisfies the dispersion relation $|k|=\omega/c$, while the zero pair is
permitted for every $k\ne0$ and $\omega>0$, both on and off this dispersion
relation. This item classifies the polarization of that class of transverse
plane waves; it adds no field-theoretic content.

Write $e=a+id$ with the real vectors $a=\operatorname{Re}e$ and
$d=\operatorname{Im}e$ of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]],
applied componentwise in $\mathbb C^3$; since $k$ is real and $k\cdot e=0$, the
real and imaginary parts of this complex equation give
$\langle k,a\rangle=\langle k,d\rangle=0$. Put $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $|\cdot|$ and $\times$ be the inner product, norm
and cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. Then:

(a) [Trace] At every fixed $x$ one has
$E(x,t)=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ with $\theta=\theta(x,t)$. The curve
$\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, $\gamma(\theta):=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$,
lies in the transverse plane
$k^\perp=\{v\in\mathbb R^3:\langle k,v\rangle=0\}$; it is the image of the unit
circle $S^1=\{(u_1,u_2)\in\mathbb R^2:u_1^2+u_2^2=1\}$ under the $\mathbb R$-linear
map $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$; it is $2\pi$-periodic in the phase parameter
$\theta$ and satisfies $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$, while the map
$t\mapsto E(x,t)$ has time period $T=2\pi/\omega$. The curve $\gamma$ is
called the **polarization trace** at $x$; it does not depend on $x$, so the
classification below is the same at every point.

(b) [Classification] Exactly one of the following three cases holds.

(i) **Linear polarization**: $\dim_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$.
When $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the trace is a nontrivial closed
segment in that span, traversed twice per period; when $a=d=0$, the trace is
the single point $\{0\}$ and $(E,B)$ is the zero wave.

(ii) **Circular polarization**: $|a|=|d|>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=0$. The
trace is the circle of radius $|a|$ in $k^\perp$, and $|E(x,t)|=|a|$ for all
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(iii) **Elliptical (nondegenerate, noncircular) polarization**:
$\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$ and not (ii). Here a **nondegenerate ellipse centred at $0$** in a real plane $P$ means
the set $L(S^1)$ for a real-linear isomorphism $L:\mathbb R^2\to P$.
The trace is such an ellipse in $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$, and the
origin lies in the relative interior of the enclosed region
$L(\{u\in\mathbb R^2:|u|\le1\})$ in that plane. If in addition $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the
parametrization is along principal axes and the semiaxis lengths are $|a|$ and
$|d|$; the general principal-axis computation is not asserted by this item.

(c) [Handedness] For $a,d\in k^\perp$, the cross product $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $a$ and to $d$
([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), hence parallel
to $k$; define the **helicity sign**
$H:=\langle a\times d,\hat k\rangle\in\mathbb R$, whose sign is taken in the
order of [[def-real-order]]. One has $H=0$ exactly in the linear case (i), and
$H\ne0$ otherwise. This library calls the polarization **right-handed** when
$H<0$ and **left-handed** when $H>0$. Geometrically, $H<0$ means that at fixed
$x$ the electric vector rotates clockwise as seen by an observer facing the
incoming wave (looking along $-\hat k$), and $H>0$ means counterclockwise;
here the screen orientation is fixed by any positive orthonormal triad
$(u,v,\hat k)$, with $u$ to the right and $v$ up for that observer.
Equivalently, $\langle E(x,t)\times\partial_tE(x,t),\hat k\rangle=\omega H$ for
every $(x,t)$. The names "right" and "left" handedness are conventional and
both conventions occur in the literature, so later statements in this library
use only the sign of $H$.

(d) [Status] This is a classification definition. It introduces the trace,
the three cases and the sign $H$, and asserts no field equation, no
propagation, energy or empirical content. The magnetic amplitude enters only
through the two amplitude conditions $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$
recalled above; the definition covers the zero wave, both on and off the
dispersion relation, and no non-plane or non-transverse field is classified.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The real vectors $a,d$ are well defined by the componentwise real and
imaginary parts of $e$; because $k$ is real, taking real and imaginary parts of
$k\cdot e=\sum_jk_j(a_j+id_j)$ gives $\langle k,a\rangle=0$ and
$\langle k,d\rangle=0$, so $a,d\in k^\perp$ and $\gamma$ takes values in
$k^\perp$. The trace formula in (a) is Euler's formula
$\exp(i\theta)=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ of [[thm-eulers-formula]] together with
the field arithmetic on the right-hand side of
$E=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a+id)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\bigr)
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)+i(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)\bigr)$
and the real-linearity of $\operatorname{Re}$: the real part is
$a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$, while the imaginary part is not a field. Since
$\theta(x,t)=k\cdot x-\omega t$ and $\omega>0$, at fixed $x$ the map
$t\mapsto\theta$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$; hence the set traced by
$E(x,t)$ as $t$ varies is the full image $\gamma(\mathbb R)$, independently of
$x$, and $\gamma$ is $2\pi$-periodic with $\gamma(\theta+\pi)=-\gamma(\theta)$
because $\cos$ and $\sin$ shift by a sign under $\theta\mapsto\theta+\pi$. The
time period is $T=2\pi/\omega$, the least positive $s$ with
$\theta(x,t+s)=\theta(x,t)-2\pi$ for all $(x,t)$; it is distinct from the
phase-parameter period $2\pi$ of $\gamma$.

For the classification, "exactly one of the three cases holds" is checked
case by case: if $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\le1$ then (i); otherwise
$\dim=2$, and either $|a|=|d|>0$ with $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, which is (ii),
or not, which is (iii). In case (i) with $\dim=1$, write $d=\lambda a$ with
$a\ne0$ (or symmetrically $a=\mu d$); then
$\gamma(\theta)=(\cos\theta-\lambda\sin\theta)a$, whose image is the segment
$\{sa:|s|\le\sqrt{1+\lambda^2}\}$ in $\mathbb R a$, traversed once in each direction between successive extrema of the scalar
factor (each such phase interval has length $\pi$). In case (ii),
expanding with the bilinearity of the inner product
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) gives
$|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2-2u_1u_2\langle a,d\rangle=|a|^2$
whenever $|a|=|d|$, $\langle a,d\rangle=0$ and $u_1^2+u_2^2=1$, so the image
of the unit circle under $(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is contained in the
circle of radius $|a|$ in the plane $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; conversely,
for every $v$ in that plane with $|v|=|a|$ the coordinates
$u_1=\langle v,a\rangle/|a|^2$ and $u_2=-\langle v,d\rangle/|d|^2$ satisfy
$u_1^2+u_2^2=1$ and $u_1a-u_2d=v$, because $a/|a|$ and $d/|d|$ are orthonormal
and $v=\langle v,a/|a|\rangle(a/|a|)+\langle v,d/|d|\rangle(d/|d|)$; hence the
trace is exactly that circle. In case (iii) the vectors $a,d$
are linearly independent, so $T:(u_1,u_2)\mapsto u_1a-u_2d$ is a linear
isomorphism of $\mathbb R^2$ onto the two-dimensional plane
$\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}$; the image of the closed unit disk under $T$ is a
compact convex subset with nonempty interior in that plane, the image of the
open disk is its nonempty interior, and the image of the unit circle is its
boundary, so the trace is a nondegenerate ellipse centred at
$0=T(0)$ with the origin in the relative interior of that enclosed region.
The trace itself is its boundary and has empty interior in the plane. If moreover
$\langle a,d\rangle=0$, then along the principal axes $a,d$ the parametrization
$u_1a-u_2d$ has the stated axis lengths because the two summands are
orthogonal: $|u_1a-u_2d|^2=u_1^2|a|^2+u_2^2|d|^2$; no computation of
principal axes for general $a,d$ is used or claimed.

For (c), the cross product $a\times d$ is orthogonal to both factors and
alternating ([[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]]), and the real Gram identity
[[thm-cross-product-norm-is-the-two-vector-gram-determinant]] says
$|a\times d|^2>0$ exactly when $a,d$ are linearly independent. Thus
$a\times d=0$ holds exactly when $a$ and $d$ are linearly dependent, that is,
in case (i); then $H=0$. Otherwise $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$, and
since $\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}\subseteq k^\perp$ are both two-dimensional,
they are equal; being orthogonal to $a$ and $d$, the vector $a\times d$ is
orthogonal to $k^\perp$, whose orthogonal complement in $\mathbb R^3$ is the
line $\mathbb R k$, so $a\times d=\mu k$ for a real $\mu$ and
$H=\mu|k|\ne0$. For the rotation identity, differentiating
$E=a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta$ along $t$ with $\partial_t\theta=-\omega$ gives
$\partial_tE=\omega(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)$, so
$E\times\partial_tE
=\omega(a\cos\theta-d\sin\theta)\times(a\sin\theta+d\cos\theta)
=\omega\bigl((\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)a\times d
+\cos\theta\sin\theta(a\times a-d\times d)\bigr)=\omega\,a\times d$
by bilinearity and alternation, and taking the inner product with $\hat k$
gives the displayed identity. As a concrete check of the convention, take
$\hat k=e_3$ with the positive orthonormal screen triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$, so
that $e_1$ points right and $e_2$ up for the observer looking along $-e_3$;
then $e=e_1-ie_2$ has $a=e_1$, $d=-e_2$,
$E(0,t)=\cos(\omega t)e_1-\sin(\omega t)e_2$ (clockwise), and
$H=\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-1<0$, consistently with the
right-handed naming. This fixes the sign convention of the cited treatment:
the source writes $E_0=\alpha-i\beta$ and calls the polarization right-handed
if and only if $\beta=\hat k\times\alpha$, which under $a=\alpha$,
$d=-\beta$ is $H=-|\alpha|^2<0$ in the circular case.

Finally, all amplitudes $e,b$ and vectors $k,a,d$ are constant and all
quantities above are computed from them by the operations of the cited items;
no limit, no integral and no field equation is used, and the definition is at
the level of classification only.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let
$(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the
whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and
phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of
[[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to
$\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and
$\hat k=k/|k|$. Then:

(a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum
Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $\rho\equiv0$ and
$J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

$$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega b,\qquad k\times b=-\frac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$

(b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations
admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)\ne(0,0)$ if and only if
$|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is
$e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a
particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero,
in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the
solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with
$e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k\times e/\omega$: a
complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every
nonzero solution $e\ne0$ and $b\ne0$.

(c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation]
For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every
$(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$,
$E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k\times E(x,t)/c$; in particular
$|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$
solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$.

(d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and
membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about
fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see
[[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane
waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and
is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular
frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$
the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]].
Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit
$\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic
fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product
of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be
those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose
convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is
used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps
$E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$

componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$,
$\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**,
$\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the
**angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**,
and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then:

(a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region
$\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an
electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class
$C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

(b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is
affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the
$e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through
$\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$.

(c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave
**nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the
magnetic field alone determines $b$, because
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$
(evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$).

(d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It
asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no
energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of
[[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The
units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is
claimed.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a
real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and
$\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential
series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number
$e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and
$B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$,
$T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map
$(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$
as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and
$y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself
([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex
derivative is also its real total derivative
([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]),
and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by
[[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word
$(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$,
$\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell
=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$,
by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with
$b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite
word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a).
The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of
$w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if
$\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking
$\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives
$\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is
immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real
linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are
constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no
matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this
definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the
Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are
defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

derivations.claim: Common data. With $k=Ke_3$ one has $|k|=K$, $|k|=\omega/c$ because $\omega=cK$, and $\hat k=e_3$; by [F4] and the coordinate formula, $e_3\times e_1=e_2$ and $e_3\times e_2=-e_1$. Hence for each choice $b=k\times e/\omega=(K/\omega)(e_3\times e)$: for $e=E_0e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)e_2$; for $e=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)$; for $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2+ie_1)$; for $e=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$, $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$; and for $e=E_0(1+i)e_1$, $b=(E_0/c)(1+i)e_2$. Also $k\cdot e=K e_3\cdot e=0$ for each of these amplitudes, since only the first two coordinates are nonzero.

Case (i), linear. For $e=E_0e_1$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=0$, so $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$ and clause (b)(i) of [F1] gives a linear trace, the segment $[-E_0,E_0]e_1$ traversed twice per period; $a\times d=E_0e_1\times0=0$ by [F4], so $H=0$. The fields are $E=\operatorname{Re}(E_0e_1e^{i\theta})=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1$ and $B=(E_0/c)\cos\theta\,e_2$, whence $|B|=|E|/c$ pointwise; this also matches $b=(E_0/c)e_2$ from step 1.1 and clause (c) of [F2].

Case (ii), circular. For $e=E_0(e_1+ie_2)$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=E_0e_2$, so $|a|=|d|=E_0>0$ and $\langle a,d\rangle=E_0^2\langle e_1,e_2\rangle=0$ by the orthonormality of [F5]; clause (b)(ii) of [F1] gives a circular polarization of radius $E_0$. The trace is $E=E_0(\cos\theta\,e_1-\sin\theta\,e_2)$ with $|E|^2=E_0^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)=E_0^2$ by [F5], and $B=\operatorname{Re}\bigl((E_0/c)(e_2-ie_1)e^{i\theta}\bigr) =(E_0/c)(\sin\theta\,e_1+\cos\theta\,e_2)$ with $|B|=E_0/c$; finally $H=\langle a\times d,e_3\rangle=E_0^2\langle e_1\times e_2,e_3\rangle=E_0^2>0$ by [F4] and [F5], so this polarization is left-handed by [F1]. For the reversed choice $e=E_0(e_1-ie_2)$ one has $d=-E_0e_2$ and $H=E_0^2\langle e_1\times(-e_2),e_3\rangle=-E_0^2<0$, which is right-handed.

Case (iii), elliptical. For $e=E_0(e_1+2ie_2)$ one has $a=E_0e_1$, $d=2E_0e_2$, which are orthogonal by [F5] and have unequal lengths, and $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=2$; since $|a|=E_0\ne2E_0=|d|$, clause (b)(ii) fails, so clause (b)(iii) of [F1] applies and, because $\langle a,d\rangle=0$, the trace is the axis-aligned ellipse with semiaxes $E_0$ and $2E_0$ along $e_1$ and $e_2$. Explicitly $E=E_0\cos\theta\,e_1-2E_0\sin\theta\,e_2$ and $|E|^2=E_0^2\cos^2\theta+4E_0^2\sin^2\theta$ by [F5], which lies between $E_0^2$ and $4E_0^2$; $b=(E_0/c)(e_2-2ie_1)$ by step 1.1, and $H=\langle E_0e_1\times2E_0e_2,e_3\rangle=2E_0^2>0$.

Case (iv), degenerate and edge cases. For $e=0$ the fields vanish identically by [F3] (the zero wave), $a=d=0$, and clause (b)(i) of [F1] covers the trace $\{0\}$; for $e=E_0(1+i)e_1$ one has $a=d=E_0e_1$, so $\dim\operatorname{span}\{a,d\}=1$, the polarization is linear, and the trace is $E=E_0(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)e_1$, whose coefficient $\cos\theta-\sin\theta=\sqrt2\cos(\theta+\pi/4)$ ranges over $[-\sqrt2,\sqrt2]$; the trace is therefore the segment $[-\sqrt2E_0,\sqrt2E_0]e_1$, and $H=\langle a\times a,e_3\rangle=0$ by alternation of the coordinate formula [F4]. No orthogonality of $a$ and $d$ is used, matching the covering clause of [F1]; the corresponding $b$ is the one computed in step 1.1.

Scope check (v). In every case step 1.1 gives $b=k\times e/\omega$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $|k|=\omega/c$, so by clause (b) of [F2] the amplitude equations hold and the corresponding fields are smooth source-free Maxwell solutions; the amplitudes $e$ and the semiaxis lengths $E_0$, $2E_0$ carry $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ by [F6], and the pointwise relation $|B|=|E|/c$ is clause (c) of [F2]. The item computes only ideal field quantities and asserts no measurement or empirical realization.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), used through the cited published suppliers ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $c>0$, $t_0\in\mathbb R$, $T>t_0$, let $a,b\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ and let $h\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times[t_0,T])$ in the extension sense that $h$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ function on $\mathbb R^3\times J$ for some open interval $J\supset[t_0,T]$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
