e0$ in both. The magnetic identity of step 3.1 reads $n	imes igl(Y_2e_t-Y_1(e_i-e_r) igr)=0$, and its argument is tangential, so $Y_1(e_i-e_r)=Y_2e_t$ by [F11]; together with $e_i+e_r=e_t$ this is exactly the system of [F3], and since $Y_1+Y_2
e0$ the solution formulas $r=(Y_1-Y_2)/(Y_1+Y_2)$, $t=2Y_1/(Y_1+Y_2)$ hold with $e_r=r\,e_i$, $e_t=t\,e_i$; here $r,t$ are scalars in $\mathbb C$ multiplying the fixed nonzero vector $e_i$, so the reflected and transmitted electric phasors are parallel to the incident one. Moreover $t
e0$ because $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$ by [F3] and [F10]; and $r=0$ if and only if $Y_1=Y_2$.

[Lossless transmitting medium, part (c)] If $\sigma_2=0$ then $k=\omega/v_2>0$ by the Statement, so $Y_2=k/(\mu_2\omega)=\omega/(v_2\mu_2\omega)=1/(v_2\mu_2)=1/Z_2$ by [F9] ($v_2\mu_2=\sqrt{\mu_2/\varepsilon_2}=Z_2$), and $Y_1=1/Z_1$ similarly; hence substituting $Y_j=1/Z_j$ into the formulas of step 4.1 gives $r=(1/Z_1-1/Z_2)/(1/Z_1+1/Z_2)=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_1+Z_2)$ and $t=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$, both real, the same formulas as in the scalar parametrisation of [F4]. The period-averaged normal fluxes at the interface: for a nonzero lossless wave with real wavevector the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_j\rangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $\omega$ the common frequency, so $\langle S_i\cdot n\rangle=|e_i|^2k_1/(2\mu_1\omega)=|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)$ because $k_1/(\mu_1\omega)=Y_1=1/Z_1$; similarly $\langle S_r\cdot n\rangle=|e_r|^2(-k_1)/(2\mu_1\omega)=-|e_r|^2/(2Z_1)$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=|e_t|^2k/(2\mu_2\omega)=|e_t|^2/(2Z_2)$. If $e_r=0$, then $h_r=0$ and $S_r=0$, so the reflected formula holds directly as well. With $R=|r|^2$ and $T=(Z_1/Z_2)|t|^2$, the identity $R+T=1$ is [F4]; since $|e_r|^2=R|e_i|^2$ and $|e_t|^2=(Z_2/Z_1)T|e_i|^2=|e_i|^2 T Z_2/Z_1$, the three fluxes are $|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)$ times $1$, $-R$ and $T$ respectively, which is the stated fraction reading.

[Ohmic transmitting medium: system and budget, part (d) first half] If $\sigma_2>0$ then $k=\kappa_2(\omega)=p+iq$ with $p,q>0$ by [F9], so $Y_2=(p+iq)/(\mu_2\omega)$ has $\operatorname{Re}Y_2=p/(\mu_2\omega)>0$ and $\operatorname{Im}Y_2=q/(\mu_2\omega)>0$; the solution formulas of step 4.1 give $r,t$, and [F3] gives $|r|^2+(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2=1$ and $|t|^2=4Y_1^2/|Y_1+Y_2|^2>0$. Since $\operatorname{Im}Y_2\ne0$, the numerator $Y_1-Y_2$ of $r$ is nonzero, so $r\ne0$ in this branch.

[Attenuated transmitted field and entering flux] With $k=p+iq$ and the common frequency, the transmitted field factorizes exactly: for $x_3\in\mathbb R$, $i(kx_3-\omega t)=-qx_3+i(px_3-\omega t)$, and [F6] gives $e^{i(kx_3-\omega t)}=e^{-qx_3}(\cos(px_3-\omega t)+i\sin(px_3-\omega t))$, so $E_t(x,t)=e^{-qx_3}\operatorname{Re}(e_t e^{i(px_3-\omega t)})$ componentwise (the exact decay factor $e^{-qx_3}$), and $H_t=e^{-qx_3}\operatorname{Re}(h_t e^{i(px_3-\omega t)})$ for the same reason since $h_t$ is a constant phasor. The period-averaged normal flux of the transmitted field is, by the cross-product form of [F7] applied to the factorized fields, $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=e^{-2qx_3}\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl((e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n\bigr)$; from $h_t=Y_2\,n\times e_t$ with $Y_2=(p+iq)/(\mu_2\omega)$ by step 4.1, $\overline h_t=\overline{Y_2}\,n\times\overline e_t=((p-iq)/(\mu_2\omega))\,n\times\overline e_t$ by [F10], and the triple-product expansion of [F11] gives $e_t\times(n\times\overline e_t)=n\,|e_t|^2-\overline e_t\,(e_t\cdot n)=n\,|e_t|^2$ because $e_t$ is tangential; hence $(e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n=(p-iq)|e_t|^2/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=e^{-2qx_3}p|e_t|^2/(2\mu_2\omega)=:F(x_3)$. At the interface $x_3=0$ this equals $(p/(\mu_2\omega))|e_t|^2/2$, and dividing by the incident flux $|e_i|^2/(2Z_1)=Y_1|e_i|^2/2$ of step 5.1 (which applies to medium 1, lossless) gives $\frac{p}{\mu_2\omega Y_1}|t|^2=\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}|t|^2$, the stated entering fraction of the incident period-averaged normal flux.

[Ohmic absorption] In the conductor the free current is the conduction current $J_f=\sigma_2E_t$ with the declared positive scalar $\sigma_2$ (the model of [F1] has no external free current), and the Ohmic dissipation density of [F8] averaged over a period is $d(x_3):=\sigma_2\langle|E_t|^2\rangle=\sigma_2|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/2$ by [F7] applied to the factorized field of step 6.1; the flux of step 6.1 is $F(x_3)=p|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(2\mu_2\omega)$. Since $2pq=\mu_2\sigma_2\omega$ by [F9], $F'(x_3)=-2q\,p|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(2\mu_2\omega)=-pq|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/(\mu_2\omega)=-\sigma_2|e_t|^2e^{-2qx_3}/2=-d(x_3)$: the flux lost per unit length is exactly the Ohmic dissipation. For every $L>0$ the integrand $d$ is continuous on $[0,L]$, hence Riemann integrable by [F13], and the exponential antiderivative is differentiable through the endpoints; the fundamental theorem [F13] gives $\int_0^Ld(x_3)\,dx_3=\sigma_2|e_t|^2(1-e^{-2qL})/(4q)=F(0)-F(L)$, where the last identity uses $p/(2\mu_2\omega)=\sigma_2/(4q)$, which is $2pq=\mu_2\sigma_2\omega$ rearranged. Since $q>0$, $e^{-2qL}\to0$ as $L\to\infty$ by [F13], and defining the improper integral as the limit of the proper integrals per [F13] gives $\int_0^\infty d(x_3)\,dx_3=\sigma_2|e_t|^2/(4q)=F(0)$: the whole entering flux is dissipated in the conductor, and with the budget of step 5.2 the reflected fraction $|r|^2$ and the absorbed fraction $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ add to $1$.

[Scope, part (e)] All conclusions are conditional on the given wave data and the interface identities [A1]; the argument used only the two tangential identities, the amplitude conditions and dispersion of [F1], the character lemma [F5], the admittance algebra [F3], the Euler form [F6] and the period averages [F7]; the normal interface identities, the optional normal-root selection rule and any outgoing condition were not used, and the oblique-incidence theorem [F2] was cited only as the consistent lossless cross-check. The interface identities are stated hypotheses on the noncompact plane; for compact interfaces they follow from [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]. No choice principle is used: every quantity is finite-dimensional algebra in the given data, and the only limiting passage is the explicit exponential improper integral of step 7.1.

citations.quote: [Interface hypothesis] assume that for all $(y,t)\in\mathbb R^{2}\times I$, with $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open interval, the one-sided traces at $(y,0,t)$ satisfy the four stationary interface identities with no free surface charge or current, $$n\cdot\bigl(\varepsilon_2E_t-\varepsilon_1(E_i+E_r)\bigr)=0,\qquad n\cdot\bigl(\mu_2H_t-\mu_1(H_i+H_r)\bigr)=0,$$ $$n\times\bigl(E_t-(E_i+E_r)\bigr)=0,\qquad n\times\bigl(H_t-(H_i+H_r)\bigr)=0 .$$

**(b) [Amplitude conditions]** the quadruple $(E,H,D,B)$ satisfies the four source-free macroscopic equations $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ on $\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot h=0,\qquad k\times e=\omega\mu\,h,\qquad k\times h=-(\omega\varepsilon+i\sigma)\,e .$$ **(c) [Structure, dispersion and solution family]** if $e\ne0$ and (b) holds, then $h=k\times e/(\omega\mu)$, $k\cdot h=0$, $e\cdot h=0$ and $k\cdot k=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega$;

**(c) [Propagating waves: reflection law and Snell's law]** if in addition $k_i,k_r,k_t\in\mathbb R^{3}$, then with $\theta_j\in[0,\pi/2]$ defined by $\sin\theta_j=|\kappa_j|/|k_j|$ (well defined because the real dispersion relation gives $|k_j|>0$; the incident and reflected angles are below $\pi/2$, and the transmitted angle may equal $\pi/2$) one has $\theta_r=\theta_i$ and, writing $v_j=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$ and $n_j=c/v_j$ for the parameters of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]], $$n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t.$$

Define: **(a) [Lossless parameters]** with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], $$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$ $v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case. **(b) [Complex propagation constant]** put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and $$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$ Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$;

[Normal-flux identity] If $Y_1>0$ is real (the incident side admittance), then $$|r|^2+\frac{\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{Y_1}\,|t|^2=1,$$ and explicitly $|t|^2=\dfrac{4Y_1^2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$ and $|r|^2=1-\dfrac{4Y_1\operatorname{Re}Y_2}{|Y_1+Y_2|^2}$. The second summand $(\operatorname{Re}Y_2/Y_1)|t|^2$ is nonnegative if and only if $\operatorname{Re}Y_2\ge0$; it is the normal-flux coefficient of a passive transmitted medium and may be negative for an active one, in which case $|r|>1$ and the identity carries no energy-conservation

Let $\varepsilon_j,\mu_j>0$ be real for $j=1,2$, put $Z_j:=\sqrt{\mu_j/\varepsilon_j}$ for the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]], and let $E_i,E_r,E_t\in\mathbb C$ with $E_i\ne0$ satisfy the two linear equations $$E_i+E_r=E_t,\qquad \frac{E_i-E_r}{Z_1}=\frac{E_t}{Z_2}.$$ Then $$\frac{E_r}{E_i}=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad \frac{E_t}{E_i}=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2},$$ and the real numbers $R:=\bigl\lvert E_r/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ and $T:=\bigl(Z_1/Z_2\bigr)\bigl\lvert E_t/E_i\bigr\rvert^2$ satisfy $$R+T=1 .$$

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$.

**Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$

**Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then

$$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$

the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Define the stored-energy density and the energy-flux vector $$u:=\tfrac12\bigl(E\cdot D+B\cdot H\bigr),\qquad S:=E\times H,$$ with the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]; $u$ carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and $S$ carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}$.

For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex numbers** by the quotient ring $$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$ ([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set $$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$ Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient.

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of $\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$, and $$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$ $$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$ If $a+bi\ne0$, then $$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$

Complex conjugation is a real-field automorphism satisfying $$\overline{z+w}=\overline z+\overline w,\qquad \overline{zw}=\overline z\,\overline w,\qquad \overline{\overline z}=z.$$ For every $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $$z\overline z=|z|^2,\qquad |z|\ge0,\qquad |z|=0\Longleftrightarrow z=0,$$ $$|zw|=|z||w|,\qquad |z+w|\le |z|+|w|.$$

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class $C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class $C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a **magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of the same class.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

**(b) [Elementary inertial-rest branch]** In the rest frame, with constant symmetric positive-definite matrices $\varepsilon,\mu\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ (the isotropic scalar cases $\varepsilon=\varepsilon\mathbf 1$, $\mu=\mu\mathbf 1$ with $\varepsilon,\mu>0$ included), the model takes

$$D=\varepsilon E,\qquad B=\mu H,\qquad J_c=\sigma E,$$

where $\sigma\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ is symmetric positive semidefinite and $J_c$ is the conduction part of the free current, $J_f=J_c+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. For a real matrix $T$, symmetric means $T^{\mathsf T}=T$, positive definite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv>0$ for every nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^3$, and positive semidefinite means $v^{\mathsf T}Tv\ge0$ for every $v$. Local, linear and nondispersive (instantaneous) response is part of this restricted assumption. In the isotropic case an exact broadband interpretation of the constant-coefficient law additionally requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$, so that the characteristic speed $1/\sqrt{\varepsilon\mu}$ does not exceed the vacuum speed $c$; without that condition, and in the anisotropic branch, the constant-coefficient law is a declared finite-band effective phase-response model and carries no universal front-speed claim.

derivations.claim: [Both polarisation families satisfy the amplitude conditions] For (s), $k_j\cdot e_j=E_j\,k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ because $k_j=\kappa+k_{j3}n$ and $\hat y\perp\kappa,n$; and $k_j\times e_j=E_jk_j\times\hat y=E_j(\kappa\times\hat y+k_{j3}n\times\hat y)=E_j(|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x)$ by [F5], which equals $\omega\mu_jh_j$ with $h_j=k_j\times e_j/(\mu_j\omega)$ by definition. For (p), $e_j=-(k_j\times\hat y)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ and $k_j\cdot e_j=0$ because $k_j\cdot(k_j\times\hat y)=0$ by the orthogonality in [F5]; further $k_j\times e_j=-(k_j\times(k_j\times\hat y))H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=\bigl[(k_j\cdot k_j)\hat y-k_j(k_j\cdot\hat y)\bigr]H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=(\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2)\hat yH_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)=\omega\mu_jH_j\hat y=\omega\mu_jh_j$, using $k_j\cdot\hat y=0$ and $k_j\cdot k_j=\varepsilon_j\mu_j\omega^2$ of [F1]. In (s), $k_j\cdot h_j=0$ by cross-product orthogonality, and $k_j\times h_j=-\omega\varepsilon_j e_j$ follows by expanding $k_j\times(k_j\times e_j)=k_j(k_j\cdot e_j)-(k_j\cdot k_j)e_j$ and using dispersion. In (p), $k_j\cdot h_j=0$ because $\hat y$ is perpendicular to $k_j$, and $k_j\times h_j=-\omega\varepsilon_j e_j$ is the definition of $e_j$. Thus all four amplitude conditions hold in both families, including zero reflected or transmitted amplitudes.

[The tangential interface identities in the fixed frame] By the orthogonal decomposition of [F5], the tangential parts of the electric amplitudes are: for (s), $e_j^\tau=e_j=E_j\hat y$; for (p), $e_j^\tau=(k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j))\hat x$ because $e_j=(k_{j3}\hat x-|\kappa|n)H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ from $k_j\times\hat y=|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x$ by [F5]. The magnetic tangential traces are obtained as follows: $h_j=H_j\hat y$ in (p), and in (s) $h_j=E_j(\kappa\times\hat y+k_{j3}n\times\hat y)/(\mu_j\omega)=E_j(|\kappa|n-k_{j3}\hat x)/(\mu_j\omega)$ with tangential part $-k_{j3}E_j\hat x/(\mu_j\omega)$ and, for the reflected wave with $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$, tangential part $+k_{13}E_r\hat x/(\mu_1\omega)$. Since the interface identities hold for all $(y,t)$ with the common $(\kappa,\omega)$, each has the form $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(W e^{i(\kappa\cdot y-\omega t)}\bigr)=0$ for a constant tangential vector $W$. Since $n=e_3$, $n\times(w_1,w_2,0)=(-w_2,w_1,0)$, so the cross-product trace identities are equivalent to these real-part identities. Fixing any $y$ and allowing $t$ to vary in $I$, the time-line proof of the amplitude-vanishing clause (a) of [F1] gives $W=0$. Concretely: the tangential electric identity gives $E_i+E_r=E_t$ in (s) and $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=E^{(p)}_t$ in (p); the tangential magnetic identity gives $k_{t3}E_t/(\mu_2\omega)=k_{13}(E_i-E_r)/(\mu_1\omega)$ in (s) and $H_i+H_r=H_t$ in (p), where $E^{(p)}_j=k_{j3}H_j/(\omega\varepsilon_j)$ by definition, and when $k_{t3}\ne0$, converting $H_j=Y^p_jE^{(p)}_j$ for $j=i,t$ and $H_r=-Y^p_1E^{(p)}_r$ (the reflected sign entering through $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$) turns the last identity into $Y^p_1(E^{(p)}_i-E^{(p)}_r)=Y^p_2E^{(p)}_t$. Writing $Y^s_1=k_{13}/(\mu_1\omega)$, $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)$, $Y^p_1=\varepsilon_1\omega/k_{13}$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/k_{t3}$ when $k_{t3}\ne0$ gives the two systems of (a).

[Solution of the systems, part (a)] In the (s) branch, $Y^s_1>0$ is real and positive, and $Y^s_2$ is real positive for $|\kappa|<K_2$, zero at the critical point, and $i eta/(\mu_2\omega)$ for $|\kappa|>K_2$; in every case $\operatorname{Re}(Y^s_1+Y^s_2)=Y^s_1+\operatorname{Re}Y^s_2\ge Y^s_1>0$, so $Y^s_1+Y^s_2
e0$. In the (p) branch with $k_{t3}
e0$, $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_1=Y^p_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^p_2=0$ or $>0$, so again $Y^p_1+Y^p_2
e0$. The admittance lemma [F3](a) therefore applies to each scalar system of step 2.1 and gives $r_\chi=(Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2)/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$ and $t_\chi=2Y^\chi_1/(Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2)$; in particular $t_\chi
e0$ because its numerator $2Y^\chi_1
e0$.

[Critical angle, part (e)] Let $|\kappa|=K_2$; then $k_{t3}=0$ by [F6], so $Y^s_2=0$ and no $Y^p_2$ is defined (a division by $k_{t3}$ is not performed). For (s), the system of step 2.1 reads $E_i+E_r=E_t$ and $Y^s_1(E_i-E_r)=0$ with $Y^s_1>0$, so $E_r=E_i$ and $E_t=2E_i$, i.e. $r_s=1$ and $t_s=2$. For (p), $E^{(p)}_t=k_{t3}H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=0$ and $E^{(p)}_i=k_{13}H_i/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$, $E^{(p)}_r=-k_{13}H_r/(\omega\varepsilon_1)$ by the fixed-direction definitions of step 2.1; the tangential electric identity $E^{(p)}_i+E^{(p)}_r=0$ gives $H_r=H_i$, and the tangential magnetic identity $H_i+H_r=H_t$ gives $H_t=2H_i$; hence $r_p=E^{(p)}_r/E^{(p)}_i=-H_r/H_i=-1$ and $t_p=E^{(p)}_t/E^{(p)}_i=0$. The transmitted normal averaged flux vanishes: $\langle S_t\cdot n\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl((e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n\bigr)$ by [F4], and with $h_t=H_t\hat y$ and $e_t=-(k_t\times\hat y)H_t/(\omega\varepsilon_2)=-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ (because $k_t=\kappa$ and $\kappa\times\hat y=|\kappa|n$ by [F5]), the vector $e_t\times\overline h_t$ is a multiple of $n\times\hat y$, which is orthogonal to $n$: $(e_t\times\overline h_t)\cdot n=0$. In the TE case $e_t=E_t\hat y$ and $h_t=|\kappa|E_tn/(\mu_2\omega)$, so $e_t\times\overline h_t$ is tangential and its normal component is also zero. The transmitted TM electric vector $-|\kappa|H_tn/(\omega\varepsilon_2)$ has a nontrivial normal component whenever $H_t\ne0$.

[Propagating branch: angles and fluxes, part (b)] Let $|\kappa|<K_2$. Then $k_{t3}=\sqrt{K_2^2-|\kappa|^2}>0$ and all three wavevectors are real by [F6]; the four admittances of step 2.1 are real and positive. With $|k_i|=|k_r|=K_1$ and $|k_t|=K_2$ from $|k_j|^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{j3}^2$, the angles $\theta_j:=\arcsin(|\kappa|/|k_j|)\in(0,\pi/2)$ are well defined by [F8] since $0<|\kappa|<\min\{K_1,K_2\}$; then $\sin\theta_r=|\kappa|/K_1=\sin\theta_i$, so $\theta_r=\theta_i$ by the strict increase of sine and of $\arcsin$ in [F8], and $K_1\sin\theta_i=|\kappa|=K_2\sin\theta_t$, which is $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ after multiplying by $c/\omega$ and using $n_j=cK_j/\omega=c(\varepsilon_j\mu_j)^{1/2}$ by [F6]; this is the same angle law as [F2]. The period-averaged normal fluxes: for (s), the flux of [F1] is $\langle S_j\rangle=|e_j|^2k_j/(2\mu_j\omega)$ with $|e_j|^2=|E^{(s)}_j|^2$ and $k_j\cdot n=k_{j3}$, so the normal fluxes are $k_{j3}|E^{(s)}_j|^2/(2\mu_j\omega)$, i.e. $Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_i|^2/2$, $-Y^s_1|E^{(s)}_r|^2/2$, $Y^s_2|E^{(s)}_t|^2/2$; for (p) the same $\langle S_j\cdot n\rangle=|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)$ equals $Y^p_j\,|E^{(p)}_j|^2/2$ up to the reflected sign, because $|e_j|^2=\mu_j|H_j|^2/\varepsilon_j$ and $|E^{(p)}_j|=|k_{j3}||H_j|/(\varepsilon_j\omega)$ give $|e_j|^2k_{j3}/(2\mu_j\omega)=k_{j3}|H_j|^2/(2\varepsilon_j\omega)$ for the incident and transmitted signs, while the reflected signed component $k_{r3}=-k_{13}$ produces the minus sign, as in the Statement. With $R_\chi=|r_\chi|^2=|E^\chi_r|^2/|E^\chi_i|^2$ and $T_\chi=(Y^\chi_2/Y^\chi_1)|t_\chi|^2=Y^\chi_2|E^\chi_t|^2/(Y^\chi_1|E^\chi_i|^2)$, the budget $R_\chi+T_\chi=1$ is [F3](b) applied with the real positive $Y^\chi_1,Y^\chi_2$.

[Total internal reflection, part (d)] Let $|\kappa|>K_2$; then $K_2<K_1$, so $n_2<n_1$, and $k_{t3}=i\beta$ with $\beta=\sqrt{|\kappa|^2-K_2^2}>0$ by [F6]. Hence $Y^s_2=k_{t3}/(\mu_2\omega)=i\beta/(\mu_2\omega)$ and $Y^p_2=\varepsilon_2\omega/(i\beta)=-i\varepsilon_2\omega/\beta$ are purely imaginary by [F7], while $Y^\chi_1>0$ is real; the admittance lemma [F3](c) gives $|r_s|=|r_p|=1$ and $|t_\chi|^2=4(Y^\chi_1)^2/((Y^\chi_1)^2+|Y^\chi_2|^2)>0$, so $t_\chi\ne0$. The transmitted wave is the evanescent branch of [F1] with $n'=n$, $\kappa_0=\kappa$ and $k_t\cdot k_t=K_2^2=\varepsilon_2\mu_2\omega^2$: the field factorizes with the decay factor $e^{-\beta x_3}$, its period-averaged normal flux vanishes identically, and its tangential averaged flux is strictly positive; since $|r_\chi|=1$, the reflected normal averaged flux equals minus the incident normal averaged flux, i.e. the reflected wave carries the whole incident normal averaged flux.

[Brewster condition, part (c)] In each finite-admittance branch the formula of step 3.1 gives $r_\chi=0$ exactly when the numerator $Y^\chi_1-Y^\chi_2$ vanishes, i.e. $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$. Assume now $\mu_1=\mu_2=:\mu$ and $|\kappa|<K_2$, so that the (p) admittances are real positive. The condition $Y^p_1=Y^p_2$ reads $\varepsilon_1/k_{13}=\varepsilon_2/k_{t3}$; substituting $\varepsilon_j=n_j^2/(c^2\mu)$ and $k_{j3}=(\omega n_j/c)\cos\theta_j$ (from $k_{13}=K_1\cos\theta_i=(\omega n_1/c)\cos\theta_i$ and $k_{t3}=K_2\cos\theta_t=(\omega n_2/c)\cos\theta_t$) gives $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$. Together with Snell's law $n_1\sin\theta_i=n_2\sin\theta_t$ of step 4.1, squaring both and eliminating $\sin^2\theta_t$ gives $(n_1^2-n_2^2)\bigl[n_2^2-(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i\bigr]=0$: indeed $n_1^2(1-\sin^2\theta_t)=n_2^2\cos^2\theta_i$ and $\sin\theta_t=(n_1/n_2)\sin\theta_i$ yield $n_1^2n_2^2-n_1^4\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^4-n_2^4\sin^2\theta_i$, i.e. $n_2^2(n_1^2-n_2^2)=(n_1^2-n_2^2)(n_1^2+n_2^2)\sin^2\theta_i$. If $n_1\ne n_2$, division by the nonzero first factor gives $\sin^2\theta_i=n_2^2/(n_1^2+n_2^2)$; since $0<\theta_i<\pi/2$ and sine is strictly increasing on $[0,\pi/2]$ with $\sin 0=0$ by [F8], this determines the unique admissible angle $\theta_B:=\arcsin\bigl(n_2/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}\bigr)\in(0,\pi/2)$, This angle is admissible: with $D:=\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, its tangential wavenumber is $K_1n_2/D<K_2$ because $n_1/D<1$. Snell's law therefore gives $\sin\theta_t=n_1/D$ and, by positivity of both cosines and the Pythagorean identity, $\cos\theta_i=n_1/D$, $\cos\theta_t=n_2/D$. Thus $n_1\cos\theta_t=n_2\cos\theta_i$, establishing $Y_1^p=Y_2^p$ and $r_p=0$; this proves sufficiency as well as uniqueness. At this angle $\cos\theta_B>0$: cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ with $\cos(\pi/2)=0$ by [F8], so $0<\theta_B<\pi/2$ gives $\cos\theta_B>\cos(\pi/2)=0$. The Pythagorean identity of [F8] then gives $\cos\theta_B=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta_B}=n_1/\sqrt{n_1^2+n_2^2}$, so $\tan\theta_B=\sin\theta_B/\cos\theta_B=n_2/n_1$ by the definition of tangent in [F8]; no other admissible angle has this tangent, because tangent is strictly increasing on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F8]. Also $r_s\ne0$ at $\theta_B$, because $Y^s_1=Y^s_2$ would give $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ (the $\mu$ factors being equal), hence $K_1^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{13}^2=|\kappa|^2+k_{t3}^2=K_2^2$ and $n_1=n_2$, contrary to hypothesis. If instead $n_1=n_2$ and $\mu_1=\mu_2$ then $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ and the two media are identical: $k_{13}=k_{t3}$ and $\varepsilon_1=\varepsilon_2$ give $Y^\chi_1=Y^\chi_2$, so $r_s=r_p=0$ and $t_s=t_p=1$ at every admissible angle (where the (p) formula applies), with no distinguished Brewster angle.

[Scope, part (f)] All clauses are conditional on the given wave data and the interface identities [A1]; the argument used the amplitude conditions and solution structure of [F1], the admittance algebra [F3], the angle conventions of [F2] and [F8], the period averages and stored-energy flux of [F4], and the complex arithmetic of [F7]; the ideal-conductor limit, absorption, dispersion, anisotropy, moving and nonlinear media, signal-speed and group-velocity statements and all empirical claims are excluded. The denominator $Y^\chi_1+Y^\chi_2$ is nonzero in every considered branch because $\operatorname{Re}Y^\chi_1>0$ and $\operatorname{Re}Y^\chi_2\ge0$; the interface identities are stated hypotheses on the noncompact plane (for compact interfaces, [[pthm-em-material-stationary-jumps]]), and no choice principle is used, all constructions being finite-dimensional algebra in the given data.

citations.quote: **(b) [Exact skin depth]** $q^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}-a\bigr)/2$, $p^{2}=\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)/2$, $pq=b/2=\mu\sigma\omega/2$, and the skin depth of [[def-em-medium-wave-parameters]] equals the exact closed expression $$\delta(\omega)=\frac{1}{q}=\frac{\sqrt{2\,(r+a)}}{b}=\frac{\sqrt{2\bigl(\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}+a\bigr)}}{\mu\sigma\omega}.$$ **(c) [Good-conductor regime]** put $t:=a/b=\varepsilon\omega/\sigma>0$. For every $t\le1/4$ the exact value satisfies the explicit bounds $$\bigl|q-\sqrt{b/2}\bigr|\le2t\sqrt{b/2}=\frac{2\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{\mu\sigma\omega}{2}},\qquad \bigl|\delta-\sqrt{2/b}\bigr|\le4t\sqrt{2/b}=\frac{4\varepsilon\omega}{\sigma}\sqrt{\frac{2}{\mu\sigma\omega}} ;$$ equivalently $\delta=\sqrt{2/(\mu\sigma\omega)}\,\bigl(1+O(\varepsilon\omega/\sigma)\bigr)$ in the declared regime $\varepsilon\omega/\sigma\le1/4$, with the displayed explicit remainder bounds.

Assume the elementary inertial-rest branch of [[post-em-material-closure]] in the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], in its isotropic scalar case: the material is at rest in the laboratory frame, $D,H$ are defined by [[def-em-polarization-magnetization]](d), and the constitutive relations of [[post-em-material-closure]](b) hold with constant scalars $\varepsilon>0$ (F$\,$m$^{-1}$), $\mu>0$ (H$\,$m$^{-1}$) and $\sigma\ge0$ (S$\,$m$^{-1}$), so that $D=\varepsilon E$, $B=\mu H$ and the free current is $J_f=\sigma E+J_{\mathrm{ext}}$ for a declared external free current $J_{\mathrm{ext}}$. Write $c>0$ for the exact vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and let $\omega>0$ (s$^{-1}$) be an angular frequency. Define:

**(a) [Lossless parameters]** with $\sqrt{\cdot}$ the nonnegative square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]],
$$v:=(\varepsilon\mu)^{-1/2}\quad(\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}),\qquad Z:=\Bigl(\frac{\mu}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)^{1/2}\quad(\Omega),\qquad n:=\frac{c}{v}=c(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}\quad(\text{dimensionless}),\qquad k(\omega):=\frac{\omega}{v};$$
$v$ is the phase speed, $Z$ the wave impedance, $n$ the refractive index relative to vacuum and $k(\omega)$ the real wavenumber of the lossless case.

**(b) [Complex propagation constant]** put $a:=\mu\varepsilon\omega^{2}>0$, $b:=\mu\sigma\omega\ge0$, $r:=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ and
$$p(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r+a}{2}},\qquad q(\omega):=\sqrt{\frac{r-a}{2}},\qquad \kappa(\omega):=p(\omega)+i\,q(\omega).$$
Then $\kappa(\omega)$ is the unique $k\in\mathbb C$ with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ and $k^{2}=\varepsilon\mu\omega^{2}+i\mu\sigma\omega=a+ib$; in the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $q=0$ and $\kappa(\omega)=k(\omega)=p(\omega)$ real. (The explicit formula is the one of [[thm-every-complex-number-has-a-square-root]]; the verification $p^{2}-q^{2}=a$, $2pq=b$ and the uniqueness of the root with $\operatorname{Re}k\ge0$, $\operatorname{Im}k\ge0$ are verified in the well-definedness paragraph below.)

**(c) [Skin depth]** call $\delta(\omega):=1/q(\omega)$ (m) the skin depth if $\sigma>0$, and set $\delta(\omega):=+\infty$ if $\sigma=0$: for $\kappa(\omega)=p+iq$ and $x_3\in\mathbb R$ the modulus of $e^{i(\kappa x_3-\omega t)}$ equals $e^{-q x_3}$ ([[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]), so $\delta$ is the distance in which that modulus decays by the factor $1/e$ in the direction of increasing $x_3$; for $\sigma=0$ there is no attenuation and $\delta$ is infinite rather than a division by zero.

**(d) [Status and scope]** This item fixes objects, units, branch conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation for a solution, no attenuation of any concrete field and no material validity. The parameters are declared for the isotropic scalar constant-coefficient branch at rest in the laboratory frame; for $\varepsilon\mu<c^{-2}$ the branch is, by [[post-em-material-closure]](b), a declared finite-band effective phase-response model with no universal front-speed claim. An exact broadband interpretation must be separately adopted and requires $\varepsilon\mu\ge c^{-2}$; that inequality alone does not adopt a broadband interpretation or establish material validity, and a finite-band interpretation remains possible when it holds. No measured value, precision or empirical statement is included.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The material assumptions, the rest-frame clause, the isotropic scalar case and the finite-band caveat are those of [[post-em-material-closure]](a)-(b) read with [[def-em-polarization-magnetization|the polarization and magnetization definitions]]; the unit system and the exact constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; the laboratory chart is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

The only content beyond notation is the well-definedness of $\kappa(\omega)$ in (b). With $a>0$, $b\ge0$ and $r=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ one has $r+a>0$ and $(r-a)(r+a)=b^2\ge0$, so $r-a\ge0$ and both defining radicands are nonnegative. If $b>0$, the same identity gives $r-a>0$, hence $q>0$; if $b=0$, uniqueness of nonnegative roots gives $r=a$ and $q=0$. Also $p>0$ because $r+a>0$. Thus $p^{2}-q^{2}=(r+a)/2-(r-a)/2=a$ and $(2pq)^{2}=4\cdot(r+a)(r-a)/4=r^{2}-a^{2}=b^{2}$, so $2pq=b$ because $p,q\ge0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); hence $\kappa^{2}=p^{2}-q^{2}+2ipq=a+ib$, by the field arithmetic of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. The square roots of $a+ib$ are exactly $\pm\kappa$: if $z^2=\kappa^2$, then $(z-\kappa)(z+\kappa)=0$, and the complex field property ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]) gives $z=\kappa$ or $z=-\kappa$. If $k=u+iv$ with $u,v\ge0$ and $k^{2}=a+ib$, then $u^{2}-v^{2}=a$, $2uv=b$ and $u^{2}+v^{2}=|k|^{2}=|k^{2}|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}=r$, where $|k^{2}|=|k|^{2}$ is the multiplicativity of the modulus ([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]) and $|a+ib|=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}$ is the modulus of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; solving gives $u^{2}=(r+a)/2=p^{2}$ and $v^{2}=(r-a)/2=q^{2}$, and since $u,v,p,q\ge0$ the uniqueness of the nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]) gives $u=p$ and $v=q$, so $k=\kappa$. In the lossless case $\sigma=0$ one has $b=0$, $r=a$, $q=0$, $p=\sqrt a=\omega(\varepsilon\mu)^{1/2}=k(\omega)$ by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. All divisions are by strictly positive real numbers, $v$ and $q$ are nonzero exactly where defined, and no choice principle is used.

**(b) [Amplitude conditions]** the quadruple $(E,H,D,B)$ satisfies the four source-free macroscopic equations $\operatorname{div}D=0$, $\operatorname{div}B=0$, $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$, $\operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$ on $\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R$ if and only if

citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

derivations.claim: [First derivatives and traces] Let $m,n\ge0$ and $x\in R$. The partial derivatives of the cosine products are $\partial_1h_{mn}(x)=-\frac{m\pi}{L_1}\sin\bigl(\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\bigr)\cos\bigl(\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\bigr)$ and $\partial_2h_{mn}(x)=-\frac{n\pi}{L_2}\cos\bigl(\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\bigr)\sin\bigl(\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\bigr)$: fix the other coordinate and apply the chain rule to $x_j\mapsto\cos\bigl(\frac{m\pi x_j}{L_j}\bigr)$ composed with the affine map, i.e. the derivative $-\sin\cdot\,\frac{m\pi}{L_j}$, together with the product rule. Evaluating with [F5] gives $\partial_1h_{mn}(0,x_2)=\partial_1h_{mn}(L_1,x_2)=0$ and $\partial_2h_{mn}(x_1,0)=\partial_2h_{mn}(x_1,L_2)=0$. Similarly, for $m,n\ge1$, $\partial_1e_{mn}(x)=\frac{m\pi}{L_1}\cos\bigl(\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\bigr)\sin\bigl(\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\bigr)$, $\partial_2e_{mn}(x)=\frac{n\pi}{L_2}\sin\bigl(\frac{m\pi x_1}{L_1}\bigr)\cos\bigl(\frac{n\pi x_2}{L_2}\bigr)$, and $e_{mn}=0$ on $\partial R$ because a sine factor vanishes whenever $x_1\in\{0,L_1\}$ or $x_2\in\{0,L_2\}$.

[One-dimensional orthogonality and norms] Let $m,m'\ge0$ and $p,p'\ge1$ be integers. By [F6], $\cos(m\pi x/L)\cos(m'\pi x/L)=\frac12\bigl[\cos\bigl(\frac{(m-m')\pi x}{L}\bigr)+\cos\bigl(\frac{(m+m')\pi x}{L}\bigr)\bigr]$, so the second fundamental theorem [F3] applied to the continuous antiderivatives, together with the integer values [F5], gives $\int_0^L\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}\cos\frac{m'\pi x}{L}\,dx=0$ for $m\ne m'$, $=\frac{L}{2}$ for $m=m'\ge1$ and $=L$ for $m=m'=0$; uniformly $\int_0^L\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}\cos\frac{m'\pi x}{L}\,dx=\delta_{mm'}\frac{L}{2}(1+\delta_{m0})$. Likewise $\int_0^L\sin\frac{p\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{p'\pi x}{L}\,dx=\frac{L}{2}\delta_{pp'}$, because $\sin\frac{p\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{p'\pi x}{L}=\frac12\bigl[\cos\frac{(p-p')\pi x}{L}-\cos\frac{(p+p')\pi x}{L}\bigr]$ and every nonzero integer multiple of $\pi$ is a zero of sine (and the case $p=p'$ leaves the constant $1$ in the first term).

[Eigen-identities] Differentiating the formulas of step 1.1 once more in the same coordinate gives $\partial_1^2h_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{m\pi}{L_1}\bigr)^2h_{mn}$ and $\partial_2^2h_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{n\pi}{L_2}\bigr)^2h_{mn}$ on $R$, so $\Delta h_{mn}=-k_{mn}^2h_{mn}$ by [F1]; the same computation gives $\partial_1^2e_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{m\pi}{L_1}\bigr)^2e_{mn}$, $\partial_2^2e_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{n\pi}{L_2}\bigr)^2e_{mn}$ and $\Delta e_{mn}=-k_{mn}^2e_{mn}$. Since each open face of $\partial R$ carries one of the normals $\pm e_1,\pm e_2$ and the corresponding normal derivative $\partial_1h_{mn}$ or $\partial_2h_{mn}$ vanishes on it by step 1.1, clause (a) and clause (b) hold.

[Rectangle orthogonality, norms and mixed integrals] Each of the functions $h_{mn}h_{m'n'}$, $e_{mn}e_{m'n'}$ and $h_{mn}e_{pq}$ is continuous on the closed rectangle $\overline R=[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]$, hence Riemann integrable there by [F2]; their sections in each coordinate are continuous, hence integrable. Fubini's theorem [F2] therefore factorizes each integral into a product of one-dimensional integrals. By step 1.2, $\int_Rh_{mn}h_{m'n'}=\frac{L_1L_2}{4}(1+\delta_{m0})(1+\delta_{n0})$ if $(m,n)=(m',n')$ and $=0$ otherwise, and $\int_Re_{mn}e_{m'n'}=\frac{L_1L_2}{4}$ if $(m,n)=(m',n')$ and $=0$ otherwise. For the mixed integral, $\int_Rh_{mn}e_{pq}=J_{mp}(L_1)J_{nq}(L_2)$ with the stated $J_{mp}$.

[Evaluation of $J$] Let $m\ge0$, $p\ge1$ and $L>0$. By [F6], $\cos\frac{m\pi x}{L}\sin\frac{p\pi x}{L}=\frac12\bigl[\sin\frac{(p+m)\pi x}{L}+\sin\frac{(p-m)\pi x}{L}\bigr]$. If $p=m$, the second sine vanishes identically and the integral of the first over $[0,L]$ is $\frac{L}{2\pi m}\bigl(1-\cos(2m\pi)\bigr)=0$ by the fundamental theorem [F3] and [F5] (here $m=p\ge1$); thus $J_{mm}=0$. If $p\ne m$, the fundamental theorem gives $J_{mp}=\frac{L}{2\pi}\Bigl[\frac{1-\cos((p+m)\pi)}{p+m}+\frac{1-\cos((p-m)\pi)}{p-m}\Bigr]=\frac{L}{2\pi}\bigl(1-(-1)^{p+m}\bigr)\Bigl[\frac{1}{p+m}+\frac{1}{p-m}\Bigr]=\frac{pL}{\pi(p^2-m^2)}\bigl(1-(-1)^{p+m}\bigr)$, using $\cos(k\pi)=(-1)^k$ and $\frac{1}{p+m}+\frac{1}{p-m}=\frac{2p}{p^2-m^2}$. Hence $J_{mp}=0$ when $m,p$ have matching parity (the case $p=m$ included) and $J_{mp}=\frac{2pL}{\pi(p^2-m^2)}$ when their parities differ. In particular $J_{01}(L)=\frac{2L}{\pi}$ for $L=L_1,L_2$, so $\int_Rh_{00}e_{11}=J_{01}(L_1)J_{01}(L_2)=\frac{4L_1L_2}{\pi^2}$.

[Dirichlet-type identities] Fix $x_2\in(0,L_2)$ and put $G_1(x_1):=h_{mn}(x_1,x_2)\partial_1h_{mn}(x_1,x_2)$ on $[0,L_1]$. By the product rule [F4], $G_1$ is differentiable on $[0,L_1]$ with $G_1'=(\partial_1h_{mn})^2+h_{mn}\partial_1^2h_{mn}$, a continuous hence integrable function, and $G_1(0)=G_1(L_1)=0$ by step 1.1; the fundamental theorem [F3] gives $\int_0^{L_1}\bigl[(\partial_1h_{mn})^2+h_{mn}\partial_1^2h_{mn}\bigr]dx_1=0$. The same argument in the second coordinate, and step 2.1 (respectively step 1.1 for the vanishing trace), give $\int_0^{L_2}\bigl[(\partial_2h_{mn})^2+h_{mn}\partial_2^2h_{mn}\bigr]dx_2=0$, and the identical argument with $e_{mn}$ in place of $h_{mn}$ gives $\int_0^{L_1}\bigl[(\partial_1e_{mn})^2+e_{mn}\partial_1^2e_{mn}\bigr]dx_1=0$ and its second-coordinate counterpart, the boundary terms vanishing because $e_{mn}$ is zero on $\partial R$. Integrating the resulting pointwise identities over the rectangle against the other coordinate and applying Fubini [F2] (all integrands are continuous on $\overline R$), then substituting $\partial_1^2h_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{m\pi}{L_1}\bigr)^2h_{mn}$, $\partial_2^2h_{mn}=-\bigl(\frac{n\pi}{L_2}\bigr)^2h_{mn}$ and the analogous two identities for $e_{mn}$ from step 2.1, yields both statements of clause (d).

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$.

Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$.

Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: [Component forms] In the orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_z)$ a transverse vector has the form $v=(v_1,v_2,0)$, and the coordinate formula for the cross product [F3] gives $e_z\times v=(e_z\times v_1e_1)+(e_z\times v_2e_2)=v_1e_2-v_2e_1=(-v_2,v_1,0)$. Hence $e_z\times\nabla_th=(-\partial_2h,\partial_1h,0)$, $e_z\times u_t=(-u_2,u_1,0)$, and $e_zh$ is the field $(0,0,h)$; every field displayed in the Statement is independent of $x_3$, so its $\partial_3$-derivative vanishes wherever the derivative is taken.

[Divergence of $e_z\times\nabla_th$] By [F2] and step 1.1, $\operatorname{div}(e_z\times\nabla_th)=\partial_1(-\partial_2h)+\partial_2(\partial_1h)+\partial_3 0=-\partial_1\partial_2h+\partial_2\partial_1h$, which is $0$ by [F5] because $h$ is $C^2$; this is the first identity of clause (a).

[Curl of $e_z\times\nabla_th$] By [F2] and step 1.1, again with the third-coordinate derivative vanishing, $\operatorname{curl}(e_z\times\nabla_th)=(\partial_2 0-\partial_3\partial_1h,\ \partial_3(-\partial_2h)-\partial_1 0,\ \partial_1\partial_1h-\partial_2(-\partial_2h))=(0,0,\partial_1^2h+\partial_2^2h)=e_z\Delta_th$, which is the second identity of clause (a) by [F4].

[Triple product, orthogonality and norm] For an arbitrary transverse $v=(v_1,v_2,0)$, step 1.1 gives $e_z\times(e_z\times v)=e_z\times(-v_2,v_1,0)=(-v_1,-v_2,0)=-v$; the coordinate formulas of [F3] give $v\cdot(e_z\times v)=v_1(-v_2)+v_2v_1+0\cdot0=0$, $e_z\cdot(e_z\times v)=0$ as the third component of $e_z\times v$ is $0$, and $|e_z\times v|^2=(-v_2)^2+v_1^2+0=v_1^2+v_2^2=|v|^2$, both sides nonnegative, so $|e_z\times v|=|v|$. At $v=\nabla_th$ these are the remaining four identities of clause (a); the case $v=0$ is included since then both sides vanish.

[Clause (b)] By [F2] and step 1.1, $\operatorname{curl}(e_zh)=(\partial_2h-\partial_3 0,\ \partial_3 0-\partial_1h,\ \partial_1 0-\partial_2 0)=(\partial_2h,-\partial_1h,0)=-e_z\times\nabla_th$, and $\operatorname{div}(e_zh)=\partial_1 0+\partial_2 0+\partial_3h=\partial_3h$, which is $0$ because $h$ is independent of $x_3$.

[Clause (c)] For $u_t=(u_1,u_2,0)$ with $\partial_3u_j=0$, [F2] gives $\operatorname{curl}(u_t)=(\partial_2 0-\partial_3u_2,\ \partial_3u_1-\partial_1 0,\ \partial_1u_2-\partial_2u_1)=(0,0,\operatorname{curl}_2u_t)=e_z\operatorname{curl}_2u_t$ and $\operatorname{div}(u_t)=\partial_1u_1+\partial_2u_2=\operatorname{div}_tu_t$; and $e_z\times u_t=(-u_2,u_1,0)$ has third component $0$, so it is transverse.
