derivations.claim: Write $w_j=\alpha_j+i\beta_j$ with $\alpha_j=\operatorname{Re}w_j$, $\beta_j=\operatorname{Im}w_j$ real and fix the component index $j$; by [F1] $e^{-i\omega t}=\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t$, so the product rule of [F2] with $(a,b)=(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ and $(c,s)=(\cos\omega t,-\sin\omega t)$ gives $z_{p,j}(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w_j\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t)$ for every real $t$. The maps $t\mapsto\omega t$, $\sin$ and $\cos$ are smooth, and the sum, scalar-multiple and product rules of [F3] give the derivatives of finite combinations, so each $z_{p,j}$ is $C^\infty$ and hence $z_p$ is $C^\infty$ by [F7].

Differentiating the display of step 1.1 componentwise with the rules of [F3] gives $z_{p,j}'(t)=\omega^{-1}(\alpha_j\sin\omega t-\beta_j\cos\omega t)$ and $z_{p,j}''(t)=\alpha_j\cos\omega t+\beta_j\sin\omega t=\operatorname{Re}((\alpha_j+i\beta_j)(\cos\omega t-i\sin\omega t))=\operatorname{Re}(w_je^{-i\omega t})$ for every $j$ and every real $t$, the middle equality by the product rule of [F2] and the last by [F1]; hence $z_p''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise.

Since $\omega(t+T)=\omega t+2\pi$, the display of step 1.1 and the period formulas $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$, $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ of [F4] give $z_{p,j}(t+T)=z_{p,j}(t)$ for every $j$ and every $t\in\mathbb R$, so $z_p$ is $T$-periodic; with steps 1.1 and 2.1 this is claim (a).

Let $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $\mathbb R$ and set $h:=z-z_p$; by step 2.1, $h''=0$ on $\mathbb R$. Fix $j$; the component $h_j$ is $C^2$, so $h_j'$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R$, which is the interior of $\mathbb R$ by [F5], with $(h_j')'=h_j''=0$; [F5] applied on the order-convex interval $\mathbb R$ therefore makes $h_j'$ a constant $b_j\in\mathbb R$. The map $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ by [F6] and differentiable at every point with derivative $h_j'-b_j=0$, the derivative of $b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ being $b_j$ by [F3]; [F5] makes $h_j-b_j\,\mathrm{id}$ a constant $a_j$, so $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ and $z=z_p+a+bt$ with $a=(a_1,\dots,a_n)$, $b=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$. If also $z=z_p+a'+b't$ on $\mathbb R$, evaluating at $t=0$ gives $a=a'$ and then differentiating at $t=0$ gives $b=b'$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique; this is claim (b).

Let $z=z_p+a+bt$ be a solution as in step 3.1. If $b=0$, then $z=z_p+a$ is $T$-periodic by step 2.2. Conversely, if $z$ is $T$-periodic, then for every $t\in\mathbb R$ the equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ together with $z_p(t+T)=z_p(t)$ of step 2.2 gives $b(t+T)=bt$, hence $bT=0$ and $b=0$ because $T>0$. The $T$-periodic solutions are therefore exactly the maps $z_p+a$ with $a\in\mathbb R^n$; their oscillating part is $z_p$ itself, whose defining formula $z_p(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-w\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$ exhibits the complex amplitude vector $-w/\omega^2$; this is claim (c).

Let $I$ be a nonempty open interval, $t_*\in I$, and let $z:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with $z''=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $I$; put $h:=z-z_p$ on $I$. Fixing $j$ and repeating the argument of step 3.1 on the order-convex interval $I$, every interior point of which lies in $I$ where the assumed derivatives exist, gives a constant $b_j$ on $I$ equal to $h_j'$, then a constant $a_j$ with $h_j=a_j+b_jt$ on $I$; hence $z=z_p+a+bt$ on $I$. Evaluating at $t_*$ gives $b=z'(t_*)-z_p'(t_*)$ and $a=z(t_*)-z_p(t_*)-bt_*$, and conversely those values reproduce $z$ on $I$, so the pair $(a,b)$ is unique. Define $Z(t):=z_p(t)+a+bt$ for all real $t$ with these $(a,b)$; by steps 2.1 and 2.2, $Z$ is a $C^\infty$ solution on $\mathbb R$ extending $z$. If $\tilde Z$ is any global $C^2$ solution on $\mathbb R$ agreeing with $z$ on $I$, then step 3.1 writes $\tilde Z=z_p+\tilde a+\tilde bt$ with a unique pair $(\tilde a,\tilde b)$; restricting to $I$ and using the uniqueness just proved gives $\tilde a=a$ and $\tilde b=b$, so $\tilde Z=Z$ and the extension is unique.

For $Z$ as in step 4.2, step 4.1 gives that $Z$ is $T$-periodic if and only if $b=0$, which by step 4.2 is equivalent to $z'(t_*)=z_p'(t_*)$. If $t$ and $t+T$ both lie in $I$, then $Z(t+T)-Z(t)=bT$ while $Z$ agrees with $z$ at those two arguments, so equality $z(t+T)=z(t)$ forces $bT=0$ and $b=0$. If $I$ contains no such pair, then the condition "$z(t+T)=z(t)$ whenever both $t$ and $t+T$ lie in $I$" has empty scope and is satisfied vacuously; the extension with any fixed nonzero $b$ obeys it and is not $T$-periodic, so the condition determines nothing about periodicity of the global extension.

Fix $t\in\mathbb R$ and a component index $j$ and define $G_j(s):=-\omega^{-3}(\alpha_j\sin\omega s-\beta_j\cos\omega s)$ for $s\in[t,t+T]$; by the rules of [F3], $G_j$ is differentiable at every point of $[t,t+T]$ with $G_j'(s)=-\omega^{-2}(\alpha_j\cos\omega s+\beta_j\sin\omega s)=z_{p,j}(s)$. The map $z_{p,j}$ is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, hence continuous on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6], hence Riemann integrable on $[t,t+T]$ by [F6]; the fundamental theorem [F6] therefore gives $\int_t^{t+T}z_{p,j}=\omega^{-3}[\beta_j(\cos(\omega(t+T))-\cos\omega t)-\alpha_j(\sin(\omega(t+T))-\sin\omega t)]=0$, the vanishing because $\cos(\omega t+2\pi)=\cos\omega t$ and $\sin(\omega t+2\pi)=\sin\omega t$ by [F4] and $\omega T=2\pi$. Summing over $j$ and dividing by $T$ gives mean zero for $z_p$ over $[t,t+T]$. For the affine part put $P(s):=as+bs^2/2$, differentiable with $P'(s)=a+bs$ by [F3]; the same fundamental theorem, the integrand $s\mapsto a+bs$ being continuous, gives $\frac1T\int_t^{t+T}(a+bs)\,ds=\frac{P(t+T)-P(t)}T=a+\frac{b((t+T)^2-t^2)}{2T}=a+b(t+\frac T2)$. Adding the two computations, the mean of $Z$ over $[t,t+T]$ is $a+b(t+T/2)$ for every real $t$, and it equals $a$ for every $t$ exactly when $b=0$, which by step 5.1 is exactly the periodicity condition; then the mean over every complete period is $a$. This completes the proof of (d) and of the lemma.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 4.2 and 5.1 distinguish the nonempty open solution interval from the possibly empty set of pairs t,t+T in I. When that pair set is empty the local periodicity test is vacuous; the unique global extension still has its classified affine drift.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 show w=0 gives z_p identically zero, and steps 3.1 and 4.1 keep the zero drift b=0 as the periodic branch; step 6.1 computes the period mean a, which may be the zero vector. The zero-frequency value is excluded by omega>0.

Step 2.2 verifies periodicity at the single shift T; step 4.1 decides periodicity by the single equation bT=0; step 5.1 uses one admissible pair t and t+T in I; the n=1 component case is covered by the fixed component index j in steps 1.1 to 2.1.

boundaries.reason: Clause (d) quantifies only over nonempty open intervals, so a degenerate interval (a single point) is outside the hypothesis; the degenerate drift case b=0 is the periodic case treated in steps 4.1 and 5.1.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 differentiates the difference h on all of R and step 6.1 integrates G_j on the closed interval from t to t+T with the fundamental theorem, G_j being continuous to the endpoints; step 5.1 evaluates the periodic equality only at pairs t and t+T that both lie in I.

The proof fixes finitely many component indices, times and the single point t_*, and applies the explicit derivative, integral and zero-derivative suppliers; the Statement declares no choice principle and step 4.2 uses only Corollary [F5].
Step 4.1: if a solution z_p+a+bt is T-periodic then b(t+T)=bt for every t, hence b=0; step 5.1 transfers the conclusion to the unique global extension Z.

Step 4.1 proves b=0 implies T-periodicity; step 5.1 transfers this to the unique global extension. By step 4.2 the condition is z-prime(t_*)=z_p-prime(t_*); no equality of the positions is required because the constant mean a is arbitrary.

Includes w=0,n=1,nonzero drift and vacuous short-interval periodicity. No Choice or empirical premise. Reader/refuter report no finding on this carrier.

citations.quote: Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so $\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. For $z\in\mathbb C$, define $$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$ whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of [[def-complex-integer-powers]] and [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
The complex exponential is entire, and $$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with $$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$ Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$, $$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$ In particular, $$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex numbers** by the quotient ring $$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$ ([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set $$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$ Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map $\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which $\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of [[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent: 1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$. 2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number. 3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$. 4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations $$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$ When these conditions hold, $$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$
The complex exponential is entire, and $$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$ for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A 	o \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) 
e 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) 
e 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 	o \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$ igl((f/g)|_{A_0} igr)'(c) \;=\;  rac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$ Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that it has the stated value. Both are proved. **Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$ is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis is $g(c) 
e 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere". **Everything is proved through [[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent. The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative** $$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$ For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$. Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{n-1}):U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$ in the componentwise Euclidean sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Then the **divergence** of $F$ is $\operatorname{div}F:=\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i$, the function $U\to\mathbb R$ whose value at $p$ is $\sum_{i<n}\partial_iF_i(p)$. The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], and the sum is the finite sum used throughout [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Since each $\partial_iF_i$ is continuous on $U$, so is $\operatorname{div}F$. Now let $n=3$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$. Following [[def-cross-product-in-r3]], write the three coordinates of a point and of a vector as $x,y,z$ rather than $0,1,2$, so that $F=(F_x,F_y,F_z)$ means $F=(F_0,F_1,F_2)$ and $\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z$ are $\partial_0,\partial_1,\partial_2$. With that naming, the **curl** of $F$ is $\operatorname{curl}F:=(\partial_yF_z-\partial_zF_y,\ \partial_zF_x-\partial_xF_z,\ \partial_xF_y-\partial_yF_x)$, a map $U\to\mathbb R^3$ each of whose coordinates is continuous on $U$. In this naming the divergence reads $\operatorname{div}F=\partial_xF_x+\partial_yF_y+\partial_zF_z$. Both operators are defined pointwise from the first partial derivatives of the components, so no differentiability of $F$ beyond $C^1$ is used and no orientation or metric structure enters beyond the standard coordinates of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. For a $C^1$ scalar function $f$ on $U$, the gradient $\nabla f=(\partial_0f,\ldots,\partial_{n-1}f)$ is that of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; in the three-coordinate naming, $\nabla f=(\partial_xf,\partial_yf,\partial_zf)$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F,G:U	o\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$, let $f:U	o\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ and let $a,b\in\mathbb R$. Then $aF+bG$ and $fF$ are $C^1$ on $U$ and $$\operatorname{div}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{div}F+b\operatorname{div}G,$$ $$\operatorname{div}(fF)=\langle
abla f,Fangle+f\operatorname{div}F.$$ If moreover $n=3$, then $$\operatorname{curl}(aF+bG)=a\operatorname{curl}F+b\operatorname{curl}G,\qquad \operatorname{curl}(fF)=
abla f	imes F+f\operatorname{curl}F.$$ Here $\operatorname{div}$, $\operatorname{curl}$ and the coordinate naming are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], $
abla f$ is the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], $\langle\cdot,\cdotangle$ is the inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $	imes$ is the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

Let $(X, d_X)$ and $(Y, d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]), let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and let $a \in X$. $f$ is **continuous at $a$** if for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ such that $$d_X(x,a) < \delta \;\Longrightarrow\; d_Y\big(f(x), f(a)\big) < \varepsilon \qquad \text{for all } x \in X .$$ $f$ is **continuous** (globally, or on $X$) if it is continuous at every point of $X$. **The same condition in balls.** Since $d_X(x,a) < \delta$ says $x \in B_X(a,\delta)$ and $d_Y(f(x),f(a)) < \varepsilon$ says $f(x) \in B_Y(f(a),\varepsilon)$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), continuity at $a$ reads: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $$f\big[B_X(a,\delta)\big] \subseteq B_Y\big(f(a), \varepsilon\big).$$ Both forms are used below and are the same statement written twice. **Both metrics matter, and both are named.** Continuity is a property of the triple $(d_X, d_Y, f)$, not of $f$ alone. When several metrics on the same underlying sets are in play, as in [[def-equivalent-metrics]], the metrics are always written out. **Quantifier order.** The $\delta$ is allowed to depend on $\varepsilon$ **and on the point $a$**. Requiring one $\delta$ to work at every point simultaneously is a strictly stronger condition, uniform continuity; it is defined on a later page of this library, and at this point in the reading order it is written out in full where needed ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, and give $\mathbb{R}$ its usual topology, the metric topology of $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]], [[def-metrizable-space]]). Let $$\mathbb{R}^n \;=\; \prod_{k < n} \mathbb{R}$$ be the product of $n$ copies of $\mathbb{R}$ ([[def-product-topology]]). As a **set** this is literally the $\mathbb{R}^n$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], both being the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$; and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the three metrics defined there. Then: 1. The product topology on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is the metric topology of $d_\infty$ ([[def-metric-topology]]). The key computation is that a $d_\infty$-ball is a box: $$B_{d_\infty}(x, r) \;=\; \prod_{k<n} (x_k - r,\ x_k + r) \qquad (r > 0),$$ a product of bounded open intervals ([[def-interval]]). 2. $d_\infty \le d_1 \le n\, d_\infty$ and $d_\infty \le d_2 \le n\, d_\infty$ pointwise, so $d_1$ and $d_2$ are each Lipschitz equivalent to $d_\infty$ ([[def-equivalent-metrics]]); here $n$ denotes the canonical natural $n \cdot 1_{\mathbb{R}}$. 3. Consequently all three metrics induce the product topology ([[thm-metric-equivalence-hierarchy]]). So $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the product topology and $\mathbb{R}^n$ carrying the topology of any one of $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are **one topological space**, and it is metrizable ([[def-metrizable-space]]). **Why $n \ge 1$.** The metric $d_\infty$ is a maximum over $n$ terms, which does not exist for $n = 0$; [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries the same hypothesis, and it is carried here for the same reason. For $n = 0$ the product is a one-point space and there is nothing to compare.

Let $(X_i, \mathcal{T}_i)_{i \in I}$ be topological spaces and let $P := \prod_{i \in I} X_i$ carry the product topology, with projections $\pi_j$ ([[def-product-topology]]). Then: 1. **The projections are continuous**, and the product topology is the coarsest topology on $P$ making all of them continuous. 2. **Characteristic property.** For every space $Z$ and every function $h : Z \to P$, $$h \text{ is continuous } \iff \pi_i \circ h \text{ is continuous for every } i \in I .$$ The functions $\pi_i \circ h$ are the **components** of $h$, and every family of functions $h_i : Z \to X_i$ arises from exactly one $h$, namely $h(z)(i) := h_i(z)$. 3. **The projections are open maps** ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]), for the product topology and for the box topology alike. They need not be closed; that failure is recorded on this page as a false statement. 4. **Surjectivity.** If every $X_i$ is nonempty then every $\pi_j$ is surjective. For $I$ a natural number this is a theorem of ZF ([[lem-finite-choice]]); for an arbitrary $I$ it is the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), and this is the only place in the item where a choice principle is used.

Let $f,g:X\to\mathbb R$ be continuous maps from a topological space. Then $f+g$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max(f,g)$, and $\min(f,g)$ are continuous. On the open cozero set $\operatorname{coz}(g)$, the quotient $f/g$ is continuous. The same holds for every finite sum, product, maximum, or minimum of continuous real-valued maps.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is continuous at every point of $S$. **No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the companion page.

derivations.claim: [Encoding] For clauses (a) and (c), assume the stated $C^1$ hypotheses. For every $k$ and every $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$, [F1] and [F2] give $E_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})=(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x))\cos\omega t+(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x))\sin\omega t$, and the same display with $\widetilde B_k$ in place of $\widetilde E_k$ gives $B_k(x,t)$; moreover, since $\widetilde E$ and $\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, their six real coordinate maps and all first partials are continuous on $D$ and the complex partials are $\partial_j\widetilde E_k=\partial_j(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k)+i\,\partial_j(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k)$, by [F4].

[Injectivity] Let $w\in\mathbb C^3$ satisfy $\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})=0$ for every real $t$. At $t=0$, [F1] gives $e^0=1$, so $\operatorname{Re}w=0$; at $t=\pi/(2\omega)$ one has $e^{-i\pi/2}=-i$ by [F1], so $0=\operatorname{Re}(-iw)=\operatorname{Im}w$ by [F2]; hence $w=\operatorname{Re}w+i\operatorname{Im}w=0$. If $w:D\to\mathbb C^3$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re}(w(x)e^{-i\omega t})=0$ for all $(x,t)$, applying the preceding conclusion at each fixed $x\in D$ gives $w(x)=0$ for every $x$, so $w\equiv0$; no continuity of $w$ is needed for this conclusion.

[Time derivative] Fix $x$ and $k$. The map $t\mapsto\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t}$ is the composition of the real-linear map $t\mapsto-i\omega t$ (which is differentiable on $\mathbb R$ with derivative $-i\omega$ and real-linear, so totally differentiable with that derivative) with $\exp$, which is real totally differentiable everywhere with derivative the multiplication $h\mapsto e^z h$ by [F3], followed by multiplication by the constant $\widetilde E_k(x)$; the chain and product rules of [F3], [F4] give derivative $-i\omega\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t}$. Taking real parts by [F2] and inserting the display of step 1.1, $\partial_tE_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde E_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})=\omega(\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k(x))\cos\omega t-\omega(\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k(x))\sin\omega t$ for every $(x,t)$; the same computation with $\widetilde B$ gives $\partial_tB_k(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde B_k(x)e^{-i\omega t})$.

[Spatial derivatives] Fix $(x,t)$ and indices $j,k$. The map $h\mapsto E_k(x+he_j,t)$ equals $h\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_k(x+he_j))$ times $\cos\omega t$ plus $h\mapsto\operatorname{Im}(\widetilde E_k(x+he_j))$ times $\sin\omega t$ on a neighbourhood of $0$ small enough that $x+he_j\in D$, by step 1.1. All assertions are pointwise identities on the open domain $D\times\mathbb R$, no existence theory for partial differential equations, no boundary condition and no choice principle are used, and the argument rests only on the cited complex, real-analysis and topological continuity suppliers.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice, as used by the variational, Sobolev and compact-spectral suppliers and by the Fredholm alternative ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $O\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded open set with $C^\infty$ boundary ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]) whose exterior $D=\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline O$ is connected, let $k>0$, and let $R>0$ with $\overline O\subset B_R(0)$. Write $A:=B_R(0)\setminus\overline O$ and let $n$ be the outward unit normal field of $A$, so that on $\partial O$ the field $n$ points into $O$; extend $n$ to a smooth normal collar by $n(p+sn(p)):=n(p)$, so $\partial_n n=0$, using [[thm-euclidean-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem]]; put $\kappa:=\operatorname{div}n|_{\partial O}$ and, for a field $E$ on $\partial O$, $E_n:=E\cdot n|_{\partial O}$. For $e_T:\partial O\to\mathbb C^3$ smooth in boundary charts and satisfying $e_T\cdot n=0$, put $$\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T:=\operatorname{div}\widetilde e_T-\partial_n(\widetilde e_T\cdot n)\quad\text{on }\partial O,$$ where $\widetilde e_T$ is any smooth extension of $e_T$ to a neighbourhood of $\partial O$; the expression is independent of the extension and equals the surface divergence of $e_T$ with respect to the Euclidean surface measure of $\partial O$. Write $\Delta$ for the Euclidean Laplacian ([[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]]), acting componentwise, and for a vector field $f=(f_1,f_2,f_3)$ on $S_R$ write $T_Rf:=(T_Rf_1,T_Rf_2,T_Rf_3)$ with $T_R$ the scalar Dirichlet-to-Neumann map of [[lem-em-sphere-outgoing-dirichlet-to-neumann-map]]. Then there is exactly one field $E\in C^\infty(\overline D;\mathbb C^3)$ with $$(\Delta+k^2)E=0\ \text{on }D,\qquad \operatorname{div}E=0\ \text{on }D,\qquad E_{\text{tangential}}=e_T\ \text{on }\partial O,$$ which is outgoing on the sphere $S_R$ in the modal sense of that lemma: its trace $f:=E|_{S_R}$ lies in $H^{1/2}(S_R;\mathbb C^3)$ and the normal derivative of $E$ on $S_R$ equals $T_Rf$ componentwise in the weak trace sense of the sphere DtN lemma. With these data the normal boundary values of $E$ on $\partial O$ satisfy the closure relation $$\partial_nE_n+(\operatorname{div}n)E_n=-\operatorname{div}_{\partial O}e_T$$ as an identity of $C^\infty$ functions on $\partial O$. No scalar Dirichlet condition is imposed on the three Cartesian components of $E$, and no decay rate, asymptotic expansion or pointwise Sommerfeld formula beyond the stated modal outgoing class is assumed.

Let $\omega>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty open set, and let $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be the vacuum constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; put $T:=2\pi/\omega$.

**(a) [Phasor encoding.]** For every pair of $C^\infty$ maps $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) define the **associated real fields** $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\qquad((x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R),$$

with the complex exponential and real part of [[def-complex-exponential]] and [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. This is the encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] specialized from plane-wave amplitudes to a general $C^\infty$ amplitude, and the complex fields are not themselves physical fields.

**(b) [Source-free class.]** The pair $(\widetilde E,\widetilde B)$ is called a **frequency-$\omega$ source-free vacuum phasor pair on $D$** when it is $C^\infty$ and satisfies, on $D$,

$$\operatorname{div}\widetilde E=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}\widetilde B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde E=i\omega\widetilde B,\qquad \operatorname{curl}\widetilde B=-i\omega\varepsilon_0\mu_0\widetilde E=-i\omega c^{-2}\widetilde E,$$

with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] applied componentwise to the complex fields. The word "source-free" records that the displayed equations carry no charge or current term; the associated real fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]], $\omega$ is the angular frequency and $T$ the period.

**(c) [Status and scope.]** This item fixes the encoding, the four phasor equations and the terminology only. It asserts no equation for the associated real fields, no outgoing or boundary condition, no existence or uniqueness statement, no energy or flux reading and no empirical content. In particular the deduction that the associated real fields satisfy the smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations with zero sources is not part of this definition; for the pairs used on the exterior-scattering page it is established by the exterior-scattering theorem recorded there. Only $C^\infty$ pairs on an open set are defined, so no boundary trace, weak or distributional class is introduced here.

### Well-definedness and conventions

The componentwise reading of the two complex fields is the one of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]: $\widetilde E$ and $\widetilde B$ are $C^\infty$ exactly when the twelve real coordinate maps $\operatorname{Re}\widetilde E_k$, $\operatorname{Im}\widetilde E_k$, $\operatorname{Re}\widetilde B_k$, $\operatorname{Im}\widetilde B_k$ ($k=1,2,3$) are $C^\infty$ on the open set $D$. The real and imaginary parts and the complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] are total on $\mathbb C$, so the associated real fields are defined for every $C^\infty$ pair, with no equation assumed and no regularity asserted of them by clause (a). Clause (b) is the subclass cut out by the four displayed equations: the divergence and curl of a $C^\infty$ complex field are the componentwise extensions of the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] to $\operatorname{Re}$ and $\operatorname{Im}$ parts, evaluated on the open set $D$, and the right-hand sides use only complex scalar multiplication by the constants $i\omega$ and $i\omega\varepsilon_0\mu_0$. In particular $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=c^{-2}$ by [[def-em-si-conventions]], a positive scalar parameter; all four equations are pointwise, so no selection of data and no choice principle enters the definition.

The units are inherited from [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]]: $\widetilde E$ and $E$ carry $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$, $\widetilde B$ and $B$ carry the tesla $\mathrm T$, the wavevector-like spatial variable $x$ carries $\mathrm m$, $t$ carries $\mathrm s$, and $\omega$ carries $\mathrm s^{-1}$. The complex fields are auxiliary amplitudes encoding the real fields; clause (b) is a condition on those amplitudes, not a new physical assertion about the real fields.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open, $c>0$ and $\omega>0$, and let $\widetilde E,\widetilde B:D\to\mathbb C^3$. Define $E,B:D\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ by $E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde B(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise ([[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]; [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] for the classes). Then: (a) [Calculus] if $\widetilde E,\widetilde B$ are $C^1$, then $E,B$ are $C^1$ and at every $(x,t)\in D\times\mathbb R$: $\partial_tE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(-i\omega\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; for each $j\in\{1,2,3\}$, $\partial_jE(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(\partial_j\widetilde E(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$; and with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] acting on the spatial variable, $\operatorname{div}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{div}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, $\operatorname{curl}E(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}((\operatorname{curl}\widetilde E)(x)e^{-i\omega t})$, and likewise for $B$. Adopt as a physical postulate of this framework the following four equations for the fields of [[def-em-fields]] and the sources of [[def-em-sources]] on the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with $\mu_0>0$, $c>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ and the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Smooth branch] Let $E,B$ be jointly $C^1$ fields with the additional derivatives required by each equation existing and continuous, and let $\rho,J$ be continuous. Then, with the divergence and curl of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]] and the partial derivative $\partial_t$ at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]], $$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE.$$ (b) [Weak branch] Let instead $E,B$ be locally integrable $\mathbb R^3$-valued fields and $\rho,J$ locally integrable scalar and vector fields on $I\times\Omega$, identified with their regular distributions ([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]). The equations are adopted classical vacuum physics in the named inertial chart; they are not deduced from charge conservation, from empirical agreement or from the special-relativity postulates, and this item by itself asserts no covariance under changes of inertial frame.

e(0,0)$ if and only if $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is $e=b=0$. If $|k|=\omega/c$, the solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with $e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k	imes e/\omega$: a complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every nonzero solution $e

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$ the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$ componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$, $\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**, $\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the **angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**, and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then: (a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. (b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through $\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$. (c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave **nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the magnetic field alone determines $b$, because $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$ (evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$). (d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is claimed. ### Well-definedness and conventions For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and $B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$, $T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map $(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and $y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex derivative is also its real total derivative ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]), and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word $(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$, $\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell =\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$, by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with $b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a). The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of $w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking $\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F$, $\nabla\operatorname{div}F$ and $\Delta F$ are all defined on $U$ and $$\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}F=\nabla\operatorname{div}F-\Delta F.$$ Here $\Delta F$ is the componentwise Laplacian of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]].
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be open and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be $C^2$. Then $\operatorname{curl}F$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ and $$\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}F)=0\qquad\text{on }U.$$
