citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the smooth modal full-Choice branch of the latter is not used. Adopt as a model assumption of the framework the following scalar aperture-diffraction model. **(a) [Data.]** Fix an angular frequency $\omega>0$ and wavenumber $k:=\omega/c$, with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Let $S\subset\{y\in\mathbb R^3:y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$ be a nonempty compact subset of a declared aperture plane $y_3=0$ with aperture radius $a>0$ (the screening plane and spatial region are read in the laboratory chart of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]), and let $\alpha$ be a finite complex measure on $\mathbb R^3$ supported in $S$ ([[def-complex-measure]], [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]) — the **aperture distribution** — with $\alpha$ read in volts so that the model field below carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ of an electric-field component and its pairings are those of [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. **(b) [Model field.]** The model assigns to every observation point $x$ with $x_3>0$ the complex scalar amplitude $$u(x):=\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y),$$ where $G_k(z)=e^{ik|z|}/(4\pi|z|)$ for $z\ne0$ is the outgoing Helmholtz kernel of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]], together with the real scalar field $U(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and the model period-averaged squared field $(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. All model predictions are declared comparisons of this squared field between observation points; no absolute radiometric power or intensity calibration is adopted. **(c) [Adopted regime and status.]** The model is the declared polarization-insensitive scalar approximation of aperture diffraction. It ignores the vector nature and polarization of the electromagnetic field, takes the aperture distribution rather than the exact screen traces as its datum, assigns no back-reaction of the diffracted field on the illumination and no screen interaction beyond the aperture, and is not derived from either branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] or from the material-closure branches of [[post-em-material-closure]]; it is a declared optical approximation, not an exact electromagnetic model. It does not assert that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and it does not identify $\alpha$ with the unknown exact Maxwell boundary traces: assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently is not a well-posed exact boundary problem, as recorded in [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]], and the error terms of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] are the controlled content of the model. No measured intensity, apparatus, sampling model, uncertainty budget, empirical comparison or quantitative radiometric calibration is adopted. ### Well-definedness and non-derivation notes For fixed $x$ with $x_3>0$ and $y$ ranging over the compact support $S$ of $\alpha$, one has $|x-y|\ge x_3>0$, so $y\mapsto G_k(x-y)$ is continuous on $S$, bounded there by $1/(4\pi x_3)$; the pairing $\int G_k(x-y)\,d\alpha(y)$ is therefore the integral of a bounded continuous complex function against a finite complex measure and is defined by [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]], with $|u(x)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}/(4\pi x_3)$ in the total variation of [[def-total-variation-of-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]. The model permits the compact closed-radius support $|y|\le a$, including aperture corners: the integral, off-support regularity and closed-radius estimates at $r\ge2a$ are established for finite measures supported in $\overline{B_a(0)}$ by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]. The consuming diffraction theorem also supplies direct kernel estimates at that same closed radius. The integral against a finite complex measure, the real-field reading and the squared field $\tfrac12|u|^2$ constitute the whole mathematical content adopted here; the physical reading uses the aperture plane and spatial region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], the relation $k=\omega/c$ and the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Neither the smooth nor the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] implies this scalar source model, and the finite-conductivity and material branches of [[post-em-material-closure]] contain no ideal aperture or screen model. The item uses no choice principle beyond those carried by the cited mathematical suppliers; the Countable Choice hypothesis is inherited verbatim from the kernel and boundary-representation suppliers and this postulate adds no choice use of its own. No derivation of the adopted data from the underlying postulates, and no empirical validation of the model, is claimed or implied by this item.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]] and [[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]] ([[def-countable-choice]]), whose trace qualification is used in clause (d); the full-Choice modal branch of the latter is not used. Adopt the scalar aperture model and its notation from [[post-em-scalar-aperture-model]]: frequency $\omega>0$, $k=\omega/c$, aperture radius $a>0$, finite complex aperture distribution $\alpha$ supported in the planar aperture $S\subset\{y_3=0\}\cap\{y:|y|\le a\}$, model field $u=G_k*\alpha$, real field $U(x,t)=\operatorname{Re}(u(x)e^{-i\omega t})$ and $T=2\pi/\omega$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-complex-exponential]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], [[def-integration-against-a-signed-or-complex-measure]]). Set $I(x):=(1/2)|u(x)|^2$. Then: (a) [Model field and Fraunhofer estimate] $u$ is $C^\infty$ on the half-space $\{x_3>0\}$ and on $\mathbb R^3\setminus S$, satisfies $(\Delta+k^2)u=0$ there, and is outgoing in the sense of [[lem-em-outgoing-source-helmholtz-and-diffraction]]: for $x=rn$ with $r\ge2a$ and $n\in S^2$, $$u(rn)=\frac{e^{ikr}}{4\pi r}\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)+O\Bigl(\frac{\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}}{r}\Bigl[\frac ar+\frac{ka^2}{r}\Bigr]\Bigr)$$ uniformly in direction, and $r(\partial_ru-iku)=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly. (b) [Fresnel estimate] write $y_t=(y_1,y_2)$ and $\xi=(\xi_1,\xi_2)$ for transverse vectors; for the planar aperture and observation $x=(\xi_1,\xi_2,z)$ with $z>0$, $b\ge0$, $|\xi|\le b$ and any declared fixed small-angle range $(a+b)/z\le\eta_0<1$, where $0<\eta_0<1$, the Fresnel approximation replaces $R=|x-y|$ by $z+|\xi-y_t|^2/(2z)$ and $1/R$ by $1/z$ in the model integral with phase error $O(k(a+b)^4/z^3)$, relative amplitude error $O((a+b)^2/z^2)$ and absolute field error $O(\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}z^{-1}[(a+b)^2/z^2+k(a+b)^4/z^3])$. (c) [Intensity and error transfer] at every $x$ with $x_3>0$ the model period average satisfies $\frac1T\int_0^TU(x,s)^2\,ds=I(x)$ ([[lem-em-period-average]]). If $u_{\rm approx}$ is any approximation of $u$ with $|u_{\rm approx}(x)-u(x)|\le\delta(x)$, then $|\frac12|u_{\rm approx}(x)|^2-I(x)|\le\frac12\delta(x)(|u(x)|+|u_{\rm approx}(x)|)$; if moreover $u(x)\ne0$ and $|u_{\rm approx}(x)-u(x)|\le\epsilon(x)|u(x)|$, the relative intensity error is at most $2\epsilon(x)+\epsilon(x)^2$. In particular the Fraunhofer and Fresnel field errors of (a) and (b) bound the corresponding intensity errors; no new approximation is introduced by passing to $I$. (d) [Trace and scope] the aperture distribution $\alpha$ is an adopted model datum and is not identified with the exact Maxwell boundary data on the screen; assigning both $u$ and $\partial_nu$ on the aperture independently does not produce a well-posed exact boundary problem ([[lem-em-helmholtz-boundary-representation]]). The construction ignores polarization and aperture back-reaction, makes no claim that $u$ or $U$ satisfies the Maxwell equations exactly, and makes no measured-intensity, apparatus, sampling or empirical claim; only comparisons of $I$ between observation points are read as model predictions.

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$. **Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$ **Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$ the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative to $\mu$** is the measure $$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$ whose measure property is supplied by [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define $$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$ The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal. Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write $$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$ ([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and $\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every** set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue measurable with $$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$ In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box $B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite parameters the value is already $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **complex measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function $$
u:\mathcal A\longrightarrow\mathbb C$$ such that: 1. $
u(\varnothing)=0$; 2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$, $$
u\left( igcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_night)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty 
u(E_n)$$ in $\mathbb C$. The codomain is the field $\mathbb C$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]), so a complex measure is finite-valued by definition: there is no complex number called $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ to allow.

Let $

A countable measurable partition of $E$ means: 1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$; 2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint; 3. $E= igcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$. The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$. For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into the definition here.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then $f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and $$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$ If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and $$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$ The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is complex-linear on it: $$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every $n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so $\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]. For $z\in\mathbb C$, define $$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$ whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of [[def-complex-integer-powers]] and [[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A 	o \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) 
e 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) 
e 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 	o \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$ igl((f/g)|_{A_0} igr)'(c) \;=\;  rac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$ Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that it has the stated value. Both are proved. **Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$ is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis is $g(c) 
e 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere". **Everything is proved through [[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent. The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].
The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with $$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$ Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$ **Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything (the sign function); both witnesses are on the companion page. **No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form: the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for continuous integrands.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]). ### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$ At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$. **This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric, not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$. ### The algebra of the inner product For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$: 1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$ termwise. 2. **Additivity in the first argument.** $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies. 3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.** $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2. 4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws in the second argument. 5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$. 6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$. That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed here.

For every real $x$, $$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$ Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.
For every real $x$, $$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$ Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). **The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then: 1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$. 2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$ 3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with $m, M$ real, then $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$ **Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is [[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] below. **Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives $\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when $u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]). Then: 1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable; 2. and in that case $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$ 3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary. Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$ Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the form used everywhere below.

Let $
u$ be a signed measure or complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$ and let $f\in L^1(
u)$. Then $$\left|\int f\,d
uight|\le \int |f|\,d|
u|.$$ More generally, for every measurable $E$, $$\left|\int_E f\,d
uight|\le \int_E |f|\,d|
u|.$$

derivations.claim: [The pushforward is a finite complex measure with the stated support and total variation] For disjoint Borel sets $E_m\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ the inverse images $\jmath^{-1}(E_m)$ are disjoint and Borel by [F3], and countable additivity of $\lambda_2$ gives $\alpha(\bigcup_mE_m)=A_0\sum_m\lambda_2(R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E_m))=\sum_m\alpha(E_m)$, while $\alpha(\varnothing)=0$; hence $\alpha$ is a complex measure, and it is finite because $\lambda_2(R)=4ab$ by [F2]. If $E\cap S=\varnothing$ then $R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E)=\varnothing$, so $\alpha$ is supported in $S$. For every countable Borel partition $\{E_m\}$ of $\mathbb R^3$, the defining values sum to $|A_0|\sum_m\lambda_2(R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E_m))=|A_0|\lambda_2(R)=4ab|A_0|$ by countable additivity and [F2]; taking the supremum over partitions gives $\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}=4ab|A_0|<+\infty$.

[Pairing identity] For a complex simple Borel function $s$, its defining sum gives $\int s\,d\alpha=A_0\int_Rs\circ\jmath\,d\lambda_2$, since each level set pulls back to $R\cap\jmath^{-1}(E)$, by [F3]. For bounded Borel $f$, choose $M>0$ bounding both real coordinates. For each positive integer $N$, partition $[-M,M]$ at $t_j:=-M+2Mj/N$, $0\le j\le N$, into half-open intervals $[t_j,t_{j+1})$ except for the last interval, which includes $M$. On the Borel preimage of the cell with coordinate indices $j,k$, set $s_N:=t_j+it_k$. This gives a finite-range Borel simple function with $\|f-s_N\|_\infty\le2\sqrt2M/N$. By [F3], the error in the left integral is at most $2\sqrt2M\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}/N$, and the error in the right integral is at most $8ab|A_0|\sqrt2M/N$, using $\lambda_2(R)=4ab$. Passing to the limit in the simple-function identities proves $\int f\,d\alpha=A_0\int_Rf\circ\jmath\,d\lambda_2$.

[Fraunhofer amplitude] Fix $n\in S^2$ and put $f(y):=e^{-ikn\cdot y}$, which is continuous on the compact support; by step 2.1, $\int e^{-ikn\cdot y}\,d\alpha(y)=A_0\int_R e^{-ik(n_1y_1+n_2y_2)}\,d\lambda_2(y_1,y_2)$ because $y=\jmath(y_1,y_2)$ and $n\cdot y=n_1y_1+n_2y_2$ by [F5]. The integrand is continuous on the compact rectangle $R$, hence Riemann integrable, so the Lebesgue integral equals the Riemann double integral by [F4], and the Riemann double integral factors as the product of the one-dimensional integrals $\int_{-a}^ae^{-ikn_1y_1}dy_1$ and $\int_{-b}^be^{-ikn_2y_2}dy_2$ by [F4]. For $n_1\ne0$ the map $y_1\mapsto e^{-ikn_1y_1}/(-ikn_1)$ is an antiderivative with derivative $e^{-ikn_1y_1}$ by the chain, algebra and trigonometric derivative rules of [F5], so the second fundamental theorem gives $\int_{-a}^ae^{-ikn_1y_1}dy_1=(e^{-ikn_1a}-e^{ikn_1a})/(-ikn_1)=2\sin(ka\,n_1)/(kn_1)=2a\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)$; for $n_1=0$ the integral is $2a=2a\operatorname{sinc}0$ by the separate value of sinc. The second factor is analogous, giving the displayed identity $4abA_0\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)$ for every direction $n$.

[Fraunhofer intensity] For $r\ge2a'$ the support bound $|y|\le a'$ of [F2] puts the model in the regime of the Fraunhofer estimate of [F1] with aperture radius $a'$, so $u(rn)=e^{ikr}(4\pi r)^{-1}\cdot4abA_0\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)+R(rn)$ with $|R(rn)|\le\|\alpha\|_{\rm TV}(\pi r)^{-1}[a'/r+k(a')^2/r]$ uniformly in direction by step 3.1. Taking moduli, $|u_{\rm F}(rn)|=\dfrac{ab|A_0|}{\pi r}\,|\!\operatorname{sinc}(ka\,n_1)|\,|\!\operatorname{sinc}(kb\,n_2)|$, so $I_{\rm F}(rn)=\frac12|u_{\rm F}(rn)|^2=\dfrac{a^2b^2|A_0|^2}{2\pi^2r^2}\operatorname{sinc}^2(ka\,n_1)\operatorname{sinc}^2(kb\,n_2)$, and the intensity-error transfer of [F1] bounds $\bigl|I(rn)-I_{\rm F}(rn)\bigr|$ by the Fraunhofer field error.

[Zeros of the pattern] By definition of sinc and the zero set of sine in [F6], $\operatorname{sinc}\xi=0$ exactly when $\xi\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$; since $k,a,b>0$ and the two factors multiply, $I_{\rm F}(rn)=0$ exactly when $ka\,n_1\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ or $kb\,n_2\in\pi\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$.

[Global maxima] First, $|\sin x|\le|x|$ for every real $x$, with equality exactly at $x=0$: for $x>0$ choose $\delta:=\min\{x/3,\pi/6\}>0$; on $[\delta,2\delta]\subseteq[0,\pi/2]$ the cosine is positive and strictly decreasing, so $|\cos t|=\cos t\le\cos\delta<1$ there, while $|\cos t|\le1$ everywhere; the second fundamental theorem, the integral triangle bound and monotonicity of [F6] give $|\sin x|=\bigl|\int_0^x\cos t\,dt\bigr|\le\int_0^x|\cos t|\,dt\le(x-\delta)+\delta\cos\delta=x-\delta(1-\cos\delta)<x$, and for $x<0$ oddness of sine in [F6] gives $|\sin x|=|\sin(-x)|<|x|$, while $x=0$ gives equality. Hence $|\!\operatorname{sinc}\xi|\le1$ with equality exactly at $\xi=0$; since $k,a,b>0$, the modulus of the product in step 4.1 equals the prefactor exactly when $ka\,n_1=0$ and $kb\,n_2=0$, that is $n_1=n_2=0$, which on $S^2$ means $n=(0,0,\pm1)$; these two poles are therefore exactly the global maxima of the pattern on $S^2$, and the model's half-space $x_3>0$ forces $n_3>0$, leaving only the positive pole.

[Scope and choice accounting] The computation is exact inside the adopted scalar model: by [F1] it inherits the Fraunhofer and Fresnel error bounds rather than re-estimating them, it makes no measured-intensity, apparatus, sampling or calibration claim, and no polarization or screen-interaction content is introduced; only model comparisons of $I$ between observation points are read from it, which is clause (c).
