citations.quote: Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart, $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of [[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class $C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and $\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. (a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density** $u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by $$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$ At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$. (b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class $C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of $E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$ and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields. (c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields: for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and $S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters the definitions. (d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$ pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated, is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of singular source support. (e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density $g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions, not an identification made at this point.

Let $\omega>0$, $k:=\omega/c$ with $c$ the vacuum speed of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\mu_0>0$ the vacuum permeability of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and $p_0\in\mathbb C^3$ (the complex dipole-moment amplitude, in $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m$). Define, on the punctured space $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and all times $t\in\mathbb R$, $$E_{\rm d}(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\Bigl(-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}\,n\times(n\times p_0)\,e^{i(kr-\omega t)}\Bigr),\qquad B_{\rm d}(x,t):=\frac1c\,n\times E_{\rm d}(x,t),$$ where $r:=|x|$ and $n:=x/r$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]), with the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]] and the componentwise real-part encoding convention of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] (the spatial amplitude here varies with $x$; no plane-wave instance is asserted). Call $(E_{\rm d},B_{\rm d})$ the **ideal harmonic electric-dipole radiation model of frequency $\omega$ and amplitude $p_0$**, and call $S_{\rm d}:=E_{\rm d}\times B_{\rm d}/\mu_0$ its model flux ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]); the model fields are read as an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]]. ### Adopted status This is an explicitly adopted ideal radiation-law model, fixed by the following declarations. 1. It is the leading transverse far-zone field of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]](c) evaluated at the harmonic transverse moment $V(u)=\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, i.e. at $p''$ for the waveform $p(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$: by part (a) of [[lem-em-harmonic-forcing-periodic-response]] the second derivative of that explicit $C^\infty$ waveform is $\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, and substituting $u=t-r/c$ into $\mu_0\,n\times(n\times V(u))/(4\pi r)$ gives exactly $E_{\rm d}$, because $e^{i(kr-\omega t)}=e^{-i\omega(t-r/c)}$. 2. The model contains no independent magnetic-dipole or higher-multipole radiation, no near-zone or static field and no other radiating component. 3. It is not asserted to solve the vacuum Maxwell equations at finite $r$, to be the field of any actual source, to satisfy any boundary condition or to have finite total energy on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. 4. For compact smooth conserved sources, comparison with these prescribed model fields uses the actual source's moment $p_{\rm act}(u)$ of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], the harmonic waveform $p_{\rm h}(u)=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u})$, their second-derivative mismatch $$M(u):=|p_{\rm act}''(u)-p_{\rm h}''(u)|,$$ and the explicit $D,\Gamma$ bounds of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] (b), (c) and (e). A bound depending only on that source's $D$ and $\Gamma$ is valid when $M\equiv0$ on the observation window, in which case the theorem's leading fields for the source's moment coincide with the model fields; for $M\not\equiv0$ the comparison carries the additional mismatch term. The source's moment is not automatically the independently prescribed $p_0$. These actual-source comparisons assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) carried by the cited theorem. The explicit ideal fields themselves and their pointwise flux definition remain choice-free. No measured, empirical or material-response content is adopted: $p_0$ is prescribed model data, not a derived polarizability. ### Well-definedness and conventions On the declared domain $r>0$, so $r=|x|$ is the positive Euclidean norm and $n=x/r$ is a unit vector; $n\times(n\times p_0)$ and its real part are defined componentwise, and $E_{\rm d}$, $B_{\rm d}$ are $C^\infty$ on $(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R$ because $r$ is $C^\infty$ there and the real and imaginary parts of $-\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p_0)e^{i(kr-\omega t)}$ are smooth combinations of the smooth functions $r^{-1}$, $x_i$, $\cos(kr-\omega t)$ and $\sin(kr-\omega t)$ ([[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[cor-complex-exponential-cartesian-form-modulus-and-eulers-identity]]). The field is transverse in the sense that $E_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$ and $B_{\rm d}\cdot n=0$, because $n\times(n\times p_0)$ is orthogonal to $n$ and $n\times E_{\rm d}$ is orthogonal to $n$ by [[lem-cross-product-is-bilinear-alternating-and-orthogonal]] applied separately to real and imaginary parts, and $B_{\rm d}=n\times E_{\rm d}/c$ holds by definition with $|B_{\rm d}|=|E_{\rm d}|/c$. The model is meaningful at $p_0=0$, where both fields and the flux vanish identically. The varying radial amplitude $1/r$ is not a plane-wave amplitude, and the componentwise real-part convention is that of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; the cross product, inner product and norms are those of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. No equation of motion of any source, no determination of $p_0$ from any charge distribution and no energy or flux reading beyond the pointwise definition of $S_{\rm d}$ in [[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]] is part of this item.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$ the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$ componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$, $\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**, $\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the **angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**, and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then: (a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. (b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through $\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$. (c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave **nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the magnetic field alone determines $b$, because $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$ (evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$). (d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is claimed. ### Well-definedness and conventions For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and $B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$, $T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map $(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and $y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex derivative is also its real total derivative ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]), and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word $(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$, $\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell =\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$, by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with $b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a). The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of $w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking $\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ and $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, and let $(E,B)$ be the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on the whole-space region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$, with the terminology and phase convention of that definition, the cross product and inner product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] extended to $\mathbb C^3$ componentwise, the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]] and $\hat k=k/|k|$. Then: (a) [Amplitude equations] $(E,B)$ satisfies the four smooth-branch vacuum Maxwell equations of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]] with $ho\equiv0$ and $J\equiv0$ on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$ if and only if $$k\cdot e=0,\qquad k\cdot b=0,\qquad k	imes e=\omega b,\qquad k	imes b=- rac{\omega}{c^2}e .$$ (b) [Dispersion, nonzero waves, two polarizations] The amplitude equations admit a nonzero solution $(e,b)
e(0,0)$ if and only if $|k|^2=\omega^2/c^2$; off this dispersion relation the only solution is $e=b=0$. On the dispersion relation both zero and nonzero solutions occur; a particular solution is nonzero exactly when its amplitudes are not both zero, in the sense of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]](c). If $|k|=\omega/c$, the solutions are exactly the pairs $(e,b)$ with $e\in\{v\in\mathbb C^3: k\cdot v=0\}$ arbitrary and $b=k	imes e/\omega$: a complex two-dimensional family; $e=0$ gives the zero wave, and for every nonzero solution $e
e0$ and $b
e0$. (c) [Transversality, orthogonality, magnitude relation and the wave equation] For every solution with $|k|=\omega/c$ and every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$: $k\cdot E(x,t)=k\cdot B(x,t)=0$, $E(x,t)\cdot B(x,t)=0$ and $B(x,t)=\hat k	imes E(x,t)/c$; in particular $|B(x,t)|=|E(x,t)|/c$. Each component of $E$ and of $B$ is a $C^\infty$ solution of the wave equation $\Delta v=c^{-2}\partial_t^2v$ of [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]] on $\mathbb R^3	imes\mathbb R$. (d) [Scope] The equivalence in (a) is between the amplitude equations and membership in the source-free smooth Maxwell branch; it says nothing about fields that solve the wave equations but not the amplitude equations (see [[pthm-em-vacuum-wave-equation]](b)). The item covers ideal whole-space plane waves only, makes no finite-energy, boundary, material or empirical claim, and is conditional on the adopted postulate.

Let $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$, $\omega>0$ with $\omega=c|k|$, let
$e\in\mathbb C^3$ with $k\cdot e=0$ and $b=k\times e/\omega$, and let $(E,B)$ be
the corresponding plane-wave solution of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]]
([[def-em-plane-wave-definition]]) on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$. Let $u$ and
$S$ be the energy density and Poynting vector of
[[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], and $g=S/c^2$, $\sigma$, $\Pi=-\sigma$ the
momentum density, Maxwell stress and momentum flux of
[[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]]. Write $T=2\pi/\omega$,
$|e|^2=e\cdot\overline e$, $\hat k=k/|k|$, and let
$\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(x,s)\,ds$ be the period average at fixed
$x$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$:

(a) [Averaged energy density] $\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}|e|^2$,
independent of $x$ and of the starting time.

(b) [Averaged Poynting vector]
$\langle S\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2\hat k$; hence
$\langle S\rangle=\langle u\rangle c\hat k$, and the period-averaged intensity
is $I:=|\langle S\rangle|=c\langle u\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2$.

(c) [Averaged momentum density, stress and momentum flux]
$\langle g\rangle=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2c}|e|^2\hat k$, and componentwise
$\langle\sigma_{ij}\rangle=-\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$, equivalently
$\langle\Pi_{ij}\rangle=\langle u\rangle\hat k_i\hat k_j$; the period-averaged
momentum flux across a plane with unit normal $n$ (with the physical balance
interpretation conditional as in (d)) is therefore
$\langle u\rangle(\hat k\cdot n)\hat k$, a pure flux along $\hat k$ with signed
coefficient $(I/c)(\hat k\cdot n)$ and magnitude $(I/c)|\hat k\cdot n|$. The
tensor identity holds for every complex transverse amplitude $e$, not only for
real or circular ones.

(d) [Balance reading with continuum coupling] For this clause additionally
adopt [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]](ii) for the empty-matter model on
$\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$: the matter energy density
$w:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, energy flux
$Q:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$, momentum density
$p:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ and momentum flux
$P:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ are all identically
zero, as are the source fields $\rho,J$. The adopted electromagnetic force
and power densities are then $f:=\rho E+J\times B=0$ and $J\cdot E=0$,
respectively; the zero matter balances are satisfied. Under this additional
interpretation premise the local identities of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]
and [[pthm-em-momentum-balance]] hold for this field; since $u,g,S,\sigma$ are $T$-periodic in $t$, the period averages of
their time derivatives vanish ([[thm-ftc-second-part]]), so averaging the
identities gives $\operatorname{div}\langle S\rangle=0$ and
$\operatorname{div}\langle\sigma\rangle=0$ consistently (both averaged fields
are in fact constant), and the reading of $u,S,g,\Pi$ as energy and momentum
densities and fluxes is that of those two theorems.

(e) [Scope] These are exact identities for the ideal plane wave; $I$ is the
intensity used by the radiation-pressure thought experiment of the companion
page and in radiation-flux arguments. No detection statistics, no finite-beam
or finite-time realisation and no empirical claim is made, and the zero
amplitude gives the zero wave and zero total energy, whereas every nonzero
amplitude gives infinite total energy over $\mathbb R^3$.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} =4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $\omega>0$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega>0$. **Scalar form.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C$. Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\overline d\bigr).$$ **Vector forms.** Let $a,d\in\mathbb C^3$, write the same symbols for the componentwise complex-bilinear extensions of the Euclidean inner product and of the cross product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] to $\mathbb C^3$, and let $\operatorname{Re}$ act componentwise. In coordinate formulas, $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is $+1$ for even permutations of $(1,2,3)$, $-1$ for odd permutations and zero for repeated indices; all displayed repeated-index sums run from 1 to 3. Then $$\frac1T\int_0^T\bigl\langle\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr),\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\bigr\rangle\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(\langle a,\overline d\rangle\bigr),\qquad \frac1T\int_0^T\operatorname{Re}\bigl(ae^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\times\operatorname{Re}\bigl(de^{-i\omega t}\bigr)\,dt=\frac12\operatorname{Re}\bigl(a\times\overline d\bigr),$$ the integrals of the real vector-valued integrands being componentwise. The real-valued functions $\operatorname{Re}(ae^{-i\omega t})$ are the time-dependent factors of the plane-wave fields of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]] at a fixed position, with the phase absorbed into $a$ and $d$; no electromagnetic interpretation is asserted. Real quadratic expressions may not be replaced by complex quadratic expressions without conjugation: the average is not $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(ad)$ in general. For $a=d=1+i$ the proved average is $\tfrac12|1+i|^2=1$, whereas $\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}((1+i)^2)=0$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set, and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so $$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$ is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$, a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations ([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]). ### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$ At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function, and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$. **This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric, not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$. ### The algebra of the inner product For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$: 1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$ termwise. 2. **Additivity in the first argument.** $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies. 3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.** $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2. 4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws in the second argument. 5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$. 6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$. That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed here.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), as carried by the surface-measure interface below ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on the unit sphere $S^2\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]), let $e_3:=(0,0,1)$ and write $n_3=n\cdot e_3$ for $n\in S^2$. Then: (a) [Zonal identity] for every continuous $f:[-1,1]\to\mathbb R$, $$\int_{S^2}f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\int_{-1}^{1}f(u)\,du.$$ (b) [Linear weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)\,f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3\int_{-1}^{1}u\,f(u)\,du.$$ (c) [Quadratic weighted moment] for every continuous $f$ and every $a\in\mathbb R^3$, $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2f(n_3)\,d\sigma(n)=2\pi\,a_3^{2}\int_{-1}^{1}u^{2}f(u)\,du+\pi\,(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^{2})f(u)\,du.$$ (d) [Moments] $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$, $\int_{S^2}n\,d\sigma=0$, $\int_{S^2}n_in_j\,d\sigma=(4\pi/3)\delta_{ij}$, and for every $a\in\mathbb R^3$ $$\int_{S^2}(n\cdot a)^2d\sigma=\frac{4\pi}{3}|a|^2,\qquad \int_{S^2}|n\times a|^2d\sigma=\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^2,$$ where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker symbol and $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]]. (e) [Scope] (a)-(d) are identities for the polar surface measure of the unit sphere with only the stated continuity of $f$; they assert no physical field, flux or radiation statement. The measure is finite, so all displayed integrals are absolutely convergent; $f$ need not be nonnegative. For the uses on this page $f$ is a rational function with denominator bounded below by $1-b>0$, hence continuous on $[-1,1]$.

Assume the setting and hypotheses of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]] and $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by its suppliers: $c>0$, $\mu_0>0$, $a>0$, $t_0<T$, jointly $C^\infty$ fields $\rho,J$ vanishing outside $\overline B_a(0)\times[t_0,T]$ and satisfying $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}J=0$; let $\varphi,A$ be the retarded potentials and $E:=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$, $B:=\nabla\times A$ the fields, with $S:=E\times B/\mu_0$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]], [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]]). Adopt the causal selection [[post-em-radiation-selection]]: these retarded fields are the fields of the source model (the compact smooth instance established by [[pthm-em-retarded-potentials]]). Define the **time-dependent electric dipole moment** $$p(u):=\int_{B_a}y\,\rho(y,u)\,dy\in\mathbb R^3$$ (componentwise, about the fixed chart origin of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]; it is the fixed-time analogue of the static source moment of [[def-em-electric-moments]]), and, as in the asymptotic theorem, $I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$, $V(n,u):=\partial_uI(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy$ and $$D(u):=\frac{a}{c}\int_{B_a}\sup_{|v-u|\le a/c}|J_{tt}(y,v)|\,dy.$$ Then: (a) [Moment identities] $p\in C^\infty(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^3)$, $p'(u)=\int_{B_a}J(y,u)\,dy$, $p''(u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u)\,dy$, $\int_{B_a}\rho_t(y,u)\,dy=0$ and the total charge $\int_{B_a}\rho(y,u)\,dy$ vanishes for every $u$. (b) [Dipole replacement error] $|V(n,u)-p''(u)|\le D(u)$ for every $n\in S^2$ and every $u\in[t_0,T]$: the explicit absolute error of the dipole approximation to the source's transverse current moment. (c) [Leading fields] With $\Gamma_E$, $\Gamma_B$ the constants of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](b) (depending only on $a,c,\mu_0$ and the listed source suprema), for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in[t_0,T]$, $r\ge2a$: $$\Bigl|E\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p''(u))\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D(u)}{4\pi r},\qquad \Bigl|B\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)-\frac{n\times E(rn,u+\tfrac rc)}{c}\Bigr|\le\frac{\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c}{r^2}.$$ The displayed dipole field approximates the actual leading far field $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$ with the stated absolute $D(u)/r$ error. Equality of these leading fields requires $n\times(n\times(V-p''))=0$; $V=p''$ and, in particular, $D(u)=0$ are sufficient. All errors are uniform in $n$ at fixed $u$. (d) [Retarded-time radiated power] The limit of [[thm-em-radiation-asymptotic-flux]](c) equals $\mu_0|p''(u)|^2/(6\pi c)+R(u)$ with the explicit absolute error $$|R(u)|\le\frac{\mu_0\bigl(2|p''(u)|D(u)+D(u)^2\bigr)}{4\pi c},\qquad\text{so}\qquad \lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S\bigl(rn,u+\tfrac rc\bigr)d\sigma=\frac{\mu_0}{6\pi c}|p''(u)|^2\ \text{ whenever } D(u)=0.$$ The evaluation uses the sphere moment $\int_{S^2}|n\times p''|^2d\sigma=(8\pi/3)|p''|^2$ of [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]](d). The limit is at fixed retarded time $u$, not at fixed observation time. (e) [Scope] The compact smooth source branch only; the dipole error is absolute and explicitly controlled by $D(u)$, and no assertion is made that slow or 'nonrelativistic' source motion alone makes $D(u)$ small -- that is a hypothesis on the source's time variation. No point charge, no moving point source, no radiation reaction, no self-force and no empirical or measurement content; the failure of the correspondence with an oscillator for rapidly varying sources is retained through $D(u)$. Separately retain the sharper actual source estimate $|B(rn,u+r/c)-n\times E_{\rm lead}(n,u,r)/c|\le\Gamma_B/r^2$, with $E_{\rm lead}=\mu_0n\times(n\times V)/(4\pi r)$; the bound against the actual E uses the combined constant displayed in (c).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy $$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$ For $\varepsilon > 0$, define $$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$ The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family generated by $\varphi$**.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose $u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$ and $u'v$ are integrable and $$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$ **The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is then not false but ill-formed; that is the false statement that deletes it on the companion page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and $$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$ If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and $$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$ The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=\prod_{i=1}^n[a_i,b_i]$ with $n\ge1$ and $a_i<b_i$. If a bounded Borel real function $f$ on $Q$ is Riemann integrable, then it is Lebesgue integrable and the two integrals agree. The corresponding assertion for complex functions holds componentwise. In particular it applies to smooth compact test integrands and their bounded Borel zero extensions from compact Jordan regions.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function ([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and $$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$ At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what [[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$, and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$. **Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$. **Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable $f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by an integrable function with no primitive and by a false statement about the integral function.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) and let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]), with $$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$ Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every $x \in I$. Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with $$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$ **Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain. **The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$ nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever $f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem, not a hypothesis of it.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then: 1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$. 2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$ 3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with $m, M$ real, then $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$ **Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is [[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] below. **Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives $\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when $u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define $$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$ The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal. Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

derivations.claim: [Model flux along the observation direction] Fix $n\in S^2$ and $r>0$. By [F1], $B_{\rm d}=n\times E_{\rm d}/c$ and $n\cdot E_{\rm d}=0$, since $n\times(n\times p_0)$ is orthogonal to $n$; hence with the vector identity $E_{\rm d}\times(n\times E_{\rm d})=n|E_{\rm d}|^2-E_{\rm d}(n\cdot E_{\rm d})$ of [F4], $S_{\rm d}\cdot n=\frac1{\mu_0}(E_{\rm d}\times B_{\rm d})\cdot n=\frac1{\mu_0c}(E_{\rm d}\times(n\times E_{\rm d}))\cdot n=\frac{|E_{\rm d}|^2}{\mu_0c}$, because $n\cdot n=1$.

[The model field is the leading field of the harmonic waveform] For $u=t-r/c$ one has $e^{i(kr-\omega t)}=e^{-i\omega u}$; since $p_{\rm h}''(u)=\operatorname{Re}(-\omega^2p_0e^{-i\omega u})$ by [F1] of the harmonic lemma as recorded in [[def-em-ideal-harmonic-dipole-model]], and $n\times(n\times\cdot)$ is real-linear by [F4], $E_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p_{\rm h}''(u))$ and $B_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)=\frac1c n\times E_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}n\times p_{\rm h}''(u)$, the last identity by the double-cross computation of [F4].

[Period average and the averaged radial power] At fixed $x=rn$ the amplitude $w=w(x)$ of [F1] is independent of $t$, and $E_{\rm d}(rn,t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$; by [F3] with $a=d=w$, $\langle|E_{\rm d}|^2\rangle=\frac12|w|^2$. Evaluating $|w|^2$ with [F4], $|w|^2=\bigl(\frac{\mu_0\omega^2}{4\pi r}\bigr)^2|n\times(n\times p_0)|^2=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4}{16\pi^2r^2}|n\times p_0|^2$, because $|n\times(n\times p_0)|=|n\times p_0|$; therefore $r^2\langle S_{\rm d}\cdot n\rangle=\frac{r^2}{\mu_0c}\langle|E_{\rm d}|^2\rangle=\frac{\mu_0\omega^4}{32\pi^2c}|n\times p_0|^2$, independent of $r$.

[Electric and magnetic fidelity bounds] Let $p_{\rm act}$ and $D,\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$ be the actual-source data of [F6]. Subtracting the two leading fields, $E_{\rm act}(rn,u+r/c)-E_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)=\bigl[E_{\rm act}-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times p_{\rm act}'')\bigr]+\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times\bigl(n\times(p_{\rm act}''-p_{\rm h}'')\bigr)$, so taking norms and using $|n\times(n\times w)|\le|w|$ of [F4] and $|p_{\rm act}''-p_{\rm h}''|=M(u)$, the first bound of [F6] gives $|E_{\rm act}-E_{\rm d}|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D(u)}{4\pi r}+\frac{\mu_0M(u)}{4\pi r}=H(u,r)$, uniformly in $n$ at fixed $u$. For the magnetic field, $|B_{\rm act}-B_{\rm d}|\le|B_{\rm act}-\frac1c n\times E_{\rm act}|+\frac1c|n\times(E_{\rm act}-E_{\rm d})|\le\frac{\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c}{r^2}+\frac{H(u,r)}{c}$ by the second bound of [F6], [F4] and the electric bound just proved. For the sharper direct estimate, [F6] gives $|B_{\rm act}-\frac1c n\times E_{\rm lead}(V_{\rm act})|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}$ with $E_{\rm lead}=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times V_{\rm act})$, and by the double-cross computation of [F4] applied to $V_{\rm act}$ and $p_{\rm h}''$, $\frac1c n\times E_{\rm lead}(V_{\rm act})-B_{\rm d}=-\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi cr}n\times(V_{\rm act}-p_{\rm h}'')$; hence $|B_{\rm act}-B_{\rm d}|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0(D(u)+M(u))}{4\pi cr}$ by the triangle inequality and $|V_{\rm act}-p_{\rm h}''|\le D+M$ from the replacement bound of [F6]. When $M\equiv0$ on the window the bounds reduce to $H=\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D}{4\pi r}\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0D}{2\pi r}$, and neither $M\equiv0$ nor $D\equiv0$ is automatic.

[Independence of the averaging start] For any real $s$, define $G(s):=\int_s^{s+T}|E_{\rm d}(rn,t)|^2dt$. By [F7] the first fundamental theorem gives $G'(s)=|E_{\rm d}(rn,s+T)|^2-|E_{\rm d}(rn,s)|^2=0$, because the exponential encoding of [F1] and the addition law give $e^{-i\omega(t+T)}=e^{-i\omega t}e^{-2\pi i}=e^{-i\omega t}$, so $t\mapsto E_{\rm d}(rn,t)$ is $T$-periodic; hence $G$ is constant by the zero-derivative corollary of [F7] and the mean $\frac1T\int_s^{s+T}|E_{\rm d}|^2=\frac1T\int_0^T|E_{\rm d}|^2$ is independent of the start, so the cross-section ratio of step 2.1 is as well.

[Matched compact-window realization] Let the window be a compact interval $W$ in the source-time line and let $a_0,b_0\in\mathbb R^3$. Choose a real $C^\infty$ cutoff $\eta$ in time, equal to $1$ on a neighbourhood of $W$, supported in a compact interval $(t_0,t_1)$ strictly containing $W$, as supplied by [F7], and set $p_\eta:=\eta\,(p_{m h}+a_0+b_0u)$. Choose a nonempty closed cube $Q\subset B_a$ and a cutoff $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_a)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ near $Q$, by [F7]. On a bounding rectangle, Fubini and integral monotonicity give $0<\operatorname{vol}(Q)\le C:=\int\chi<\infty$; set $\sigma:=\chi/C$, which is nonnegative, smooth, supported in $B_a$ and has $\int\sigma=1$ and set $ho(y,u):=-p_\eta(u)\cdot
abla\sigma(y)$, $J(y,u):=p_\eta'(u)\sigma(y)$; both are $C^\infty$ and vanish outside $\overline B_a(0)	imes[t_0,t_1]$, and $\partial_uho+\operatorname{div}J=-p_\eta'\cdot
abla\sigma+p_\eta'\cdot
abla\sigma=0$, so the conservation equation holds. Integrating by parts on a rectangle containing $B_a$ and using Fubini as in [F7], $\int_{B_a}ho(y,u)\,dy=-p_\eta(u)\cdot\int_{B_a}
abla\sigma=0$, so the total charge vanishes, and $\int_{B_a}y_iho(y,u)\,dy=-\sum_jp_{\eta,j}(u)\int_{B_a}y_i\partial_j\sigma(y)\,dy=p_{\eta,i}(u)$ because $\int_{B_a}y_i\partial_j\sigma=-\delta_{ij}\int_{B_a}\sigma=-\delta_{ij}$ by the same integration by parts; hence the actual moment of the source is $p_{m act}=p_\eta$. On $W$ one has $\eta\equiv1$, so $p_{m act}''=p_{m h}''$ there and the mismatch $M$ vanishes on the window; applying the fidelity bounds of step 2.2 to this source preserves every finite-radius and source-variation error term $D,\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$ computed from it, and outside the window the moment is tapered, so no eternal harmonic moment is asserted.

[Angular pattern] Dividing the averaged radial power of step 2.1 by $I_{\rm inc}=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0c}$ of [F2] gives $\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(n)=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4|n\times p_0|^2}{16\pi^2|e|^2}$, and substituting $\mu_0^2=\frac1{\varepsilon_0^2c^4}$ from [[def-em-si-conventions]] gives the displayed second form $\frac{\omega^4|n\times p_0|^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2c^4|e|^2}$; with step 3.1 this is clause (a).

[Total cross section] Write $p_0=u+iv$ with $u,v\in\mathbb R^3$; by [F4], $|n\times p_0|^2=|n\times u|^2+|n\times v|^2$ for every $n$, so integrating the pattern of step 4.1 over $S^2$ and using $\int_{S^2}|n\times a|^2d\sigma_{S^2}=\frac{8\pi}{3}|a|^2$ of [F5] for the real vectors $u$ and $v$ gives $\int_{S^2}|n\times p_0|^2d\sigma_{S^2}=\frac{8\pi}{3}(|u|^2+|v|^2)=\frac{8\pi}{3}|p_0|^2$; hence $\sigma=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4}{16\pi^2|e|^2}\cdot\frac{8\pi}{3}|p_0|^2=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4|p_0|^2}{6\pi|e|^2}$, and the $\varepsilon_0$ form follows from $\mu_0^2=\frac1{\varepsilon_0^2c^4}$. For the scalar branch $p_0=\alpha e$, [F4] gives $|n\times p_0|^2=|\alpha|^2|n\times e|^2=|\alpha|^2|e|^2|n\times\hat e|^2$ and $|p_0|^2=|\alpha|^2|e|^2$, so both displayed substitutions hold; this is clause (b).

[Scope and choice accounting] Clause (d) is the exact scope: the cross sections are conditional predictions of the adopted model, $p_0$ is prescribed data rather than a derived response, and no measured, material, multipole, self-force or finite-size claim is made; the $p_0=0$ case gives zero model fields and zero cross sections while the nonzero $I_{\rm inc}$ still normalizes the ratios. The only choice principle used is the Countable Choice carried by the actual-source theorem and the sphere-moment interface of [F5], both invoked in the finite-window and integration steps; the period averages, the double-cross algebra, the division by the incident flux and the integration of the pattern use only finite sums and the explicit suppliers [F3], [F4], so no further choice is made.

boundaries.reason: The incident data fix a nonzero wavevector and a nonzero amplitude, the sphere is nonempty, and the actual-source clause is conditional on a source satisfying the cited hypotheses; there is no empty family case.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement records that p_0=0 gives zero scattered fields and cross sections while the nonzero incident intensity still defines the ratios; step 5.1 treats the scalar branch alpha=0 by the same algebra, and step 2.2 treats the matched case of vanishing mismatch.

Step 3.1 proves independence of the averaging start with one derivative of the accumulated integral G(s); step 4.1 divides once by the single incident intensity; step 5.1 integrates the pattern once over the sphere.

The Statement excludes the degenerate incident data and proves the ratio independent of r>0; step 5.1 decomposes a general complex p_0 into real and imaginary parts and so includes p_0=0; the scalar branch p_0=alpha e includes alpha=0.

Step 4.1 holds for every r>0 and every direction on the sphere, and step 3.1 for every real averaging start s, including any chosen interval endpoints; the actual-source bounds of step 2.2 are asserted at events rn and u+r/c for source-time u in the closed interval and r>=2a.

Countable Choice is declared for [F6] and [F5] and enters through their hypotheses; step 6.1 accounts the cross-section algebra as choice-free, and step 3.2 constructs one cutoff and one bump explicitly.

boundaries.reason: The theorem asserts formulas, inequalities and an independence statement; it contains no biconditional between named systems.
No converse implication is asserted; in particular the fidelity bounds are one-way estimates rather than equivalences.
