citations.quote: Assume the framework's spacetime, field and worldline objects of [[post-em-minkowski-physical-model]], [[def-em-lab-geometry]], [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]], with the SI units of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and clause (i) of the adopted Lorentz coupling [[post-em-lorentz-coupling]]: a constant charge parameter $q\in\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-sources]] (a), an externally supplied rest mass $m>0$, a future timelike $C^2$ massive worldline $x:J\to A$ with four-velocity $U$, and a prescribed field $F$ of [[def-em-electromagnetic-tensor]] that is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of the graph of $x$ and is generated externally to the particle; the adopted equation of motion is $$m\,\frac{dU}{d\tau}=q\,\Phi(U),\qquad \eta(\Phi(u),w)=F(w,u),$$ $U$ the four-velocity of [[def-em-relativistic-worldlines-frames]] (b) with $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$. Let $t\mapsto r(t)$ be the laboratory chart reading of the worldline, $v:=r'$ its coordinate velocity and $\gamma:=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, so that $U=\gamma(c,v)$ ([[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]] (e)). Then, wherever the worldline is $C^2$: (a) [Coordinate force and power] with the coordinate three-momentum $p:=m\gamma v$ of [[pthm-sr-momentum-and-four-force]] (a), $$\frac{dp}{dt}=q\,(E+v\times B),\qquad \frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}=q\,E\cdot v,$$ the derivatives taken with respect to the chart time $t$ and $E,B$ the components of $F$ in the laboratory frame. (b) [Norm preservation] $s\mapsto\eta(U(s),U(s))$ is constant on $J$ with value $-c^2$; in particular a solution with future timelike initial data remains future timelike, and $|v(t)|<c$ wherever the reading is differentiable ([[lem-em-antisymmetric-tensor-contraction]]). (c) [Controlled low-speed expansion] for every $\delta\in(0,1)$, on any interval where $|v|/c\le\delta$, $$|\gamma-1|\le\frac{|v|^2/c^2}{2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma-1-\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2}\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\Bigl(\frac{|v|^2}{c^2}\Bigr)^{2},$$ and consequently $$|p-mv|\le m|v|\,\frac{|v|^2}{2c^2(1-\delta^2)^{3/2}},\qquad \Bigl|\gamma mc^2-mc^2-\tfrac12m|v|^2\Bigr|\le\frac{3}{8}(1-\delta^2)^{-5/2}\frac{m|v|^4}{c^2};$$ the constants depend only on $\delta$, so the bounds are uniform in $|v|/c\le\delta$. These are pointwise algebraic expansions; they assert no approximation of the trajectory over a time interval, which would require a separate stability argument. (d) [Scope] The charge is constant, $m>0$ is an externally supplied parameter and $F$ is a prescribed exterior field: the particle's own field, radiation reaction and any self-force are excluded, as are magnetic monopoles and zero or variable mass; the nonrelativistic coordinate law is not adopted as exact, and (c) is a controlled kinematic expansion, not a trajectory approximation. The statement is conditional on the adopted postulates and makes no empirical claim.

Let the laboratory region and its chart be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the units of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. (a) [Charge parameter] The framework takes a real **charge parameter** $q\in\mathbb R$, measured in coulombs, attached to a source; its sign is the sign of the source and it is a parameter of the model. Charge quantisation is not asserted. (b) [Smooth source fields] A **smooth (volume) source field** on $\Omega\times I$ is a pair $(\rho,J)$ of maps $\rho:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$, $J:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is continuous on $\Omega\times I$ and of class $C^1$ wherever a displayed equation differentiates it; $\rho$ is the **frame charge density** (C m$^{-3}$) and $J$ the **frame current density** (A m$^{-2}$). For each fixed $t\in I$ retain the compact Jordan branch: if $V\subseteq\Omega$ is compact and Jordan measurable, define $$Q_R(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)dy$$ by [[def-riemann-integral-over-a-jordan-set]], with integrability supplied by [[thm-continuous-functions-on-compact-jordan-sets-are-integrable]]. For the full measurable-volume branch assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), as required by the published Lebesgue-measure interface. If $V$ is any bounded Lebesgue-measurable subset with compact closure $\overline V\subseteq\Omega$, define $$Q(V,t):=\int_V\rho(y,t)d\lambda_3(y)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}F_t(y)\mathbf{1}_V(y)d\lambda_3(y),$$ where $F_t=\rho(\cdot,t)$ on $\Omega$ and $0$ elsewhere; the signed integral is defined through its positive and negative parts ([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]], [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]). The function $F_t$ is Borel, and hence Lebesgue measurable: for every open $O\subseteq\mathbb R$ its preimage inside the open set $\Omega$ is relatively open in $\Omega$, hence open in $\mathbb R^3$, and the closed complement of $\Omega$ is added precisely when $0\in O$ ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]). This integral is absolutely finite: $\rho(\cdot,t)$ is bounded on the compact $\overline V$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]], $V$ has finite Lebesgue measure by [[prop-lebesgue-measure-is-sigma-finite-and-finite-on-bounded-sets]], and the monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral ([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) bound $\int|F_t|\mathbf{1}_Vd\lambda_3\le M_t\lambda_3(V)<\infty$, the indicator integral being its simple-function value ([[prop-the-nonnegative-integral-agrees-with-the-simple-integral]]); the positive and negative parts are measurable by [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]. On the compact Jordan branch, under the same Countable Choice assumption, $Q=Q_R$ by [[lem-riemann-lebesgue-comparison-for-distribution-test-integrands]]. The empty region has charge zero in both branches. The current flux remains defined independently: for each oriented surface patch in $\Omega$ the current flux at time $t$ is the surface integral of $J(\cdot,t)$ in the induced orientation, as defined in [[def-oriented-unit-normal-and-flux-of-a-surface-patch]]. Point sources and sheet sources are not source fields in this sense; they are different objects, defined by their own pairings when the framework uses them. (c) [Covariant identification] Write $j:=(c\rho,J)$, so $j^0=c\rho$ and $j^i=J^i$. The framework adopts as a model premise the identification of the charge-current of a source with a vector field of the affine Minkowski model, and hence the component transformation law of [[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]] for $j$ between inertial charts. This is a model premise, not a theorem about physical currents. (d) [Frame density, scalar multiplier and the normalized material branch] Suppose additionally that the identified $j$ is $C^1$ and $j=\rho_0U$, with a $C^1$ future timelike vector field $U$ and a $C^1$ real scalar multiplier $\rho_0$. Since $U^0>0$, define the normalized chart direction $u:=U/U^0$, so $u^0=1$, $u^i=U^i/U^0$. Then $j=(\rho_0U^0)u$ and, because the electromagnetic convention is $j^0=c\rho$, $$\rho=\rho_0U^0/c,\qquad J^i=\rho_0U^i=c\rho\,u^i.$$ Pointwise equality $\rho=\rho_0$ holds if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-c)=0$, including the zero-multiplier case. Where $\rho_0\ne0$, equality is equivalent to $U^0=c$, which does not alone imply $U^i=0$ for an arbitrary future timelike $U$. Thus a scalar multiplier is not automatically a Lorentz rest charge density. The direction $u$ is chart normalized, with no unit or proper-four-velocity normalization imposed in this general branch; if its coordinate velocity interpretation is adopted, the spatial velocity is $v^i:=cu^i$. For the separate convective source model, explicitly assume that $U$ is the material proper-time four-velocity, normalized by $\eta(U,U)=-c^2$ as in [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]. This is an additional model condition, not a consequence of the factorization $j=\rho_0U$. In that branch, $U=\gamma(c,v)$, $|v|<c$, $\gamma=(1-|v|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, and $$\rho=\gamma\rho_0,\qquad J=\rho v.$$ Here $\rho_0$ is the rest charge density of this stipulated convective model: in a comoving inertial frame $U=(c,0,0,0)$ and $j=(c\rho_0,0,0,0)$. The equality $\rho=\rho_0$ then holds exactly where $\rho_0=0$ or $v=0$ (equivalently $\gamma=1$). Both signs of charge and the zero-density case are retained. (e) [Scope] This definition fixes the source objects of the smooth branch and their transformation interface. It asserts no conservation law (that is proved for stated source classes) and no regularity of singular sources.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]]. (a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$ carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant $\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of $\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}} =4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$ or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the framework by $$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$ in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$, so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$. (b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$ and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where $1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$ carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$. (c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram (kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$. (d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light, which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Fix a wavevector $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ and a positive angular frequency $\omega>0$; here $k$ carries the unit $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $\omega$ the unit $\mathrm s^{-1}$ in the SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]]. Fix complex amplitudes $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$, where $e$ carries the unit $\mathrm V\,\mathrm m^{-1}$ and $b$ the unit T of the electric and magnetic fields of [[def-em-fields]]. Let $k\cdot x$ denote the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $\exp$ and $\operatorname{Re}$ be those of the encoding definition [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]], whose convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex expressions is used throughout. Define, for each $t\in\mathbb R$, maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ by $$E(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),\qquad B(x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b\,\exp(i(k\cdot x-\omega t))\bigr),$$ componentwise, and put $|k|:=\sqrt{\langle k,k\rangle}$, $\hat k:=k/|k|$ and $T:=2\pi/\omega$. Terminology: $k$ is the **wavevector**, $\hat k$ the **propagation direction**, $|k|$ the **wavenumber**, $\omega$ the **angular frequency**, $T$ the **period**, $e,b$ the **complex amplitudes**, and $\theta(x,t):=k\cdot x-\omega t$ the **phase**. Then: (a) [Objects, domain and regularity] Both maps are of class $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, as verified below; on the whole-space laboratory region $\Omega=\mathbb R^3$, $I=\mathbb R$ of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] they are an electric and a magnetic field of [[def-em-fields]] of every finite class $C^k$, $k\ge1$, read in the frame basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. (b) [Phase and periodicity] At fixed $x$ the map $t\mapsto\theta(x,t)$ is affine with derivative $-\omega<0$, so the phase decreases in time (the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention); $E$ and $B$ depend on $(x,t)$ only through $\theta$ and are $T$-periodic in $t$. (c) [Zero and nonzero waves] $(E,B)$ is the identically zero pair on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ if and only if $e=b=0$; call the wave **nonzero** otherwise. The electric field alone determines $e$ and the magnetic field alone determines $b$, because $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for all real $\theta$ forces $w=0$ (evaluate at $\theta=0$ and at $\theta=\pi/2$). (d) [Status] This item fixes objects, conventions and terminology only. It asserts no field equation, no dispersion relation, no transversality, no energy claim and no polarization classification; those are the content of [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] and [[def-em-polarization-definition]]. The units and the propagation constant $c$ are those of [[def-em-si-conventions]], and no empirical realization or measurement is claimed. ### Well-definedness and conventions For every $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the phase $\theta(x,t)$ is a real number, so $i\theta(x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\theta(x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series of [[def-em-complex-plane-wave]]; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined, so each $E_j$ and $B_j$ is a well-defined real-valued function. Since $\omega>0$ and $k\ne0$, $T=2\pi/\omega>0$ and $|k|>0$, so $\hat k$ is defined. The joint map $(x,t)\mapsto(E(x,t),B(x,t))$ has the open set $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ as its domain. For regularity, let $q=(k_1,k_2,k_3,-\omega)$ and $y=(x_1,x_2,x_3,t)$. The exponential has derivative itself ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), its complex derivative is also its real total derivative ([[thm-complex-differentiability-real-linearity-wirtinger-and-cauchy-riemann]]), and the real-linear map $\operatorname{Re}$ commutes with differentiation by [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]. Thus for every coordinate word $(j_1,\ldots,j_m)$ and component $\ell$, $\partial_{y_{j_m}}\cdots\partial_{y_{j_1}}E_\ell =\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_\ell\prod_{r=1}^m(iq_{j_r})\exp(iq\cdot y)\bigr)$, by induction using the same chain rule; the identical formula holds with $b_\ell$ for $B_\ell$. These expressions are continuous for every finite word, proving the $C^\infty$ assertion in (a). The equivalence in (c) is the elementary injectivity of $w\mapsto\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\cdot})$ on $\mathbb C^3$: if $\operatorname{Re}(w\,e^{i\theta})=0$ for every real $\theta$, then taking $\theta=0$ gives $\operatorname{Re}w=0$ and taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $\operatorname{Re}(iw)=-\operatorname{Im}w=0$, so $w=0$, and the converse is immediate. The complex notation is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field; the symbols $e$ and $b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields. No electromagnetic equation, no matter model and no physical interpretation is introduced by this definition; in particular the complex amplitudes need not satisfy the Maxwell amplitude equations, and the plane-wave expressions above are defined for every $e,b\in\mathbb C^3$.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$ ([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define $$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$ and define its **modulus** by $$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$ The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]], [[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points $x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with $$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$ and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]). Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). **The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $\omega>0$, $T:=2\pi/\omega$, $n\ge1$ and $w\in\mathbb C^n$; use the real part and complex exponential of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]] and [[def-complex-exponential]]. Define $z_p:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ by $z_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}(-w\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})$ componentwise ([[def-derivative]] for the derivative below). Then: (a) $z_p$ is $C^\infty$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and satisfies $z_p''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$; it is $T$-periodic. (b) every $C^2$ solution $z:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ of $z''(t)=\operatorname{Re}(we^{-i\omega t})$ on $\mathbb R$ has the form $z(t)=z_p(t)+a+bt$ with unique $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$. (c) such a solution is $T$-periodic if and only if $b=0$; the $T$-periodic solutions are exactly $z_p(t)+a$, $a\in\mathbb R^n$, and their oscillating part has complex amplitude $-w/\omega^2$. (d) [Local solutions and exact global extension] Let $I$ be any nonempty open interval, $t_*\in I$, and let $z:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$ with the same harmonic equation on $I$. Then $z=z_p+a+bt$ on $I$ for a unique pair $a,b\in\mathbb R^n$, with $b=z'(t_*)-z_p'(t_*)$ and $a=z(t_*)-z_p(t_*)-bt_*$. The same explicit formula defines its unique global harmonic-ODE extension $Z$ on $\mathbb R$. This extension is $T$-periodic exactly when $b=0$, equivalently $z'(t_*)=z_p'(t_*)$; when $b=0$ its mean over every complete period is $a$. For general drift, the mean of its global extension over $[t,t+T]$ is $a+b(t+T/2)$. Thus periodic preparation can be imposed on the global response without requiring a driven nonlinear family to exist on $\mathbb R$. If $I$ contains at least one pair $t,t+T$, equality at that pair forces $b=0$. If $I$ contains no such pair, a condition expressed only as $z(t+T)=z(t)$ wherever both arguments belong to $I$ is vacuous and does not imply periodicity of the global extension. All affine-drift local solutions remain classified, and the original global branches (a)-(c) remain intact.

Assume Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) as carried by [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]] and [[lem-em-sphere-zonal-moments]] ([[def-countable-choice]]); the period-average and cross-section algebra itself uses no choice. Adopt the ideal harmonic electric-dipole radiation model of [[def-em-ideal-harmonic-dipole-model]] with frequency $\omega>0$, wavenumber $k=\omega/c$ and amplitude $p_0\in\mathbb C^3$; let $E_{\rm d},B_{\rm d},S_{\rm d}$ be its fields and model flux. Let $\kappa\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ with $|\kappa|=\omega/c$, $e\in\mathbb C^3\setminus\{0\}$ with $\kappa\cdot e=0$, $b:=\kappa\times e/\omega$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and let $(E_{\rm inc},B_{\rm inc})$ be the corresponding plane-wave fields of [[def-em-plane-wave-definition]] on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$; by [[pthm-em-plane-wave-maxwell]] they satisfy the smooth-branch source-free vacuum Maxwell equations, and by [[pthm-em-wave-energy-average]](b) their period-averaged energy flux has magnitude $I_{\rm inc}=\frac{\varepsilon_0c}{2}|e|^2=\frac{|e|^2}{2\mu_0c}$ ([[def-em-si-conventions]]). Define the **model differential scattering cross section** by $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(n):=\frac{r^2\langle S_{\rm d}(rn,\cdot)\cdot n\rangle}{\langle S_{\rm inc}\cdot\hat\kappa\rangle},\qquad n\in S^2,\ r>0,$$ where $\hat\kappa:=\kappa/|\kappa|$, $S_{\rm inc}:=E_{\rm inc}\times B_{\rm inc}/\mu_0$ ([[def-em-vacuum-energy-flux]]), and $\langle f\rangle:=\frac1T\int_0^Tf(s)\,ds$, $T=2\pi/\omega$, is the period average at fixed observation point. Then: (a) [Angular pattern] the ratio is independent of $r$ and of the averaging start, and for every $n\in S^2$ $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(n)=\frac{\omega^4|n\times p_0|^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2c^4|e|^2}=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4|n\times p_0|^2}{16\pi^2|e|^2}.$$ (b) [Total cross section] with $d\sigma_{S^2}$ the surface measure of the unit sphere, $\sigma:=\int_{S^2}\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}\,d\sigma_{S^2}$ equals $$\sigma=\frac{\omega^4|p_0|^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0^2c^4|e|^2}=\frac{\mu_0^2\omega^4|p_0|^2}{6\pi|e|^2};$$ if $p_0=\alpha e$ for a complex scalar $\alpha$ (the scalar polarizability, in $\mathrm F\,\mathrm m^2$), then $\sigma=\frac{\omega^4|\alpha|^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0^2c^4}$ and $\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(n)=\frac{\omega^4|\alpha|^2}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2c^4}|n\times\hat e|^2$ with $\hat e:=e/|e|$. (c) [Fidelity for arbitrary actual sources and matched windows] Let an actual compact smooth conserved source satisfy the exact hypotheses of [[pthm-em-dipole-radiation]], with spatial support radius $a>0$, source-time interval $[\tau_0,\tau_1]$, moment $p_{\rm act}(u)$, variation bound $D(u)$ and constants $\Gamma_E,\Gamma_B$. These source data are independent of the prescribed model amplitude $p_0$. Put $$p_{\rm h}(u):=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega u}),\qquad M(u):=|p_{\rm act}''(u)-p_{\rm h}''(u)|.$$ For $n\in S^2$, $u\in[\tau_0,\tau_1]$, $r\ge2a$, define $$H(u,r):=\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}[D(u)+M(u)].$$ The actual retarded fields and the model fields satisfy, uniformly in $n$, $$|E_{\rm act}(rn,u+r/c)-E_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)|\le H(u,r),$$ $$|B_{\rm act}(rn,u+r/c)-B_{\rm d}(rn,u+r/c)|\le\frac{\Gamma_B+\Gamma_E/c}{r^2}+\frac{H(u,r)}c.$$ Also retain the sharper direct source-leading-field consequence $$|B_{\rm act}-B_{\rm d}|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}+\frac{\mu_0[D(u)+M(u)]}{4\pi cr}$$ at the same events. If $p_{\rm act}''=p_{\rm h}''$ on a specified finite window, $M\equiv0$ there and these give the full matched dipole bounds; in particular they imply the coarser electric bound $\Gamma_E/r^2+\mu_0D/(2\pi r)$. Neither moment matching nor $D\equiv0$ is automatic. A sound sufficient matched branch is $p_{\rm act}=p_{\rm h}+a_0+b_0u$ on an open neighbourhood of the window (any fixed real vectors $a_0,b_0$). Such a branch has actual compact realizations over any finite window: choose a smooth time cutoff $\eta$ equal to $1$ near the window, let $p_\eta:=\eta\,(p_{\rm h}+a_0+b_0u)$, choose a nonnegative smooth spatial bump $\sigma$ with support inside $B_a$ and integral $1$, and set $\rho:=-p_\eta\cdot\nabla\sigma$, $J:=p_\eta'\sigma$. Then continuity holds and the actual moment is $p_\eta$; outside the window it is tapered. Apply the actual-source theorem with the resulting $D$ and $\Gamma$, retaining every finite-radius and source-variation error. No eternal harmonic moment of a compact-time source is asserted. (d) [Scope] conditional predictions of the adopted ideal model: no measured cross section, no frequency-domain response law (the amplitude $p_0$ is prescribed model data), no magnetic-dipole or higher-multipole content, no self-force, material response, finite-size or empirical claim; the scalar-$\alpha$ clause records a declared proportional response, not a derived polarizability. In all complex-amplitude formulas $|v|^2=\sum_i|v_i|^2$ is the Hermitian norm square; $n\times v$ is complex-linear for real $n$. The $p_0=0$ case gives zero scattered fields and cross sections while the nonzero incident intensity still defines the ratios. Actual-source fidelity assumes only the explicitly quantified mismatch and source hypotheses; it does not turn the model cross section into a measured or self-consistent scattering prediction.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement. > For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by > $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that > $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their components and their limits are as in [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]. ### The derivative Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$ the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ ([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$ **The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$ satisfies the limit condition, as proved in [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences. **The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.** For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is $\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of $f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by [[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2: > $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable > at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$. Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is defined, and the coordinates are read off it. **Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at $c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]. ### The integral Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ ([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component $f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then $$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$ **That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by [[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is $\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$. **Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set $$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$ so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]]. **Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and $\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with $$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$ since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and $\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by [[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]]. **Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with $a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$, $\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of [[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and [[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled coordinate by coordinate.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$ **Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything (the sign function); both witnesses are on the companion page. **No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form: the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for continuous integrands.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). **The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that $(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for $\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one $\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function ([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and $$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$ At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what [[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$, and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$. **Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$. **Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable $f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by an integrable function with no primitive and by a false statement about the integral function.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$ with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) $$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$ In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$: $$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$ the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for every partition $P$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A 	o \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) 
e 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) 
e 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 	o \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$ igl((f/g)|_{A_0} igr)'(c) \;=\;  rac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$ Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that it has the stated value. Both are proved. **Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$ is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis is $g(c) 
e 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere". **Everything is proved through [[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent. The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$
For all $u,v,w\in\mathbb R^3$, the cross product is bilinear and alternating, $\langle u\times v,w\rangle=\det[u\ v\ w]$, and $u\times v$ is orthogonal to both $u$ and $v$.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$ **Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything (the sign function); both witnesses are on the companion page. **No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form: the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for continuous integrands.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and $$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $$m \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; M \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b],$$ with $m, M$ real. Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]), so its Darboux sums and integrals are defined ([[def-darboux-sums]], [[def-darboux-integral]]), and for **every** partition $P$ of $[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) $$m(b-a) \;\le\; L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) \;\le\; M(b-a) .$$ In particular, taking $f$ to be the constant function with value $c$: $$\int_a^b c \;=\; c\,(b-a) ,$$ the constant function being integrable, with $L(f,P) = U(f,P) = c(b-a)$ for every partition $P$.

derivations.claim: [Uniform smallness of the velocity and of $\gamma-1$] Let $K\subset I$ be a nonempty compact interval containing $0$ in its interior (any compact subinterval of $I$ containing $0$ will do); the expansion hypothesis gives $|v_\eta(t)|\le|\eta||\dot r_1(t)|+C_K\eta^2\le|\eta|(\|\dot r_1\|_K+C_K)$ for $|\eta|<\min\{\eta_0,1\}$ and $t\in K$, where $\|\dot r_1\|_K$ is finite by continuity on the compact $K$. Choose $\eta_1\in(0,\min\{\eta_0,1\})$ with $\eta_1(\|\dot r_1\|_K+C_K)\le c/2$; then for $0<|\eta|<\eta_1$ every $t\in K$ has $|v_\eta(t)|/c\le1/2$, so the low-speed clause of [F1] with $\delta=1/2$ gives $|\gamma_\eta(t)-1|\le\frac{|v_\eta(t)|^2}{2c^2(1-1/4)^{3/2}}\le C_1\eta^2$ for a constant $C_1$ depending only on $K,\eta_1$ and the data, uniformly in $t\in K$.

[Uniform convergence of the scaled momentum and of its derivative] With $\gamma_\eta=(1-|v_\eta|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ and $P_\eta:=m\gamma_\eta v_\eta$, write $\frac1\eta P_\eta=m\gamma_\eta\frac{v_\eta}\eta=m\frac{v_\eta}\eta+m(\gamma_\eta-1)\frac{v_\eta}\eta$; by the expansion hypothesis $\frac{v_\eta}\eta\to\dot r_1$ uniformly on $K$ with error $C_K|\eta|$, and by step 1.1 $|\gamma_\eta-1|\le C_1\eta^2$ while $\bigl|\frac{v_\eta}\eta\bigr|\le\|\dot r_1\|_K+C_K|\eta|$ is uniformly bounded, so $\frac{P_\eta}\eta\to m\dot r_1$ uniformly on $K$ as $\eta\to0$ with $\eta\ne0$. Moreover, dividing the exact coordinate force law of [F1] by $\eta$ gives, for $t\in K$ and $\eta\ne0$, $\frac1\eta P_\eta'(t)=q\bigl[E_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(t),t)+v_\eta(t)\times B_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(t),t)\bigr]$, and this right-hand side converges uniformly on $K$ to $qE_{\rm inc}(x_0,t)$: the spatial Lipschitz bound of [F2] on a compact tube around $\{x_0\}\times K$ gives $|E_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(t),t)-E_{\rm inc}(x_0,t)|\le C|r_\eta(t)-x_0|\to0$ uniformly by the expansion, while $|v_\eta(t)\times B_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(t),t)|\le|v_\eta(t)|\sup|B_{\rm inc}|\le C_2|\eta|$ by [F2] and the bilinearity and norm bound of [F5].

[First-order equation] Fix $\eta\ne0$ with $|\eta|<\eta_1$ and fix a component index $i$. The scalar map $t\mapsto(P_\eta)_i(t)$ is $C^1$ on $K$ with continuous derivative $(P_\eta')_i=q\eta[E_{\rm inc}+v_\eta\times B_{\rm inc}]_i$, so $(P_\eta')_i$ is Riemann integrable on every closed subinterval of $K$ by [F5]; splitting at $0$ and applying the second fundamental theorem [F5] to the intervals $[0,t]$ for $t\ge0$ and $[t,0]$ for $t\le0$ (with the orientation convention of the displayed one-sided differences) gives, for every $t\in K$, $\frac{(P_\eta)_i(t)-(P_\eta)_i(0)}\eta=\int_0^t\frac{(P_\eta')_i(s)}\eta\,ds=q\int_0^t[E_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(s),s)+v_\eta(s)\times B_{\rm inc}(r_\eta(s),s)]_i\,ds$. By the uniform convergence of step 2.1 applied componentwise, the integrands converge uniformly on $K$ to $qE_{\rm inc}(x_0,\cdot)_i$, so the integral bound of [F5] lets $\eta\to0$: the left side tends to $m[(\dot r_1)_i(t)-(\dot r_1)_i(0)]$ and the right side to $q\int_0^tE_{\rm inc}(x_0,s)_i\,ds$. The fundamental theorem [F5] differentiates the right side in $t$ to $qE_{\rm inc}(x_0,t)_i$, and the left side is differentiable with derivative $m(\ddot r_1)_i(t)$; hence $m\ddot r_1(t)=qE_{\rm inc}(x_0,t)$ componentwise on $K$. Every point $t\in I$ lies in such a compact $K\subset I$ containing $0$, so the identity holds on all of $I$ and is clause (a).

[Harmonic classification and the induced dipole] Equation (a) reads $\ddot r_1(t)=\operatorname{Re}(w e^{-i\omega t})$ on $I$ with $w=(q/m)e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}$ by [F2]. By the local-clause of the harmonic lemma [F3], on $I$ one has $r_1=z_p+a+bt$ for a unique pair $(a,b)$, the same formula defines the unique global extension $Z$ of $r_1$, and $b=0$ exactly when $Z$ is $T$-periodic, equivalently when $r_1'(0)=z_p'(0)=\operatorname{Re}(iw/\omega)$ (differentiating $z_p$ at $0$ with the rules of [F5]). Preparation (P) therefore says exactly $b=0$, so on $I$ we have $r_1=z_p+a$ with $a$ the mean of the periodic extension over every complete period by [F3]. Then $q(r_1-a)=qz_p(t)=\operatorname{Re}(-qw\omega^{-2}e^{-i\omega t})=\operatorname{Re}(p_0e^{-i\omega t})$ with $p_0=-qw/\omega^2=-\frac{q^2}{m\omega^2}e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}$, because $w=(q/m)e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}$; writing $e'=e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}$ one has $|e'|=|e|$ by [F5], so $p_0=\alpha e'$ with $\alpha=-\frac{q^2}{m\omega^2}$. The arbitrary mean $a$ is retained and no mean or periodicity of the nonlinear family is asserted; this is clause (b).

[Thomson cross section] Apply the cross-section formula of [F4] with the incident amplitude $e$ and dipole amplitude $p_0$ of step 4.1: $\sigma=\frac{\omega^4|p_0|^2}{6\pi\varepsilon_0^2c^4|e|^2}$, and $|p_0|^2=\frac{q^4}{m^2\omega^4}|e|^2$ because $|e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}|=1$; substituting cancels $\omega^4$ and $|e|^2$ and gives $\sigma_{\rm T}=\frac{q^4}{6\pi\varepsilon_0^2m^2c^4}$. Multiplying out, $\frac{8\pi}{3}\bigl(\frac{q^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0mc^2}\bigr)^2=\frac{8\pi}{3}\cdot\frac{q^4}{16\pi^2\varepsilon_0^2m^2c^4}=\frac{q^4}{6\pi\varepsilon_0^2m^2c^4}$, the same value, and it depends neither on $\omega$ nor on the phase factor beyond the unimodular $e'$; this is clause (c).

[Scope and choice accounting] Clause (d) records the exact content: the result is a conditional first variation of the adopted external-force law under the stated family and preparation hypotheses, with the affine drift retained in general and set to zero only by (P) for (b) and (c); no existence, persistence, stability or self-consistency of the family, no self-force, radiation reaction or material content, and no empirical, atomic or frequency-response claim is made. The $\eta^2$ scaling statement is a remark on the leading model: for nonzero $\eta$ the incident amplitude $\eta e$ and the induced amplitude $\eta p_0$ scale together, so the ratio defining $\sigma_{\rm T}$ is unchanged; at $q=0$ the amplitude $p_0=-\frac{q^2}{m\omega^2}e\,e^{i\kappa\cdot x_0}$ and $\sigma_{\rm T}$ vanish by direct substitution without any division by $q$. The only choice principle used is the Countable Choice carried by the cross-section theorem [F4]; the uniform-limit, integral and harmonic-classification arguments use only the explicit suppliers [F1], [F3], [F5] and finite compact intervals.

citations.quote:
Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), with orientation fixed as a positive ray of
the determinant line $\Lambda^4V$
([[def-determinant-line-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]])
and with the corresponding class of positively oriented ordered bases of $V$
([[def-orientation-of-a-finite-dimensional-real-vector-space]]); by
[[prop-orientations-and-positive-basis-classes-agree-in-positive-dimension]] the
positive ray selects exactly one such class for $\dim V=4>0$.

An **inertial frame** of the model is a tuple $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ consisting
of an event $o\in A$ and an ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $V$ that is

1. **$\eta$-orthonormal**: $\eta(e_a,e_b)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{ab}$ for all $a,b$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]);
2. **future**: $e_0\in C^+$, i.e. $e_0$ is future timelike; and
3. **positively oriented**: the ordered basis lies in the positive-basis class
   selected by the fixed orientation.

The event $o$ is the **origin** of the frame and $e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3$ are its
**basis vectors**.

**Inertial charts.** For an inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$, define

$$E:\mathbb R^4\longrightarrow V,\qquad E(u):=\sum_{a=0}^3u^ae_a .$$

Then $E$ is a linear isomorphism ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]):
it is linear by construction, and it is bijective because
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is an ordered basis, every $v\in V$ having exactly one
coordinate list $u$ with $v=\sum_au^ae_a$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). The **inertial
chart** of the frame is the map

$$x:A\longrightarrow\mathbb R^4,\qquad x(p):=E^{-1}(p-o),$$

and its values $x^a(p)$ are the **inertial coordinates of the event $p$** in the
frame. Since $E$ and $v\mapsto p+v$ are bijections, $x$ is a bijection
$A\to\mathbb R^4$; and $x(p)=0$ exactly when $p-o=0_V$, that is, exactly when
$p=o$.

**Transition law.** Let $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be another inertial frame
with chart $x'$, and let $M=(M^b_a)$ be the change-of-basis matrix defined by
$e'_a=\sum_bM^b_ae_b$, a $4\times4$ real matrix that is invertible because both
families are ordered bases. Then $E'(u)=\sum_au^ae'_a=E(Mu)$ for all
$u\in\mathbb R^4$, for the matrix-vector product $Mu$ in the coordinates of the
first frame, because $\sum_au^a\sum_bM^b_ae_b=\sum_b(\sum_aM^b_au^a)e_b$; hence
$E'=E\circ M$ and $E'^{-1}=M^{-1}\circ E^{-1}$, so for every event $p$,

$$x'(p)=M^{-1}\bigl(x(p)-x(o')\bigr)=M^{-1}x(p)-M^{-1}x(o') .$$

In particular the transition between two inertial charts is an affine map of
$\mathbb R^4$ with invertible linear part $M^{-1}$ and constant part
$-M^{-1}x(o')$, and it is a bijection of $\mathbb R^4$ with inverse
$u\mapsto Mu+x(o')$, which is the transition in the reverse direction.

**The inertial atlas.** The **inertial atlas** of the model is the family of
all inertial frames together with their inertial charts. Its charts are
available at every event by [[lem-future-oriented-inertial-frames-exist]], which
supplies for every $o\in A$ an inertial frame with origin $o$; and any two of
its charts are related by the affine transition displayed above.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and let
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an $\eta$-orthonormal ordered basis. Write
$v=v^0e_0+v^1e_1+v^2e_2+v^3e_3$ for the coordinates of $v$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]) and

$$\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert:=\sqrt{(v^1)^2+(v^2)^2+(v^3)^2}.$$

Then $\eta(v,v)=-(v^0)^2+\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert^2$, and the timelike set
$T:=\{v\in V:\eta(v,v)<0\}$ satisfies

$$T=T_+\cup T_-,\qquad T_+:=\{v:v^0>\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad T_-:=\{v:v^0<-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\}.$$

The sets $T_+$ and $T_-$ are nonempty, disjoint, open in $V$ (for the metric
topology of the distance $d(u,w):=\lVert c(u)-c(w)\rVert_2$ induced by the
coordinates $c(v):=(v^0,v^1,v^2,v^3)$), convex and path-connected, and they are
exactly the two connected components of $T$. In every $\eta$-orthonormal
ordered basis the two displayed coordinate sets coincide with the two
components of $T$ in some order, and they may be interchanged relative to a
previously fixed naming of the components. Moreover

$$\operatorname{cl}(T_+)=\{v:v^0\ge\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{v:v^0\le-\lvert v_{\mathrm{vec}}\rvert\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(T_+)\cap\operatorname{cl}(T_-)=\{0\}.$$

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]). Put

$$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)=\{w\in V:\eta(e_0,w)=0\},$$

the equality holding because a vector $w=\sum_aw^ae_a$ satisfies
$\eta(e_0,w)=-w^0$ by $\eta$-orthonormality, so $\eta(e_0,w)=0$ exactly when
$w$ is a linear combination of $e_1,e_2,e_3$. In particular $S$ is the linear
subspace of $V$ spanned by the three spatial basis vectors of the frame, and
$V=S\oplus\operatorname{span}(e_0)$.

Let $\delta$ be the restriction of $\eta$ to $S$, i.e.
$\delta(w,z):=\eta(w,z)$ for $w,z\in S$. Writing $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and
$z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ and using $\eta(e_i,e_j)=\delta_{ij}$ for $i,j\ge1$, one
has

$$\delta(w,z)=w^1z^1+w^2z^2+w^3z^3,\qquad \delta(w,w)=(w^1)^2+(w^2)^2+(w^3)^2 .$$

Hence $\delta$ is a symmetric bilinear form on $S$ that is positive definite:
$\delta(w,w)\ge0$, with equality exactly for $w=0$ by uniqueness of coordinates
in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$
([[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]]). Thus $\delta$
is an inner product on the real vector space $S$
([[def-inner-product-space]]); the induced function

$$\lvert w\rvert:=\sqrt{\delta(w,w)}=\bigl\lVert(w^1,w^2,w^3)\bigr\rVert_2$$

is the Euclidean norm of the coordinate vector of $w$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and it is a norm on $S$
([[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]]). The ordered basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $S$ is $\delta$-orthonormal, and it is declared **positively
oriented** in $S$ by the convention that an ordered triple $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of
elements of $S$ is positively oriented when the ordered basis
$(e_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $V$ is positively oriented for the fixed orientation of
$V$. The pair $(S,\delta)$, together with this orientation and the frame's
basis, is the **Euclidean spatial structure of the inertial frame**
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$.

**Vector product.** For $w=\sum_{i=1}^3w^ie_i$ and $z=\sum_{i=1}^3z^ie_i$ in
$S$, define the **vector product** $w\times z$ to be the unique element of $S$
whose coordinates are

$$(w\times z)^1=w^2z^3-w^3z^2,\qquad (w\times z)^2=w^3z^1-w^1z^3,\qquad (w\times z)^3=w^1z^2-w^2z^1 .$$

This is well defined by uniqueness of coordinates in the basis
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. It is bilinear in $(w,z)$, alternating
($z\times w=-(w\times z)$ and $w\times w=0$), and it satisfies, for all
$w,z,y\in S$,

$$\delta(w\times z,y)=\det\begin{pmatrix}w^1&z^1&y^1\\ w^2&z^2&y^2\\ w^3&z^3&y^3\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lvert w\times z\rvert^2=\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2-\delta(w,z)^2 .$$

The first identity is the expansion of the determinant along its columns, both
sides equalling $\sum_i(w\times z)^iy^i$; the second is Lagrange's identity,
obtained by expanding $\lvert w\times z\rvert^2+\delta(w,z)^2$ and comparing
termwise with $\lvert w\rvert^2\lvert z\rvert^2$ using
$\lvert w\rvert^2=\delta(w,w)$
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

**Frame dependence.** The objects $S$, $\delta$, $\lvert\cdot\rvert$ and
$\times$ belong to the spatial three-space of the **named** inertial frame:
replacing the spatial basis by another $\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented
basis of $S$ transforms coordinates by an orientation-preserving orthogonal
matrix, under which $\delta$, the norm and the displayed identities are
unchanged, while a general change of inertial frame with a different time axis
$e_0$ changes $S$ itself and hence changes the domains of $\delta$ and $\times$.
The Lorentz form, the fixed orientation of $V$, and the time orientation $C^+$
are data of the model independent of the named inertial frame
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]). The Euclidean spatial structure instead
requires the choice of a time axis $e_0$; it is not an additional
frame-independent structure on the whole of $V$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]), with associated quadratic form
$q(v)=\eta(v,v)$. A vector $v\in V$ is

- **timelike** when $q(v)<0$;
- **null**, or **lightlike**, when $v\neq 0$ and $q(v)=0$;
- **spacelike** when $q(v)>0$;
- **causal** when it is timelike or null.

The zero vector $0\in V$ satisfies $q(0)=0$ and is consequently **none** of
timelike, null or spacelike: the null case explicitly excludes it, and the
timelike and spacelike cases exclude it by $q(0)=0$ together with the strict
inequalities. The **causal character** of a nonzero vector $v$ is the sign of
the real number $q(v)$, and the three names are attached to the three signs as
above. When no confusion arises, the pairing $\eta$ itself is written
$\langle v,w\rangle:=\eta(v,w)$.

**Each nonzero vector has exactly one causal character.** For a nonzero
$v\in V$ the real number $q(v)$ satisfies exactly one of $q(v)<0$, $q(v)=0$,
$q(v)>0$ by trichotomy of the order on $\mathbb R$, so $v$ is timelike, null or
spacelike, and no two of the three alternatives can hold at once. The causal
vectors are therefore exactly the nonzero vectors that are timelike or null,
and the zero vector is causal in no sense introduced here.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space with a chosen time
orientation $C^+$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear map with
$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Then:

(i) $L$ is a linear isomorphism of $V$; for every ordered $\eta$-orthonormal
basis the matrix $M$ of $L$ satisfies $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ with
$\eta_0=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and conversely every invertible matrix
$M$ with $M^{T}\eta_0M=\eta_0$ is the matrix of a linear Lorentz map in that
basis.

(ii) $\det L=\pm1$. The composition of two Lorentz maps is a Lorentz map, the
identity is a Lorentz map, and the inverse of a Lorentz map is a Lorentz map;
the sets $SO(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):\det L=1\}$,
$O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta):=\{L\in O(V,\eta):L(C^+)=C^+\}$ and
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)=SO(V,\eta)\cap O^{\uparrow}(V,\eta)$ are subgroups of
$O(V,\eta)$, which itself is a subgroup of the general linear group $GL(V)$.

(iii) $\eta(Lv,Lv)=\eta(v,v)$ for all $v\in V$; hence $L$ preserves the causal
character of every nonzero vector (timelike, null or spacelike) and maps the
set of null vectors onto itself. If $L$ is proper, then the oriented volume
form is preserved:
$\epsilon(Lv_0,\dots,Lv_3)=\epsilon(v_0,\dots,v_3)$ for all
$v_0,\dots,v_3\in V$ ([[def-oriented-minkowski-volume-form]]); if
$\det L=-1$ the two sides differ by the sign $-1$.

(iv) $L(C^+)$ is one of the two components $C^+,C^-$ of the timelike set, so
exactly one of $L(C^+)=C^+$ and $L(C^+)=C^-$ holds; $L$ is orthochronous in
the first case and non-orthochronous in the second, and $L(C^+)=C^+$ holds if
and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

(v) The affine Lorentz maps of
[[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]] form a group under composition: the
composition and the inverse of affine Lorentz maps are affine Lorentz maps,
and every affine Lorentz map is a bijection of $A$.

Let $(V,\eta)$ be a $4$-dimensional Lorentz vector space
([[def-lorentz-form-and-inertia]]) equipped with a time orientation $C^+$
([[def-time-orientation-and-future-causal-sets]]), and let
$(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the corresponding oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski
space ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]).

**(a) Linear Lorentz maps.** A **linear Lorentz map** is a linear map
$L:V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) such that

$$\eta(Lv,Lw)=\eta(v,w)\qquad\text{for all }v,w\in V.$$

The set of all linear Lorentz maps is denoted $O(V,\eta)$.

**(b) Matrix criterion.** Let $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an ordered
$\eta$-orthonormal basis of $V$ ([[lem-lorentz-form-has-orthonormal-basis]]),
so that $\eta_0:=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ is the matrix of $\eta$ in
that basis, and let $M$ be the matrix of $L$ in that basis
([[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]). Then $L$ is a linear
Lorentz map if and only if

$$M^{T}\eta_0 M=\eta_0,$$

where the product is matrix multiplication
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Every linear Lorentz map is a
linear isomorphism of $V$ ([[def-linear-isomorphism-and-invertible-linear-map]]),
and the criterion itself does not depend on the $\eta$-orthonormal basis used.
The three assertions of this clause are proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

**(c) Proper and orthochronous maps; the Lorentz group.** A linear Lorentz map
$L$ is **proper** if $\det L=+1$ ([[def-determinant-of-a-linear-operator]]) and
**orthochronous** if $L(C^+)=C^+$, a condition on the image of the set $C^+$.
The set of proper orthochronous linear Lorentz maps is denoted
$SO^{+}(V,\eta)$. The set $O(V,\eta)$ is called the **(full) Lorentz group** of
$(V,\eta)$ and $SO^{+}(V,\eta)$ the **proper orthochronous Lorentz group**;
that these sets are groups under composition is proved in
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]], which also shows
that $L$ is orthochronous if and only if $L(C^+)$ is contained in $C^+$.

**(d) Affine Lorentz maps.** An **affine Lorentz map** is a map $F:A\to A$
for which there exist $p_0\in A$ and a linear Lorentz map $L$ with

$$F(p_0+v)=F(p_0)+Lv\qquad\text{for all }v\in V.$$

Equivalently $F(p)=F(p_0)+L(p-p_0)$ for all $p\in A$, and $L$ is then unique:
it is recovered as $Lv=F(p+v)-F(p)$ for every $p\in A$, so it is independent
of the base event. $F$ is called **proper** (respectively **orthochronous**)
when its linear part $L$ is. If $x$ is the chart of an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), then

$$x(F(p))=M\,x(p)+b\qquad\text{for all }p\in A,$$

where $M$ is the matrix of $L$ in the frame's ordered basis and
$b:=x(F(o))-Mx(o)\in\mathbb R^4$; the two sides are column vectors in
$\mathbb R^4$.

**(e) Convention.** In this framework, unless stated otherwise, the term
**Lorentz transformation** means a proper orthochronous affine Lorentz map.
Improper or non-orthochronous Lorentz maps are always named explicitly.

The composition of two affine Lorentz maps is affine Lorentz with linear part
the composition of the linear parts, and the identity and the inverse of an
affine Lorentz map are again such maps; these facts are part of
[[lem-lorentz-map-preserves-metric-and-causal-structure]].

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]), let
$n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $v : n \to V$ be a finite list
([[def-linear-combination-and-span]]).

1. **The span of the image of a list.** Whether or not $v$ is injective,
   $$\operatorname{span}(v[n]) \;=\; \Bigl\{\, \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i \;:\; \lambda : n \to F \,\Bigr\} .$$
2. **Coordinates.** $v$ is an ordered basis of $V$ ([[def-linear-basis]]) **if and
   only if** for every $x \in V$ there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with
   $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$. When that holds, this $\lambda$ is called the
   **coordinate list of $x$ with respect to the ordered basis $v$**, and
   $\lambda_i$ its **$i$-th coordinate**.

The coordinate list is attached to the **ordered** basis and not to the basis as
a set: reordering the list permutes the coordinates of every vector, as the
companion page shows on a worked example in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be linear. It is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$S:W\to V$ such that

$$S\circ T=\operatorname{id}_V,\qquad T\circ S=\operatorname{id}_W.$$

Such an $S$ is the **inverse linear map** of $T$, denoted $T^{-1}$. The two
inverse equations make $T$ bijective and determine $T^{-1}$ uniquely. An
invertible linear map is also called a **linear isomorphism**, and $V$ and $W$
are **linearly isomorphic**, written $V\cong W$, when such a map exists.

derivations.claim: Fix the inertial frame and chart $x$ of the given data; by [L1] one has $D=E^{-1}(q-p)$, and in the $\eta$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the interval of the pair is $\eta(q-p,q-p)=-(D^0)^2+|D_s|^2$ in the notation of [L2].

Since $q-p$ is spacelike, [L3] gives $\eta(q-p,q-p)>0$, so $-(D^0)^2+|D_s|^2>0$, that is $(D^0)^2<|D_s|^2$; hence $D_s\ne 0$ and $e:=D_s/|D_s|$ is a well-defined unit spatial vector, the quotient $c:=D^0/|D_s|$ satisfies $|c|<1$ and is an admissible boost parameter, and $(c+1)/2$ and $(c-1)/2$ also lie in $(-1,1)$.

Fix a real number $b$ with $|b|<1$, put $\beta:=be$, $B_b:=B(\beta)$ and $e'_a:=B_b^{-1}e_a=B(-\beta)e_a$ for $a=0,1,2,3$. By [L5] and [L6] the map $B_b^{-1}=B(-\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map, so $(e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an $\eta$-orthonormal, future, positively oriented ordered basis of $V$, hence $(o;e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ is an inertial frame of the model by [L1]. Writing $x_b$ for its chart, $M_b$ for the matrix of $B_b$ in the ordered basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $E_b(u):=\sum_a u^a e'_a$, one has $E_b(u)=B_b^{-1}(E(u))$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^4$ by linearity of $B_b^{-1}$, hence $E_b^{-1}=E^{-1}B_b$ and $x_b(r)=E_b^{-1}(r-o)=E^{-1}(B_b(r-o))=E^{-1}(B_b(E(x(r))))=M_b\,x(r)$ for every $r\in A$, because $r-o=E(x(r))$ and $E^{-1}B_bE$ is the matrix map $u\mapsto M_bu$.

By linearity of $B_b$, subtracting the chart identity of step 3.1 at $p$ from the identity at $q$ gives $x_b(q)-x_b(p)=M_bD$, and its time component is $(M_bD)^0=\gamma_b(D^0-b|D_s|)$, where $\gamma_b:=(1-b^2)^{-1/2}>0$: the first row of $M_b$ gives $(M_bD)^0=\gamma_b(D^0-\beta\cdot D)$, and $\beta\cdot D=b\,(e\cdot D_s)=b|D_s|$ by [L8]. Since $D^0=c|D_s|$, this reads $x_b^0(q)-x_b^0(p)=\gamma_b|D_s|(c-b)$, which is positive for $b<c$, zero for $b=c$ and negative for $b>c$; moreover each matrix entry of $M_b$, namely $\gamma_b$, $-\gamma_b b\,e_i$ and $\delta^i_j+(\gamma_b-1)e_ie_j$, is a continuous function of $b$ on $(-1,1)$, because $b\mapsto\gamma_b$ is continuous and positive there with $\gamma_b\to 1$ as $b\to 0$, so every coordinate $x_b^a(r)$ is continuous in $b$.
The frame of step 3.1 with parameter $b:=c$, admissible by step 2.1, has chart $x_0:=x_c$ satisfying $x_0^0(q)-x_0^0(p)=0$ by step 4.1; this is assertion (b).

The frames of step 3.1 with parameters $b_+:=(c-1)/2$ and $b_-:=(c+1)/2$, both admissible by step 2.1, have $x_{b_+}^0(q)-x_{b_+}^0(p)=\gamma_{b_+}|D_s|(c-b_+)>0$ and $x_{b_-}^0(q)-x_{b_-}^0(p)=\gamma_{b_-}|D_s|(c-b_-)<0$ by step 4.1, since $c-b_+=(c+1)/2>0>c-b_-=(c-1)/2$; taking $x_+:=x_{b_+}$ and $x_-:=x_{b_-}$ this is assertion (c).

Assertion (a) is step 2.1 read in an arbitrary inertial chart; assertion (d) is the construction of steps 3.1 and 4.1, comprising the chart identity $x_b=B(be)\circ x$, the time-difference formula, the sign trichotomy relative to $c=D^0/|D_s|$ and the continuous dependence on $b$; assertions (b) and (c) are steps 5.1 and 5.2. Only inertial charts of the model and one explicitly constructed basis per parameter are used, "simultaneous" is the equality of the frame's $x^0$ coordinate as required in (e), and no choice principle is used since each parameter is a single explicit real number.
