$\eta'_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$;

(iv) the coordinate partial-derivative operators satisfy
$\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$ when applied to scalar functions
at points where their coordinate representations are totally differentiable.
Consequently, at every event where the component functions of $J$ are totally
differentiable, the divergence is invariant,
$\partial'_aJ'^a=\partial_aJ^a$. These total differentials exist at every
event if $\ell\ge1$; for $\ell=0$ this clause applies only at events where the
specified components are totally differentiable, and does not assert
covariance from the existence of separate partial derivatives alone. For a
$\mathcal C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one has
$\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_c\partial_aT^{ac}$;

(v) alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each
slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies
$\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon_{abcd}$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$, whereas a general
Lorentz matrix with $\det=-1$ changes its sign;

(vi) let $J$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field with components
$(J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3)$ in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as
$J_{\mathrm{cov}}:=(J^1,J^2,J^3)$ and denote by $\partial_i$ the spatial
partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation
$\partial_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to
$\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i=0$, and under the passive boost with
parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ ($\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$,
$\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$) the components transform as
$J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and
$J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}
+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta
-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$;

(vii) if $U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike vector field and $\rho_0$ a
$\mathcal C^1$ scalar field, then $J:=\rho_0U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field
and its first component is $J^0=\rho_0U^0$. Future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$
in every inertial chart, so one may define the normalized chart direction
$u:=U/U^0$ and the coordinate density $\rho:=J^0$. Then $u^0=1$,
$u^i=U^i/U^0$, $\rho=\rho_0U^0$, and $J=\rho u$ pointwise. The coordinate
density $\rho$ and scalar multiplier $\rho_0$ are different objects:
$\rho=\rho_0$ if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$; at points where
$\rho_0\neq0$ equality holds exactly when $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ is a
normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity
normalization. In an $x^0=ct$ convention the associated spatial coordinate
velocity, if interpreted as such, has components $cu^i$; physical
current/density identification requires its own model premise.

**Interpretation boundary.** The identification of a physical charge-current
with a vector field, and of $\rho$ with a measured charge density, is a model
premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the
transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert
that any physical current transforms as a vector.

Let $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] in an
inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$. For every
$\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ the following
hold.

(i) $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map:
$\eta(B(\boldsymbol\beta)v,B(\boldsymbol\beta)w)=\eta(v,w)$ for all $v,w\in V$,
$\det B(\boldsymbol\beta)=+1$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)(C^+)=C^+$.

(ii) $B(\mathbf 0)$ is the identity, and for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ the image
of the frame vector $e_0$ is
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)e_0=\gamma\,(e_0-\beta_1e_1-\beta_2e_2-\beta_3e_3)$, so
the map $\boldsymbol\beta\mapsto B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is injective and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ fixes $0_V$; moreover every vector $y$ with
coordinates $(0,y_{\mathrm{vec}})$ and
$\boldsymbol\beta\cdot y_{\mathrm{vec}}=0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)y=y$.

(iii) $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)B(\boldsymbol\beta)
=B(\boldsymbol\beta)B(-\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{id}_V$; in particular
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is invertible with
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$, and $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ and
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ are inverse bijections of $V$.

(iv) If $u$ is a future timelike unit vector with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$, $u^0>0$ and
$|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$, then the boost with parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0$ satisfies
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)u=e_0$.

(v) If a vector $x$ has $x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$, then the first coordinate of
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)x$ is $\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})>0$;
if $x^0<-|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|$ then that first coordinate is negative. In
particular $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ maps the future open cone
$\{x:x^0>|x_{\mathrm{vec}}|\}$ into itself.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let
$S:=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be its spatial three-space with
Euclidean form $\delta$ ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]),
and let $L:V\to V$ be a proper orthochronous Lorentz map
([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]). Write $u:=Le_0$, with coordinates
$(u^0,u_{\mathrm{vec}})$ in the frame, so that $\eta(u,u)=-1$ and $u^0>0$.
Then:

(i) $|u_{\mathrm{vec}}|<u^0$ and the parameter
$\boldsymbol\beta:=u_{\mathrm{vec}}/u^0\in\mathbb R^3$ satisfies
$|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$;

(ii) the linear map $\widehat R:=B(\boldsymbol\beta)L$ satisfies
$\widehat Re_0=e_0$ and $\widehat R(S)=S$, and its restriction $R:S\to S$ preserves $\delta$ and has determinant $+1$ ([[def-spatial-rotation-of-an-inertial-frame]]);
hence $\widehat R$ is the extension $\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ of the unique
map $R:=\widehat R|_S$; this extension is a spatial rotation of the frame and
$L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ is a product of a passive boost and a
spatial rotation;

(iii) conversely, for every $\boldsymbol\beta$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$ and
every linear map $R:S\to S$ preserving $\delta$ with $\det R=1$, the extension
$\widehat R(v^0e_0+w):=v^0e_0+Rw$ ($w\in S$), denoted
$\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$ in the frame basis, is a proper orthochronous Lorentz map and
the product $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ is a proper orthochronous Lorentz
map;

(iv) the factorization $L=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)\widehat R$ of (ii) is unique: if
$B(-\boldsymbol\beta_1)\widehat R_1=B(-\boldsymbol\beta_2)\widehat R_2$ with
$|\boldsymbol\beta_i|<1$ and spatial rotations $\widehat R_i$, then
$\boldsymbol\beta_1=\boldsymbol\beta_2$ and $R_1=R_2$;

(v) $L$ is a passive boost, that is $L=B(\boldsymbol\beta')$ for some
$|\boldsymbol\beta'|<1$, if and only if the rotation $R$ in (ii) is the
identity, and then $\boldsymbol\beta'=-\boldsymbol\beta$ with
$\boldsymbol\beta$ the parameter of (i).

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame of the model
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), and let
$x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$ be its coordinates, so that a vector is written
$x=x^0e_0+x^1e_1+x^2e_2+x^3e_3$ and the spatial part is the coordinate
column $x_{\mathrm{vec}}=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ of $\mathbb R^3$ with its standard
Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

For $\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^3$ with $|\boldsymbol\beta|<1$, where
$|\boldsymbol\beta|$ is the Euclidean norm, set

$$\gamma(\boldsymbol\beta):=(1-|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)^{-1/2}\ \ge 1,$$

with equality exactly for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ and strict inequality
for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$; here the power is the rational power
([[def-rational-power]], [[lem-rational-power-laws]]). The **passive Lorentz
boost with parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$** is the linear map
$B(\boldsymbol\beta):V\to V$ ([[def-linear-map]]) defined by its action on
coordinates: for $\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$,

$$x'^0=\gamma\,(x^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}),\qquad x'_{\mathrm{vec}}=x_{\mathrm{vec}}+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\,(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}})\,\boldsymbol\beta-\gamma\,\boldsymbol\beta\,x^0,$$

and for $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$, $B(\mathbf 0):=\operatorname{id}_V$.
Here $x'$ denotes the coordinates of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ applied to the
vector with coordinates $x$, and $\boldsymbol\beta\cdot x_{\mathrm{vec}}$ is
the Euclidean scalar product. Equivalently, in the ordered basis
$(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ the matrix of $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is

$$\begin{pmatrix}\gamma & -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\\ -\gamma\boldsymbol\beta & I_3+\dfrac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}\,\boldsymbol\beta\boldsymbol\beta^{T}\end{pmatrix},$$

that is, $B^0{}_0=\gamma$, $B^0{}_i=B^i{}_0=-\gamma\beta_i$ for
$i=1,2,3$, and
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}\beta_i\beta_j$
for $i,j=1,2,3$, with the spatial block replaced by
$I_3$ when $\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$. In the $1+1$ case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\beta e_1$ this reads
$x'^0=\gamma(x^0-\beta x^1)$ and $x'^1=\gamma(x^1-\beta x^0)$. The vector
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is called the **boost parameter**; it is dimensionless and
mathematically independent of any unit convention.

**Consistency of the definition.** The displayed formulas assign to every
coordinate pair $(x^0,x_{\mathrm{vec}})$ a pair
$(x'^0,x'_{\mathrm{vec}})$; writing the result as the matrix product above and
using that $\mathbb R^4$ is identified with coordinates through
[[thm-unique-coordinates-with-respect-to-an-ordered-basis]] (see
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]), the map
$v\mapsto E(M(E^{-1}(v)))$ is the unique linear map with that matrix. The case
$\boldsymbol\beta=\mathbf 0$ is declared separately because the expression
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ is undefined there. That the two cases fit
together is the limit computation recorded next.

**The limit as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$.** For
$\boldsymbol\beta\neq\mathbf 0$ the identity
$\gamma^2-1=|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\gamma^2$ gives

$$\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^{2}}=\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\gamma+1}.$$

Since $|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\le3/4$ forces $1\le\gamma\le2$, the bounds
$|\beta_i|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|$ and $|\beta_i\beta_j|\le|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$
(from the Euclidean norm convention, [[def-abs-value]], [[lem-of-abs-value]])
show that $\gamma\to1$ as $\boldsymbol\beta\to\mathbf 0$; here continuity of
the positive-base power at fixed exponent $-1/2$ is
[[thm-real-power-continuity-and-derivatives]], with real and rational powers
identified by [[thm-real-power-agrees-with-rational-exponent]]. Hence
$(\gamma-1)/|\boldsymbol\beta|^2\to1/2$, so
$B^i{}_j=\delta^i{}_j+\frac12\beta_i\beta_j+o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ and
$B(\boldsymbol\beta)\to I$ entrywise, without a hidden division by zero.
Here $o(|\boldsymbol\beta|^2)$ denotes a remainder whose ratio to
$|\boldsymbol\beta|^2$ tends to $0$ through nonzero parameters: the ratio
of each spatial remainder is bounded by
$|\gamma^2/(\gamma+1)-1/2|\to0$. The time-space entries obey
$|\gamma\beta_i|\le2|\boldsymbol\beta|\to0$, and the time-time entry tends to
$1$ by $\gamma\to1$. The
definition asserts no Lorentz property: that $B(\boldsymbol\beta)$ is a proper
orthochronous Lorentz map with inverse $B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$ is proved in
[[lem-boost-is-proper-orthochronous-with-inverse]], and its collinear
composition law in
[[lem-collinear-boost-composition-and-velocity-addition]]. The physical
reading of $c\boldsymbol\beta$ as a relative velocity is not part of this
definition ([[def-lorentz-map-and-lorentz-group]]).

For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$.

This is the right-handed **cross product**. The displayed coordinates are those of the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), and inner products and norms are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

derivations.claim: Adapted oriented frame. By [F1] the rest space $n^\perp$ is a three-dimensional inner product space; [F2] gives an orthonormal basis $(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ of $n^\perp$. The ordered frame $(n,u_1,u_2,u_3)$ is orthonormal; if its orientation class is negative, replace $u_3$ by $-u_3$, which keeps orthonormality and makes the frame positively oriented. Writing $e_0:=n$, $e_1,e_2,e_3$ for this frame, the components satisfy $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and $\varepsilon_{0123}=+1$. Only finitely many choices are made.

Hodge dual on the six basis forms. Let $\theta^a$ be the dual coframe and set $a_i:=\theta^0\wedge\theta^i$ and $s_1:=\theta^2\wedge\theta^3$, $s_2:=\theta^3\wedge\theta^1$, $s_3:=\theta^1\wedge\theta^2$. Evaluating the definition $(*F)_{ab}=\tfrac12\varepsilon_{ab}{}^{cd}F_{cd}$ on the basis forms, using $\varepsilon^{0123}=-1$ and the antisymmetry of $\varepsilon$, gives $$(*a_i)=-s_i,\qquad (*s_i)=a_i\qquad(i=1,2,3).$$ Indeed the only nonzero contributions come from the complementary index pair, and $\varepsilon_{0i}{}^{jk}=+\epsilon_{ijk}$ and $\varepsilon_{ij}{}^{0k}=-\epsilon_{ijk}$ for spatial indices. Consequently $*(*F)=-F$ on every two-form, since $*^2=-1$ on each of the six basis forms. For $F=\tfrac12F_{ab}\theta^a\wedge\theta^b$ the dual is $(*F)=e_i s_i-b_i a_i$ whenever the components $e_i=F_{i0}$ and $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ are used, by direct substitution into the definition.

Components of $e$ and $b$ and reconstruction (a),(b). With $n=e_0$ one has $n^a=\delta^a_0$, $n_a=-\delta_a^0$, so $e_0=F_{00}=0$, $e_i=F_{i0}$ and $b_0=(*F)_{00}=0$, $b_i=(*F)_{i0}=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ by step 1.2. Hence $e(n)=e_0=0$ and $b(n)=b_0=0$. Antisymmetry gives $F_{0i}=-F_{i0}=-e_i$, and inverting the relation $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ with the identity $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ijl}=2\delta_{kl}$ gives $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$. Comparing components with $n^\flat\wedge e$ (whose only nonzero components are $(n^\flat\wedge e)_{0i}=-e_i$) and with $*(n^\flat\wedge b)$ (whose only nonzero components are $*(n^\flat\wedge b)_{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$, computed as in step 1.2) gives $F=n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$, and $*(*F)=-F$ by step 1.2. Identifying the horizontal covectors $e,b$ with their metric dual vectors $e^\sharp,b^\sharp\in n^\perp$, the map $F\mapsto(e^\sharp,b^\sharp)$ is thus a linear isomorphism from the six-dimensional space of alternating bilinear forms onto $n^\perp\oplus n^\perp$, with inverse given by these component formulae.

Invariants (c). Raising indices with the diagonal metric, $F^{0i}=e_i$, $F^{i0}=-e_i$ and $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$, while $(*F)^{0i}=b_i$, $(*F)^{i0}=-b_i$ and $(*F)^{ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}e_k$; counting both orders in each antisymmetric pair, $$\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=\tfrac12\big(-2|e|^2+2|b|^2\big)=|b|^2-|e|^2,\qquad F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=-2(e\cdot b)-2(b\cdot e)=-4\,(e\cdot b).$$ Evaluating the normalized alternating four-form on $(e_0,\dots,e_3)$, only the three terms $2[F_{01}F_{23}-F_{02}F_{13}+F_{03}F_{12}]=2[e_1b_1+e_2b_2+e_3b_3]$ survive, so $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon$.

Invariance and observer components. For a proper orthochronous inertial transition with matrix $\Lambda$, [F3] gives $F\prime_{ab}=(\Lambda^{-1})^c{}_a(\Lambda^{-1})^d{}_bF_{cd}$. The contractions $I_1,I_2$ and the coefficient of $F\wedge F$ are unchanged, because inverse index factors cancel against the metric factors and the oriented volume form is preserved. For the component lists $(e,b)$ in this paragraph, each frame uses its own time-axis observer, whose components in that frame are $(1,0,0,0)$; these lists compare different observers. Under $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(1,R)$, $R\in SO(3)$, the covariant law and step 2.1 give $(e\prime,b\prime)=(Re,Rb)$. For the passive boost along $e_1$, substitution of the inverse matrix from [F4] gives $e\prime_1=e_1$, $b\prime_1=b_1$ and $$e\prime_2=\gamma(e_2+\beta b_3),\quad e\prime_3=\gamma(e_3-\beta b_2),\quad b\prime_2=\gamma(b_2-\beta e_3),\quad b\prime_3=\gamma(b_3+\beta e_2).$$ For a fixed physical observer, its primed vector components instead satisfy $n\prime=\Lambda n$, and the associated horizontal covectors transform by the covariant law; that is a distinct comparison.

Optional identification (d). Let $c>0$ and suppose that in the frame one has $F^{i0}=E_i/c$, $F^{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ for spatial data $E,B$. Then $F_{i0}=\eta_{ii}\eta_{00}F^{i0}=-E_i/c$, so $e_i=-E_i/c$; and $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}(-\epsilon_{jkl}B_l)=B_i$ by step 2.1. Substituting into step 3.1 gives $\tfrac12F_{ab}F^{ab}=|B|^2-|E|^2/c^2$, $F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}=4(E\cdot B)/c$ and $F\wedge F=-2(E\cdot B)\varepsilon/c$, so $\kappa=(F\wedge F)_{0123}=-2E\cdot B/c$ and $E\cdot B=-c\kappa/2$. Under the passive boost along $e_1$ the component law $F'^{ab}=\Lambda^a{}_c\Lambda^b{}_dF^{cd}$ of [F3] and [F4], evaluated directly on the six components of $F$, gives $F'^{10}=E_1/c$, $F'^{20}=\gamma(E_2/c-\beta B_3)$, $F'^{30}=\gamma(E_3/c+\beta B_2)$, $F'^{23}=-B_1$, $F'^{13}=\gamma(B_2+\beta E_3/c)$ and $F'^{12}=\gamma(-B_3+\beta E_2/c)$; translating back by the identification and writing $v=\beta c$ this is exactly $E'_1=E_1$, $B'_1=B_1$, $E'_\perp=\gamma(E+v\times B)_\perp$, $B'_\perp=\gamma(B-v\times E/c^2)_\perp$, which are the stated vector formulae under the right-handed cross product [F5]. At $\beta=0$, $\gamma=1$ and the identities are immediate.

The invariant quadratic polynomials. Let $P$ be a homogeneous quadratic polynomial in the six components of $F$ that is invariant under all proper orthochronous maps; by the isomorphism of step 2.1, $P$ is a quadratic form in $(e,b)$, say $P=e^{\mathsf T}Ae+b^{\mathsf T}Bb+e^{\mathsf T}Cb$ with $A,B$ symmetric. Invariance under the rotations $R\oplus R$ of step 4.1 means $R^{\mathsf T}AR=A$, $R^{\mathsf T}BR=B$ and $R^{\mathsf T}CR=C$ for every $R\in SO(3)$. The half-turns $R=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1)$ and $R=\operatorname{diag}(-1,-1,1)$ are proper rotations, and since $R$ is diagonal the conditions read $R_{ii}M_{ij}R_{jj}=M_{ij}$ entrywise; together they force every off-diagonal entry of $A$ and of $B$ to vanish, while the cyclic permutation matrix (a proper rotation) forces the surviving diagonal entries to be equal, so $A=aI_3$ and $B=bI_3$. The same two half-turns force every off-diagonal entry of $C$ to vanish, and the cyclic permutation forces its diagonal entries to agree, so $C=cI_3$. Hence $P=a|e|^2+b|b|^2+c\,(e\cdot b)$ for real $a,b,c$. Invariance under the boost of step 4.1 applied to $e=(0,1,0)$, $b=0$, which is sent to $e'=(0,\gamma,0)$, $b'=(0,0,\gamma eta)$, gives $a=a\gamma^2+b\gamma^2 eta^2$, i.e. $(a+b)\gamma^2 eta^2=0$, hence $a+b=0$ for $ eta
e0$ (and by continuity of the polynomial identity in $ eta$ also for $ eta=0$). Thus $P=a(|e|^2-|b|^2)+c\,(e\cdot b)=-a\,I_1-	frac c4\,I_2$, so $I_1$ and $I_2$ span the invariant quadratic polynomials. They are linearly independent: at $b=0$, $e
e0$ one has $I_1=-|e|^2
e0$, $I_2=0$, and at $e=b
e0$ one has $I_1=0$, $I_2=-4|e|^2
e0$. Finally $F\wedge F=2(e\cdot b)\varepsilon=-	frac12I_2\varepsilon$, and $I_2=F_{ab}(*F)^{ab}$ changes sign if the orientation is reversed with $\eta$ and $F$ held fixed, because then $\varepsilon$ is replaced by $-\varepsilon$ and hence $*F$ by $-*F$.

routine_steps.claim: Clauses (a) and (b) are steps 1.2 and 2.1, clause (c) is steps 3.1 and 5.1, and clause (d) is step 4.2. The proof is finite-dimensional linear algebra on the oriented Lorentz vector space with the stated index conventions; the only choices are the finite Gram–Schmidt and orientation adjustments of step 1.1; clause (d) is an optional identification of components with fields of the electromagnetic framework and the theorem asserts no field equation, no dynamics, no measurement, no energy condition and no transformation beyond the stated component law. No choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Step 2.1 identifies horizontal covectors with rest-space vectors by metric duality. Its isomorphism F -> (e^sharp,b^sharp) includes the zero form and has codomain n^perp direct-sum n^perp.

The zero form and the vanishing of individual components are handled: $F=0$ gives $e=b=0$ and the reconstruction of step 2.1 degenerates to $0=0$, while $e$ or $b$ may vanish separately with the other nonzero.

The Hodge dual squares to $-1$ rather than $+1$ on two-forms (step 1.2), and the two independent invariants $I_1,I_2$ form a basis of the invariant quadratics (step 5.1); the optional identification of clause (d) carries the single factor $c$ throughout.

The degenerate cases are admitted: an electric-only two-form has $b=0$ and a magnetic-only one has $e=0$, both consistent with the reconstruction; the invariant-basis argument of step 5.1 uses two independent witnesses precisely so that neither $e$ nor $b$ is assumed nonzero.

The boost parameter ranges over the open interval $(-1,1)$: no endpoint at $\beta=\pm1$ is used, and step 4.2 evaluates the passive boost at $\beta=0$, where $\gamma=1$ and the component identities are immediate.
Step 1.1 makes finitely many choices (a Gram-Schmidt basis and possibly one sign change), and the rest of the proof is finite-dimensional algebra; step 6.1 records that no choice principle is used.

The only equivalence proved is the component equivalence in (b): the reconstruction of (a) holds for the field assembled from the components, as step 2.1 verifies in the adapted frame by the comparison of the $0i$ and $ij$ components.

The converse direction follows by substituting the component formulae back into $n^\flat\wedge e-*(n^\flat\wedge b)$; step 2.1 inverts $b_i=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}\epsilon_{ijl}=2\delta_{kl}$ to recover $F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}b_k$.

derivations.claim: The field. Define the smooth symmetric field by $T^{00}=x^0$, $T^{01}=T^{10}=-x^1$, $T^{11}=x^0$, all other components zero. By [F2] its force density has components $f^0=\partial_0x^0+\partial_1(-x^1)=1-1=0$, $f^1=\partial_0(-x^1)+\partial_1x^0=0$ and $f^2=f^3=0$; hence $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ on all of affine Minkowski space and $T$ is locally conserved.

The slice integral is not conserved. Let $L>0$, $c_2<d_2$, $c_3<d_3$, put $A=(d_2-c_2)(d_3-c_3)>0$ and $K=[0,L]\times[c_2,d_2]\times[c_3,d_3]$, and let $Q^0(s)=\int_KT^{00}(s,x)\,d^3x=A\int_0^Lx^0(s)\,dx^1=ALs$. For $s_1<s_2$, [F1] applied to the sub-box with $f=0$ gives $Q^0(s_2)-Q^0(s_1)=-\big(\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_1^+}T^{10}-\int_{[s_1,s_2]\times K_1^-}T^{10}\big)-0$, and $T^{10}=-x^1$ takes the constant values $-L$ on $K_1^+=\{x^1=L\}$ and $0$ on $K_1^-=\{x^1=0\}$, so the side-flux difference equals $-A(s_2-s_1)\cdot(L-0)=-AL(s_2-s_1)$ and $Q^0(s_2)-Q^0(s_1)=AL(s_2-s_1)\ne0$ whenever $s_1<s_2$; the transverse fluxes vanish because $T^{2b}=T^{3b}=0$. For example $A=6$, $L=2$ and $s_2-s_1=3$ give the value $36$.

The $b=0$ identity. The temporal faces contribute $\int_{F_0^+}T^{00}-\int_{F_0^-}T^{00}=A\int_{x_1}^{x_2}x^0\Big|_{t_2}dx^1-A\int_{x_1}^{x_2}x^0\Big|_{t_1}dx^1=A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$; the faces with $a=1$ contribute $\int_{F_1^+}T^{10}-\int_{F_1^-}T^{10}=A\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x^1\Big|_{x_2}dx^0-A\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x^1\Big|_{x_1}dx^0=A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$; the transverse faces vanish because $T^{2b}=T^{3b}=0$. The sum of face differences is $2A(t_2-t_1)(x_2-x_1)$, equal to the bulk integral of step 1.1, verifying [F1] for $b=0$.

The $b=1$ identity and the remaining components. For $b=1$, the temporal faces contribute $\pm A\int_{x_1}^{x_2}x^1\,dx^1$ with opposite signs, which cancel, and the faces with $a=1$ contribute $\pm A\int_{t_1}^{t_2}x^0\,dx^0$, which also cancel; the transverse faces vanish. citations.quote:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $V$ be a $4$-dimensional real vector space ([[def-vector-space]],
[[def-dimension]]). A **Lorentz form** on $V$ is a symmetric bilinear form
$\eta:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]])
such that

1. $\eta$ is nondegenerate: both radicals
   $\operatorname{rad}_L(\eta)=\{u:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }v\}$ and
   $\operatorname{rad}_R(\eta)=\{v:\eta(u,v)=0\text{ for every }u\}$ are
   $\{0\}$ ([[def-matrix-radicals-rank-and-nondegeneracy-of-a-bilinear-form]]);
   and
2. $\eta$ has **inertia** $(3,1,0)$: in some (equivalently, in every) basis of
   $V$ in which the matrix of $\eta$ is diagonal, exactly three diagonal
   entries are positive, exactly one is negative, and none is zero
   ([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]).

The inertia of a symmetric bilinear form is the triple $(p,q,r)$ of numbers of
positive, negative and zero diagonal entries of any diagonalizing basis, and it
is independent of the diagonalizing basis by Sylvester's law of inertia
([[def-definiteness-inertia-and-signature-data-over-the-reals]]); hence clause 2
is a property of $\eta$ itself and not of a chosen basis. The **associated
quadratic form** of $\eta$ is

$$q(v):=\eta(v,v),\qquad v\in V .$$

A **Lorentz vector space of signature $(-,+,+,+)$** is a pair $(V,\eta)$
consisting of a $4$-dimensional real vector space $V$ and a Lorentz form $\eta$
on $V$; the name records that the diagonal normal form of $\eta$ has one
negative entry followed by three positive entries. No positive-definite
structure on $V$ is assumed or implied by this definition, and $q$ takes both
negative and positive values on nonzero vectors: a basis in which
$\eta$ is diagonal with diagonal entries $-1,1,1,1$ exists by clause 2, and on
its first vector $q$ is $-1$, while on each of the other three it is $+1$.

derivations.claim: First expansion. By [F1], using that $\eta^{ab}$ is constant, $$\partial_aT^{ab}=\partial_a\big[(\varepsilon+P)n^an^b\big]+\eta^{ab}\partial_aP=n^b\,\partial_a\big[(\varepsilon+P)n^a\big]+(\varepsilon+P)\,n^a\partial_an^b+\partial^bP,$$ where $\partial_a[(\varepsilon+P)n^a]=(\partial_a\varepsilon+\partial_aP)n^a+(\varepsilon+P)\partial_an^a=D\varepsilon+DP+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta$ with $DP:=n^a\partial_aP$, while $n^a\partial_an^b=a^b$ and $\partial_an^a=\vartheta$.

Reconstruction of the identity. Since $h^{bc}=\eta^{bc}+n^bn^c$, one has $\partial^bP=h^{bc}\partial_cP-n^bDP$. Substituting into step 1.1 cancels $n^bDP$ and gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=n^b(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)+(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP$. By [F2] the vector $Y^b:=(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP$ is in $n^\perp$.

Equivalence with the two equations. Contracting the identity of step 2.1 with $n_b$ gives $n_b\partial_aT^{ab}=n_bn^b(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)+n_bY^b=-(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta)$ because $n_bn^b=-1$ and $Y\in n^\perp$. Hence conservation $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ implies $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$, and substituting this back into the identity of step 2.1 gives $Y^b=0$; conversely, if both $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$ and $Y=0$ hold, then the identity of step 2.1 gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$. The two equations displayed are exactly the energy-balance equation and the Euler equation.

derivations.claim: $(n,\rho)$ satisfies the dust equations. By the definitions of $\gamma$ and the Minkowski metric, $\eta(n,n)=-(n^0)^2+(n^1)^2=-\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=-1$, and $n^0=\gamma>0$ in the chart's time orientation, so $n$ is a future unit timelike constant field; by [F3] $\partial_an^b=0$ and hence $n^a\partial_an^b=0$. The profile depends only on $x^2,x^3$, so $n^a\partial_a\rho=\gamma(\partial_0\rho+\beta\partial_1\rho)=0$; and $\partial_an^a=0$, so $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=n^a\partial_a\rho+\rho\,\partial_an^a=0$. By [F1] the field $T^{ab}=\rho\,n^an^b$ is conserved.

Nonnegative variant and support. If $\rho_0\ge0$ is allowed to vanish, the same equations $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ hold, and [F1] gives conservation, with the inertial-flow statement on $\{\rho_0>0\}$; a compactly supported nonnegative transverse profile gives the same exact solution and the same finite-box constancy. The profile is independent of $x^1$, so a nonzero profile is not compactly supported in all three spatial variables; the flow lines are $x^1=\beta x^0+\text{const}$, $x^2,x^3$ constant.

Finite slice integrals are constant. Let $\bar K=[c_1,d_1]\times[c_2,d_2]\times[c_3,d_3]$ with $c_i<d_i$ and $Q^b(s)=\int_{\bar K}T^{0b}(s,x)\,d^3x$. Since $T^{0b}=\rho\,n^0n^b=\gamma n^b\rho_0(x^2,x^3)$ is independent of $x^0$, each $Q^b(s)$ is constant in $s$. The same conclusion follows from [F2]: the force density vanishes by step 1.1, the transverse face terms vanish because $T^{2b}=T^{3b}=0$, and the two $x^1$-faces carry the same pointwise integrand $T^{1b}=\rho_0\gamma\beta n^b$ and enter with opposite signs, so their contributions cancel although the individual face flux need not vanish.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open set with an inertial chart $x$, let $c,K>0$ be numerical constants, let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and let $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be a smooth real scalar field ([[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]). For every smooth compactly supported $h:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ define the first variation $$\delta S(\varphi)[h]:=-\frac{K}{c}\int_\Omega\Big(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\varphi\,\partial_bh+V'(\varphi)h\Big)\,d^4x,$$ a finite Riemann integral by compact support of $h$ ([[lem-sr-compact-variation-and-fundamental-lemma]]\,(c)). Then (a) $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=\dfrac{K}{c}\int_\Omega\big(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi)\big)h\,d^4x$, where $\Box\varphi:=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$; (b) $\delta S(\varphi)[h]=0$ for every such $h$ if and only if $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$. The equation in (b) is called the scalar-field equation of this model. The statement is the first variation of the action on compactly supported variations; it asserts nothing about convergence of $S$ on unbounded domains, no boundary term, no dynamics beyond the equivalence in (b) and no empirical fact. No choice principle is used. Precisely, with $L(\phi):=\tfrac12\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi\partial_b\phi+V(\phi)$, define the relative action $S_h(s):=-(K/c)\int_\Omega[L(\varphi+sh)-L(\varphi)]\,d^4x$. Its integrand has support in $\operatorname{supp}h$, so it is defined for every real $s$ even when either background action diverges; $S_h\prime(0)=\delta S(\varphi)[h]$.

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be any nonempty open set with inertial chart $x$, let $c,K>0$ be numerical constants, and let $V:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $\varphi:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. For each smooth symmetric $(0,2)$ tensor $h$ with compact support, set $g_{ab}(s)=\eta_{ab}+s h_{ab}$. Choose $s_0>0$ so that these matrices are nondegenerate with negative determinant for $|s|<s_0$; outside $\operatorname{supp}h$ they equal $\eta$. Put $D_h(s,x):=[\tfrac12 g^{ab}(s,x)\partial_a\varphi(x)\partial_b\varphi(x)+V(\varphi(x))]\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}$ and define the relative action $$\mathcal A_h(s):=-\frac Kc\int_\Omega[D_h(s,x)-D_h(0,x)]\,d^4x.$$ This is the integral of a compactly supported density difference, without assuming either background density has a finite integral. (a) $\mathcal A_h$ is differentiable at $0$ and $$\mathcal A_h\prime(0)=\frac1{2c}\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x,\qquad T^{ab}:=K[\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi-\eta^{ab}(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi))],$$ with indices raised by $\eta$. (b) $T$ is smooth and symmetric, and is the unique continuous symmetric $(2,0)$ field for which $\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x=2c\mathcal A_h\prime(0)$ for every such $h$. It is called the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of this scalar-field density. (c) The result holds on unrestricted open $\Omega$, uses only compactly supported metric variations, and imposes no convergence or boundary condition at infinity. If the full background action happens to exist, the relative action is its variation difference and gives the same derivative. No choice principle is used.

In the setting of [[lem-sr-scalar-field-hilbert-stress-energy]], with $\varphi$ smooth and $T$ the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of the scalar-field action, $$\partial_aT^{ab}=K\big(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi)\big)\partial^b\varphi\qquad\text{on }\Omega,$$ where $\partial^b=\eta^{bc}\partial_c$ and $\Box\varphi=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b\varphi$. In particular every solution of the scalar-field equation $\Box\varphi=V\prime(\varphi)$ has conserved tensor, $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$. Conversely conservation implies the scalar-field equation at every point where $d\varphi\ne0$, and hence throughout an open set on which $d\varphi$ is nowhere zero. In full generality conservation is equivalent to the pointwise product condition $(\Box\varphi-V\prime(\varphi))d\varphi=0$; it need not imply the scalar equation where $d\varphi=0$. Off shell the balance holds with the four-force density $f^b=K(\Box\varphi-V'(\varphi))\partial^b\varphi$. No choice principle is used.

Put $D_h(s,x):=[\tfrac12 g^{ab}(s,x)\partial_a\varphi(x)\partial_b\varphi(x)+V(\varphi(x))]\sqrt{-\det g(s,x)}$ and define the relative action $$\mathcal A_h(s):=-\frac Kc\int_\Omega[D_h(s,x)-D_h(0,x)]\,d^4x.$$ This is the integral of a compactly supported density difference, without assuming either background density has a finite integral. (a) $\mathcal A_h$ is differentiable at $0$ and $$\mathcal A_h\prime(0)=\frac1{2c}\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x,\qquad T^{ab}:=K[\partial^a\varphi\partial^b\varphi-\eta^{ab}(\tfrac12\partial_d\varphi\partial^d\varphi+V(\varphi))],$$ with indices raised by $\eta$. (b) $T$ is smooth and symmetric, and is the unique continuous symmetric $(2,0)$ field for which $\int_\Omega T^{ab}h_{ab}\,d^4x=2c\mathcal A_h\prime(0)$ for every such $h$. It is called the Hilbert stress-energy tensor of this scalar-field density. (c) The result holds on unrestricted open $\Omega$, uses only compactly supported metric variations, and imposes no convergence or boundary condition at infinity. If the full background action happens to exist, the relative action is its variation difference and gives the same derivative. No choice principle is used.

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $\rho:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$ with $\rho>0$, let $n:\Omega\to V$ be a $C^1$ field which is future timelike and satisfies $\eta(n,n)=-1$ everywhere (a future unit timelike field, [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(c)), and set $T^{ab}:=\rho\,n^an^b$ (a $C^1$ symmetric $(2,0)$ field). Then, on $\Omega$, (a) $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ if and only if both $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ (continuity) and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ (inertial flow); (b) if $\rho\ge0$ is allowed to vanish, the implication $\partial_aT^{ab}=0\Rightarrow n^a\partial_an^b=0$ is asserted only on the open set $\{\rho>0\}$, and no assertion is made where $\rho=0$; (c) Under the conservation hypothesis $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ in (a), if $J$ is an interval and $x:J\to\Omega$ is a $C^2$ curve with $x'(s)=n(x(s))$ for all $s$ (an integral curve of $n$), then $x''(s)=0$: the flow lines of an inertial unit field are affine straight lines in the affine structure of $A$. For the nonnegative-density branch in (b), the same conclusion holds for an integral curve whose image lies in $\{\rho>0\}$, under conservation there. The lemma is the exact mathematical content of the dust equations; it asserts no matter model, no interaction and no empirical fact. No choice principle is used.

Let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be open, let $\varepsilon,P:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$, let $n:\Omega\to V$ be a $C^1$ future unit timelike field ($\eta(n,n)=-1$) and set $T^{ab}:=(\varepsilon+P)n^an^b+P\eta^{ab}$. Write $D\varepsilon:=n^a\partial_a\varepsilon$, $\vartheta:=\partial_an^a$, $a^b:=n^a\partial_an^b$ and $h^{bc}:=\eta^{bc}+n^bn^c$ (these formulas define the first-order expansion scalar, acceleration and raised rest projection for the stipulated $C^1$ field; they agree with [[def-sr-observer-congruence-and-kinematics]] and [[def-flat-covariant-derivative-on-affine-minkowski-space]] when $\Omega$ is nonempty and the field is smooth). Then the identity $$\partial_aT^{ab}=n^b\big(D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta\big)+\big((\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP\big)$$ holds on $\Omega$, and consequently $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ on $\Omega$ if and only if $D\varepsilon+(\varepsilon+P)\vartheta=0$ and $(\varepsilon+P)a^b+h^{bc}\partial_cP=0$ on $\Omega$. The two equations are the energy-balance and Euler equations of the model; the lemma asserts no equation of state, no thermodynamic relation and no causality condition. No choice principle is used.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski model
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), $c>0$, and let
$(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial frame with stationary observer $n:=e_0$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]); let $E_n,q_n$ be the observer
quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]].

**(a)** For every $P\in\mathrm{cl}(C^+)$ the coordinate components of $P$ in
the frame are $(P^0,P^1,P^2,P^3)=(E_n(P)/c,\,q^1,q^2,q^3)$, where
$q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3q^ie_i$; if $P$ is future timelike then
$E^2=m(P)^2c^4+c^2\sum_{i=1}^3(q^i)^2$ with $E=E_n(P)$.

**(b)** Let $x:I\to A$ be a $C^1$ future timelike worldline
([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]]) whose chart coordinate path is
$t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$, with coordinate velocity $w:=r'$ and
$\gamma_w:=(1-|w|^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$
([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]],
[[def-rational-power]]); then $|w|<c$, the four-velocity is
$U=\gamma_w(c,w)$ by [[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]\,(e),
and for $P=mU$ with $m>0$ constant the components are $P=m\gamma_w(c,w)$, that
is $E_n(P)=m\gamma_wc^2$ and $q_n(P)=\sum_{i=1}^3m\gamma_ww^ie_i$.

**(c)** Let $B(\beta)$ be the passive boost of [[def-lorentz-boost]] with
parameter $\beta=(v/c)s$, where $v\in\mathbb R$, $|v|<c$, and
$s\in\mathbb R^3$ is a unit spatial coordinate vector ($s\cdot s=1$), and let $P'$
denote the components of the same vector $P$ after the coordinate change
$x'=B(\beta)x$, with $B(\beta)$ here denoting its frame matrix. Put
$\gamma_v:=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, $\mathbf p:=(P^1,P^2,P^3)$,
$p_\parallel:=s\cdot\mathbf p$, $\mathbf p_\parallel:=p_\parallel s$ and
$\mathbf p_\perp:=\mathbf p-p_\parallel s$, with the same projections
defining the primed components. Then

$$P'^0=\gamma_v\bigl(P^0-(v/c)\,p_\parallel\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\parallel=\gamma_v\bigl(\mathbf p_\parallel-(v/c)P^0s\bigr),\qquad \mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp,$$

equivalently $E'=\gamma_v(E-v\,p_\parallel)$,
$p'_\parallel=\gamma_v(p_\parallel-vE/c^2)$, $\mathbf p'_\perp=\mathbf p_\perp$. The quadratic
combination is invariant,
$E'^2-c^2|\mathbf p'|^2=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m(P)^2c^4$ for future timelike
$P$, while for future null $P$ one has $E=c|\mathbf p|$ and
$E'=c|\mathbf p'|$ in both coordinate systems; in particular the invariant
mass is frame-independent.

Let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and $(o';e'_0,e'_1,e'_2,e'_3)$ be inertial frames whose bases are related by a boost along the common first spatial direction with parameter $v$, $|v|<c$:

$$e'_0=\gamma\Bigl(e_0+\frac{v}{c}e_1\Bigr),\qquad e'_1=\gamma\Bigl(e_1+\frac{v}{c}e_0\Bigr),\qquad e'_2=e_2,\qquad e'_3=e_3,$$

where $\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$, with charts $x$, $x'$ ([[def-lorentz-boost]], [[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]). For arbitrary origins put $b:=-B(v/c)x(o')$, the constant translation vector, and write the affine transition as

$$x'^0=\gamma\Bigl(x^0-\frac{v}{c}x^1\Bigr)+b^0,\qquad x'^1=\gamma\Bigl(x^1-\frac{v}{c}x^0\Bigr)+b^1,\qquad x'^2=x^2+b^2,\qquad x'^3=x^3+b^3.$$

Then:

**(i) Clock rate.** The straight worldline $y(\lambda):=x^{-1}\bigl(\lambda,\tfrac{v}{c}\lambda+a_1,a_2,a_3\bigr)$ (coordinate velocity $(v,0,0)$, the worldline of a clock at rest in the frame $x'$) is future timelike, and the elapsed proper time between $\lambda_0<\lambda_1$ is $(\lambda_1-\lambda_0)/(c\gamma)$; equivalently $d\tau/dt=1/\gamma$ along $y$, where $t$ is the coordinate time of $x$.

**(ii) Length comparison.** For $L_0>0$ let $y_a,y_b$ be the two straight worldlines at rest in the frame $x'$ through the events with $x'$-coordinates $(\lambda,0,0,0)$ and $(\lambda,L_0,0,0)$. Then (a) at equal $x'$-times their $x'$-coordinate separation is $L_0$, while (b) at equal $x$-times their $x$-coordinate separation is $L_0/\gamma$, so the measuring frame $x$ assigns the length $L_0/\gamma$ to a rod of rest length $L_0$ at rest in $x'$; (c) symmetrically, for two worldlines at rest in $x$ with constant $x$-spatial separation $(L_0,0,0)$ along the boost direction, the separation at equal $x'$-times is $L_0/\gamma$. In each case the comparison uses events at equal time in the measuring frame; comparing equal times of the other frame is a different pair of events.

**(iii) Simultaneity.** If $x^0(q)-x^0(p)=0$ and $x^1(q)-x^1(p)=L$, then $x'^0(q)-x'^0(p)=-\gamma\frac{v}{c}L$; in particular simultaneity in the chart $x$ is not simultaneity in the chart $x'$ whenever $vL\ne0$.

**(iv) Velocity transformation.** Let $y:J\to A$ be a $C^1$ future causal curve which in the chart $x$ is $t\mapsto(ct,r(t))$ with coordinate velocity $w(t):=r'(t)\in\mathbb R^3$, $|w(t)|\le c$ (the strict inequality is the timelike branch). Then the coordinate velocity $w'$ of $y$ in the chart $x'$ is given by $w'_1=(w_1-v)/(1-vw_1/c^2)$ and $w'_\perp=w_\perp/\bigl(\gamma(1-vw_1/c^2)\bigr)$, the denominators being positive; moreover $|w'|<c$ when $|w|<c$, and $|w'|=c$ exactly when $|w|=c$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the relativistic particle model, on top of the
flat spacetime model of [[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]] and the SI unit
conventions of [[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]], together with
the framework's idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks and ideal light
signals:

**(i) Mass and momentum.** Every massive classical particle of the model
carries a positive constant invariant mass parameter $m>0$ and has
four-momentum $P=mU$, where $U$ is the four-velocity of its future timelike
worldline ([[def-sr-regular-causal-curve-and-worldline]],
[[def-sr-four-velocity-and-four-acceleration]],
[[thm-sr-proper-time-and-observer-decomposition]]); $P$ is a vector of $V$
whose SI unit is kilogram metre per second. The formula is adopted only for
$m>0$; the case $m=0$ is not defined by it and is the separate premise
[[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]]. In particular $\eta(P,P)=-m^2c^2$
is a consequence of the four-velocity normalisation, not a separate
assumption.

**(ii) Observer measurement identification.** Relative to a future unit
observer $n$, the model identifies the measured energy of the particle with
$E_n(P)$, its measured spatial momentum with $q_n(P)$, its kinetic energy with
$T_n(P)=E_n(P)-mc^2$ and its rest energy with $mc^2$, where $E_n,q_n,T_n$ are
the quantities of [[def-sr-observed-energy-momentum-and-kinetic-energy]]; the
units are the joule, kilogram metre per second and kilogram of
[[def-sr-si-units-and-coordinate-conventions]]. This clause is a formulation
convention identifying mathematical quantities with the quantities the model
calls measured; it is not a measurement report and no experiment is claimed.

**(iii) Isolated collision balance.** An isolated collision is represented by
a mass-specified on-shell collision datum at an event, with finite nonempty
incoming and outgoing lists of the massive particles of (i) and/or the ideal
massless particles of [[post-sr-ideal-massless-particle-momentum]], and with
no external four-momentum transfer or omitted leg. The interaction is
idealized as confined to that event. The sum of the incoming four-momenta equals the sum of the
outgoing four-momenta, in the sense of the collision data of
[[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: the model adopts
$Q_{\mathrm{in}}=Q_{\mathrm{out}}$ for such an isolated datum. No particular
collision is asserted to occur, and no mechanism, probability, cross section
or amplitude is supplied by this clause.

**(iv) Equation of motion for a stipulated force.** Put
$H_c^+:=\{U\in C^+:\eta(U,U)=-c^2\}$. A stipulated force law is a given
map $F:D\to V$ on a given subset $D\subseteq A\times H_c^+$,
with force components in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m/\mathrm s^2$. No regularity
away from the specified worldline is assumed. Along a given $C^2$ massive worldline
$x:I\to A$ with $(x(s),U(s))\in D$ for all $s\in I$, the model's particle
equation is $m\,dU/d\tau=F(x,U)$, with
$dU/d\tau$ the proper-time derivative of
[[def-sr-proper-time-derivative-and-four-force]], so that the stipulated $F$
is the four-force of the motion. A particular force law, and the existence,
uniqueness and domain of solutions of the resulting equation, are not adopted
here and belong to a separate model.

Empirical support for these assumptions is a nonlogical relation of the
framework, not a proof; the idealisations of point particles, ideal clocks,
ideal light signals and flat spacetime are inherited and travel to every
consumer of this premise.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski model ([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), fix an independent numerical parameter $c>0$, and let $\Omega\subseteq A$ be a nonempty open set.

(a) A **stress-energy tensor** on $\Omega$ of class $C^k$, $k\ge0$ (with $C^0$ meaning continuous), is a $C^k$ symmetric type-$(2,0)$ tensor field $T$ on $\Omega$ in the sense of [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]: at every $p\in\Omega$ the map $T(p):V^*\times V^*\to\mathbb R$ is bilinear and symmetric, so in every inertial chart its components satisfy $T^{ab}=T^{ba}$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iii)).

(b) In each inertial chart $x$ of the model ([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]) define the component families $\varepsilon_x:=T^{00}$, $\pi_x^i:=T^{0i}/c=T^{i0}/c$ and $S_x^{ij}:=T^{ij}$. These are numerical component and scaling conventions involving the fixed positive number $c$; their transformation behaviour is inherited from $T$ and no physical units or measurement interpretation form part of this mathematical definition.

(c) When $k\ge1$, the **four-force density** of $T$ is the $C^{k-1}$ field whose inertial components are $f^b:=\partial_aT^{ab}$, where $\partial_a$ are the coordinate partial derivatives of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] and the sum over $a$ is the standard contraction of a contravariant index with a coordinate derivative. The components $\partial_aT^{ab}$ transform as a vector, so $f$ is a well-defined vector field on $\Omega$ independent of the inertial chart: under an inertial transition $x'=\Lambda x+a$ the components satisfy $\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_d\,\partial_cT^{cd}$ ([[thm-sr-tensor-and-current-transformation]]\,(iv)), which is exactly the vector transformation law of clause (i) applied to the components $f^b$. For $k\ge1$ one says that $T$ is **locally conserved**, or **balanced**, on $\Omega$ when $f=0$ on $\Omega$, and that $T$ is **balanced against the four-force density** $f$ when $\partial_aT^{ab}=f^b$.

(d) The definition asserts no conservation of any prescribed symmetric field $T$: whether a given $T$ is conserved, whether it arises from an action or a matter model, and whether any of its integrals over a slice converges are separate hypotheses stated elsewhere. No choice principle is used. For a merely continuous tensor ($k=0$) the component conventions and pointwise contractions of (b) are defined, while the divergence, the four-force density and the balance terminology of (c) require the additional $C^1$ hypothesis; no derivative of a merely continuous field is asserted.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be the affine Minkowski space, let $x$ and $x'$ be
inertial charts whose transition is the affine map $x'(p)=\Lambda x(p)+b$ with
linear part $\Lambda$ (a proper orthochronous Lorentz matrix by
[[lem-inertial-chart-transitions-are-affine-lorentz]]), and let
$\Omega\subseteq A$ be an open subset. Fix $\ell\in\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}$ and $r,s\in\mathbb N$. Let $J:\Omega\to V$, $k:\Omega\to V^*$ and $T:\Omega\to T^{r,s}(V)$ be a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ vector field, a $\mathcal C^\ell$ covector field and a
$\mathcal C^\ell$ type-$(r,s)$ tensor field on $\Omega$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]], with components $J^a$, $k_a$ and
$T^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}$ in the chart $x$, and primed components in
the chart $x'$. Use indices $a,b\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ and $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, summing every repeated upper/lower index. All component identities compare the same event $p$; as coordinate functions their arguments are $u=x(p)$ and $u\prime=x\prime(p)=\Lambda u+b$. Then:

(i) $J'^a=\Lambda^a{}_bJ^b$: a contravariant index gains the factor
$\Lambda^a{}_b$, that is, components transform by multiplication with the
transition matrix;

(ii) $k'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_ak_b$: a covariant index gains the factor
$(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a$. If $\theta(p)=k_ax^a(p)+\theta_0$ is an affine scalar
function with constant covector $k$ and constant $\theta_0$, then
$\theta(p)=k'_ax'^a(p)+\theta'_0$ with $k'$ as above and
$\theta'_0:=\theta_0-k'_ab^a$, so the phase function is invariant when the
constant term is transformed together with the covector;

(iii) $T'^{a_1\dots a_r}{}_{b_1\dots b_s}
=\Lambda^{a_1}{}_{c_1}\cdots\Lambda^{a_r}{}_{c_r}
(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_1}{}_{b_1}\cdots(\Lambda^{-1})^{d_s}{}_{b_s}
T^{c_1\dots c_r}{}_{d_1\dots d_s}$: every contravariant index gains a factor
$\Lambda$ and every covariant index a factor $\Lambda^{-1}$, and the law is
consistent with the multilinear evaluation of $T(p)$ after substituting the
transformed basis. Every contraction of one contravariant with one covariant
index is invariant, and the metric components satisfy
$\eta'_{ab}=\eta_{ab}$;

(iv) the coordinate partial-derivative operators satisfy
$\partial'_a=(\Lambda^{-1})^b{}_a\partial_b$ when applied to scalar functions
at points where their coordinate representations are totally differentiable.
Consequently, at every event where the component functions of $J$ are totally
differentiable, the divergence is invariant,
$\partial'_aJ'^a=\partial_aJ^a$. These total differentials exist at every
event if $\ell\ge1$; for $\ell=0$ this clause applies only at events where the
specified components are totally differentiable, and does not assert
covariance from the existence of separate partial derivatives alone. For a
$\mathcal C^1$ type-$(2,0)$ field $T$ one has
$\partial'_aT'^{ab}=\Lambda^b{}_c\partial_aT^{ac}$;

(v) alternating covariant tensor fields transform by the covariant law on each
slot; the oriented volume form of the model satisfies
$\epsilon'_{abcd}=\epsilon_{abcd}$, since $\det\Lambda=+1$, whereas a general
Lorentz matrix with $\det=-1$ changes its sign;

(vi) let $J$ be a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field with components
$(J^0,J^1,J^2,J^3)$ in an inertial chart, and write the spatial block as
$J_{\mathrm{cov}}:=(J^1,J^2,J^3)$ and denote by $\partial_i$ the spatial
partial derivatives in the chart. Then the continuity equation
$\partial_aJ^a=0$ is equivalent to
$\partial_0J^0+\sum_i\partial_iJ^i=0$, and under the passive boost with
parameter $\boldsymbol\beta$ ($\Lambda=B(\boldsymbol\beta)$,
$\Lambda^{-1}=B(-\boldsymbol\beta)$) the components transform as
$J'^0=\gamma(J^0-\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})$ and
$J'_{\mathrm{cov}}=J_{\mathrm{cov}}
+\frac{\gamma-1}{|\boldsymbol\beta|^2}(\boldsymbol\beta\cdot J_{\mathrm{cov}})\boldsymbol\beta
-\gamma\boldsymbol\beta J^0$;

(vii) if $U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ future timelike vector field and $\rho_0$ a
$\mathcal C^1$ scalar field, then $J:=\rho_0U$ is a $\mathcal C^1$ vector field
and its first component is $J^0=\rho_0U^0$. Future timelikeness gives $U^0>0$
in every inertial chart, so one may define the normalized chart direction
$u:=U/U^0$ and the coordinate density $\rho:=J^0$. Then $u^0=1$,
$u^i=U^i/U^0$, $\rho=\rho_0U^0$, and $J=\rho u$ pointwise. The coordinate
density $\rho$ and scalar multiplier $\rho_0$ are different objects:
$\rho=\rho_0$ if and only if $\rho_0(U^0-1)=0$; at points where
$\rho_0\neq0$ equality holds exactly when $U^0=1$. The vector $u$ is a
normalized chart direction; it is not assumed to have unit or four-velocity
normalization. In an $x^0=ct$ convention the associated spatial coordinate
velocity, if interpreted as such, has components $cu^i$; physical
current/density identification requires its own model premise.

**Interpretation boundary.** The identification of a physical charge-current
with a vector field, and of $\rho$ with a measured charge density, is a model
premise of the electromagnetic framework; this item is a statement about the
transformation of components of specified fields and does not by itself assert
that any physical current transforms as a vector.

derivations.claim: Clause (a). The adopted scalar model includes the field equation $\Box\varphi=V'(\varphi)$ on $\Omega$; [F1] then gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=K\cdot0\cdot\partial^b\varphi=0$ on $\Omega$. By [F5] the vanishing is independent of the inertial chart in which the components are computed.

Clause (b). The adopted dust model is exactly the pair of equations $\partial_a(\rho n^a)=0$ and $n^a\partial_an^b=0$ with $\rho>0$; the forward direction of [F2] gives $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ for $T=\rho\,n\otimes n$, and the reverse direction gives that conservation with $\rho>0$ implies both equations.

Clause (c). The adopted fluid model is the pair of equations obtained by setting both bracket expressions of [F3] to zero; by the equivalence in [F3] this is exactly $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ for $T=(\varepsilon+P)n\otimes n+P\eta^{-1}$, in both directions.

Clause (d). The definition [[def-sr-stress-energy-tensor-and-force-density]] states explicitly in its clause (d) that it asserts no conservation of any prescribed symmetric field, and the present theorem derives conservation only from the adopted model equations of clauses (a)–(c); accordingly for a $C^1$ symmetric field prescribed on $\Omega$ that is not obtained from one of the adopted models together with its field equations, no conservation is asserted, and any conservation statement about such a field would be an additional explicit premise.

Clause (e), conditional homogeneous-dust reading. Consider a homogeneous dust realization with comoving identical particles of rest mass $m>0$ and rest number density $
u>0$, so that the adopted reading gives $ho=
u mc^2$, and consider a rest rectangular parcel of rest volume $V_0$. Take the tensor $T=ho\,n\otimes n$ in the rest frame, where $n=e_0$, so that $T^{00}=ho$ and all other components vanish. The passive boost with parameter $ eta$ along the parcel's motion direction has $\Lambda^0{}_0=\gamma$ and is proper orthochronous ([[def-lorentz-boost]]), so the rank-two law of [F5] gives $T'^{00}=\Lambda^0{}_a\Lambda^0{}_bT^{ab}=(\Lambda^0{}_0)^2ho=\gamma^2ho$; thus $T'^{00}=\gamma^2
u mc^2=(\gamma mc^2)(\gamma
u)$. In a frame related to the rest frame by that boost the simultaneous volume of the parcel is $V_0/\gamma$ by the length-contraction part of [F4] (parallel length $1/\gamma$, transverse lengths unchanged), so the particle number density in that frame is $
u'=N/(V_0/\gamma)=\gamma
u$; by the massive-particle reading [F4] each particle carries energy $\gamma mc^2$. Hence the two factors in $\gamma^2ho$ correspond respectively to particle energy and volume/density in the boosted frame. This is a conditional interpretation of the factorization within the homogeneous particle realization; it is not a derivation of the continuum model from microscopic dynamics.

Empty-domain branch. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, [[post-sr-matter-models-and-evolution]] supplies only the unique empty fields described by [[def-ck-tensor-field-on-minkowski-space]]. Their component derivatives and products are empty maps; every equality asserted at a point of $\Omega$ is therefore vacuous, including the two directions of the dust and fluid equivalences. There is no nonempty parcel in $\Omega$ to which clause (e)'s conditional realization can apply. This proves the separate mathematical empty-domain clause without invoking the named nonempty-domain suppliers on that domain.

In the nonempty adopted-model branch, clauses (a), (b), (c) and (d) are steps 1.1–1.4 and clause (e) is step 1.5; the separate mathematical empty-domain clause is step 1.6. Every conservation conclusion is a conditional deduction from the adopted model equations; the theorem asserts no interaction, force law, cross section, measurement or empirical fact, contains no empirical premise and makes no claim about arbitrary prescribed tensors. All choices are finite; no choice principle is used.

boundaries.evidence: Nonempty adopted matter branch is explicitly distinguished from the empty mathematical branch. Step 1.6 proves vacuous pointwise equations and dust/fluid equivalences using unique empty maps, with no nonempty Hilbert/stress-energy/stationarity supplier and no parcel realization.
The zero-force branch is clause (a): on-shell solutions have $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$ by step 1.1, while the dust and fluid branches reduce to their displayed equations in steps 1.2 and 1.3.

Each clause treats one model at a time, and step 1.5 uses one particle species, one rest mass and one rest parcel; the two factors of $\gamma^2\rho$ are matched one-to-one with particle energy and number density.

Degenerate model data are covered by the hypotheses inherited from the postulate: the fluid branch admits $\varepsilon+P=0$ and the scalar branch admits $V\equiv0$; steps 1.1-1.3 use only the model equations and never divide by a quantity that may vanish.

The interpretation of step 1.5 compares the parcel in the rest and boosted frames using the length-contraction formulas of [F4], and the boost parameter stays in the open interval $(-1,1)$; no limiting endpoint of a boost interval is taken.
The theorem applies the adopted equations, the rank-two transformation law and the boost matrix; step 2.1 records that only finite choices occur and no choice principle is used.

Forward directions of clauses (b) and (c): step 1.2 passes from the dust equations to conservation, and step 1.3 passes from the two fluid equations to $\partial_aT^{ab}=0$, both through the equivalences of [F2] and [F3].
